Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) whether a train is rerouted around a partially blocked segment, (ii) the exact arrival/departure times at every station (or waypoint), and (iii) the discrete speed level used on each traversed track segment.  
The objective minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable, respecting the blockage, and obeying all safety‑related head‑way constraints.

---

### 1. Sets and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t*. |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s*. |
| **B ⊆ S** | Segments that are **partially blocked** during the disruption. |
| **D** | Discrete speed levels, indexed by *d* (e.g. 30, 50, 70, 90 km h⁻¹). |
| **Lₛ** | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| **v_d** | Speed (km h⁻¹) associated with speed level *d* (constant for all trains). |
| **τₛ,d = Lₛ / v_d** | Travel time on segment *s* when speed level *d* is used (h). |
| **ε_d** | Energy consumption per km at speed level *d* (kWh km⁻¹). |
| **Δₜ** | Planned (unperturbed) departure time of train *t* from its origin (h). |
| **θₜ,n** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n* (h). |
| **hₛ** | Minimum head‑way (time gap) required between two successive trains travelling **in the same direction** on segment *s* (h). |
| **M** | Large constant (e.g. 10 000 h) for big‑M formulations. |
| **α, β > 0** | Weights for delay and energy in the objective. |
| **dirₜ ∈ {+1,‑1}** | Travel direction of train *t* (+1 = northbound, ‑1 = southbound). |
| **Cₛ = 1** | Capacity of a single‑track segment (one train per direction). |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **xₜᵈᵉᵗ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the **detour** (bypass) around the blocked zone; 0 ⇒ original route. |
| **aₜ,n** ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n* (n = 0 … Nₜ, where 0 = origin, Nₜ = final destination). |
| **dₜ,n** ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **yₜ,s,d** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *d*. |
| **zₜ,s** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies segment *s* (any speed).  (Derived from *y*.) |
| **Δₜᵈᵉˡᵃʸ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *t* at its final destination:  Δₜᵈᵉˡᵃʸ = aₜ,Nₜ – Aₜ^{sched}. |
| **Eₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption of train *t* (kWh). |

Auxiliary definitions  

\[
z_{t,s}= \sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S
\]

\[
\text{Travel time on }s\text{ at speed }d:\;\tau_{s,d}= \frac{L_s}{v_d}
\]

\[
\text{Energy on }s\text{ at speed }d:\;e_{s,d}= \varepsilon_d\,L_s
\]

---

### 3. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\; \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t^{delay}\;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t}
\]

*First term penalises total passenger delay, second term penalises total energy use. The planner can tune α and β to obtain the desired trade‑off.*

---

### 4. Core constraints  

#### 4.1 Routing (detour) choice  

For every train the set of traversed segments must be exactly those of the chosen route:

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t}\sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}= (1-x_t^{det})\;|R_t|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t^{det}}\sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}= x_t^{det}\;|R_t^{det}|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

where  

* **Rₜ** – ordered list of segments of the **original** route of train *t*.  
* **Rₜ^{det}** – ordered list of segments of the **detour** (bypass) that avoids the blocked zone.  

Thus a train either uses all original segments (if *xₜ^{det}=0*) or all detour segments (if *xₜ^{det}=1*).

#### 4.2 Exactly one speed level per used segment  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}= z_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S
\]

\[
z_{t,s}\le 1\qquad\forall t,s
\]

If a segment is not traversed (zₜ,s = 0) all y‑variables for that segment are forced to 0.

#### 4.3 Time‑flow (arrival/departure)  

For every consecutive pair of stations (n, n+1) on the **selected** route of train *t*:

\[
a_{t,n+1}\;\ge\; d_{t,n}\;+\;\sum_{d\in D}\tau_{s_{t,n},d}\;y_{t,s_{t,n},d}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;n=0,\dots,N_t-1
\]

where *sₜ,n* is the segment linking station *n* to *n+1* on the chosen route (original or detour, dictated by *xₜ^{det}*).

Dwell‑time constraint  

\[
d_{t,n}\;\ge\; a_{t,n}+ \theta_{t,n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;n=0,\dots,N_t
\]

#### 4.4 Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

A blocked segment may only be traversed at a speed not exceeding the allowed maximum *vₛ^{max}* (data). This is enforced by forbidding the corresponding binary variables:

\[
y_{t,s,d}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in B,\;d\in D\text{ with }v_d>v_s^{max}
\]

If the blockage completely forbids passage, set *vₛ^{max}=0* so that all *y* on that segment become 0.

#### 4.5 Bidirectional conflict on a single‑track segment  

For every unordered pair of trains *(t, k)* that could meet on the same **single‑track** segment *s* (i.e. they travel in opposite directions on *s*), introduce a binary ordering variable *c_{t,k,s}* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k,\text{exit}(s)} &\ge a_{t,\text{enter}(s)} + \tau_{s,d}\,y_{t,s,d} - M\,(1-c_{t,k,s})\\
a_{t,\text{exit}(s)} &\ge a_{k,\text{enter}(s)} + \tau_{s,d}\,y_{k,s,d} - M\,c_{t,k,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t<k,\;s\in S_{\text{single}}
\]

*`enter(s)`* and *`exit(s)`* denote the upstream and downstream stations of segment *s*.  
The big‑M formulation guarantees that the two trains do **not** occupy the segment simultaneously.

#### 4.6 Same‑direction head‑way  

If two trains travel **in the same direction** on the same segment *s*, a minimum head‑way *hₛ* must be respected. Using a binary ordering variable *u_{t,k,s}* :

\[
a_{k,\text{enter}(s)} \ge a_{t,\text{exit}(s)} + h_s - M\,(1-u_{t,k,s})
\qquad\forall t\neq k,\;s\in S
\]

#### 4.7 Energy accounting  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D} e_{s,d}\; y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because *eₛ,d* = ε_d · Lₛ is a known constant, the expression is linear.

#### 4.8 Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_t^{delay}= a_{t,N_t} - A_t^{sched}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

where *Aₜ^{sched}* is the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (data).  
Enforce non‑negativity (early arrival is not penalised):

\[
\Delta_t^{delay}\ge 0\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 4.9 Logical linking of routing and segment‑direction variables  

A speed‑level binary may be positive only if the segment belongs to the **chosen** route:

\[
y_{t,s,d}\le
\begin{cases}
1-x_t^{det} & \text{if } s\in R_t\\[2pt]
x_t^{det}   & \text{if } s\in R_t^{det}\\[2pt]
0           & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;d\in D
\]

---

### 5. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t^{delay}\;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{Routing constraints (4.1)}\\
&\text{Exactly‑one‑speed per segment (4.2)}\\
&\text{Time‑flow constraints (4.3)}\\
&\text{Block‑occupancy limits (4.4)}\\
&\text{Bidirectional conflict (4.5)}\\
&\text{Same‑direction head‑way (4.6)}\\
&\text{Energy accounting (4.7)}\\
&\text{Delay definition (4.8)}\\
&\text{Logical linking (4.9)}\\
&x_t^{det}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,d}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
c_{t,k,s},u_{t,k,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n},d_{t,n},\Delta_t^{delay},E_t\ge 0\qquad\forall t,n
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries listed above, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

### 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Provide for each train: origin, destination, scheduled departure Δₜ, dwell times θₜ,n, and direction.  
   For each segment: length Lₛ, whether it belongs to the blocked set B, and the maximum admissible speed *vₛ^{max}* (0 if completely blocked).  
   Define the discrete speed set D together with speeds *v_d* and energy coefficients ε_d.  
   Choose the weighting parameters α, β and a sufficiently large M.  

2. **Model building** – Encode the sets, parameters and the constraints above in a MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).  

3. **Solve** – The solver returns optimal values of:  
   * *xₜ^{det}* (detour decision),  
   * *yₜ,s,d* (selected speed level on each traversed segment),  
   * *aₜ,n*, *dₜ,n* (arrival/departure times),  
   * *Δₜ^{delay}* (resulting delay) and *Eₜ* (energy use).  

4. **Interpretation** –  
   * If *xₜ^{det}=1* the train is rerouted around the blockage; otherwise it follows its original line.  
   * The unique speed level on each segment is given by the *d* for which *yₜ,s,d=1*.  
   * Arrival times give the realized timetable; the total delay and energy are directly read from the objective components.  

5. **What‑if analysis** – By varying α and β the planner can explore the trade‑off between punctuality and energy efficiency, or impose a hard cap on total energy and minimise delay only.

---

### 7. Model highlights  

| Element | Why it is needed |
|---------|------------------|
| **Binary detour variable** *xₜ^{det}* | Allows the optimizer to decide whether a train should be rerouted around the partially blocked segment. |
| **Binary speed‑level variables** *yₜ,s,d* | Discretises the speed‑management problem, keeping the formulation linear while capturing the speed‑energy relationship. |
| **Arrival/Departure times** *aₜ,n*, *dₜ,n* | Provide a detailed timetable; they are linked to speed choices through travel‑time equations. |
| **Bidirectional conflict binaries** *c_{t,k,s}* | Guarantee that two trains travelling in opposite directions never occupy a single‑track segment simultaneously (head‑on safety). |
| **Same‑direction head‑way binaries** *u_{t,k,s}* | Enforce a minimum time gap between successive trains moving in the same direction on the same track. |
| **Block‑occupancy constraints** | Model the physical limitation that a blocked segment can only be used at reduced speed or not at all. |
| **Energy accounting** | Provides the second objective component and links speed decisions to energy consumption. |
| **Weighted objective** | Lets the railway operator balance service quality (delay) against sustainability (energy). |

The formulation above is **complete, linear, and ready for implementation** in any standard MILP solver. It captures the essential interactions between train rescheduling, rerouting, and speed management under a partial segment blockage, while ensuring a conflict‑free, feasible timetable.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) which route each train will take (including possible detours around a partially blocked segment), (ii) the speed level used on every traversed segment, and (iii) the exact arrival/departure times.  
The objective minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption. All constraints are linear; the model is therefore a mixed‑integer linear program (MILP).

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *i*. |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered along the line). |
| **L** | Set of admissible speed levels, indexed by *ℓ* (ℓ = 1 … |L|). |
| **R** ⊆ S × S | Set of admissible **detour arcs** (s → s′) that can replace the nominal next segment. |
| **B** ⊆ S | Set of **partially blocked** segments. |
| **K** | Number of parallel lanes (or directions) on a segment (K = 1 for single‑track). |
| **Nₛ** ⊆ {1,…,K} | Set of lanes that are in conflict on segment *s* (e.g., opposite directions on a single track). |
| **P₍ᵢ₎** | Set of feasible **paths** for train *i* (each path is an ordered list of segments). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| τₛ | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| v_ℓ | Nominal speed for level ℓ (km /min). |
| e_ℓ | Energy consumption per km at speed level ℓ (kWh/km). |
| dᵢ⁰ | Original (planned) departure time of train *i* from its origin (min). |
| aᵢ⁰ | Original (planned) arrival time of train *i* at its destination (min). |
| γᵢₛ | Minimum dwell time of train *i* on segment *s* (0 if none) (min). |
| πₛ | Minimum headway required between two trains on the same lane of segment *s* (min). |
| πₛᴮ | Minimum headway inside a blocked sub‑segment (πₛᴮ ≤ πₛ). |
| αₛ ∈ [0,1] | Fraction of segment *s* that is blocked (αₛ = 0 ⇒ no blockage, αₛ = 1 ⇒ fully blocked). |
| wᴰ , wᴱ | Positive weights for total delay and total energy in the objective. |
| M | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|--------|
| xᵢₚ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* follows path *p* ∈ Pᵢ. |
| yᵢₛℓ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* traverses segment *s* with speed level ℓ. |
| aᵢₛ ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *i* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| bᵢₛ ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *i* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| zᵢₛk ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* occupies lane *k* on segment *s*. |
| uᵢₛ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* passes blocked segment *s* **after** the blockage; 0 ⇔ **before**. |
| wᵢⱼₛ ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable: 1 ⇔ train *i* passes segment *s* before train *j*. |
| Δᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *i* (arrival at destination – aᵢ⁰). |
| Eᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption of train *i*. |

---

### 4. Model  

#### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\; w^{D}\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_{i}\;+\;w^{E}\sum_{i\in T}E_{i}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

#### 4.2 Path‑selection  

\[
\sum_{p\in P_{i}}x_{i p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T \tag{P1}
\]

A segment belongs to a path *p* iff it appears in the ordered list \(\mathcal{S}_{p}\).  

\[
y_{i s\ell}\le\sum_{p\in P_{i}:s\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}x_{i p}\qquad\forall i,s,\ell \tag{P2}
\]

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L}y_{i s\ell}= \sum_{p\in P_{i}:s\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}x_{i p}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{P3}
\]

Thus each traversed segment receives exactly one speed level.

#### 4.3 Time propagation on a segment  

Travel time on *s* with speed level ℓ: \(\tau_{s\ell}= \dfrac{\tau_{s}}{v_{\ell}}\).

\[
b_{i s}=a_{i s}+ \sum_{\ell\in L}\tau_{s\ell}\,y_{i s\ell}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{T1}
\]

For two consecutive segments *s* → *s′* on the selected path of train *i*:

\[
a_{i s'}\ge b_{i s}\qquad\forall i,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen path} \tag{T2}
\]

#### 4.4 Departure, dwell and delay  

\[
a_{i s_{\text{origin}}}\ge d_{i}^{0}\qquad\forall i \tag{D1}
\]

\[
b_{i s}\ge a_{i s}+ \gamma_{i s}\,y_{i s\ell}\qquad\forall i,s,\ell \tag{D2}
\]

Delay at the destination (last segment \(s^{\text{dest}}_{i}\)):

\[
\Delta_{i}= a_{i s^{\text{dest}}_{i}}-a_{i}^{0}\qquad\forall i \tag{D3}
\]

#### 4.5 Blockage handling (partial segment)  

If segment *s* is partially blocked (αₛ>0) the train must either finish before the blockage starts or start after it ends:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i s} &\ge \overline{b}_{s}-M\,(1-u_{i s})\\
b_{i s} &\le \underline{b}_{s}+M\,u_{i s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,\;s\in B \tag{B1}
\]

where \([\underline{b}_{s},\overline{b}_{s}]\) is the time window of the blockage.  

If the blockage only reduces the usable length, enforce a minimum travel time on the **unblocked** part:

\[
b_{i s}-a_{i s}\;\ge\;(1-\alpha_{s})\;\tau_{s}^{\min}\qquad\forall i,\;s\in B \tag{B2}
\]

with \(\tau_{s}^{\min}= \dfrac{\tau_{s}}{\max_{\ell}v_{\ell}}\).

#### 4.6 Lane occupation and conflict avoidance  

Link lane‑occupation to segment usage:

\[
z_{i s k}\le \sum_{\ell\in L}y_{i s\ell}\qquad\forall i,s,k \tag{L1}
\]

Capacity on each lane:

\[
\sum_{i\in T}z_{i s k}\le 1 \qquad\forall s,\;k=1,\dots,K \tag{L2}
\]

Temporal headway on the same lane (or opposite directions on a single track):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j s}&\ge b_{i s}-M\,(1-w_{i j s})\\
a_{i s}&\ge b_{j s}-M\,w_{i j s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s,\;k\in N_{s} \tag{L3}
\]

The binary \(w_{i j s}\) decides which train is first; the constraints guarantee a separation of at least πₛ (or πₛᴮ inside a blocked sub‑segment).

#### 4.7 Energy consumption  

\[
E_{i}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}\,\tau_{s}\,y_{i s\ell}\qquad\forall i \tag{E}
\]

Because exactly one speed level is chosen on each traversed segment, the expression is linear.

#### 4.8 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{i p},\,y_{i s\ell},\,z_{i s k},\,u_{i s},\,w_{i j s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i s},\,b_{i s},\,\Delta_{i},\,E_{i}\ge 0\qquad\forall i,s,\ell,k,j.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{D}\sum_{i}\Delta_{i}+w^{E}\sum_{i}E_{i}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(P1)–(P3)} &&\text{path and speed‑level selection}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{time propagation}\\
&\text{(D1)–(D3)} &&\text{departure, dwell and delay}\\
&\text{(B1)–(B2)} &&\text{partial‑blockage handling}\\
&\text{(L1)–(L3)} &&\text{lane capacity and headway}\\
&\text{(E)} &&\text{energy calculation}\\
&\text{binary / non‑negative domains.}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries that encode routing, speed‑level choice, lane occupation, blockage‑ordering and train‑ordering. Consequently the formulation belongs to the class **MILP** and can be solved directly with any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, S, L, R, B* and the feasible path collection *Pᵢ* for each train. Provide segment lengths τₛ, speed limits v_ℓ, energy coefficients e_ℓ, original times dᵢ⁰, aᵢ⁰, dwell times γᵢₛ, headways πₛ (and πₛᴮ for blocked parts), blockage windows \([\underline{b}_{s},\overline{b}_{s}]\) and the blockage fractions αₛ.  
2. **Weight selection** – Choose wᴰ and wᴱ to reflect the planner’s preference between punctuality and energy saving.  
3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to a solver. The optimal solution yields for every train:  
   * the selected path (xᵢₚ),  
   * the speed level on each traversed segment (yᵢₛℓ),  
   * the exact arrival/departure times (aᵢₛ, bᵢₛ),  
   * the total delay Δᵢ and energy Eᵢ.  
4. **Post‑processing** – Translate the binary decisions into a human‑readable timetable and a set of executable speed profiles for the train‑control system.

The formulation captures **rerouting around partial blockages, bidirectional conflict resolution, speed‑level management, delay minimisation and energy efficiency** in a single, linear mixed‑integer model – exactly the integrated TRSMP problem described in the introduction.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
*Indices, sets and parameters*  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**  | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**  | Set of track segments (including both directions), indexed by *s* |
| **N**  | Set of stations, indexed by *n* |
| **A ⊂ S × S** | Set of admissible directed arcs (segment → segment) that a train may traverse (includes possible rerouting arcs) |
| **D ⊂ T × T** | Set of ordered train‑pair conflicts (train *i* and *j* share a segment in opposite directions) |
| **K**  | Set of discrete speed‑profile “plans” that can be assigned to a train on a given arc (plan *k* = a feasible speed‑time envelope) |
| **Δ**  | Length of the basic time‑discretisation interval (minutes) |
| **L_s** | Physical length of segment *s* (km) |
| **v^max_s**, **v^min_s** | Upper / lower speed limits on segment *s* (km/h) |
| **a^max**, **a^min** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h²) |
| **E_{t,s,k}** | Energy consumption (kWh) of train *t* when traversing segment *s* by plan *k* |
| **τ^{nom}_{t,s}** | Nominal travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (minutes) under the original timetable |
| **τ^{win}_{s} = [τ^{start}_s , τ^{end}_s]** | Disruption time window on segment *s* (minutes) – the segment is blocked for one direction during this interval |
| **M**  | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) |
| **ε**  | Small positive constant (e.g. 0.1 min) used to enforce strict ordering |

*Decision variables*  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **x_{t,s,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* using speed‑profile plan *k*; 0 otherwise |
| **y_{t,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses segment *s* (any plan); 0 otherwise ( = Σ_k x_{t,s,k}) |
| **z_{t,i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *t* departs station *i* before arriving at station *j* (ordering variable) |
| **α_{t,s}** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (minutes from horizon start) |
| **β_{t,s}** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s* (minutes) |
| **γ_{t,n}** | continuous ≥0 | Dwell (stop) time of train *t* at station *n* (minutes) |
| **δ_{t,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* within the disruption window (i.e. suffers a blockage) |
| **π_{t,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* is **rerouted** on segment *s* (i.e. uses the opposite‑direction track) |

*Assumptions (explicitly stated)*  

1. **Time‑discretisation** – all times are measured in minutes and are multiples of a base interval Δ.  
2. **Speed‑profile linearisation** – each admissible speed‑profile plan *k* on a segment *s* is pre‑computed and represented by a constant travel time τ_{s,k} and associated energy E_{t,s,k}. This yields a MILP‑compatible representation of the otherwise nonlinear speed‑management problem.  
3. **Bidirectional conflict** – only pairs of trains travelling in opposite directions on the same physical track can conflict. If a segment is blocked for one direction during τ^{win}_s, the opposite direction may be used only if a rerouting decision π_{t,s}=1 is taken.  
4. **Single‑track capacity** – at any instant a physical segment can be occupied by at most one train (including both directions).  
5. **Dwell‑time bounds** – each station *n* has a minimum dwell γ^{min}_n (e.g. 1 min) and a maximum dwell γ^{max}_n (e.g. 5 min).  
6. **Cancellation not modelled** – all trains in T must be scheduled (cancellation could be added by a binary “cancel” variable but is omitted for clarity).  

---

### 1. Objective function  

The integrated model simultaneously minimises total delay and total energy consumption.  
Let **D_{t,n} = α_{t,s_{in}(n)} – α^{nom}_{t,n}** be the arrival‑delay of train *t* at station *n* (α^{nom}_{t,n} is the scheduled arrival time).  
The objective is a weighted sum:

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{n\in N} w^{delay}\, D_{t,n}}_{\text{total passenger‑delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} w^{energy}\,E_{t,s,k}\,x_{t,s,k}}_{\text{total energy consumption}} .
\]

*Weights* \(w^{delay},w^{energy}>0\) reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

### 2. Core constraints  

#### 2.1 Plan selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S .
\tag{C1}
\]

If a train uses a segment, exactly one speed‑plan is chosen.

#### 2.2 Travel‑time linking  

For each selected plan the departure time at the downstream end equals the upstream arrival plus the plan’s travel time:

\[
\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\,x_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S .
\tag{C2}
\]

#### 2.3 Station continuity (flow)  

Let *s_{in}(n)* and *s_{out}(n)* be the incoming and outgoing segments of station *n* for train *t*. The departure from a station equals arrival plus dwell:

\[
\beta_{t,s_{out}(n)} = \alpha_{t,s_{in}(n)} + \gamma_{t,n} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; n\in N .
\tag{C3}
\]

#### 2.4 Dwell‑time bounds  

\[
\gamma^{min}_n \le \gamma_{t,n} \le \gamma^{max}_n \qquad \forall t\in T,\; n\in N .
\tag{C4}
\]

#### 2.5 Disruption‑window feasibility  

A train may traverse a blocked segment only if it either (i) passes **outside** the disruption window or (ii) is rerouted to the opposite track.  

\[
\alpha_{t,s} \ge \tau^{end}_s + \epsilon \;-\; M\,\delta_{t,s} \qquad
\beta_{t,s} \le \tau^{start}_s - \epsilon \;+\; M\,\delta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{C5}
\]

If \(\delta_{t,s}=0\) the train must be completely before the window or after it; if \(\delta_{t,s}=1\) the constraint is relaxed (big‑M).  

Rerouting is allowed only when the opposite‑direction track is free:

\[
\pi_{t,s} \le 1 - \sum_{i\in T\setminus\{t\}} y_{i,\text{opp}(s)} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{C6}
\]

If another train already occupies the opposite track, rerouting is forbidden.

#### 2.6 Single‑track capacity (conflict avoidance)  

For any two trains *i* and *j* that share a physical segment (including opposite directions when no rerouting is used) their occupation intervals must not overlap:

\[
\alpha_{i,s} \ge \beta_{j,s} - M\,(1 - u_{ij,s}) \qquad
\alpha_{j,s} \ge \beta_{i,s} - M\,(u_{ij,s}) \qquad
\forall (i,j)\in D,\; s\in S .
\tag{C7}
\]

Binary variable \(u_{ij,s}\in\{0,1\}\) decides the ordering of the two conflicting trains on segment *s*.

#### 2.7 Train‑order (reordering) variables  

If the timetable is allowed to change the sequence of trains on a segment, the ordering variables must be consistent with the binary conflict variables:

\[
u_{ij,s} + u_{ji,s} = 1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in D,\; s\in S .
\tag{C8}
\]

#### 2.8 Route feasibility (path selection)  

Each train must follow a feasible path from its origin to its destination. Let **P_t** be the set of admissible arcs for train *t*. For every node (segment) the flow conservation holds:

\[
\sum_{(s',s)\in A,\; s\in P_t} y_{t,s} - \sum_{(s,s'')\in A,\; s\in P_t} y_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } s \text{ is the origin segment of } t,\\
-1 & \text{if } s \text{ is the destination segment of } t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall t\in T .
\tag{C9}
\]

Thus the binary usage variables \(y_{t,s}\) define a simple path.

#### 2.9 Coupling of rerouting and segment usage  

If a train is rerouted on segment *s*, it must also use that segment:

\[
\pi_{t,s} \le y_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{C10}
\]

Conversely, if a train uses the opposite‑direction track, the original direction cannot be used:

\[
y_{t,\text{opp}(s)} \le 1- \pi_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{C11}
\]

#### 2.10 Delay definition (for objective)  

Let \(A^{nom}_{t,n}\) be the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. The delay variable is defined as:

\[
D_{t,n} = \alpha_{t,s_{in}(n)} - A^{nom}_{t,n} \qquad \forall t,n .
\tag{C12}
\]

Optionally, enforce non‑negativity (only tardiness penalised):

\[
D_{t,n} \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,n .
\tag{C13}
\]

---

### 3. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{n\in N} w^{delay}\,D_{t,n}
      +\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} w^{energy}\,E_{t,s,k}\,x_{t,s,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C13)}\\
& x_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
u_{ij,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
\pi_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& \alpha_{t,s},\beta_{t,s},\gamma_{t,n},D_{t,n}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model simultaneously decides **(i)** the binary route (including possible rerouting), **(ii)** the ordering of conflicting bidirectional trains, **(iii)** the selection of a discrete speed‑profile plan for each traversed segment, and **(iv)** the resulting arrival/departure times and dwell times, while minimising a weighted combination of passenger delay and energy consumption.  

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisation for time‑window and conflict ordering), thus the formulation is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** suitable for exact solvers (e.g., CPLEX, Gurobi) or for decomposition‑based solution approaches as discussed in the accompanying study.

**Variables**

- \(y_{i,s,t}\in\{0,1\}\) – train \(i\) occupies segment \(s\) (or its opposite) during time period \(t\).  
- \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) – train \(i\) is cancelled (1) or operates (0).  
- \(a_i\ge 0\) – actual arrival time of train \(i\) at its destination station (hours).  
- \(d_i\ge 0\) – departure time from the same station, \(d_i = a_i+\text{dwell}_i\).  
- \(v_{i,s,t}\ge 0\) – average speed of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) during period \(t\) (km/h).  
- \(w_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) – selection of breakpoint \(k\) for the piece‑wise linear energy approximation on segment \(s\).  
- \(e_{i,s}\ge 0\) – energy consumed by train \(i\) on segment \(s\).

**Parameters (data to be provided)**  

- \(I\) – set of trains, indexed by \(i\).  
- \(S\) – set of directed track segments, indexed by \(s\); for each physical segment two opposite‑direction copies are created (original \(s\) and opposite \(s^{\mathrm{op}}\)).  
- \(T\) – set of discrete time periods, indexed by \(t\).  
- \(\text{a}_i^0\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) (baseline).  
- \(\text{dwell}_i\) – minimum dwell time at the destination station.  
- \(L_s, U_s\) – lower and upper speed limits on segment \(s\).  
- \(\alpha_s,\beta_s\) – coefficients for the quadratic energy model on segment \(s\) (\(E = \alpha_s v^2+\beta_s\)).  
- \(C^{\text{cancel}}_i\) – penalty cost for cancelling train \(i\).  
- \(\omega^{\text{delay}},\omega^{\text{energy}},\omega^{\text{cancel}}\) – weighting factors in the objective.  
- \(M\) – big‑M constant (e.g., \(10^5\)).  
- \(\Delta t_t\) – length of time period \(t\) (hours).  
- \(\text{NextSeg}_s\) – the directed successor segment of \(s\) in the normal (or rerouted) route.  
- \(\mathcal{K}_s\) – ordered set of break‑points for the piece‑wise linear approximation on segment \(s\), with known speed values \(v_{s,k}\) and corresponding energy values \(e_{s,k}= \alpha_s v_{s,k}^2+\beta_s\).  
- \(\mathcal{D}\subseteq S\) – set of segments that are partially blocked.  
- \([t^{\text{start}}_s, t^{\text{end}}_s]\) – disruption time window for each blocked segment \(s\in\mathcal{D}\).

**Objective (minimize weighted sum of delay, energy, and cancellations)**  

\[
\min\;
\omega^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_i-\text{a}_i^0\bigr)
\;+\;
\omega^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{t\in T}
\bigl(\alpha_s v_{i,s,t}^2+\beta_s\bigr)\;\Delta t_t\;y_{i,s,t}
\;+\;
\omega^{\text{cancel}}\sum_{i\in I} C^{\text{cancel}}_i\,z_i
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Cancellation linking** – a train cannot occupy any segment if it is cancelled  

\[
y_{i,s,t}\le 1-z_i \qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S,\; t\in T
\]

2. **Arrival feasibility with cancellation**  

\[
a_i \ge \text{a}_i^0 - M\,z_i \qquad \forall i\in I
\]

3. **Departure definition**  

\[
d_i = a_i + \text{dwell}_i \qquad \forall i\in I
\]

4. **Speed limits (active only when the segment is used)**  

\[
L_s\, y_{i,s,t} \le v_{i,s,t} \le U_s\, y_{i,s,t}+U_s(1-y_{i,s,t})
\qquad \forall i,s,t
\]

5. **Capacity (conflict avoidance on each directed segment)**  

\[
\sum_{i\in I} y_{i,s,t} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S,\; t\in T
\]

6. **Disruption handling** – blocked segment cannot be used during its disruption window; the opposite direction may be used instead  

\[
y_{i,s,t}=0 \qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in\mathcal{D},\;
 t^{\text{start}}_s\le t\le t^{\text{end}}_s
\]

7. **Flow conservation (one‑period travel approximation)** – if a train uses segment \(s\) at period \(t\) it must continue on its successor at the next period  

\[
y_{i,s,t} \le y_{i,\text{NextSeg}_s,\,t+1}+M\,z_i
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S,\; t\in T\setminus\{ \max T\}
\]

8. **Piece‑wise linear energy representation**  

   a) Exactly one breakpoint is selected for each \((i,s)\) that is actually used  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_s} w_{i,s,k}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \sum_{t} y_{i,s,t}>0\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
\]

   b) Energy equals the value of the selected breakpoint  

\[
e_{i,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_s} e_{s,k}\, w_{i,s,k}
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
\]

9. **Link energy to the objective (already embedded in the objective term).**  

All variables are bounded as indicated (binary or non‑negative continuous).  

---

**Assumptions made (clearly stated)**  

- Travel time on a segment is approximated by one time period; more accurate travel‑time coupling can be introduced by additional binary variables or a deterministic travel‑time matrix.  
- The opposite‑track reroute is represented by a separate directed copy of each physical segment; the model allows a train to switch to that copy only when the original segment is blocked.  
- Energy on a segment is approximated by a piece‑wise linear function of speed; the break‑points \(\mathcal{K}_s\) and their energy values are supplied as data.  
- Big‑M constant \(M\) is sufficiently large to deactivate constraints when a train is cancelled.  

The formulation above gives a complete MILP description of the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockages, ready to be implemented in any MILP solver.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The formulation below captures the whole problem described in the prompt: a high‑speed railway suffers a *partial segment blockage* (only one side of a track is unavailable for a given time window).  Trains may be **re‑routed** to the opposite side, **re‑ordered** on shared tracks, and must obtain **feasible speed profiles** that respect acceleration limits and minimise energy use.  The model is a pure mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) – all non‑linearities are linearised with standard big‑M techniques.

---

### 1. Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, *i = 1,…,|I|* |
| **N** | Set of stations (including origins and destinations), *n* |
| **K** | Set of track segments between two consecutive stations, *k = (n,n+1)* |
| **S = {L,R}** | Two possible **sides** (left/right) of a bidirectional segment |
| **B ⊂ K** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (partial blockage) |
| **U ⊂ K** | Sub‑set of *fully blocked* segments (never usable) |
| **T** | Set of discrete time‑intervals, *t = 1,…,|T|* (Δt = length of an interval) |
| **L** | Set of admissible speed levels, *ℓ ∈ L* (e.g. 0, 30, 60, … km h⁻¹) |
| **Vℓ** | Physical speed of level ℓ (km h⁻¹) |
| **αℓ** | Energy consumption coefficient for level ℓ (kWh per interval) |
| **distₖ** | Length of segment *k* (km) |
| **dwellᵢₙ** | Minimum dwell time of train *i* at station *n* (min) |
| **schedᵢ** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (min) |
| **blockStartₖ,ₛ**, **blockEndₖ,ₛ** | Start / end of the disruption window on side *s* of blocked segment *k* (min) |
| **Mₜ** | Large constant ≥ any feasible time difference (e.g. 10⁶ min) |
| **wᴰ**, **wᴱ** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |

*Assumption 1*: All trains travel the same route (the line) except that on a blocked segment they may choose side *L* or *R*.  
*Assumption 2*: Speed can only take values from the discrete set **L**; the set is fine enough to approximate a continuous speed curve.  

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **rᵢₛ** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* on every blocked segment it traverses. |
| **xᵢₖₛ** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* occupies side *s* of segment *k* (used to couple side choice with capacity). |
| **oᵢⱼₖ** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* **enters** segment *k* before train *j* (ordering on that side). |
| **aᵢₙ** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *n*. |
| **dᵢₙ** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *n* ( = aᵢₙ + dwellᵢₙ). |
| **τᵢₖ** | continuous ≥0 | **Entry time** of train *i* onto segment *k* ( = dᵢₙ for k = (n,n+1)). |
| **φᵢₖ** | continuous ≥0 | **Exit time** of train *i* from segment *k* ( = aᵢₙ₊₁). |
| **zᵢₜℓ** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* travels with speed level ℓ during interval *t*. |
| **vᵢₜ** | continuous ≥0 | Physical speed of train *i* during interval *t* (linear combination of speed levels). |
| **Δᵢ** | continuous ≥0 | Total delay of train *i* ( = aᵢ,last – schedᵢ). |
| **Eᵢ** | continuous ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train *i*. |

---

### 3. Linear relationships  

*Speed level ↔ speed*  

\[
v_{i,t}= \sum_{\ell\in L} V_{\ell}\;z_{i,t,\ell}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;t\in T
\]

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{i,t,\ell}=1\qquad\forall i\in I,\;t\in T
\]

*Energy*  

\[
E_i = \sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{\ell\in L}\alpha_{\ell}\;z_{i,t,\ell}\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

*Dwell*  

\[
d_{i,n}=a_{i,n}+dwell_{i,n}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;n\in N
\]

*Link entry/exit of a segment with station times*  

\[
\tau_{i,k}=d_{i,n},\qquad \phi_{i,k}=a_{i,n+1}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;k=(n,n+1)
\]

*Travel‑time – distance relation* (linearised by a pre‑computed coefficient  
\(c_{\ell,k}= \dfrac{dist_k}{V_{\ell}}\))

\[
\phi_{i,k}-\tau_{i,k}= \sum_{t\in T_k}\sum_{\ell\in L} c_{\ell,k}\;z_{i,t,\ell}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;k\in K
\]

where **Tₖ** is the set of intervals that intersect segment *k* (the model can be built so that each interval belongs to exactly one segment).

*Acceleration / deceleration*  

\[
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}\le a_{\max}\,\Delta t\qquad\forall i\in I,\;t=1,\dots,|T|-1
\]

\[
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1}\le d_{\max}\,\Delta t\qquad\forall i\in I,\;t=1,\dots,|T|-1
\]

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
w^{D}\sum_{i\in I}\Delta_i\;+\;
w^{E}\sum_{i\in I}E_i}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_i = a_{i,\text{last}}-sched_i\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

Both terms are linear.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Side choice on blocked segments  

For every train that traverses a blocked segment (*k∈B*)  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

\[
x_{i,k,s}=r_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;k\in B,\;s\in S
\]

If side *s* of segment *k* is the **closed** side during the disruption, it cannot be used:

\[
x_{i,k,s}=0\qquad\forall i\in I,\;k\in B,\;s\text{ closed}
\]

#### 5.2 Capacity – no overlap on the same side  

For any pair of distinct trains *(i,j)* that may share side *s* of segment *k* :

\[
o_{i j k}+o_{j i k}= x_{i,k,s}+x_{j,k,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S
\]

Big‑M disjunctive constraints enforce the temporal ordering:

\[
\tau_{j,k}\ge \phi_{i,k}-M_t\bigl(1-o_{i j k}\bigr)\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S
\]

\[
\tau_{i,k}\ge \phi_{j,k}-M_t\;o_{i j k}\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S
\]

If a train does **not** use side *s* of *k* (i.e. \(x_{i,k,s}=0\)), the corresponding ordering binary is forced to 0 by the first equation, thereby de‑activating the big‑M constraints.

#### 5.3 Ordering consistency across consecutive segments  

If train *i* precedes *j* on segment *k*, the same ordering must hold on the next segment *k+1* (provided both trains travel that segment):

\[
o_{i j,k+1}\ge o_{i j,k}-(1-x_{i,k+1,s})-(1-x_{j,k+1,s})\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K\setminus\{k_{\max}\},\;s\in S
\]

A symmetric inequality can be added; together they prevent overtaking inside a block of consecutive segments.

#### 5.4 Disruption‑window exclusion  

For each blocked side *s* of segment *k∈B* :

\[
\tau_{i,k}\ge \text{blockEnd}_{k,s}\;-\;M_t\,(1-x_{i,k,s})\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

\[
\phi_{i,k}\le \text{blockStart}_{k,s}\;+\;M_t\,(1-x_{i,k,s})\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

If a train uses the closed side (\(x_{i,k,s}=1\)) it must be completely **outside** the disruption interval; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

#### 5.5 Speed limits  

\[
V_{\min}\le v_{i,t}\le V_{\max}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;t\in T
\]

Because *v* is a convex combination of the admissible levels, the bounds are automatically satisfied; they are kept for numerical robustness.

#### 5.6 Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_i = a_{i,\text{last}}-sched_i\qquad\forall i\in I
\]

#### 5.7 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{i,s},\;x_{i,k,s},\;o_{i j k},\;z_{i,t,\ell}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{i,n},\,d_{i,n},\,\tau_{i,k},\,\phi_{i,k},\,v_{i,t},\,\Delta_i,\,E_i \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{D}\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-sched_i\bigr)
      \;+\;w^{E}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L}\alpha_{\ell}\,z_{i,t,\ell}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 &&\forall i\in I\\
& x_{i,k,s}=r_{i,s} &&\forall i\in I,\;k\in B,\;s\in S\\
& x_{i,k,s}=0 &&\forall i\in I,\;k\in B,\;s\text{ closed}\\[2pt]
& d_{i,n}=a_{i,n}+dwell_{i,n} &&\forall i,n\\
& \tau_{i,k}=d_{i,n},\;\phi_{i,k}=a_{i,n+1} &&\forall i,\;k=(n,n+1)\\
& \phi_{i,k}-\tau_{i,k}= \sum_{t\in T_k}\sum_{\ell\in L}c_{\ell,k}\,z_{i,t,\ell}
   &&\forall i,k\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L}z_{i,t,\ell}=1 &&\forall i,t\\
& v_{i,t}= \sum_{\ell\in L}V_{\ell}\,z_{i,t,\ell} &&\forall i,t\\
& v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}\le a_{\max}\Delta t &&\forall i,\;t<|T|\\
& v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1}\le d_{\max}\Delta t &&\forall i,\;t<|T|\\[2pt]
& o_{i j k}+o_{j i k}= x_{i,k,s}+x_{j,k,s}
   &&\forall i<j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S\\
& \tau_{j,k}\ge \phi_{i,k}-M_t\bigl(1-o_{i j k}\bigr)
   &&\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S\\
& \tau_{i,k}\ge \phi_{j,k}-M_t\,o_{i j k
   } &&\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K,\;s\in S\\
& o_{i j,k+1}\ge o_{i j,k}-(1-x_{i,k+1,s})-(1-x_{j,k+1,s})
   &&\forall i\neq j,\;k\in K\setminus\{k_{\max}\},\;s\in S\\[2pt]
& \tau_{i,k}\ge \text{blockEnd}_{k,s}-M_t(1-x_{i,k,s})
   &&\forall i,\;k\in B,\;s\text{ closed}\\
& \phi_{i,k}\le \text{blockStart}_{k,s}+M_t(1-x_{i,k,s})
   &&\forall i,\;k\in B,\;s\text{ closed}\\[2pt]
& V_{\min}\le v_{i,t}\le V_{\max} &&\forall i,t\\
& \Delta_i = a_{i,\text{last}}-sched_i &&\forall i\\
& \text{domain restrictions (binary / non‑negative)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries listed above.  Consequently the model is a **pure MILP**.

---

### 7. How the model works  

* **Route choice** – binary variables `rᵢₛ` enforce that each train picks exactly one side of the blocked segment; the side‑usage variables `xᵢₖₛ` link that choice to the capacity constraints.  
* **Conflict‑free timetable** – ordering binaries `oᵢⱼₖ` together with the big‑M disjunction guarantee that two trains never occupy the same side of a segment simultaneously.  Consistency constraints keep the ordering the same on consecutive segments, eliminating overtaking inside a block.

* **Objective** – a weighted sum of total passenger delay (difference between realised and scheduled final arrival) and total electrical energy consumption.

For realistic instances (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a few hundred time intervals) the formulation is tractable; additional decomposition or heuristic refinements (e.g. the IP‑plan decomposition described in the paper) can be applied if needed.

**Variables**

| Symbol | Description | Type | Domain |
|--------|-------------|------|--------|
| \(x_{i,j,k}\) | Train \(i\) uses route option \(k\) on segment \(j\) (0 = normal side, 1 = alternative side) | Binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(y_{i,t}\) | Train \(i\) starts its journey at discrete time‑point \(t\) | Binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(v_{i,j}\) | Speed of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) | Continuous | \(v^{\min }_j \le v_{i,j}\le v^{\max }_j\) |
| \(d_i\) | Departure time of train \(i\) from its origin | Continuous | \(\ge 0\) |
| \(a_i\) | Arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination | Continuous | \(\ge 0\) |
| \(\text{ord}_{i,i',j}\) | Train \(i\) passes segment \(j\) before train \(i'\) (only for non‑blocked segments) | Binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |

**Parameters**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal I\) | Set of trains |
| \(\mathcal J\) | Ordered set of track segments (origin → destination) |
| \(\mathcal K_j=\{0,1\}\) | Route‑option set for segment \(j\) |
| \(\mathcal T\) | Discrete start‑time set (e.g., 0, 0.25, 0.5 h …) |
| \(\hat a_i\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) (used for delay) |
| \(L_j\) | Length of segment \(j\) (km) |
| \(v^{\min }_j, v^{\max }_j\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(j\) |
| \(\kappa_j\) | Capacity of segment \(j\) (max number of trains simultaneously) |
| \(j^{\text{blk}}\) | Segment that is partially blocked |
| \(k^{\text{blk}}\) | Side of \(j^{\text{blk}}\) that is unavailable during the disruption |
| \([t^{\text{disc}}_{\text{st}},t^{\text{disc}}_{\text{en}}]\) | Disruption time window |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) | Objective weights |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time |

**Objective**

\[
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(a_i-\hat a_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}
\bigl(v_{i,j}\bigr)^{2}\,L_j}_{\text{energy (≈ \(v^{2}\)·distance)} }.
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Unique start time** for each train  
\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} y_{i,t}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I .
\]

2. **Departure time equals chosen start time**  
\[
d_i = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} t\,y_{i,t}\qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I .
\]

3. **Exactly one route option on the blocked segment**  
\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_{j^{\text{blk}}}} x_{i,j^{\text{blk}},k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I .
\]

4. **Blocked side cannot be used during the disruption window**  
For every train that would occupy the blocked side while the disruption is active,
\[
x_{i,j^{\text{blk}},k^{\text{blk}}}\;+\; y_{i,t}\le 1
\qquad
\forall i\in\mathcal I,\; \forall t\in\mathcal T:
t\in[t^{\text{disc}}_{\text{st}},t^{\text{disc}}_{\text{en}}].
\]

5. **Speed limits**  
\[
v^{\min }_{j}\le v_{i,j}\le v^{\max }_{j}\qquad 
\forall i\in\mathcal I,\; \forall j\in\mathcal J .
\]

6. **Travel time on a segment** (link speed to time)  
\[
\tau_{i,j}= \frac{L_j}{v_{i,j}}\qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I,\; \forall j\in\mathcal J .
\]

7. **Flow conservation (cumulative travel)** – the arrival at the destination must be after the departure plus all segment travel times:  
\[
d_i + \sum_{j\in\mathcal J}\tau_{i,j}\;\le\; a_i \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I .
\]

8. **Capacity on each segment** (big‑M ordering for segments of capacity 1; for higher capacity a simple sum‑overlap formulation can be used).  
   For \(\kappa_j=1\) and any two distinct trains \(i,i'\):
   \[
   \text{ord}_{i,i',j} + \text{ord}_{i',i,j}=1,
   \]
   \[
   d_i + \sum_{p\le j}\tau_{i,p} \;+\; M\bigl(1-\text{ord}_{i,i',j}\bigr)\;\le\;
   d_{i'} + \sum_{p\le j}\tau_{i',p}\qquad 
   \forall i\neq i',\; \forall j\neq j^{\text{blk}}.
   \]

   For segments with \(\kappa_j>1\) a linearised overlap count ensures  
   \[
   \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\zeta_{i,j}\le\kappa_j,
   \]
   where \(\zeta_{i,j}=1\) iff train \(i\) occupies segment \(j\) (derived from start‑time and travel‑time variables).

9. **Route‑option consistency** – a train may travel on a segment only on the side it has selected:  
\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_j} x_{i,j,k}=1\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall j\in\mathcal J .
\]

**Assumptions (explicitly stated)**  

* Time is discretised only for the departure decision; all intra‑segment travel times are continuous.  
* Energy consumption on a segment is approximated by a quadratic function of speed (\(\propto v^{2}\)).  
* The big‑M constant \(M\) is chosen larger than the maximal possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 h).  
* For simplicity, capacity constraints are expressed with ordering binaries when \(\kappa_j=1\); higher capacities can be handled by a linear overlap‑count formulation (not detailed here).  
* The disruption blocks only one side of a single segment; the other side remains fully usable.  

The model above is a complete mixed‑integer linear program (with a quadratic objective) that simultaneously chooses departure times, route sides on the blocked segment, speeds on every segment, and the ordering of trains on shared tracks, so as to minimise a weighted sum of total passenger delay and energy consumption while respecting all operational and safety constraints.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
*Goal: minimise the total secondary delay of all trains while respecting safety, capacity and routing constraints. The model is presented in three logical blocks (rerouting, re‑ordering, rescheduling) but is written as a single‑stage MILP that can be solved directly or used as a master‑problem in a decomposition scheme.*

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = *N*) |
| **N** | Set of network nodes (stations, signal blocks, junctions), indexed by *i* |
| **E** | Set of directed track‑segments (edges)  *(i → j)*, indexed by *e = (i,j)* |
| **R** | Set of admissible routes for each train, indexed by *r*. For a given train *t* the subset is *Rₜ ⊆ R*. |
| **Pₑ** | Set of time‑points (discrete planning horizon) at which a train may occupy edge *e*, indexed by *p* (p = 0,…,P). |
| **Sₑ** | Set of successor edges of *e* (i.e. edges that can be travelled after *e* without a conflict). |
| **K** | Set of “conflict pairs’’ (t₁,t₂) that share at least one common edge (including opposite directions). |

*Assumption 1*: The planning horizon is discretised into equal time‑steps Δt (e.g. 30 s). All departure/arrival times are expressed as integer multiples of Δt.

*Assumption 2*: For each train *t* a finite set of feasible routes *Rₜ* is pre‑computed (e.g. by a shortest‑path algorithm or a route‑selection heuristic).  

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| **xₜʳ** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* ∈ *Rₜ*, 0 otherwise |
| **yₜₑₚ** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies edge *e* during time‑step *p*, 0 otherwise |
| **sₜ** | continuous ≥0 | scheduled (original) departure time of train *t* (given data) |
| **dₜ** | continuous ≥0 | **secondary delay** of train *t* (decision variable to be minimised) |
| **aₜₑₚ** | continuous ≥0 | arrival time of train *t* at the **head** of edge *e* at step *p* (used for propagation) |
| **wₜₖ** | binary | 1 if train *t* must wait for the other train in conflict pair *k=(t, t′)*, 0 otherwise |
| **zₜₑₚ** | binary | auxiliary variable to linearise “train *t* leaves edge *e* at step *p*’’ (see constraints) |
| **πₜₑₚ** | continuous ≥0 | **cumulative delay** of train *t* when it starts to traverse edge *e* at step *p* (used for propagation). |

*Assumption 3*: Trains travel at a constant (pre‑defined) speed on each edge; thus the traversal time τₑ (in time‑steps) is known for every edge *e*.

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \sum_{t\in T} d_{t}
\]

*Interpretation*: minimise the sum of secondary delays (total passenger‑/freight‑delay). If a trade‑off with energy consumption is desired, an additional term  
\(\alpha \sum_{t,e,p} y_{t e p}\) (proportional to travelled distance) can be added – this is left as a modelling extension.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Edge‑usage consistency with the chosen route**  

For each train *t* and each edge *e*:

\[
\sum_{p\in P_e} y_{t e p}= \sum_{r\in R_t} \delta_{e}^{r}\, x_{t r}
\tag{4}
\]

where \(\delta_{e}^{r}=1\) if edge *e* belongs to route *r*, 0 otherwise.  
*Interpretation*: a train occupies exactly the edges that belong to its selected route.

### 4.2 Temporal feasibility (travel time)  

3. **Traversal time on an edge** – if a train enters edge *e* at step *p* it must stay τₑ steps on it:

\[
\sum_{q=p}^{p+\tau_{e}-1} y_{t e q} \ge \tau_{e}\, z_{t e p} \qquad \forall t, e, p
\tag{5}
\]

\(z_{t e p}=1\) iff the train *starts* traversing *e* at step *p*.  

4. **Linking start‑variables to occupancy**  

\[
z_{t e p} \le y_{t e p} \qquad \forall t,e,p
\tag{6}
\]
\[
z_{t e p} \le y_{t e (p+\tau_{e}-1)} \qquad \forall t,e,p
\tag{7}
\]

These linearise the “continuous block’’ of occupancy.

### 4.3 Capacity / Safety (single‑track)  

5. **At most one train on an edge at a given time**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t e p} \le 1 \qquad \forall e\in E,\; p\in P_e
\tag{8}
\]

(If the edge is double‑track, the RHS can be set to 2.)

### 4.4 Conflict‑pair waiting (re‑ordering)  

6. **If two trains share an edge, one must wait for the other**  

For each conflict pair *k = (t, t′) ∈ K* and each common edge *e* :

\[
\sum_{p\in P_e} p\, y_{t e p} + M\, w_{t k} \le 
\sum_{p\in P_e} p\, y_{t' e p} + M \qquad \forall e\in E_{k}
\tag{9}
\]

where \(E_{k}\) is the set of edges shared by the pair, and *M* is a big‑M larger than the horizon.  
If \(w_{t k}=1\) train *t* is forced to depart the shared edge after train *t′* (FIFO‑like).  

7. **Exactly one waiting direction per conflict pair**  

\[
w_{t k}+ w_{t' k}=1 \qquad \forall k=(t,t')\in K
\tag{10}
\]

(If simultaneous occupancy is allowed, the RHS can be ≤1.)

### 4.5 Delay propagation (rescheduling)  

8. **Definition of secondary delay** – the actual departure time equals scheduled plus delay:

\[
a_{t\,\text{origin}\,0}= s_{t}+d_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{11}
\]

9. **Arrival time at the head of an edge** – if a train starts edge *e* at step *p* its arrival time equals the start time plus accumulated delay:

\[
a_{t e p}= s_{t}+d_{t}+p\Delta t \qquad \forall t,e,p \text{ with } z_{t e p}=1
\tag{12}
\]

10. **Propagation of delay to the next edge** – when a train leaves edge *e* at step *p+τₑ‑1* it may have to wait for a predecessor train on the successor edge *e′* (if conflict exists). This is linearised by the waiting variables:

\[
\pi_{t e' (p+τ_{e})} \ge \pi_{t e p}+ \tau_{e}\Delta t 
+ M\, w_{t k} \qquad \forall (t,t')\in K,\; e\in E_{k},\; e' \in S_{e}
\tag{13}
\]

The cumulative delay variable \(\pi\) is used only for the purpose of linking successive edges; the final secondary delay *dₜ* is the value of \(\pi\) when the train reaches its destination node.

11. **Terminal condition** – the secondary delay equals the cumulative delay at the last edge of the chosen route:

\[
d_{t}= \pi_{t\,e^{\text{last}}\,p^{\text{last}}}\qquad 
\forall t\in T,\; e^{\text{last}}\in \text{route}_{t},\; p^{\text{last}}\in P_{e^{\text{last}}}
\tag{14}
\]

### 4.6 Logical linking of route and timing  

12. **If an edge is not selected by the route, it cannot be occupied**  

\[
y_{t e p} \le \sum_{r\in R_t}\delta_{e}^{r} x_{t r} \qquad \forall t,e,p
\tag{15}
\]

13. **Non‑negativity / binary restrictions**  

\[
x_{t r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t e p}\in\{0,1\},\; w_{t k}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t e p}\in\{0,1\}
\]
\[
d_{t}\ge 0,\; a_{t e p}\ge 0,\; \pi_{t e p}\ge 0
\tag{16}
\]

---

## 5. Model Summary  

The complete MILP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} d_t \\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(1)–(16)} \quad \text{(as listed above)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; binary variables appear only linearly, therefore the model belongs to the **mixed‑integer linear programming** class.

---

## 6. Remarks & Extensions  

1. **Energy‑aware objective** – add a term \(\beta\sum_{t,e,p} y_{t e p}\) (β > 0) to penalise total travelled distance or to approximate energy consumption.

2. **Variable train speeds** – replace the constant τₑ by a decision variable τₑₜ (bounded between min/max travel times) and add a linear relationship with energy consumption if required.

3. **Overlaps / safety margins** – introduce a fixed “overlap’’ time 𝜏ᵒ that must be kept clear behind a stopped train. This can be modelled by extending the occupancy of the preceding edge by 𝜏ᵒ steps (add a constraint similar to (5) with τₑ+𝜏ᵒ).

4. **Decomposition** – the model can be split into a master problem (variables *xₜʳ* and *wₜₖ* – rerouting & re‑ordering) and a sub‑problem (variables *y, d, π* – rescheduling). Benders cuts can be generated from the sub‑problem to improve convergence.

5. **Scalability** – for large networks the set *Pₑ* can be limited by a time‑window around the scheduled passage time (e.g., ± 30 min) to keep the number of binary variables tractable.

---

### References (selected)

* Pellegrini et al., 2014, 2015, 2019 – MILP formulations for rtRTMP.  
* Keita et al., 2020 – three‑stage decomposition (rerouting, reordering, rescheduling).  
* Samà et al., 2016 – route‑selection graph model.  
* Zhan et al., 2024 – two‑stage approach for complete blockages.  

*(All references are taken from the introductory text; the model above follows the same notation and assumptions.)*

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for rolling‑stock rescheduling with infrastructure‑availability constraints**  

The model combines two sub‑problems that are solved iteratively (or within a Benders‑type exact scheme):

1. **Composition model** – decides which rolling‑stock unit (RSU) is assigned to each scheduled train‑trip and which **shunting movements** (SM) are performed at the considered stations (Utrecht Centraal, Rotterdam Centraal).  
2. **Infrastructure model** – checks that every chosen shunting movement can be executed on a free track segment at the required time; if not, it forces a short delay of conflicting passenger‑train services (or forbids the movement).

Below the complete linear formulation is given.  Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are explicitly stated (marked **Assumption**).

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of **train‑trips** (passenger services) in the original timetable (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(R\) | Set of **rolling‑stock units** (RSUs) available for the day (indexed by \(r\)). |
| \(S\) | Set of **stations** where shunting is allowed (here \(S=\{Utrecht, Rotterdam\}\)). |
| \(M_s\) | Set of **shunting movement types** that can be performed at station \(s\) (e.g., “enter depot”, “exit depot”, “swap composition”). Index by \(m\). |
| \(K_s\) | Set of **track‑slots** (time‑intervals) on which a shunting movement can be placed at station \(s\) (indexed by \(k\)). |
| \(P\) | Set of **passenger‑train events** that occupy a track at a station (indexed by \(p\)). |
| \(D\) | Set of **disruption blocks** (full blockages) that are active during the planning horizon (indexed by \(d\)). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \(a_t\) | Planned **departure time** of trip \(t\) (minutes from midnight). | timetable |
| \(b_t\) | Planned **arrival time** of trip \(t\). | timetable |
| \(c_{rt}\) | **Compatibility**: 1 if RSU \(r\) can serve trip \(t\) (right length, power, etc.), 0 otherwise. | rolling‑stock database |
| \(cap_t\) | Passenger **capacity** of trip \(t\) (seats). | timetable |
| \(demand_t\) | Expected **passenger demand** on trip \(t\). | demand forecast |
| \(len_m\) | **Duration** (in minutes) of shunting movement type \(m\). | engineering data |
| \(track_{sk}\) | Length of track‑slot \(k\) at station \(s\) (in minutes) – i.e., the time window that is free if not occupied. | infrastructure schedule |
| \(M^{max}\) | Maximum number of shunting movements that may be performed at a station during the disruption. | policy |
| \(\Delta^{max}\) | Maximum **allowed delay** (minutes) that a passenger‑train event may receive to make room for a shunting movement. | buffer policy |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight for **operational cost** of using a shunting movement (e.g., crew cost). | decision‑maker |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for **deviation from original plan** (delays, cancellations). | decision‑maker |
| \(\gamma\) | Weight for **similarity** to the original rolling‑stock circulation (penalise re‑assignments). | decision‑maker |
| \(\epsilon\) | Small positive constant to linearise “big‑M” constraints. | modelling |
| \(M_{big}\) | Large constant (big‑M) – e.g. horizon length (1440 min). | modelling |

**Assumption 1** – All times are expressed in integer minutes; the planning horizon is 0 … 1440.

**Assumption 2** – Each shunting movement occupies a **single track‑slot** at a station; overlapping movements on the same slot are forbidden.

**Assumption 3** – A passenger‑train event \(p\) corresponds to a train occupying a track at a station during a known interval \([s_p^{start}, s_p^{end}]\).  

**Assumption 4** – The disruption blocks are modelled as a set of time intervals during which certain tracks are unavailable; the model only permits shunting on tracks that are *not* blocked.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \(x_{rt}\) | binary | 1 if RSU \(r\) is assigned to trip \(t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{r}^{init}\) | binary | 1 if RSU \(r\) starts the day at its *original* depot (i.e., unchanged). |
| \(z_{smk}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement type \(m\) is scheduled on track‑slot \(k\) at station \(s\). |
| \(\theta_{smk}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Start time** of shunting movement \((s,m,k)\). |
| \(\delta_{p}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Delay** applied to passenger‑train event \(p\) (minutes). |
| \(c_t\) | binary | 1 if trip \(t\) is **canceled** (i.e., not served). |
| \(u_{smk}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \((s,m,k)\) is **rejected** by the infrastructure model (used for Benders cuts). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The objective is a weighted sum of three (conflicting) goals:

1. **Operational cost of shunting** – minimise number and duration of shunting movements.  
2. **Service quality** – minimise total passenger‑train delay and cancellations.  
3. **Plan similarity** – penalise changes of RSU assignments compared with the original circulation.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\alpha \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{m\in M_s}\sum_{k\in K_s} z_{smk}}_{\text{(A) shunting cost}} \\
& + \underbrace{\beta \Big( \sum_{p\in P}\delta_{p} \;+\; \sum_{t\in T} c_{t}\, cap_{t}\Big)}_{\text{(B) passenger impact}} \\
& + \underbrace{\gamma \sum_{r\in R}\Big(1- y_{r}^{init}\Big)}_{\text{(C) deviation from original plan}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

*Explanation*  

* (A) each performed shunting movement incurs a fixed cost \(\alpha\) (crew, fuel).  
* (B) each minute of delay is penalised, and each cancelled trip incurs a penalty proportional to its capacity (lost seats).  
* (C) if a RSU is not kept at its original start location (\(y_r^{init}=0\)), we pay \(\gamma\).

All three weights can be tuned by the decision‑maker.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Rolling‑stock assignment  

1. **Each trip is served by at most one RSU (or cancelled).**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{rt} + c_t = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

2. **Compatibility between RSU and trip.**  

\[
x_{rt} \le c_{rt} \qquad \forall r\in R,\; t\in T .
\]

3. **Flow conservation of RSUs (circulation).**  
   For each RSU, the sequence of trips it serves must be feasible in time.  
   Let \(succ(t)\) be the set of trips that can follow \(t\) (arrival of \(t\) ≤ departure of \(t'\) – turnaround time \(\tau\)).  

\[
\sum_{t'\in succ(t)} x_{rt'} \;-\; \sum_{t\in pred(t')} x_{rt} = 0 \qquad \forall r\in R,\; t\in T .
\]

   (A compact way is to use a **time‑expanded network**; the above is a simplified representation.)

4. **Similarity to original circulation.**  
   If RSU \(r\) starts the day at its original depot we set \(y_r^{init}=1\). This can be forced by a parameter \(orig_r\in\{0,1\}\) that indicates whether the original plan uses RSU \(r\) at the first trip.  

\[
y_r^{init} \le \sum_{t\in T_{start}} x_{rt} \qquad \forall r\in R,
\]

   where \(T_{start}\) are the trips that start the day at the depot.

### 5.2 Shunting‑movement scheduling  

5. **Only a limited number of shunting movements per station.**  

\[
\sum_{m\in M_s}\sum_{k\in K_s} z_{smk} \le M^{max} \qquad \forall s\in S .
\]

6. **Each track‑slot can host at most one shunting movement.**  

\[
\sum_{m\in M_s} z_{smk} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S,\; k\in K_s .
\]

7. **Start time of a shunting movement must lie inside its allocated slot and respect the slot length.**  

\[
\theta_{smk} \ge \text{slotStart}_{sk}\, z_{smk} \qquad \forall s,m,k,
\]
\[
\theta_{smk} + len_m \le \text{slotEnd}_{sk}\, z_{smk} + M_{big}(1-z_{smk}) \qquad \forall s,m,k .
\]

8. **Shunting movements must not overlap passenger‑train events on the same track.**  
   For each passenger‑train event \(p\) that uses the same track at station \(s\) we enforce a **big‑M** disjunction: either the shunting finishes before the passenger train starts, or it starts after the passenger train ends, possibly after delaying the passenger train by \(\delta_p\).  

\[
\theta_{smk} + len_m \le s_p^{start} + M_{big}\, u_{smkp} \qquad \forall s,m,k,p,
\]
\[
s_p^{start} + \delta_p \le \theta_{smk} + M_{big}\,(1-u_{smkp}) \qquad \forall s,m,k,p,
\]

   where binary \(u_{smkp}\) selects the side of the disjunction.  

9. **Passenger‑train delays are limited.**  

\[
0 \le \delta_p \le \Delta^{max} \qquad \forall p\in P .
\]

10. **If a shunting movement cannot be scheduled (infeasibility detected by the infrastructure model), it must be rejected.**  

\[
z_{smk} \le 1 - u_{smk} \qquad \forall s,m,k,
\]

   where \(u_{smk}=1\) is a Benders cut generated by the infrastructure model indicating that the combination of movements \(\{z_{smk}=1\}\) violates track availability.

### 5.3 Interaction constraints (Benders / iterative coupling)  

11. **Cut generation (exact algorithm).**  
   After solving the composition sub‑problem, the infrastructure model checks feasibility. If a set \(C\subseteq\{(s,m,k)\mid z_{smk}=1\}\) is infeasible, a cut of the form  

\[
\sum_{(s,m,k)\in C} z_{smk} \le |C|-1
\]

   is added to the master problem. In the MILP we model this by the binary variables \(u_{smk}\) and constraint (10) above.  

12. **Iterative heuristic – one‑by‑one insertion.**  
   In the heuristic version the master problem is solved, then each selected shunting movement is **fixed** (set \(z_{smk}=1\)) and the infrastructure model is solved; if infeasible, the movement is discarded (\(z_{smk}=0\)). This behaviour is reproduced by the same MILP if the solver is instructed to branch on \(z_{smk}\) sequentially (or by adding the cuts after each iteration).

---

## 6. Summary of the Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \alpha \sum_{s,m,k} z_{smk}
      + \beta \Big(\sum_{p}\delta_{p} + \sum_{t}c_t\,cap_t\Big)
      + \gamma \sum_{r}(1-y_r^{init}) \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r}x_{rt}+c_t = 1 &&\forall t\in T \\
& x_{rt}\le c_{rt} &&\forall r,t \\
& \sum_{t'\in succ(t)}x_{rt'}-\sum_{t\in pred(t')}x_{rt}=0 &&\forall r,t \\
& y_r^{init}\le \sum_{t\in T_{start}}x_{rt} &&\forall r \\
& \sum_{m,k}z_{smk}\le M^{max} &&\forall s\in S\\
& \sum_{m}z_{smk}\le 1 &&\forall s,k\\
& \theta_{smk}\ge \text{slotStart}_{sk}\,z_{smk} &&\forall s,m,k\\
& \theta_{smk}+len_m\le \text{slotEnd}_{sk}+M_{big}(1-z_{smk}) &&\forall s,m,k\\
& \theta_{smk}+len_m\le s_p^{start}+M_{big}u_{smkp} &&\forall s,m,k,p\\
& s_p^{start}+\delta_p\le \theta_{smk}+M_{big}(1-u_{smkp}) &&\forall s,m,k,p\\
& 0\le\delta_p\le\Delta^{max} &&\forall p\\
& z_{smk}\le 1-u_{smk} &&\forall s,m,k\\
& x_{rt},z_{smk},c_t,u_{smkp},u_{smk},y_r^{init}\in\{0,1\} &&\\
& \theta_{smk},\delta_p\ge 0 && .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Remarks & Possible Extensions  

* **Multi‑period rolling‑stock circulation** – the model can be enriched with a time‑expanded network where each node corresponds to a *departure* event of a trip and arcs represent feasible dead‑head or shunting moves.  
* **Crew‑availability** – additional binary variables can be introduced to ensure that a shunting driver is present for each movement.  
* **Capacity‑balancing** – a penalty term \(\beta_2\sum_t \max\{0, demand_t - \sum_{r} cap_r x_{rt}\}\) can be added to avoid under‑capacity on heavily demanded trips.  
* **Robustness** – stochastic parameters for disruption duration can be handled by a two‑stage robust formulation where the first stage decides \(x\) and \(z\), while the second stage (recourse) adjusts \(\delta_p\).  

The presented MILP captures the essential trade‑offs discussed in the introductory text: **(i)** selecting rolling‑stock assignments and shunting movements that keep the plan close to the original, **(ii)** limiting passenger‑train delays and cancellations, and **(iii)** guaranteeing that every shunting movement can be realised on the available infrastructure. By iterating between the composition and infrastructure sub‑problems (or by embedding Benders cuts), the model can be solved to optimality for realistic instances or used within the fast heuristic described in the paper.
