Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) for a Partially Blocked Segment**  

The model decides for every train whether it uses the original track or the opposite (detour) track, fixes its departure/arrival times, chooses a feasible speed level on each travelled segment and minimises a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption while respecting all operational constraints (headway, blockage, acceleration, etc.).

---

### 1. Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Set of trains to be scheduled |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Ordered set of track **segments** (the line is divided into consecutive pieces) |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,|K|\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g. low/medium/high) |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | Sub‑set of segments that are **blocked** during a known time window |
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km) |
| \(\nu_k\) | Nominal speed of level \(k\) (km h\(^{-1}\)) |
| \(e_k\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at level \(k\) (kWh km\(^{-1}\)) |
| \(d_i^{\text{orig}}, a_i^{\text{orig}}\) | Original (planned) departure/arrival times of train \(i\) (min) |
| \([\underline t_s,\overline t_s]\) | **Blockage window** on a blocked segment \(s\in B\) (no train may occupy the original track inside this interval) |
| \(\gamma\) | Minimum head‑way (minutes) required between two trains on the same physical track |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min) |
| \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\) | Weights in the objective (delay vs. energy) |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|--------------|
| \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Route choice of train \(i\): 0 = original track, 1 = opposite (detour) track |
| \(d_i\ge 0\) | continuous | Actual departure time of train \(i\) from its origin |
| \(a_i\ge 0\) | continuous | Actual arrival time of train \(i\) at its destination |
| \(t_{i,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Enter** time of train \(i\) into segment \(s\) |
| \(u_{i,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Leave** time of train \(i\) from segment \(s\) |
| \(y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 iff train \(i\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\) |
| \(\Delta_i^{\text{dep}}\ge 0,\;\Delta_i^{\text{arr}}\ge 0\) | continuous | Positive departure/arrival delay of train \(i\) |
| \(z_i\ge 0\) | continuous | Total (positive) delay of train \(i\) (linearised, see §3) |
| \(b_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Ordering variable: 1 iff train \(i\) passes segment \(s\) **before** train \(i'\) (used only when both use the same track) |
| \(\theta_{i,s,k,k'}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Linearisation of the product \(y_{i,s,k}\,y_{i,s+1,k'}\) (needed for acceleration constraints) |

---

### 3. Linearisation of delay  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_i^{\text{dep}} &\ge d_i - d_i^{\text{orig}} ,&
\Delta_i^{\text{dep}} &\ge d_i^{\text{orig}} - d_i ,\\
\Delta_i^{\text{arr}} &\ge a_i - a_i^{\text{orig}} ,&
\Delta_i^{\text{arr}} &\ge a_i^{\text{orig}} - a_i ,\\
z_i &\ge \Delta_i^{\text{dep}} + \Delta_i^{\text{arr}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(z_i\) equals the sum of positive departure + arrival delay.

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\sum_{i\in T} z_i \;+\; \beta\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} e_k\,L_s\,y_{i,s,k}
}
\]

*First term*: total (positive) delay, weighted by \(\alpha\).  
*Second term*: total energy consumption (energy per km × segment length × binary speed‑level decision), weighted by \(\beta\).

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1  Schedule flow (timing)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,1} &= d_i &&\forall i\in T,\\
u_{i,s} &= t_{i,s} + \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s}{\nu_k}\;y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i\in T,\;s\in S,\\
t_{i,s+1} &= u_{i,s} &&\forall i\in T,\;s=1,\dots,|S|-1,\\
a_i &= u_{i,|S|} &&\forall i\in T .
\end{aligned}
\]

The travel time on a segment equals the length divided by the selected speed level (the fraction \(\frac{L_s}{\nu_k}\) is a constant).

#### 5.2  Exactly one speed level per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T,\; s\in S .
\]

#### 5.3  Acceleration / deceleration limits  

Let \(\tau^{\text{acc}}_{k,k'}\) be the minimal extra travel time needed to accelerate from level \(k\) (in segment \(s\)) to level \(k'\) (in segment \(s+1\)), and \(\tau^{\text{dec}}_{k,k'}\) the corresponding deceleration term.  

Linearisation of the product \(y_{i,s,k}y_{i,s+1,k'}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{i,s,k,k'} &\le y_{i,s,k},\\
\theta_{i,s,k,k'} &\le y_{i,s+1,k'},\\
\theta_{i,s,k,k'} &\ge y_{i,s,k}+y_{i,s+1,k'}-1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Acceleration / deceleration feasibility:

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,s+1} &\ge u_{i,s} + \sum_{k,k'\in K}\tau^{\text{acc}}_{k,k'}\;\theta_{i,s,k,k'} ,\\
t_{i,s+1} &\ge u_{i,s} + \sum_{k,k'\in K}\tau^{\text{dec}}_{k,k'}\;\theta_{i,s,k,k'} .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a simpler model is preferred, the above can be replaced by a bound on the change of speed level (e.g. \(|k-k'|\le 1\)).

#### 5.4  Head‑way (capacity) on the **same physical track**  

Two trains that use the **same** track (both \(x_i=0\) or both \(x_i=1\)) must be separated by at least \(\gamma\) minutes on any common segment.  
For every ordered pair \((i,i')\) with \(i<i'\) and every segment \(s\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i',s} &\ge u_{i,s}+ \gamma - M\bigl(\,|x_i-x_{i'}| + (1-b_{i,i',s})\bigr),\\
t_{i,s}   &\ge u_{i',s}+ \gamma - M\bigl(\,|x_i-x_{i'}| + b_{i,i',s}\bigr),\\
b_{i,i',s}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the two trains are on **different** tracks (\(|x_i-x_{i'}|=1\)), the big‑M term deactivates the constraints, allowing them to pass simultaneously.

#### 5.5  Blockage of the original track  

The original track cannot be used on any blocked segment \(s\in B\) inside the blockage window \([\underline t_s,\overline t_s]\). This is enforced by forbidding the binary speed‑level variables on that track:

\[
\boxed{\;\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,k}\;\le\; x_i \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in B\;}
\]

If \(x_i=0\) (original track) the left‑hand side must be 0, i.e. the train cannot traverse the blocked segment; if \(x_i=1\) the constraint is inactive.

#### 5.6  Departure/arrival windows (optional service limits)  

\[
d_i^{\text{orig}} \le d_i \le d_i^{\text{orig}} + M,\qquad
a_i^{\text{orig}} \le a_i \le a_i^{\text{orig}} + M \qquad\forall i\in T .
\]

These simply keep the solution within a reasonable horizon.

#### 5.7  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_i,\;y_{i,s,k},\;b_{i,i',s},\;\theta_{i,s,k,k'}\in\{0,1\},\\
&d_i,\;a_i,\;t_{i,s},\;u_{i,s},\;\Delta_i^{\text{dep}},\;\Delta_i^{\text{arr}},\;z_i\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\sum_{i\in T}z_i\;+\;\beta\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}e_k\,L_s\,y_{i,s,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(5.1) – (5.7) listed above} \\[1mm]
&\text{Binary / non‑negative domain restrictions.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 7. Discussion  

* **Variables** – The model jointly decides (i) **route choice** (\(x_i\)), (ii) **departure/arrival times** (\(d_i,a_i\)), (iii) **segment‑by‑segment speed level** (\(y_{i,s,k}\)), and (iv) **ordering** on each segment to guarantee safety headways.  
* **Objective** – A weighted sum lets the planner trade‑off punctuality (delay) against sustainability (energy).  
* **Constraints** – All operational realities described in the narrative are captured:  
  * The *blocked segment* cannot be used on the original track (5.5).  
  * *Bidirectional conflicts* are avoided by the head‑way constraints (5.4) which become active only when two trains share the same physical track.  
  * *Acceleration/deceleration feasibility* is ensured by the linearised product constraints (5.3).  
  * *Timetable feasibility* follows from the flow equations (5.1) and the delay linearisation (3).  

Because every term is linear and every product of binaries has been linearised with auxiliary binaries, the model is a **pure MILP** that can be handed directly to any commercial or open‑source MIP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, HiGHS, …).  

The formulation therefore provides a complete, mathematically rigorous description of the **integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem (TRSMP)** under a partial segment blockage, ready for computational experiments or real‑world deployment.

Text:
**Sets**

\(I\) – set of trains, indexed by \(i\)  
\(J=\{0,1\}\) – route choice, 0 = original route, 1 = reroute  
\(L\) – ordered set of line segments, indexed by \(\ell\)  
\(K\) – set of admissible speed levels, indexed by \(k\)  
\(T=\{0,\dots ,T^{\max }\}\) – discrete time periods (Δ = 1 min)  

**Parameters**

\(\hat s_i\) – planned (nominal) start time of train \(i\) (min)  
\(\text{len}_{\ell}\) – physical length of segment \(\ell\) (km)  
\(v_{\ell k}\) – speed (km/h) of speed level \(k\) on segment \(\ell\)  
\(e_{\ell k}\) – energy consumption rate (kWh·h\(^{-1}\)) for level \(k\) on segment \(\ell\)  
\(B^{\text{start}}, B^{\text{end}}\) – start and end of the blockage window (min) on the blocked segment \(\ell^{b}\)  
\(\underline d,\overline d\) – minimum / maximum dwell time at stations (min)  
\(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M)  

**Decision variables**

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{ij}&\in\{0,1\}       &&\text{1 iff train }i\text{ uses route }j,\\
z_i   &\in\{0,1\}       &&\text{1 iff train }i\text{ is cancelled},\\
s_i    &\ge 0           &&\text{actual start time of train }i,\\
d_{i\ell}&\ge 0         &&\text{departure time from the upstream end of segment }\ell,\\
a_{i\ell}&\ge 0         &&\text{arrival time at the downstream end of segment }\ell,\\
t_{i\ell}&\ge 0         &&\text{travel time on segment }\ell,\\
v^{k}_{i\ell}&\in\{0,1\}&&\text{1 iff speed level }k\text{ is chosen for train }i\text{ on }\ell,\\
y_{i\ell\tau}&\in\{0,1\}&&\text{1 iff train }i\text{ occupies segment }\ell\text{ during minute }\tau,\\
o_{i\ell}&\in\{0,1\}    &&\text{1 iff train }i\text{ traverses segment }\ell .
\end{aligned}
\]

**Objective function**

\[
\min\; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I} w^{\text{delay}}\bigl(s_i-\hat s_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{k\in K}
    w^{\text{energy}}\,e_{\ell k}\,v^{k}_{i\ell}\,t_{i\ell}}_{\text{total energy consumption}} .
\]

\(w^{\text{delay}},w^{\text{energy}}\) are user‑defined weights.

**Constraints**

1. **Route selection (or cancellation)**
\[
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}+z_i=1 \qquad \forall i\in I .
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage**  
   (original route uses every segment, reroute skips the blocked segment \(\ell^{b}\))
\[
\begin{aligned}
o_{i\ell^{b}} &= x_{i0}-x_{i1} &&\forall i\in I,\\
o_{i\ell} &= 1-z_i &&\forall i\in I,\;\ell\neq\ell^{b}.
\end{aligned}
\]

3. **Exactly one speed level per travelled segment**
\[
\sum_{k\in K} v^{k}_{i\ell}=o_{i\ell} \qquad \forall i\in I,\;\ell\in L .
\]

4. **Travel time definition (linearised with big‑M)**
\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i\ell} &\ge \frac{\text{len}_\ell}{v_{\ell k}}\; \frac{60}{ }\,v^{k}_{i\ell}
            &&\forall i,\ell,k,\\
t_{i\ell} &\le \frac{\text{len}_\ell}{v_{\ell k}}\; \frac{60}{ }\,v^{k}_{i\ell}
            +M\bigl(1-v^{k}_{i\ell}\bigr)
            &&\forall i,\ell,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

(The factor 60 converts hours to minutes.)

5. **Temporal linking of departure, travel and arrival**
\[
a_{i\ell}=d_{i\ell}+t_{i\ell}+M(1-o_{i\ell}) 
\qquad \forall i,\ell .
\]

6. **Continuity between consecutive segments**
Let the ordered list be \(\ell_1,\dots ,\ell_{|L|}\). For every \(p=1,\dots ,|L|-1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{i,\ell_{p+1}} &\ge a_{i,\ell_{p}}-M(1-o_{i,\ell_{p}}),\\
d_{i,\ell_{p+1}} &\le a_{i,\ell_{p}}+M(1-o_{i,\ell_{p}}) .
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall i\in I .
\]

7. **Start time at origin**
\[
s_i = d_{i,\ell_1}+M(1-o_{i,\ell_1}) \qquad \forall i\in I .
\]

8. **Dwell‑time limits at intermediate stations**
For every interior segment \(\ell_p\) (\(p=1,\dots ,|L|-1\)):
\[
\underline d \le d_{i,\ell_{p+1}}-a_{i,\ell_{p}} \le \overline d
\qquad \forall i\in I .
\]

9. **Cancellation linking**
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_i &\le M(1-z_i),\\
d_{i\ell},\,a_{i\ell},\,t_{i\ell} &\le M(1-z_i) \qquad \forall i,\ell .
\end{aligned}
\]

10. **Occupancy definition**
\[
y_{i\ell\tau}\le o_{i\ell},\qquad
y_{i\ell\tau}\le \frac{a_{i\ell}-\tau}{ }+\!M(1-o_{i\ell}),\qquad
y_{i\ell\tau}\le \frac{\tau+1-d_{i\ell}}{ }+\!M(1-o_{i\ell}),
\qquad \forall i,\ell,\tau .
\]

(These linear constraints force \(y_{i\ell\tau}=1\) only when \(\tau\) lies in the interval
\([d_{i\ell},a_{i\ell})\).)

11. **Blockage restriction** – only trains on the rerouted track may occupy the blocked segment during the blockage window:
\[
y_{i,\ell^{b},\tau}\le 1-x_{i0}
\qquad \forall i\in I,\;\tau\in\{B^{\text{start}},\dots ,B^{\text{end}}\}.
\]

12. **Bidirectional conflict on all (non‑blocked) segments**
\[
\sum_{i\in I} y_{i\ell\tau}\le 1 
\qquad \forall \ell\in L\setminus\{\ell^{b}\},\;\tau\in T .
\]

13. **Binary and non‑negativity restrictions**
\[
x_{ij},z_i,v^{k}_{i\ell},y_{i\ell\tau},o_{i\ell}\in\{0,1\},
\qquad
s_i,d_{i\ell},a_{i\ell},t_{i\ell}\ge 0 .
\]

---

### Remarks (assumptions)

* The route‑segment mapping is simplified: the original route uses every segment; the reroute simply skips the blocked segment.  
* Speed levels are pre‑defined; the model selects one per travelled segment.  
* Time is discretised in 1‑minute intervals for conflict constraints; a coarser Δ can be used to reduce model size.  
* Large constant \(M\) must dominate any feasible time value (e.g., 10 000 min).  

The above equations constitute a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockage**, covering variables, objective, and all constraints required for a conflict‑free, energy‑aware schedule.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model)*  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains  \(t\in T\) (|T| = *n*). |
| **S** | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD‑sections)  \(s\in S\). |
| **N(s)** | Set of neighbour sections of *s* (immediate upstream/down‑stream sections). |
| **\( \mathcal{P}_t\subseteq S\)** | Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (the route). |
| **\(L_s\)** | Physical length of section *s* (km). |
| **\(v^{\max}_{t,s}\)** | Maximum admissible speed of train *t* in section *s* (km/h). |
| **\(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\)** | Service‑braking deceleration of train *t* (km/h²). |
| **\(a^{\text{acc}}_{t}\)** | Maximum acceleration of train *t* (km/h²). |
| **\(d^{\text{stop}}_{t,s}\)** | Minimum braking distance (in km) required for train *t* to stop from speed \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\) (computed from \(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\)). |
| **\( \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\)** | Minimum dwell (station‑stop) time of train *t* in section *s* (minutes). |
| **\( \Delta^{\text{max}}_{t}\)** | Upper bound on admissible delay for train *t* (minutes). |
| **\(M\)** | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation (e.g. 10⁶). |
| **\( \beta\)** | Weight for secondary objective (e.g. number of re‑orderings). |

*Assumptions* (explicitly stated)

1. **Deterministic timetable** – the original (unperturbed) arrival/departure times at the entry of each section are known and denoted by \(\bar a_{t,s},\;\bar d_{t,s}\).  
2. **Single‑track sections** – at most one train can occupy a section at a given instant (conflict definition).  
3. **DTG separation** – the safety distance between two consecutive trains *i* (ahead) and *j* (behind) in the same section is the **braking distance of the rear train** computed from its current speed (speed‑dependent).  
4. **Continuous speed profile is approximated by a piece‑wise constant speed equal to the section‑wise speed limit \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\).** This yields a linear expression for the braking distance.  
5. **Switches** are modelled as separate sections with possibly different speed limits.  
6. **Rescheduling actions** allowed: (i) **retiming** (add delay to a train at any section), (ii) **reordering** (swap the order of two trains that would otherwise conflict), (iii) **local rerouting** (choose an alternative parallel route; modelled by a binary variable that activates a different route set \(\mathcal{P}^{\text{alt}}_{t}\)). For brevity only (i) and (ii) are fully modelled; (iii) is indicated as an optional extension.  

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Actual arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of section *s*. |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Actual departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of section *s*. |
| \(\delta_{t}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual final arrival and scheduled final arrival). |
| \(x_{i,j,s}\) | binary | **Ordering variable**: 1 if train *i* is scheduled **ahead of** train *j* in section *s* (i.e. *i* leaves the section before *j* enters). |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | **Brake‑indication activation**: 1 if a brake‑indication point for train *t* lies **inside** section *s* (i.e. the train must start braking already in *s*). |
| \(z_{t}\) | binary | **Re‑ordering flag**: 1 if train *t* participates in at least one ordering change (used for secondary objective). |
| *(optional)* \(r_{t,k}\) | binary | Route‑selection variable: 1 if train *t* uses alternative route *k* (for local rerouting). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The primary aim is to **minimise total passenger/operational delay**; a secondary aim is to keep the number of re‑orderings low (to avoid massive timetable disruption).  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\; \beta\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}_{\text{Number of reordered trains}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*If a third objective (e.g., minimise total energy consumption) is required, it can be added linearly with an appropriate weight.*

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1. Timing propagation (travel time)  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of sections \((s,s')\) on its route (\(s'\) is the downstream neighbour of *s* in \(\mathcal{P}_t\)):

\[
d_{t,s} + \frac{L_s}{v^{\max}_{t,s}} \;\le\; a_{t,s'} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t\setminus\{ \text{last}\}
\tag{1}
\]

If a dwell is required (station section), we enforce a minimum dwell time:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t\text{ where } \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}>0
\tag{2}
\]

The departure time cannot be earlier than the arrival time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,s
\tag{3}
\]

### 4.2. Delay definition  

Let \(\bar a_{t}^{\text{final}}\) be the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (last section *s\_f*).  

\[
\delta_{t} \;=\; a_{t,s_f} - \bar a_{t}^{\text{final}} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{4}
\]

Upper bound on admissible delay (to keep the model bounded):

\[
\delta_{t} \;\le\; \Delta^{\text{max}}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5}
\]

### 4.3. DTG‑based separation (speed‑dependent safety distance)  

For any two trains *i* and *j* that share a section *s* (i.e. \(s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j\)), the **rear train must not enter the section before the front train has progressed at least its braking distance**.  
Let the **braking distance** of train *j* when travelling at its section speed limit be  

\[
B_{j,s}= \frac{(v^{\max}_{j,s})^{2}}{2\,a^{\text{br}}_{j}} \quad\text{(in km)} .
\tag{6}
\]

The time needed to travel this distance at speed \(v^{\max}_{j,s}\) is  

\[
\theta_{j,s}= \frac{B_{j,s}}{v^{\max}_{j,s}} \quad\text{(in minutes)} .
\tag{7}
\]

The ordering binary \(x_{i,j,s}\) decides which train is ahead:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} \; &\ge\; d_{i,s} + \theta_{j,s} - M(1-x_{i,j,s}) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j \\
a_{i,s} \; &\ge\; d_{j,s} + \theta_{i,s} - M x_{i,j,s} \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

Only one of the two inequalities is active; the big‑M term deactivates the non‑selected one.

### 4.4. Consistency of ordering variables  

For any pair of trains sharing a section, exactly one ordering must hold:

\[
x_{i,j,s}+x_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\tag{9}
\]

If the original timetable already defines a precedence, we can *force* that ordering (optional, used to penalise re‑ordering):

\[
x_{i,j,s}= \bar x_{i,j,s} \quad\text{if re‑ordering not allowed for this pair}
\tag{10}
\]

where \(\bar x_{i,j,s}\) is 1 if train *i* is scheduled ahead of *j* in the baseline timetable.

### 4.5. Brake‑indication point (binary \(y_{t,s}\))  

A brake‑indication may be required inside a section when the distance to the **end‑of‑authority (EoA)** is less than the braking distance. Let \(E_{t,s}\) be the distance from the upstream end of *s* to the EoA (known from the signalling layout). The condition  

\[
E_{t,s} \le B_{t,s}
\]

is linearised with a binary:

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{t,s} - B_{t,s} &\le M y_{t,s} \\
E_{t,s} - B_{t,s} &\ge \epsilon - M (1-y_{t,s}) \qquad (\epsilon>0\text{ small})
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

If \(y_{t,s}=1\) the train must start braking **inside** section *s*. This is enforced by tightening the departure time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\le\; a_{t,s} + \theta_{t,s} \qquad\text{if } y_{t,s}=1
\tag{12}
\]

which can be linearised as  

\[
d_{t,s} \le a_{t,s} + \theta_{t,s} + M(1-y_{t,s})
\tag{13}
\]

### 4.6. Linking re‑ordering flag  

If a train participates in at least one ordering change, set \(z_t=1\):

\[
z_{t} \;\ge\; x_{i,j,s} - \bar x_{i,j,s} \qquad \forall i\neq t,\; \forall j,\; \forall s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\tag{14}
\]

(Any positive deviation from the baseline ordering forces \(z_t=1\).)

### 4.7. Optional: Local rerouting  

If alternative routes are available, a binary \(r_{t,k}\) selects one:

\[
\sum_{k\in K_t} r_{t,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{15}
\]

All timing constraints (1)–(3) are then written using the selected route \(\mathcal{P}_{t}^{(k)}\). This extension does **not** affect the core model presented above.

---

## 5. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}z_{t} \\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(1)–(5)} &&\text{(time propagation, dwell, delay)}\\
&\text{(6)–(9)} &&\text{(DTG speed‑dependent separation and ordering)}\\
&\text{(10) (optional)} &&\text{baseline ordering fixation}\\
&\text{(11)–(13)} &&\text{brake‑indication activation}\\
&\text{(14)} &&\text{link to re‑ordering flag}\\
&\text{(15) (optional)} &&\text{route selection}\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
& x_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t}\in\{0,1\},\; r_{t,k}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Remarks on Linearisation  

* The product of a binary and a continuous variable (e.g., \(x_{i,j,s}\theta_{j,s}\)) is avoided because \(\theta_{j,s}\) is a **parameter** (pre‑computed from speed limits).  
* Big‑M values should be chosen tight:  
  * For ordering constraints (8), \(M\) can be set to the horizon length (e.g., total schedule horizon in minutes).  
  * For brake‑indication linearisation (11)–(13), \(M\) can be the maximum possible travel time of a section.  

---

## 7. How the Model Captures DTG Features  

| DTG feature | How it appears in the MILP |
|-------------|---------------------------|
| **Speed‑dependent separation** | Braking distance \(B_{t,s}\) and corresponding time \(\theta_{t,s}\) depend on the section speed limit \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\). Constraint (8) enforces that the trailing train cannot enter until the leading train has progressed at least \(\theta\) minutes, i.e., the physical braking distance. |
| **Brake‑indication point inside a section** | Binary \(y_{t,s}\) indicates that the distance to the EoA is smaller than the braking distance, forcing the departure time to respect the braking curve (13). |
| **Distinction between switches and regular track** | Switches are modelled as separate sections with their own \(L_s\) and speed limits; the same constraints apply, allowing different braking distances on switches. |
| **Retiming, reordering, optional rerouting** | Retiming is achieved by the continuous arrival/departure variables; reordering is modelled by the binary ordering variables \(x_{i,j,s}\) and penalised via \(z_t\); optional rerouting is captured by route‑selection binaries \(r_{t,k}\). |
| **Integration with existing RECIFE‑MILP** | All constraints are linear extensions of the classic RECIFE‐MILP (which uses fixed‑block separation). The only modification is the replacement of a constant block‑based headway by the speed‑dependent \(\theta\) term. |

---

### 8. Possible Extensions  

* **Multiple speed profiles** – introduce binary variables to select among a set of admissible speed profiles per section, adding extra constraints for acceleration/deceleration limits.  
* **Moving‑block / virtual‑block** – replace the fixed EoA distance \(E_{t,s}\) by a dynamic safety margin behind the rear of the preceding train (requires additional binary linking).  
* **Stochastic delays** – replace deterministic \(\Delta^{\max}_t\) by scenario‑based variables and minimise expected delay.  

---

**The formulation above provides a complete, linear (mixed‑integer) description of the conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem for railway operations under distance‑to‑go signalling, ready to be implemented in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).**

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The formulation below captures (i) the binary decisions needed to reschedule/re‑route trains when a partial‑track blockage occurs, (ii) the continuous decisions that define a feasible speed profile for every train on every track segment, and (iii) the trade‑off between service quality (delay) and energy consumption.  All sets, parameters, variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable placeholders are introduced and flagged as **assumptions**.  

---

### 1.   Index Sets and Basic Data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run in the planning horizon. |
| **S** = {1,…, |S|} | Set of stations (including the depot) visited by the trains. |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of directed track **segments** (i→j) that can be traversed. |
| **B** ⊆ E | Subset of segments that are **blocked** for a given disruption (partial‑track blockage). |
| **K** = {1,…, Kmax} | Set of **speed‑profile intervals** (time‑distance discretisation) used to describe a feasible speed/acceleration pattern on a segment. |
| **P** = {1,…, Pmax} | Set of **pre‑computed feasible plans** for each train (a plan = a combination of departure/arrival times, route choice and a feasible speed‑profile on every traversed segment).  (Generated in a preprocessing step.) |
| **Ω** = {(t,p) | t∈T , p∈P } | Set of all train‑plan pairs. |

**Assumption 1 – Discretisation.**  
Every segment (i→j) is divided into Kmax equally‑spaced “position‑time” intervals.  Within each interval the train either **cruises**, **accelerates**, or **decelerates** at a constant rate.  The physical limits (max speed v̂, max acceleration â⁺, max deceleration â⁻) are enforced by linear inequalities on the interval variables (see §4.2).

**Assumption 2 – Pre‑computed Plans.**  
For each train *t* a (large but finite) catalogue of feasible plans *p*∈P is generated by a separate speed‑profile generation routine (e.g., using a piecewise‑linear approximation of the optimal control problem).  Each plan already satisfies all train‑dynamics constraints on unrestricted segments; only the **conflict‑avoidance** constraints (track‑capacity & bidirectional usage) are left to the MILP.

---

### 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{tp}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* adopts plan *p*; 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{e}^{t}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* (i→j) in the direction indicated by *e*; 0 otherwise. |
| \(u_{e}^{t}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* traverses the **opposite** direction on the same physical track (i←j) (i.e. uses the opposite track of a bidirectional line). |
| \(c_{e}^{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Entry time** of train *t* onto segment *e* (the time at which the front of the train reaches the upstream node of *e*). |
| \(d_{e}^{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Exit time** of train *t* from segment *e* (the time at which the rear of the train clears the downstream node of *e*). |
| \(w_{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at its final destination and the original scheduled arrival). |
| \(e_{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of interval‑wise energy use, see §4.3). |

---

### 3. Parameters  

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| \(T_{t}^{\text{sched}}\) | Original scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (baseline). |
| \(R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\) ⊆ E | Set of segments traversed by train *t* under plan *p*. |
| \(a_{tp}^{\text{enter}}(e)\) | Planned **entry time** onto segment *e* in plan *p* (continuous). |
| \(a_{tp}^{\text{exit}}(e)\) | Planned **exit time** from segment *e* in plan *p*. |
| \(E_{tp}\) | Planned **energy** (kWh) of train *t* under plan *p* (computed from the speed‑profile). |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for typical “if‑then” linearisation (e.g., 10⁶ s). |
| \(\Delta\) | Minimum **headway** (seconds) required between two successive trains using the same physical track in the same direction. |
| \(\Delta^{\text{opp}}\) | Minimum **headway** for opposite‑direction trains on a shared single‑track segment (e.g., safety margin). |
| \(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\) | Weighting coefficients for the two objectives (delay and energy). |
| \(\tau^{\text{block}}_{e} = [\underline{t}_{e},\overline{t}_{e}]\) | **Blocking time window** for segment *e*∈B (no train may occupy the blocked side during this interval). |
| \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment *e*. |
| \(v_{\max}\) , \(a_{\max}^{+}\) , \(a_{\max}^{-}\) | Physical limits on speed, acceleration and deceleration (used in the preprocessing of plans). |

---

### 4.   Model Formulation  

#### 4.1   Plan‑Selection Constraints  

1. **Exactly one plan per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{1}
   \]

2. **Link plan choice to segment usage**  
   For every train *t* and every segment *e*:  
   \[
   z_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{e\in R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\}} \qquad 
   u_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{ \text{opposite direction of }e\in R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\}}
   \tag{2}
   \]
   (Here \(\mathbf{1}_{\{\cdot\}}\) is 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.)

3. **Derive entry/exit times from the selected plan**  
   \[
   c_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; a_{tp}^{\text{enter}}(e) \qquad
   d_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; a_{tp}^{\text{exit}}(e) \qquad \forall t,e
   \tag{3}
   \]

4. **Delay definition** (final‑destination segment is denoted by \(e^{\text{dest}}_{t}\))  
   \[
   w_{t}= d_{e^{\text{dest}}_{t}}^{\,t}- T_{t}^{\text{sched}} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{4}
   \]
   (If a train is cancelled we may set \(w_{t}=M\) and enforce a special “cancellation” plan; omitted here for brevity.)

5. **Energy aggregation**  
   \[
   e_{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; E_{tp} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{5}
   \]

#### 4.2   Conflict‑Avoidance (Track‑Capacity) Constraints  

All constraints below are linearised using big‑M.  They guarantee that at any instant the physical track capacity is not exceeded and that a blocked side cannot be used.

1. **Headway for trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical track**  

   For any ordered pair of distinct trains \((t_{1},t_{2})\) and any segment *e* (direction i→j):  
   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{2}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{1}} + \Delta - M\bigl(1 - z_{e}^{t_{1}} - z_{e}^{t_{2}} + y_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\bigr)
   \tag{6a}
   \]
   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{1}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{2}} + \Delta - M\bigl(1 - z_{e}^{t_{1}} - z_{e}^{t_{2}} + (1-y_{t_{1}t_{2}e})\bigr)
   \tag{6b}
   \]
   where \(y_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\in\{0,1\}\) decides the ordering (which train passes first).  If either train does not use *e* (\(z_{e}^{t}=0\)), the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

2. **Opposite‑direction conflict on a single‑track segment**  

   Let the physical track underlying segment *e* be shared for both directions.  Define a binary variable \(s_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\in\{0,1\}\) that orders opposite‑direction trains.  The constraints become:  

   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{2}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{1}} + \Delta^{\text{opp}} - M\bigl(1 - z_{e}^{t_{1}} - u_{e}^{t_{2}} + s_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\bigr)
   \tag{7a}
   \]
   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{1}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{2}} + \Delta^{\text{opp}} - M\bigl(1 - u_{e}^{t_{1}} - z_{e}^{t_{2}} + (1-s_{t_{1}t_{2}e})\bigr)
   \tag{7b}
   \]

3. **Blockage‑side exclusion** – trains are not allowed to occupy the blocked side of a segment during its blockage window.  If segment *e*∈B is blocked on the **original** track direction (i→j), then only the opposite direction may be used, and only **outside** the window:  

   \[
   c_{e}^{t} \ge \overline{t}_{e} \;-\; M\bigl(1- z_{e}^{t}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,\; e\in B
   \tag{8a}
   \]
   \[
   d_{e}^{t} \le \underline{t}_{e} \;+\; M\bigl(1- z_{e}^{t}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,\; e\in B
   \tag{8b}
   \]

   If a train traverses the **opposite** side (variable \(u_{e}^{t}=1\)), the same constraints are applied with \(\underline{t}_{e},\overline{t}_{e}\) swapped, i.e. the opposite side is **available** during the whole horizon (or a different blockage window could be defined).

#### 4.3   Energy‑Delay Trade‑off Objective  

The planner wants a timetable that (i) limits passenger‑related delay and (ii) keeps total traction energy low.  A weighted linear combination is used:

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{\beta_{1}\sum_{t\in T} w_{t}}_{\text{Total passenger delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\beta_{2}\sum_{t\in T} e_{t}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}}
\tag{9}
\]

*Typical values:* \(\beta_{1}=1\) (minutes of delay) and \(\beta_{2}=0.01\) (kWh → monetary equivalence); any other relative weighting can be chosen by the railway operator.

---

### 5.   Additional Feasibility Constraints (Optional Enhancements)  

| Constraint | Description |
|------------|--------------|
| **Minimum dwell time** at stations: \(c_{(i\!-\!j)}^{t}+ \tau^{\text{dwell}} \le c_{(j\!-\!k)}^{t}\). |
| **Maximum travel time** on a segment (to prevent unrealistic speed): \(d_{e}^{t} - c_{e}^{t} \le L_{e}/v_{\min} + M(1-z_{e}^{t})\). |
| **Cancellation option** – introduce a binary \(\kappa_{t}\) (1 if cancelled).  Set \(w_{t}=M\kappa_{t}\) and force \(x_{tp}=0\) for all regular plans; a special “cancellation plan” with zero energy is added to the catalogue. |
| **Train‑order re‑routing** – allow a train to change its route after the blockage (different \(R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\) for each plan).  The model already captures this through the plan catalogue. |

---

### 6.   Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \beta_{1}\sum_{t} w_{t} \;+\; \beta_{2}\sum_{t} e_{t} \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{(1)–(5)} && \text{plan‑selection and definition of delay/energy}\\
& \text{(6a)–(6b)} && \text{same‑direction headway}\\
& \text{(7a)–(7b)} && \text{opposite‑direction headway}\\
& \text{(8a)–(8b)} && \text{blockage exclusion}\\
& \text{optional feasibility constraints (dwell, max speed, cancellation)}\\
& x_{tp}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{e}^{t},u_{e}^{t}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t_{1}t_{2}e},s_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\in\{0,1\}\\
& c_{e}^{t},d_{e}^{t},w_{t},e_{t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; therefore the problem is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.  Solving it yields:

* for each train *t* the selected **rescheduling plan** (new departure/arrival times, possible rerouting, and a feasible speed trajectory);  
* a **conflict‑free timetable** respecting headway and blockage restrictions;  
* the **total expected delay** and **energy consumption**, allowing the decision maker to evaluate the disruption‑recovery performance.

---

### 7.   Remarks on Model Construction  

* **Plan generation** (Assumption 1) is the computationally heavy preprocessing step; a rich plan set improves solution quality but enlarges the MILP.  The decomposition approach described in the source text (IP model + train‑plan selection) is directly applicable: the master problem decides the binary \(x_{tp}\) while the sub‑problems verify feasibility of the speed profile.  
* **Scalability** can be enhanced by (i) limiting the plan catalogue to the *k* most promising plans per train, (ii) applying a *local‑branching* cut to explore the neighbourhood of a current solution, and (iii) using the adaptive refinement of interval granularity described in the paper.  
* The presented MILP is **complete** (all necessary variables and constraints are listed) and **self‑contained**; it can be directly fed to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, SCIP, etc.) after instantiating the data.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)  
Partial‑Segment‑Blockage, Bidirectional Conflict, Delay + Energy Trade‑off**

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered from origin to destination) |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete), indexed by *k* |
| **R** | Set of admissible routes (ordered list of segments) for each train, indexed by *r* |
| **B ⊆ S** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (partial blockages) |
| **P** | Set of ordered pairs of trains that travel on the same physical track in opposite directions (used for head‑on conflict) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment *s* | km |
| \(v_k\) | Speed associated with level *k* | km h\(^{-1}\) |
| \(c_k\) | Energy consumption rate at speed level *k* | kWh km\(^{-1}\) |
| \(\tau_t^{0}\) | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* | min |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight on total delay (≥0) | – |
| \(\beta\) | Weight on total energy (≥0) | – |
| \(\gamma_s\) | Usable fraction of segment *s* (0 < γ ≤ 1). For unblocked segments γ\(_s\)=1. |
| \(\Delta_{s}^{\text{head}}\) | Minimum head‑way time (min) required between two trains that occupy segment *s* in opposite directions |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min) |
| \(\text{Cap}_s\) | Nominal capacity of segment *s* (number of trains that can simultaneously occupy it, e.g. 1 for a single‑track line) |

All data are assumed known from the timetable, network geometry and the incident report.

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* (rerouting decision) |
| \(d_t\) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from its origin (min) |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the upstream end of segment *s* (entry time) |
| \(b_{t,s}\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the downstream end of segment *s* (exit time) |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k* |
| \(e_t\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at destination and planned arrival) |
| \(E_t\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train *t* (kWh) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
\alpha\sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\;
\beta\sum_{t\in T} E_t}
\]

*First term* penalises total delay; *second term* penalises total energy consumption. The weights \(\alpha,\beta\) allow the planner to stress punctuality, sustainability or a balanced trade‑off.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑selection  
\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Link route choice to segment‑usage  
\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R}\delta_{t,r,s}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

\(\delta_{t,r,s}=1\) if segment *s* belongs to route *r* for train *t*, otherwise 0 (pre‑computed).

#### 5.3 At most one speed level per traversed segment  
\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4 Travel‑time on a segment (big‑M linearisation)  

For every \(t,s,k\):
\[
b_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} - M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \tag{R4a}
\]
\[
b_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} + M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \tag{R4b}
\]

When \(y_{t,s,k}=1\) the travel time equals \(L_s/v_k\); otherwise the constraints are relaxed.

#### 5.5 Continuity between consecutive segments  

Let \(\text{next}_t(s)\) denote the downstream neighbour of *s* on the **chosen** route of train *t* (if any). Then  

\[
a_{t,\text{next}_t(s)} \ge b_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a downstream neighbour} \tag{R5}
\]

#### 5.6 Origin departure and minimum dwell  

\[
d_t \ge \tau_t^{0} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R6a}
\]
\[
a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R6b}
\]

A minimal dwell time at the origin (boarding) can be added as \(d_t \ge \tau_t^{0}+p_t\) if required.

#### 5.7 Partial‑blockage capacity  

Only a fraction \(\gamma_s\) of the nominal capacity may be used on a blocked segment:

\[
\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\le \bigl\lceil\gamma_s\;\text{Cap}_s\bigr\rceil
\qquad\forall s\in B \tag{R6c}
\]

For a single‑track line \(\text{Cap}_s=1\); thus the RHS becomes 0 or 1 depending on \(\gamma_s\).

#### 5.8 Bidirectional head‑way (conflict) constraints  

For every unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) and every segment *s* that both may occupy (i.e. \(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=1\) and \(\sum_k y_{t',s,k}=1\)):

\[
a_{t',s} \ge b_{t,s}+ \Delta_{s}^{\text{head}} 
- M\Bigl(2- \sum_{k}y_{t,s,k} - \sum_{k}y_{t',s,k}\Bigr)
\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S \tag{R7}
\]

and the symmetric version with *t* and *t'* swapped. The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when at least one of the two trains does **not** occupy the segment.

#### 5.9 Energy consumption definition  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s\,c_k\, y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R8}
\]

Because each \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary and at most one per segment, the expression stays linear.

#### 5.10 Delay definition (linearisation)  

Let \(a_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) be the arrival time at the destination (the *b* of the last segment). The delay is the positive part of \((a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0})\). Introduce a non‑negative auxiliary variable \(e_t\) and binary \(\delta_t\):

\[
e_t \ge a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0} \tag{R9a}
\]
\[
e_t \le M\,\delta_t \tag{R9b}
\]
\[
a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0} \le M\,(1-\delta_t) \tag{R9c}
\]

Thus \(e_t = \max\{0, a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0}\}\).

#### 5.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\qquad y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,r,s,k\\
&d_t,\;a_{t,s},\;b_{t,s},\;e_t,\;E_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Model Summary (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t} e_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t} E_t\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. }&
\sum_{r}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r}\delta_{t,r,s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R2}\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}\le 1 &&\forall t,s \tag{R3}\\
&b_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} - M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k \tag{R4a}\\
&b_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} + M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k \tag{R4b}\\
&a_{t,\text{next}_t(s)}\ge b_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \text{ with next} \tag{R5}\\
&d_t\ge \tau_t^{0} &&\forall t \tag{R6a}\\
&a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t &&\forall t \tag{R6b}\\
&\sum_{t}\sum_{k} y_{t,s,k}\le \lceil\gamma_s\text{Cap}_s\rceil &&\forall s\in B \tag{R6c}\\
&a_{t',s}\ge b_{t,s}+ \Delta_{s}^{\text{head}}-M\bigl(2-\sum_k y_{t,s,k}-\sum_k y_{t',s,k}\bigr) &&\forall t<t',s \tag{R7}\\
&E_t = \sum_{s}\sum_{k} L_s c_k y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t \tag{R8}\\
&e_t \ge a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0},\; e_t\le M\delta_t,\; a_{t}^{\text{dest}}-\tau_t^{0}\le M(1-\delta_t) &&\forall t \tag{R9}\\
&x_{t,r},y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; d_t,a_{t,s},b_{t,s},e_t,E_t\ge0 &&\forall t,r,s,k
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 7. Remarks & Practical Use  

* **Big‑M** must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 min).  
* The model is **linear**; all non‑linearities (max, division) are handled by binary variables and big‑M constraints.  
* The number of binary variables grows with \(|T|\times|S|\times|K|\) (speed decisions) plus \(|T|\times|R|\) (route choices) and \(|T|^2\times|S|\) (conflict constraints). For large networks a decomposition (Benders, column generation) or a time‑indexed formulation may be required.  
* By varying \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can explore the trade‑off curve between punctuality and energy efficiency.  
* The model directly yields a **conflict‑free timetable** (\(a_{t,s},b_{t,s}\)) and a **feasible speed profile** (\(y_{t,s,k}\)) that respects the partial blockage and bidirectional head‑way requirements, thus guaranteeing that the rescheduled timetable is executable at the train‑control level.

---  

**This MILP fully captures the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockages, including rerouting decisions, bidirectional conflict resolution, delay minimisation, and energy‑efficiency optimisation.**

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) – MILP Formulation**  

Below is a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) model that simultaneously decides (i) which trains are rerouted to the opposite track side during a partial segment blockage, (ii) the order in which trains use a shared track side, and (iii) the discrete speed level (hence travel time and energy) for every train‑section. The model minimizes a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable.  

---

### 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of line segments that may be blocked, indexed by *s* |
| **I** | Ordered set of track sections (or stations) traversed by the trains, indexed by *i* |
| **K** | Set of discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (|K| = K) |
| **τ<sub>i,k</sub>** | Travel time of a train on section *i* when speed level *k* is used |
| **e<sub>i,k</sub>** | Energy consumption of a train on section *i* when speed level *k* is used |
| **sched<sub>t,i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (given) |
| **minDwell<sub>i</sub>, maxDwell<sub>i</sub>** | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station *i* |
| **T<sub>start,s</sub>, T<sub>end,s</sub>** | Beginning and ending time of the blockage on segment *s* (blocked side unavailable in this window) |
| **M** | Large constant > planning horizon (big‑M) |
| **w₁, w₂** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |

#### Decision variables  

* **x<sub>t,s</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if train *t* is rerouted to the *alternative* side of segment *s* (otherwise it uses the normal side).  
* **y<sub>t₁,t₂,s</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if train *t₁* passes *before* train *t₂* on the *same* side of segment *s*.  
* **a<sub>t,i</sub> ≥ 0** – Arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (or at the beginning of section *i*).  
* **d<sub>t,i</sub> ≥ 0** – Departure time of train *t* from station *i*.  
* **u<sub>t,i,k</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on section *i* (exactly one level per section).  

---

### 2. Objective function  

\[
\min\;
w_{1}\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w_{2}\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

*`a<sub>t,last</sub>` denotes the arrival time at the final destination of train *t*.  

---

### 3. Constraints  

#### 3.1 Travel‑time relationship (feasibility)  
For every train *t* and every section *i≠1*:  

\[
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I\setminus\{1\}
\]

#### 3.2 Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i} &\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\; i\in I\\
d_{t,i} &\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 3.3 Speed‑level selection (one level per section)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,i,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

#### 3.4 Blockage‑availability (respect disruption window)  

Let `enter_s(t)` be the index of the station where train *t* would **enter** segment *s* on the normal side.  

\[
a_{t,\text{enter}_s(t)} \;\ge\; T_{\text{end},s} \;-\; M\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If \(x_{t,s}=0\) (no reroute) the train may enter only after the blockage ends; if \(x_{t,s}=1\) the big‑M term deactivates the restriction, allowing entrance earlier on the alternative side.

#### 3.5 Side‑choice definition  

\[
z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}} = 1 - x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

\(z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}}\) is 1 when train *t* uses the normal side, 0 otherwise.

#### 3.6 Conflict‑avoidance on a shared side (ordering)  

Consider any unordered pair \(\{t_1,t_2\}\subset T\) such that both trains can occupy segment *s* on the **same** side (i.e. \(z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}=z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}=1\)).  

*Exactly one ordering* (linearized):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\le z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}\\
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\le z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}\\
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\ge z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}+z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}-1
\end{aligned}
\]

*Temporal precedence* (let `enter_s(t)` and `exit_s(t)` be the indices of the entry/exit stations of segment *s* for train *t*):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t_1,\text{exit}_s(t_1)} &\le a_{t_2,\text{enter}_s(t_2)} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_1,t_2,s}\bigr)\\
a_{t_2,\text{exit}_s(t_2)} &\le a_{t_1,\text{enter}_s(t_1)} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_2,t_1,s}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall \{t_1,t_2\},\; s\in S
\]

If \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}=1\) the first inequality forces train *t₁* to leave the segment before train *t₂* enters it; the second inequality is relaxed by the big‑M term, and vice‑versa.

The same set of constraints is applied to the **alternative** side by replacing \(z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}}\) with \(x_{t,s}\).

#### 3.7 Planning‑horizon bounds  

\[
0 \le a_{t,i} \le H,\qquad 0 \le d_{t,i} \le H
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

---

### 4. Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
      + w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}u_{t,i,k} &&\forall t,i\neq 1\\
& d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i\\
& d_{t,i}\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i\\
& \sum_{k\in K}u_{t,i,k}=1 &&\forall t,i\\
& a_{t,\text{enter}_s(t)} \ge T_{\text{end},s} - M\,x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
& \text{(ordering constraints 3.6 for every pair of trains sharing a side of segment } s\text{)}\\
& 0\le a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\le H &&\forall t,i\\
& x_{t,s},y_{t_1,t_2,s},u_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,i,k
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; products of binaries have been replaced by the standard big‑M linearizations shown in Section 3.6.  

---

### 5. Interpretation  

| Model part | Role in the timetable |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| **x<sub>t,s</sub>** | Decides whether a train uses the blocked side (0) or reroutes to the opposite side (1). |
| **y<sub>t₁,t₂,s</sub>** | Determines the temporal order of two trains on the same side, guaranteeing head‑on and rear‑end safety. |
| **u<sub>t,i,k</sub>** | Selects a discrete speed/energy profile for each train‑section, linking travel time and energy consumption. |
| **Travel‑time constraints** | Enforce that arrivals follow departures plus the travel time of the chosen speed level. |
| **Dwell constraints** | Respect minimum/maximum station‑stop times. |
| **Blockage constraint** | Prevents entry onto a blocked side during its outage unless the train has been rerouted. |
| **Ordering constraints** | Ensure conflict‑free usage of a shared track side (both normal and alternative). |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total tardiness (delay) and total energy use, allowing the operator to balance punctuality versus sustainability. |

---

### 6. Practical notes  

* **Big‑M** should be set larger than the planning horizon *H* plus the longest possible travel time on any section.  
* Generate the pairwise conflict set only for trains whose routes overlap on a given side; this strongly reduces the number of `y` variables.  
* If a segment *s* is never blocked, fix \(x_{t,s}=0\) for all *t* to simplify the model.  
* The formulation can be easily extended (e.g., adding penalties for cancellations, crew costs, or a hard energy cap) while preserving linearity.  

---

**Result** – The formulation above constitutes a *complete, linear MILP* ready to be solved with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). It yields an optimal, conflict‑free timetable together with executable speed profiles for all trains under partial‑segment‑blockage disruptions, while jointly optimising delay and energy consumption.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
The model below follows the two‑stage decomposition described in the paper (rerouting + reordering → rescheduling) and is written in a compact, linear form that can be fed directly to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  
All symbols are defined in the **Variables** section; the **Assumptions** paragraph explains the (reasonable) data that are not explicitly given in the text.

---

## 1.  Sets, parameters and assumptions  

| Symbol | Meaning | Remarks |
|--------|---------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that have to be dispatched in the disruption horizon | – |
| **N** = {1,…,|N|} | Set of *nodes* (stations, block sections, points) of the railway graph | – |
| **A** ⊆ N×N | Set of directed *arcs* (track sections) connecting nodes | Each arc *a* = (i,j) has a physical length `len_a` and a speed limit `v_a`. |
| **R_t** = {r₁,…,r_{|R_t|}} | Set of admissible **routes** for train *t* (pre‑computed by a routing‑selection routine) | A route *r* is an ordered list of arcs  `r = (a₁,…,a_{|r|})`. |
| **π(t,r,a)** = 1 if arc *a* belongs to route *r* of train *t*, 0 otherwise | – |
| **τ₀₍t,i₎** | Planned (pre‑disruption) arrival time of train *t* at node *i* | From the published timetable. |
| **Δ₀₍t,i₎** | Planned departure time of train *t* from node *i* (τ₀₍t,i₎ + dwell₍t,i₎) | – |
| **dwell₍t,i₎** | Minimum dwell time required at node *i* for train *t* (passenger exchange, crew change) | – |
| **M** | A big‑M constant, larger than the maximal possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10⁴ s) | Used for logical constraints. |
| **ε** | Small positive number (e.g., 1 s) to enforce strict precedence when needed. |
| **Cₐ** | Capacity of arc *a* (maximum number of trains that can occupy the arc simultaneously) – usually 1 for a single‑track block, >1 for multi‑track. |
| **β** | Weight of secondary delay in the objective (β ≥ 0). If only delay minimisation is required set β = 0. |
| **γ** | Weight of energy consumption (optional, see Section 4). Set γ = 0 if not used. |
| **e₍t,a₎** | Energy consumption of train *t* while travelling arc *a* (kWh) – assumed linear with travelled distance. |
| **S₍t,i₎** | Safety overlap (in seconds) that must be kept clear behind a stopped train *t* at node *i* (relevant for stations). | Assumed given. |

### Modelling assumptions (explicitly stated)

1. **Pre‑computed route set** – For each train *t* a limited set *Rₜ* of feasible routes is supplied (e.g., by a routing‑selection heuristic).  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – The travel time on arc *a* for train *t* is `len_a / v_a`; any speed reduction caused by a delay is ignored (the model works with scheduled speeds).  
3. **Single‑track block capacity** – `Cₐ = 1` unless otherwise indicated.  
4. **FIFO reordering only** – The binary ordering variables enforce a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) rule when two trains share the same block. This matches the “pair‑wise waiting” interpretation described in the paper.  
5. **Secondary delay only** – Primary delay (caused by the disruption) is a known input `δ₀ₜ` (e.g., a 5‑min blockage). The model decides on **secondary** delay `δₜ` that is added to the timetable.  
6. **No overtaking** – Trains cannot overtake each other on the same route segment; this is enforced by ordering constraints.  
7. **Linear energy term** – Energy consumption is linear in the travelled distance; any regenerative braking or speed‑profile optimisation is ignored.  

All missing data (e.g., dwell times, safety overlaps) are assumed to be provided by the railway operator; the model remains valid for any concrete instance.

---

## 2.  Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `x_{t,r}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* ∈ Rₜ, 0 otherwise. |
| `s_{t,i}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Departure** time of train *t* from node *i* (after any waiting). |
| `a_{t,i}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Arrival** time of train *t* at node *i*. |
| `δ_t` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Secondary delay** of train *t* (the decision variable we minimise). |
| `w_{t₁,t₂,a}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t₁* must wait for train *t₂* on arc *a* (i.e., *t₁* follows *t₂* on that arc). |
| `z_{t₁,t₂}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t₁* is scheduled **before** train *t₂* on any common arc (global ordering variable). |
| `e_t` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total energy consumption** of train *t* (optional). |

Auxiliary definitions (derived from variables, not decision variables):

- `A_t = { a ∈ A | ∑_{r∈Rₜ} π(t,r,a)·x_{t,r} = 1 }` – the set of arcs actually used by train *t* (determined by the chosen route).  
- `N_t = { i ∈ N | ∃ a∈A_t with i as tail or head }` – nodes visited by train *t*.

---

## 3.  Objective function  

The primary goal is to **minimise the total secondary delay** of all trains; a secondary (optional) goal is to minimise the overall energy consumption.

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \delta_t}_{\text{total secondary delay}}
\;+\;
\beta \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \delta_t}_{\text{(same term for weighting)}}
\;+\;
\gamma \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total energy (optional)}}
}
\]

Because the first two terms are identical, the weight **β** can be used to give extra emphasis to delay (e.g., β = 1). If only delay is considered set β = 0 and γ = 0.

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc‑usage linking** – an arc belongs to the selected route  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} \pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r}= y_{t,a}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a\in A
\tag{R2}
\]

where `y_{t,a}` ∈ {0,1} is a derived binary (can be introduced explicitly if the solver does not allow products of binaries). For a pure linear model we keep `y_{t,a}` as a variable with:

\[
y_{t,a}\le \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r},\qquad
y_{t,a}\ge \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r} - (1-M_{ta})\;,
\]

with `M_{ta}=|R_t|` (big‑M) – essentially forcing `y_{t,a}` = 1 iff the chosen route contains arc *a*.

### 4.2 Timing (arrival / departure) constraints  

3. **Arrival = departure of previous node + travel time** (for each used arc)  

For every train *t* and every arc *a = (i,j)*:

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a}\;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,a})\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a=(i,j)\in A
\tag{T1}
\]

If the arc is not used (`y_{t,a}=0`) the constraint is relaxed by the big‑M term.

4. **Dwell time at nodes**  

\[
s_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} \;+\; \text{dwell}_{t,i}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; i\in N_t
\tag{T2}
\]

5. **Link to the original timetable (primary delay)**  

The first node (origin) of each train has a known planned departure `Δ₀₍t,origin₎`. The secondary delay `δ_t` is added to that time:

\[
s_{t,\text{origin}_t}\;=\; \Delta_{0(t,\text{origin})} \;+\; \delta_{t}
\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{T3}
\]

If a train already suffers a known primary delay `δ₀ₜ` (e.g., due to a blockage), we can set  

\[
\delta_t \ge \delta_{0t}
\tag{T3b}
\]

### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance (capacity & ordering)  

6. **Capacity on each arc** – at most `Cₐ` trains can occupy the arc simultaneously. Using a time‑indexed formulation would be non‑linear, therefore we enforce a *pairwise* ordering on each shared arc:

For any two distinct trains `t₁ ≠ t₂` that both use arc *a* (`y_{t₁,a}=y_{t₂,a}=1`), exactly one of them must go first:

\[
s_{t₁,j} \;\ge\; s_{t₂,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a} \;-\; M\,(1-w_{t₁,t₂,a})\qquad
\forall a=(i,j),\; t₁<t₂,\; t₁,t₂\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

\[
w_{t₁,t₂,a}+w_{t₂,t₁,a}= y_{t₁,a}\; y_{t₂,a}\qquad\forall a,\;t₁<t₂
\tag{C2}
\]

`w_{t₁,t₂,a}=1` means *t₁* follows *t₂* on arc *a*; the big‑M term de‑activates the inequality when the two trains do not share the arc.

7. **FIFO reordering on a common block** – If two trains share **any** arc, the global ordering variable `z_{t₁,t₂}` must be consistent with the local waiting variables:

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}\;\ge\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\qquad \forall a\in A,\; t₁<t₂
\tag{C3}
\]

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}+z_{t₂,t₁}=1 \qquad \forall t₁<t₂
\tag{C4}
\]

Thus the model respects a first‑in‑first‑out rule across the whole network (the “pair‑wise waiting” interpretation).

### 4.4 Safety‑overlap constraints (optional, for stations)  

8. **Overlap behind a stopped train** – If train *t* stops at node *i* (i.e., `s_{t,i}` is a departure after a dwell), the following train must not enter the block until the overlap is cleared:

\[
s_{t',i'} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; S_{t,i} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{t',t})\qquad
\forall (t,t')\in T^2,\; t\neq t',\; i\in N_t\cap N_{t'}
\tag{O1}
\]

Only active when `z_{t',t}=1` (train *t'* is scheduled after *t*).  

### 4.5 Energy consumption (optional)  

9. **Linear energy accumulation**  

\[
e_t \;=\; \sum_{a\in A} e_{t,a}\, y_{t,a} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

where `e_{t,a}` is a known parameter (kWh) for train *t* on arc *a* (e.g., proportional to `len_a`).  

---

## 5.  Complete MILP formulation  

Putting together all parts, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}e_t \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} && \text{route selection} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{temporal feasibility} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{capacity / FIFO ordering} \\
&\text{(O1)} && \text{safety overlaps (if required)} \\
&\text{(E1)} && \text{energy accounting (optional)} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,a}\in\{0,1\},\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t₁,t₂}\in\{0,1\}\\
&\delta_t\ge 0,\; s_{t,i}\ge 0,\; a_{t,i}\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (products of binaries) are eliminated by the auxiliary variables `y_{t,a}` and the big‑M linearizations shown in (R2) and (C2).

---

## 6.  How the model matches the paper’s contribution  

| Paper element | MILP counterpart |
|---------------|-------------------|
| **Two‑stage decomposition** – first solve rerouting + reordering, then rescheduling. | The binary variables `x_{t,r}` and `z_{t₁,t₂}` together decide routes and a FIFO order (sub‑problem). The timing variables `s_{t,i}, a_{t,i}, δ_t` constitute the rescheduling sub‑problem, but they are linked in a single MILP for clarity. |
| **Pair‑wise waiting interpretation** | Variables `w_{t₁,t₂,a}` encode “train *t₁* waits for train *t₂* on arc *a*”. |
| **Delay propagation** (optional, global optimum model) | The timing constraints (T1) automatically propagate any secondary delay downstream; the FIFO ordering ensures that a delay of an upstream train forces downstream trains to wait, i.e., full delay propagation. |
| **Safety‑relevant overlaps** | Constraint (O1) adds the mandatory clearance time behind a stopped train. |
| **Energy consideration** | Objective term `γ Σ e_t` and linear energy accumulation (E1). |
| **Runtime‑efficient formulation** | By fixing the route set *Rₜ* a priori, the number of binary `x_{t,r}` variables stays small; the remaining binary variables are only needed for pairs of trains that actually share a block, dramatically reducing the combinatorial explosion. |

---

## 7.  Remarks for implementation  

* **Big‑M values** – Choose `M` larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 s) but not excessively large to avoid numerical issues.  
* **Pre‑processing** – Build the pair set `{(t₁,t₂,a) | t₁≠t₂, a∈A, ∃r₁∈R_{t₁}, r₂∈R_{t₂} with a∈r₁∧a∈r₂}`; only those pairs need `w` variables.  
* **Decomposition in practice** – In a real‑time system one may first solve a reduced MILP with only `x` and `z` (sub‑optimal, very fast) and then fix those decisions in the full timing MILP. The formulation above already contains both stages, so the solver can be instructed to stop after the first stage if a time limit is reached.  
* **Extension to stochastic disruptions** – The same structure can be used in a two‑stage stochastic MILP by adding scenario indices and expectation terms; this is left for future work.  

---

**End of model**. The formulation is ready to be coded in any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …) and to be solved with a state‑of‑the‑art mixed‑integer optimizer.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model simultaneously decides  

* which side of a partially blocked track segment each train will use,  
* the order in which trains occupy a shared (single‑track) portion,  
* the exact arrival / departure times at every station,  
* the speed profile of each train in each discretised time interval,  

so that total passenger delay and the energy spent for traction are minimised while respecting safety, capacity and physical‑dynamic constraints.  

All symbols, variables, objective and constraints are given below; the formulation is a pure mixed‑integer linear program (any non‑linear term is linearised with auxiliary variables and big‑M constructions).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(\mathcal I\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\). |
| \\(\mathcal K_i\\) | Ordered list of stations visited by train \\(i\\); index \\(k\\). |
| \\(\mathcal S=\{L,R\}\\) | Two possible **track sides** (left / right) of a segment. |
| \\(\mathcal L\\) | Set of track segments; each segment may have two sides. |
| \\(\mathcal L_i\subseteq\mathcal L\\) | Segments traversed by train \\(i\\) (in order). |
| \\(\mathcal T\\) | Set of discrete time‑intervals for speed decisions, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(\mathcal P\\) | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one segment, i.e. \\((i,j)\in\mathcal P\\) iff \\(\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j\neq\emptyset\\). |
| \\(\mathcal B\\) | Set of blocked side‑time windows, each element \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \\(d_{\ell}\\) | Length of segment \\(\ell\\). | km |
| \\(v^{\min},v^{\max}\\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed. | km/h |
| \\(a^{\max},d^{\max}\\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration. | km/h² |
| \\(\Delta t\\) | Length of a speed‑interval \\(t\\). | h |
| \\(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k}\\) | Minimum dwell time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\). | h |
| \\(\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \\(i\\) at its final destination. | h |
| \\(c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\\) | Weight for the delay of train \\(i\\) in the objective. | – |
| \\(c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\) | Energy‑cost coefficients (quadratic speed term and absolute speed‑change term). | – |
| \\(M\\) | Big‑M constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 h). | – |
| \\(N\\) | Big‑N constant larger than any feasible speed change (e.g. 500 km/h). | – |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data and train characteristics.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(r_{i,s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) uses side \\(s\\) of a two‑sided segment; exactly one side must be chosen. |
| \\(o_{i,j}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is scheduled **before** train \\(j\\) on every common segment; for each pair \\(o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1\\). |
| \\(a_{i,k}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\). |
| \\(d_{i,k}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(k\\). |
| \\(v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Speed of train \\(i\\) during interval \\(t\\) (assumed constant inside the interval). |
| \\(\\Delta v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Absolute speed change between intervals \\(t\\) and \\(t+1\\); linearised (see §4). |
| \\(\\alpha_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) accelerates in interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(\\beta_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) decelerates in interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(z_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is present on the track during interval \\(t\\) (links speed variables to the timetable). |
| \\(y_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) occupies a **blocked** side during interval \\(t\\) (used to enforce blockage). |

---

## 4. Linearisation of non‑linear terms  

*Absolute speed change*  

\[
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\]

*Acceleration / deceleration limits*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The quadratic energy term \\(v_{i,t}^{2}\\) is replaced by a piece‑wise‑linear (PW‑L) approximation using SOS2 variables; the resulting linear auxiliary variable is denoted by \\(e_{i,t}\\) (the formulation below keeps the term symbolic – in a real implementation it is linearised).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
\Bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}\,e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\,\Delta v_{i,t}\Bigr)}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

The first term penalises lateness at the final destination; the second term is a standard linear‑quadratic proxy for traction energy (quadratic speed term + absolute speed‑change term).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Route‑choice (side) selection  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I . \tag{R1}
\]

### 6.2. Blockage handling  

For each blocked side‑time window \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\in\mathcal B\\) and each train \\(i\\):

*If the train would occupy the blocked side during the window it is forbidden:*  

\[
y_{i,t}=0 \qquad\forall t\text{ with }t\Delta t\in[T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]. \tag{B1}
\]

*If the train uses the blocked side it must start **after** the window:*  

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} y_{i,t}\,\Delta t \;\ge\; T^{\text{end}}-T^{\text{start}} \;-\; M\,(1-r_{i,s^{*}}) . \tag{B2}
\]

The binary \\(y_{i,t}\\) is linked to the side‑choice:

\[
y_{i,t}\le r_{i,s^{*}} \qquad\forall i,t,s^{*}\in\mathcal S . \tag{B3}
\]

### 6.3. Precedence on shared (single‑track) portions  

For every pair \\((i,j)\in\mathcal P\\) that share at least one segment:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P . \tag{P1}
\]

If \\(o_{i,j}=1\\) (train \\(i\\) precedes \\(j\\)) then, for each common segment \\(\ell\\in\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j\\),

\[
d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} + \frac{d_{\ell}}{v^{\max}} \le a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,(1-o_{i,j}) . \tag{P2}
\]

The exit/enter times of a segment are expressed through the station times (see §6.5).  

### 6.4. Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min}\,z_{i,t} \le v_{i,t} \le v^{\max}\,z_{i,t} \qquad\forall i,t . \tag{S1}
\]

### 6.5. Station‑time logic (arrival / departure)  

*Dwell time*  

\[
d_{i,k} \ge a_{i,k} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in\mathcal K_i . \tag{D1}
\]

*Travel between consecutive stations*  

Let \\(\ell(i,k)\\) be the segment linking station \\(k\\) to \\(k+1\\) for train \\(i\\). Then

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k} + \frac{d_{\ell(i,k)}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} v_{i,t}\,\beta_{i,\ell(i,k),t}} . \tag{D2}
\]

The binary \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) selects the speed interval used on segment \\(\ell\\):

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta_{i,\ell,t}=1,\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\le z_{i,t},\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\}\;\;\forall i,\ell,t . \tag{D3}
\]

### 6.6. Linking side choice to segment usage  

If a segment \\(\ell\\) belongs to side \\(s(\ell)\\),

\[
z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} \qquad\forall i,\ell . \tag{L1}
\]

where \\(z_{i,\ell}\\) is a binary indicating that train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(\ell\\) (derived from the \\(\beta\\) variables).  

### 6.7. Acceleration / deceleration linearisation (already given in §4)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned} \tag{A1}
\]

### 6.8. Domain definitions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i,s},\,o_{i,j},\,\alpha_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,t},\,z_{i,t},\,y_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},\,d_{i,k},\,v_{i,t},\,\Delta v_{i,t},\,e_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Complete MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)
      +\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
        \bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\Delta v_{i,t}\bigr)\\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)} &&\sum_{s} r_{i,s}=1 &&\forall i,\\
&\text{(B1)–(B3)} &&\text{blockage constraints} &&\forall i,t,s^{*},\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{precedence on shared tracks} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\\
&\text{(S1)} &&v^{\min}z_{i,t}\le v_{i,t}\le v^{\max}z_{i,t} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(A1)} &&\text{acceleration / deceleration limits} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(D1)–(D3)} &&\text{arrival / departure and segment‑speed linking} &&\forall i,k,\ell,\\
&\text{(L1)} &&z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} &&\forall i,\ell,\\
&\text{(Linearisation)} &&\Delta v_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\;
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\\
&&&e_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t}^{2}\;\text{(PW‑L)} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{Domain} &&\text{binary / non‑negative variables as listed.}
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

### How the model works  

* **Route choice** (R1) forces each train to pick a side of every two‑sided segment.  
* **Blockage constraints** (B1‑B3) either forbid the blocked side during the disruption window or force the train to start using it only after the window has ended.  
* **Precedence variables** \\(o_{i,j}\\) guarantee a conflict‑free ordering on any single‑track portion (P1‑P2).  
* **Speed variables** \\(v_{i,t}\\) together with binaries \\(z_{i,t}\\) and \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) describe the speed profile and link it to the travel time between stations (D2).  
* **Acceleration / deceleration limits** (A1) and the linearised absolute speed‑change variables \\(\Delta v_{i,t}\\) capture realistic train dynamics and appear in the energy part of the objective.  
* **Arrival / departure times** obey minimum dwell times (D1) and are computed from the speed‑derived travel times (D2‑D3).  
* The **objective** minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and the energy proxy, allowing the planner to trade‑off punctuality against energy consumption via the coefficients \\(c^{\text{delay}}_{i},c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\).

The formulation is ready to be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). By adjusting the big‑M/N values, the granularity of the time‑interval \\(\Delta t\\) and the piece‑wise‑linear approximation of the quadratic speed term, the model can be scaled to realistic high‑speed railway instances while preserving the exact coupling between train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockages.
