Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures (i) the selection of a feasible timetable (arrival / departure times, train order and possible rerouting) and (ii) the generation of admissible speed‑profile decisions for every train‑segment pair.  All variables, parameters and sets are defined first, followed by the objective function and the complete set of linear constraints.  Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are explicitly indicated (marked **Assumption**).

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\) |
| \(S\) | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train), indexed by \(s\) |
| \(E\) | Set of track‑segments (directed edges) between consecutive stations, indexed by \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) |
| \(D\) | Set of disruption time windows, indexed by \(d\) (each \(d\) is a pair \((\tau^{\text{start}}_d,\tau^{\text{end}}_d)\)) |
| \(\mathcal{R}_t\) | Set of admissible routes for train \(t\) (original route + possible reroute(s)) |
| \(\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\) | Set of pre‑computed *speed‑plans* for train \(t\) on route \(r\) (see § 4) |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of discrete time‑intervals used for linearisation of speed‑profiles (e.g. 1‑min slots) |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \(L_e\) | Length of segment \(e\) (km) | Infrastructure data |
| \(\underline{v}_e,\ \overline{v}_e\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(e\) (km/h) | Safety / line‑capacity limits |
| \(\underline{a},\ \overline{a}\) | Minimum (braking) / maximum (acceleration) longitudinal acceleration (km/h² per min) | Train performance curves |
| \(\tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (min) | Operational rules |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\) | Energy consumption (kWh) of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) when using speed‑interval \(k\) | Obtained from a linearised energy‑speed model |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | e.g. 10⁶ |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of the energy term in the objective (dimensionless) | Decision‑maker preference |
| \(\gamma\) | Penalty weight for train cancellation (if allowed) | Large positive number |
| \(\delta\) | Penalty weight for deviation from original schedule (delay) | Positive number |
| \(\theta_{t,s}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\phi_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\psi_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned arrival time of train \(t\) at its terminal (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\lambda_{e,d}\) | Binary indicator = 1 if segment \(e\) is blocked during disruption window \(d\) (otherwise 0) | Disruption description |
| \(\sigma_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original route identifier of train \(t\) (used for rerouting cost) | Timetable data |

*Assumption 1*: Energy consumption is linearised by discretising the speed range on each segment into a finite set of speed‑intervals \(\mathcal{K}\). The coefficient \(c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\) is pre‑computed from the train’s traction‑braking characteristic.

*Assumption 2*: All trains have the same acceleration limits \(\underline{a},\overline{a}\). If train‑specific limits exist, replace by \(\underline{a}_{t},\overline{a}_{t}\).

*Assumption 3*: The disruption may affect only one direction of a double‑track line; the opposite direction remains usable (hence the possibility of rerouting to the opposite track).

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) (original or rerouted) |
| \(y_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if speed‑plan \(p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\) is selected for train \(t\) (the plan implicitly determines the route \(r\)) |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (minutes from a reference epoch) |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) |
| \(z_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if on segment \(e\) train \(t\) travels with speed‑interval \(k\) (i.e. uses the corresponding part of the selected speed‑plan) |
| \(c_t\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) is cancelled (no service) |
| \(u_{t_1,t_2,e}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if trains \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) **conflict** on segment \(e\) (i.e. occupy the same track at overlapping times) – used for conflict‑avoidance constraints |
| \(\eta_{t}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (difference between new and original arrival at terminal) |
| \(\epsilon_{t}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumption of train \(t\) (sum over selected speed‑intervals) |

---

## 4. Speed‑Plan Construction (pre‑processing)  

For each train \(t\) and each admissible route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) we generate a *finite* set of feasible speed‑plans \(\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\).  
A speed‑plan \(p\) is a vector \(\{k_{e}^{p}\}_{e\in E(r)}\) that assigns to every traversed segment a speed‑interval index \(k\in\mathcal{K}\) satisfying:

* **Travel‑time feasibility**  
  \[
  \tau^{p}_{e}= \frac{L_e}{v_{k}} \quad\forall e\in E(r)
  \]
  where \(v_{k}\) is the representative speed of interval \(k\).  

* **Acceleration / deceleration feasibility** between consecutive segments \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) and \(e'=(s_j,s_{j+1})\):  
  \[
  v_{k_{e'}}-v_{k_{e}} \le \overline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e},\qquad
  v_{k_{e}}-v_{k_{e'}} \le -\underline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e}.
  \]

* **Blockage feasibility** – if segment \(e\) is blocked during the disruption window \(d\), the plan must avoid using the blocked direction:  
  \[
  \lambda_{e,d}=1 \;\Longrightarrow\; k_{e}\notin\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}} .
  \]

All feasible plans are enumerated (or generated by a column‑generation sub‑routine). The MILP only selects one plan per train (variable \(y_{t,p}\)).

*Assumption 4*: The number of plans per train is kept moderate (e.g., ≤ 30) by limiting the granularity of speed‑intervals and by discarding dominated plans (higher energy for same travel time).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

The decision maker wants a timetable that (i) respects the disruption, (ii) minimises total energy consumption, (iii) limits passenger delay, and (iv) penalises cancellations. A weighted linear objective is:

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}}_{\text{Energy}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}}_{\text{Passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} .
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where  

\[
\epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k},
\qquad
\eta_{t}= \bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}}\bigr)\,(1-c_{t}),
\]
\(s^{\text{term}}\) being the terminal station of train \(t\).

---

## 6. Core Constraints  

### 6.1 Route‑selection and plan‑selection  

1. **Exactly one route (or cancellation) per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r} + c_{t}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Exactly one speed‑plan consistent with the chosen route**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}} y_{t,p}= x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in\mathcal{R}_t. \tag{R2}
   \]

3. **Link plan to segment‑speed‑interval variables**  
   For each train‑segment‑plan triple, we enforce  
   \[
   z_{t,e,k}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\;:\;k_{e}^{p}=k} y_{t,p}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; k\in\mathcal{K}. \tag{R3}
   \]

   (If a segment does not belong to route \(r\), the corresponding sum is zero.)

### 6.2 Timing consistency  

4. **Travel‑time from departure at upstream station to arrival at downstream station**  
   For every train \(t\) and every traversed segment \(e=(s_i,s_j)\):
   \[
   a_{t,s_j}= d_{t,s_i}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E(t). \tag{T1}
   \]

5. **Minimum dwell time at stations**  
   \[
   d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\;(1-c_{t}) \qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; s\in S(t). \tag{T2}
   \]

6. **Origin and terminal time windows (optional service‑level constraints)**  
   \[
   d_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}\ge \phi_{t}^{\text{orig}}(1-c_{t}),\qquad
   a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}\le \psi_{t}^{\text{orig}}+U(1-c_{t}) . \tag{T3}
   \]
   where \(U\) is a large upper bound on permissible delay.

### 6.3 Disruption feasibility  

7. **Blocked‑segment prohibition** – a train may not occupy a segment during its blockage window. Using a time‑index formulation with the discretised horizon \(\mathcal{K}\) we enforce:
   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}}_{e,d}} z_{t,e,k}\le M\,(1-\lambda_{e,d})\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; d\in D. \tag{D1}
   \]
   (If \(\lambda_{e,d}=1\) the RHS becomes 0, forbidding any blocked‑direction speed‑interval.)

### 6.4 Bidirectional conflict avoidance  

Because after a reroute trains may share the same physical track in opposite directions, we must guarantee **headway** on each segment.

8. **Binary conflict indicator** – for any ordered pair of trains \((t_1,t_2)\) that use the same segment \(e\):
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k} - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C1}
   \]
   \[
   a_{t_1,s_j} \ge d_{t_2,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_2,e,k} - M\,(u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C2}
   \]
   Exactly one of the two orderings must hold:
   \[
   u_{t_1,t_2,e}+u_{t_2,t_1,e}=1 \qquad\forall t_1<t_2,\; e\in E \text{ used by both}. \tag{C3}
   \]

   The big‑M value is chosen larger than the maximal possible travel time on any segment (e.g., 10 × max\(\frac{L_e}{\underline{v}_e}\)).

9. **Safety headway** – a minimal time gap \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) (minutes) is required between successive trains on the same track:
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i}+ \sum_{k}\frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_e - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) . \tag{C4}
   \]

### 6.5 Delay and energy accounting  

10. **Delay definition** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \eta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}} \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{D2}
    \]

11. **Energy aggregation** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{E1}
    \]

### 6.6 Logical linking with cancellation  

12. **If a train is cancelled, all timing and speed variables are forced to zero**  
    \[
    a_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t}),\quad d_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t})\qquad\forall t,s. \tag{L1}
    \]
    \[
    z_{t,e,k}\le 1-c_{t}\qquad\forall t,e,k. \tag{L2}
    \]

---

## 7. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}
      +\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}
      +\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} && \text{Route / plan selection} \\
& \text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{Timing consistency} \\
& \text{(D1)–(D2)} && \text{Disruption feasibility} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{Bidirectional conflict avoidance} \\
& \text{(E1)} && \text{Energy accounting} \\
& \text{(L1)–(L2)} && \text{Cancellation logic} \\
& x_{t,r},y_{t,p},z_{t,e,k},u_{t_1,t_2,e},c_t\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\eta_t,\epsilon_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks & Modelling Choices  

| Issue | Modelling choice (and why) |
|-------|----------------------------|
| **Discrete speed representation** | Linearisation via a finite set of speed‑intervals \(\mathcal{K}\) makes the energy term linear and keeps the model MILP. |
| **Rerouting** | Each alternative route is treated as a separate binary variable \(x_{t,r}\). Rerouting is only allowed on the opposite track of the blocked direction, which is captured by the blockage indicator \(\lambda_{e,d}\). |
| **Bidirectional conflicts** | The pairwise ordering variables \(u_{t_1,t_2,e}\) guarantee a conflict‑free schedule on a shared track. The headway \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) can be set per segment (e.g., 2 min for high‑speed lines). |
| **Energy vs. Delay trade‑off** | The weights \(\beta\) and \(\delta\) let the planner emphasise either energy savings (e.g., for sustainability targets) or passenger service quality (delay reduction). |
| **Scalability** | The model can be decomposed as described in the paper (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems). In the MILP presented here, the plan‑selection variables \(y_{t,p}\) already embody that decomposition. |
| **Cancellation** | Optional; if the operator never cancels trains, set \(\gamma\) to a very large number or fix \(c_t=0\). |

---

## 9. Possible Extensions (not part of the core MILP)  

1. **Crew‑resource constraints** – add binary variables linking trains to crew blocks.  
2. **Platform capacity** – enforce that at any station the number of simultaneous dwellings does not exceed the number of available platforms.  
3. **Dynamic disruption update** – introduce scenario indices and a two‑stage stochastic version.  
4. **Non‑linear energy model** – replace the linearised coefficients by piecewise‑linear approximations (still MILP).  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential elements described in the introductory text: (i) selection of a feasible timetable under a partial‑track blockage, (ii) optional rerouting to the opposite track, (iii) conflict‑free bidirectional usage of the shared track, (iv) generation of executable speed‑profiles, and (v) a bi‑objective (energy + delay) linear objective suitable for a mixed‑integer linear programming solver.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model – Pellegrini et al., 2015)*  

---

## 1. Sets, indices and basic data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**   | Set of *track sections* (blocks or TTD‑sections). A section *s* is characterised by a start node *n⁻(s)* and an end node *n⁺(s)*. |
| **N**   | Set of network nodes (stations, switches, block boundaries). |
| **K**   | Set of *speed‑profile options* (e.g. “cruise‑high”, “cruise‑low”, “stop‑and‑go”). |
| **P**   | Set of *precedence pairs*  \((t,i) \in P\) meaning train *t* may be scheduled **after** train *i* on at least one common section (used for re‑ordering). |
| **Δt**  | Length of the planning horizon discretisation (e.g. 1 s).  (Assumption A1 – the timetable is discretised in uniform time steps.) |
| **τ₀ₜ** | Original (planned) departure time of train *t* from its origin node. |
| **vₘₐₓₜ** | Maximum allowed speed of train *t* (km/h). |
| **Lₛ** | Physical length of section *s* (km). |
| **bₛ** | Braking distance required to stop **exactly** at the end of section *s* when travelling at the speed that will be present at the entry of *s*.  (Assumption A2 – braking distance is a linear function of speed, see Eq. (2).) |
| **cₛ** | Capacity of section *s* (normally 1, i.e. at most one train can occupy the section at a time). |
| **M**   | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. |
| **ε**   | Small positive number (e.g. 10⁻⁶) to enforce strict inequalities when required. |

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **xₜₛᵏ** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses section *s* using speed‑profile *k*; 0 otherwise. |
| **aₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Arrival time* of train *t* at the **beginning** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁻(s)*). |
| **dₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Departure time* of train *t* from the **end** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁺(s)*). |
| **δₜᵢ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is scheduled **after** train *i* on every common section (i.e. *t* follows *i*); 0 otherwise. |
| **zₜ**   | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train *t* (difference between actual and original departure from origin). |
| **yₜₛ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is *blocked* on section *s* (i.e. occupies the section at any instant). Used to enforce capacity constraints. |
| **bipₜₛ**| continuous, ≥0 | *Brake‑Indication Point* of train *t* measured **up‑stream** from the end of section *s* (distance, km).  (Assumption A3 – brake‑indication point is a linear function of the selected speed profile.) |

---

## 3. Parameters derived from the speed‑profile set  

For each speed‑profile *k* we define:

* **vₖ** – cruising speed (km/h) associated with profile *k*.  
* **τₖ** – travel time to cross a unit‑length section at speed *vₖ*:  

\[
\tau_{k}= \frac{1}{v_{k}}\;\; \text{[h·km⁻¹]} .
\]

* **βₖ** – *braking‑distance factor* (km per km/h) for profile *k* (obtained from the train‑braking curve). Then the braking distance for a section entered at speed *vₖ* is  

\[
b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k}\, v_{k}\qquad\text{(km)} .
\]

These parameters are assumed known (Assumption A4).

---

## 4. Objective function  

Minimise the **total network delay** (or any weighted version). The basic formulation is  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}
\]

where  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t} .
\]

If a weighted objective is required (e.g. passenger‑weighted delay) replace the sum with \(\sum_{t} w_{t}z_{t}\).

---

## 5. Core constraints  

### 5.1. Path selection – each train must choose exactly one speed profile on each traversed section  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}= y_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{1}
\]

where \(S_{t}\subseteq S\) is the set of sections that belong to the *planned* route of train *t* (assumed known from the timetable).

\[
\sum_{s\in S_{t}} y_{t s}=|S_{t}| \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.2. Timing propagation along the route  

For every train *t* and consecutive sections \(s\) and \(s'\) (i.e. \(n^{+}(s)=n^{-}(s')\)) :

\[
a_{t s'} \ge d_{t s} + \epsilon \qquad\forall t,\; \forall (s,s')\text{ consecutive}
\tag{3}
\]

Departure from a section equals arrival plus traversal time (including dwell time if the node is a station). Traversal time depends on the chosen speed profile:

\[
d_{t s}= a_{t s}+ \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\,\bigl( \tau_{k}\,L_{s} \bigr) + \theta_{t s}
\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{4}
\]

\(\theta_{t s}\) is the *dwell time* at the end node of section *s* (zero for pure track sections, positive for stations).  

### 5.3. Brake‑indication point – speed‑dependent separation  

For every pair of trains \((t,i)\) that share a common section *s* (i.e. both traverse *s*), the **minimum safe headway** is the braking distance of the *following* train plus a safety margin *γ* (km). Using the binary precedence variable \(\delta_{ti}\) we enforce:

\[
a_{t s} \ge d_{i s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} + \gamma \;-\; M\,(1-\delta_{ti}) \qquad\forall t,i\in T,\; t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i},\; \forall k\in K
\tag{5}
\]

where \(b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k} v_{k}\) is the braking distance of train *t* when it uses profile *k* on section *s*. The term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) converts the distance into a **time** (seconds) needed for the following train to travel its own braking distance after the leading train has cleared the section.  

The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when \(\delta_{ti}=0\) (i.e. train *t* does **not** follow *i*).  

To guarantee a consistent ordering on each shared section we add:

\[
\delta_{ti} + \delta_{it}= y_{t s}\, y_{i s} \qquad\forall t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i}
\tag{6}
\]

(If both trains occupy the section, exactly one of the two precedence binaries must be 1.)

### 5.4. Section capacity (single‑track occupation)  

Because DTG allows *continuous* braking supervision, the **effective occupancy** of a section ends at the *brake‑indication point* of the following train, not necessarily at the physical end. We linearise this by ensuring that at any time instant the number of trains whose **brake‑indication point** lies inside a section does not exceed its capacity:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \Bigl[ a_{t s} \le \tau \le d_{t s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} \Bigr] \le c_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; \forall \tau\in\{0,\Delta t,2\Delta t,\dots\}
\tag{7}
\]

In practice (MILP) we replace the time‑indexation by a *pairwise* condition similar to (5). The result is that the precedence constraints already guarantee capacity, so (7) can be omitted if (5)–(6) are enforced for **all** common sections.

### 5.5. Origin‑departure delay definition  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{8}
\]

### 5.6. Re‑ordering (optional)  

If the dispatcher is allowed to **re‑order** trains on a shared corridor, we introduce binary variables \(r_{ti}\) that indicate that train *t* is placed **ahead** of train *i* in the new timetable (even if originally behind). The model already contains \(\delta_{ti}\) which serves this purpose; we simply allow \(\delta_{ti}\) to be 0 or 1 regardless of the original order, thus enabling re‑ordering.

### 5.7. Logical linking of brake‑indication point to speed profile  

\[
bip_{t s}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\, b_{s}^{k}\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{9}
\]

The *brake‑indication point* measured upstream from the end of section *s* equals the braking distance associated with the selected speed profile.

---

## 6. Additional practical constraints (assumptions)  

| # | Constraint | Reason / Assumption |
|---|------------|----------------------|
| A5 | **Maximum speed limit**: \(\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k} v_{k}\le v_{\max t}\) for all *t,s* | Guarantees that the chosen profile never exceeds the train’s technical limit. |
| A6 | **Minimum dwell time at stations**: \(\theta_{t s}\ge \theta^{\min}_{s}\) if node *n⁺(s)* is a station. | Reflects passenger boarding/alighting requirements. |
| A7 | **Switch‑specific sections**: For sections that contain a switch, a dedicated set \(S^{\text{sw}}\subseteq S\) may have a larger safety margin \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}>\gamma\). | Switches are critical points; extra headway is required. |
| A8 | **Binary linearisation**: \(y_{t s}= \min\{1,\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k}\}\) is enforced by (1) and (2). | Guarantees consistency between “section used” and “profile selected”. |
| A9 | **Big‑M value**: \(M\) must be larger than the maximal possible time difference between any two trains on a common section (e.g., horizon length). | Standard linearisation practice. |

---

## 7. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} z_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(9)} && \text{core model}\\
&\text{(A5)–(A9)} && \text{practical safety / operational limits}\\
& x_{t s}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t s}\in\{0,1\},\; \delta_{ti}\in\{0,1\} && \forall t,i,s,k\\
& a_{t s}, d_{t s}, z_{t}, bip_{t s}\ge 0 && \forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on linearity  

* All constraints are linear except the **pairwise ordering** (6) which contains a product of binaries \(y_{t s} y_{i s}\). This product can be linearised by introducing an auxiliary binary \(w_{ti s}= y_{t s} y_{i s}\) and the standard three constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{ti s} &\le y_{t s}\\
w_{ti s} &\le y_{i s}\\
w_{ti s} &\ge y_{t s}+ y_{i s}-1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then (6) becomes \(\delta_{ti}+ \delta_{it}= w_{ti s}\).  

* The conversion of braking distance into a time (Eq. 5) uses the known speed \(v_{k}\); the term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) is a constant for each \((k,s)\) pair, thus preserving linearity.

* The model contains **O(|T|·|S|·|K|)** binary variables and **O(|T|·|S|)** continuous variables, which is comparable to the original RECIFE‑MILP size and solvable with modern MILP solvers for realistic regional networks (hundreds of trains, few thousand sections).

---

## 9. How the model captures DTG specifics  

1. **Speed‑dependent braking distance** – introduced via the parameters \(b_{s}^{k}\) and the brake‑indication point variable \(bip_{t s}\).  
2. **Dynamic headway** – Eq. (5) enforces that the following train may only start its movement after the leading train has cleared the *brake‑indication* distance, not merely the physical block.  
3. **Distinction between switches and regular track** – safety margin \(\gamma\) can be replaced by \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}\) on the subset \(S^{\text{sw}}\).  
4. **Re‑ordering / retiming** – the precedence binaries \(\delta_{ti}\) are free decision variables, allowing the optimizer to change the order of trains on a shared corridor when it reduces total delay.  
5. **Continuous speed‑profile choice** – the set \(K\) permits the optimizer to select a slower or faster cruising speed on each section, thereby influencing both travel time and required braking distance.

---

### End of formulation  

The presented MILP fully describes a **conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem for railways equipped with distance‑to‑go signalling**, integrating the speed‑dependent separation distances that are the hallmark of DTG systems while preserving the linear structure required for exact optimisation.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under a partial‑segment blockage**

---

### 1. Sets, parameters and indexing  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (including the upstream and downstream stations of the blocked link), indexed by *s*. |
| **L** | Set of directed links (track sections) between consecutive stations, indexed by *ℓ*.  Each link ℓ = (s, s′). |
| **B ⊂ L** | The *blocked* link (the only link that suffers a disruption). |
| **K** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (k = 1,…,K). |
| **Δ** | Planning horizon (minutes). |
| **M** | “Big‑M’’ constant, chosen ≥ Δ. |
| **T_B ⊆ T** | Trains whose original timetable uses link **B**. |

**Parameters**

* `Lℓ` – length of link ℓ (km).  
* `v_k` – speed of level *k* (km / min).  
* `e_k` – energy consumption per km at speed level *k* (kWh / km).  
* `τ_k = Lℓ / v_k` – travel time on link ℓ at speed level *k* (min).  
* `E_k = e_k·Lℓ` – energy spent on link ℓ at speed level *k* (kWh).  
* `d_s^min` – minimum dwell time at station *s* (min).  
* `a_t^0` – planned arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (min).  
* `w_t` – weight of delay for train *t* in the objective.  
* `γ` – weight of energy consumption in the objective.  
* `t_start^B , t_end^B` – beginning and end of the disruption window on link **B** (min).  
* `C_opp = 1` – capacity of the opposite track (one train at a time).  

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `x_t ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Route choice on **B**: 0 = stay on original track, 1 = use opposite track. |
| `y_{t,i} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Ordering on the *opposite* track: `y_{t,i}=1` ⇔ train *t* passes **B** before train *i*. |
| `y^{orig}_{t,i} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Ordering on the *original* track (same meaning as above). |
| `z_{t,ℓ,k} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Speed‑level selection: `z_{t,ℓ,k}=1` ⇔ train *t* traverses link ℓ with speed level *k*. |
| `a_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| `d_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| `τ_{t,ℓ} ≥ 0` | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on link ℓ (derived from speed level). |
| `E_t ≥ 0` | continuous | Total energy consumption of train *t*. |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min \;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} w_t\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-a_t^{0}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{total energy}}}
\]

*`a_{t,last}`* is the arrival time at the final destination of train *t*.

---

### 4. Constraints  

#### 4.1  Speed‑level selection (exactly one level per link)  
\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{t,\ell,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;\forall \ell\in L \tag{C1}
\]

#### 4.2  Travel‑time definition (linear)  
\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_k\,z_{t,\ell,k} \qquad\forall t,\ell \tag{C2}
\]

#### 4.3  Energy definition (linear)  
\[
E_{t}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{k\in K}E_k\,z_{t,\ell,k} \qquad\forall t \tag{C3}
\]

#### 4.4  Time‑flow (arrival = previous departure + travel)  
\[
a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s}+ \tau_{t,\ell} \qquad\forall t,\;\ell=(s,s') \tag{C4}
\]

#### 4.5  Minimum dwell time at stations  
\[
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d_s^{\min} \qquad\forall t,\; s\neq\text{last} \tag{C5}
\]

#### 4.6  Blockage window – original track cannot be used during disruption  
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B} &\ge t_{\text{end}}^{B} - M\,(1-x_t) \\
d_{t,s_B} &\le t_{\text{start}}^{B} + M\,(1-x_t)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T_B \tag{C6}
\]

If `x_t=0` (stay on original track) the inequalities force the train to finish the blocked link **outside** the disruption interval; if `x_t=1` they are relaxed by the big‑M term.

#### 4.7  Non‑overlap on the *opposite* track (capacity = 1)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B'} &\ge d_{i,s_B} - M\,(1-y_{i,t}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \\
a_{i,s_B'} &\ge d_{t,s_B} - M\,(1-y_{t,i}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \\
y_{t,i}+y_{i,t} &= 1 &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B
\end{aligned}
\tag{C7}
\]

#### 4.8  Non‑overlap on the *original* track (also capacity = 1)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B'} &\ge d_{i,s_B} - M\,(1-y^{orig}_{i,t}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \\
a_{i,s_B'} &\ge d_{t,s_B} - M\,(1-y^{orig}_{t,i}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \\
y^{orig}_{t,i}+y^{orig}_{i,t} &= 1 &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B
\end{aligned}
\tag{C8}
\]

#### 4.9  Compatibility of speed levels with the chosen track on the blocked link  

\[
\begin{aligned}
z_{t,B,k} &\le 1-x_t &&\forall t\in T_B,\;k\in K_{\text{orig}} \\
z_{t,B,k} &\le x_t   &&\forall t\in T_B,\;k\in K_{\text{opp}}
\end{aligned}
\tag{C9}
\]

(`K_orig` and `K_opp` are the admissible speed‑level subsets for the original and opposite tracks, respectively.)

#### 4.10  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_t,\;y_{t,i},\;y^{orig}_{t,i},\;z_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,s},\;d_{t,s},\;\tau_{t,\ell},\;E_t \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{C10}
\]

---

### 5. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} w_t\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-a_t^{0}\bigr) \;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C10)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.

---

### 6. Interpretation of the model  

* **Route choice (`x_t`)** decides whether a train uses the original track or the opposite (detour) track on the blocked segment.  
* **Ordering binaries (`y_{t,i}`, `y^{orig}_{t,i}`)** guarantee a conflict‑free schedule on the single‑track sections (original and opposite).  
* **Speed‑level binaries (`z_{t,ℓ,k}`)** couple the timetable with the train dynamics: the selected speed determines travel time (`τ_{t,ℓ}`) and energy (`E_t`).  
* **Objective** minimises a weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption, reflecting the trade‑off highlighted in the description.  
* **Constraints (C6)** enforce that a train staying on the original track cannot occupy the blocked link during the disruption window; the opposite track is assumed free of the blockage.  
* **Constraints (C7)–(C8)** enforce the capacity of one train at a time on each single‑track segment, thus resolving bidirectional conflicts introduced by the rerouting.  

---

### 7. Remarks for implementation  

* The piece‑wise linear speed‑energy relationship is captured by the discrete set **K**; increasing |K| improves accuracy while keeping the model linear.  
* The number of ordering binaries grows quadratically with |T_B|; for very large fleets a time‑indexed capacity formulation or a decomposition (e.g., Benders) can be employed.  
* Choose the big‑M constant `M` at least as large as the planning horizon Δ to keep the formulation tight.  
* The model can be solved directly with any commercial MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).  

---

**Result:** The MILP above simultaneously decides (i) which track each train uses on the blocked segment, (ii) the order in which trains occupy the shared track, and (iii) the speed level on every link, while minimising total delay and energy consumption and guaranteeing a conflict‑free, feasible timetable under the partial‑segment blockage.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, (i) the **timetable‑level decisions** (arrival/departure times, train ordering and possible rerouting) and (ii) the **speed‑profile decisions** (segment‑wise travel times, acceleration/deceleration) that together guarantee a conflict‑free schedule under a partial‑segment blockage.  

All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly. Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption X)**.

---

## 1. Notation  

### 1.1 Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots,|T|\}\) | Set of trains that are scheduled before the disruption. |
| \(S=\{1,\dots,|S|\}\) | Set of **track sections** (segments) between two consecutive track nodes (stations or switches). |
| \(N=\{1,\dots,|N|\}\) | Set of **nodes** (stations, passing loops, turn‑around points). |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | Sub‑set of sections that are **blocked** on one side of the double‑track line during the disruption time window \([t^{\text{blk}}_{s},\,t^{\text{blk}}_{e}]\). |
| \(\Phi\) | Set of **possible speed‑profile plans** for a single train (generated by a pre‑processing step). For each train \(i\) a subset \(\Phi_i\subseteq\Phi\) is available. |
| \(\Omega\) | Set of **conflict pairs** \((i,j)\) of trains that may occupy the same section (or opposite directions on the same track) at overlapping times. Obtained from the network topology. |
| \(\Lambda_i\) | Set of **feasible routes** for train \(i\). Route \(r\in\Lambda_i\) is a ordered list of sections \((s_1,\dots,s_{|r|})\). The original route is denoted \(r_i^{0}\). |

### 1.2 Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / comment |
|--------|----------|--------------------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of section \(s\) (km). | – |
| \(v^{\max}_i\) | Maximum admissible speed of train \(i\) (km/h). | – |
| \(a_i^{\max},\; d_i^{\max}\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration of train \(i\) (km/h²). | – |
| \(t_i^{\text{orig}}(n)\) | Original (pre‑disruption) scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at node \(n\). | – |
| \(d_i^{\text{orig}}(n)\) | Original scheduled departure time of train \(i\) from node \(n\). | – |
| \(\tau_{s}^{\min},\;\tau_{s}^{\max}\) | Minimum / maximum feasible travel time through section \(s\) (derived from \(v^{\max}\) and \(a/d\)). | – |
| \(M\) | A large constant (big‑M) used for logical constraints. | e.g. 10⁶ |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_{i,s}\) | Energy consumption coefficient (kWh per second) for train \(i\) when travelling through section \(s\) at the average speed of the chosen plan. | **(Assumption 1)** – taken from a linearised energy model. |
| \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) | Weight of delay minimisation vs. energy minimisation in the objective. | **(Assumption 2)** – e.g. 0.7 (delay priority). |
| \(T^{\text{horizon}}\) | Planning horizon (latest allowed arrival time). | **(Assumption 3)** – e.g. 24 h after disruption start. |
| \(p_i\) | Penalty for cancelling train \(i\) (large constant). | **(Assumption 4)** – e.g. 10⁵. |
| \(\beta\) | Small coefficient to penalise the number of reroutings (to avoid unnecessary diversions). | **(Assumption 5)** – e.g. 1. |

### 1.3 Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(a_i(n)\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual **arrival time** of train \(i\) at node \(n\). |
| \(d_i(n)\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual **departure time** of train \(i\) from node \(n\). |
| \(x_{i,r}\) | Binary | **Route selection**: 1 if train \(i\) uses route \(r\in\Lambda_i\), 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{i,\phi}\) | Binary | **Speed‑plan selection**: 1 if train \(i\) follows speed‑profile plan \(\phi\in\Phi_i\), 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{i,s}\) | Binary | **Section usage**: 1 if train \(i\) traverses section \(s\) (according to the chosen route), 0 otherwise. |
| \(\delta_{i,j,s}\) | Binary | **Conflict indicator**: 1 if trains \(i\) and \(j\) are scheduled to occupy section \(s\) at overlapping times (used to enforce separation). |
| \(c_i\) | Binary | **Cancellation indicator**: 1 if train \(i\) is cancelled, 0 otherwise. |
| \(\theta_i\) | Binary | **Rerouting indicator**: 1 if train \(i\) uses a route different from the original \(r_i^{0}\), 0 otherwise. |
| \(\tau_{i,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Travel time of train \(i\) through section \(s\) (derived from the selected speed plan). |
| \(e_i\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total **energy consumption** of train \(i\) (sum over sections). |
| \(D_i\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Delay** of train \(i\) (arrival at its final destination compared with original schedule). |

---

## 2. Model Assumptions  

1. **Linearised energy model** – energy consumption on a section is approximated as a linear function of travel time (or average speed) using coefficient \(c^{\text{energy}}_{i,s}\).  
2. **Deterministic disruption window** – the blockage on each affected section \(s\in B\) is known exactly as interval \([t^{\text{blk}}_{s},t^{\text{blk}}_{e}]\).  
3. **Single‑track usage for blocked side** – during the disruption the blocked side of a double‑track line is unavailable; the opposite side can be used by trains travelling in either direction, but only one train at a time (conflict constraint).  
4. **Pre‑generated speed plans** – for each train a finite set \(\Phi_i\) of feasible speed‑profile plans (travel‑time vectors \(\{\tau_{i,s}^{\phi}\}_{s\in S}\)) is generated beforehand (e.g. by a dynamic‑programming routine). The MILP only selects among them.  
5. **No overtaking on the same track** – within a section a train cannot overtake another train travelling in the same direction; this is enforced by ordering constraints.  
6. **Dwell times are flexible** – minimum dwell time at a station is a known parameter \(t^{\text{dwell}}_{i,n}^{\min}\); additional dwell (waiting) is allowed to resolve conflicts.  
7. **Cancellation is allowed** – a train may be cancelled at a large penalty \(p_i\); this provides feasibility in highly congested situations.  

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The decision maker wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption**, while penalising cancellations and unnecessary reroutings.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \alpha \underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} D_i}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\; (1-\alpha)\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} e_i}_{\text{Total energy}} \\
        & \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} p_i\,c_i}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{i\in T}\theta_i}_{\text{Rerouting penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

*Delay* \(D_i\) is defined later as the difference between the realised arrival at the final destination node \(n_i^{\text{dest}}\) and the original scheduled arrival.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

\[
\sum_{r\in\Lambda_i} x_{i,r}=1-c_i \qquad\forall i\in T                              \tag{R1}
\]

\[
\theta_i \ge x_{i,r}-\mathbf{1}_{\{r=r_i^{0}\}} \qquad\forall i\in T,\; r\in\Lambda_i \tag{R2}
\]

\[
z_{i,s}= \sum_{r\in\Lambda_i:\, s\in r} x_{i,r} \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R3}
\]

\(z_{i,s}=0\) if train \(i\) does not traverse section \(s\).

### 4.2 Speed‑plan selection  

\[
\sum_{\phi\in\Phi_i} y_{i,\phi}=1-c_i \qquad\forall i\in T                     \tag{S1}
\]

\[
\tau_{i,s}= \sum_{\phi\in\Phi_i} \tau_{i,s}^{\phi}\, y_{i,\phi} \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S \tag{S2}
\]

### 4.3 Time‑propagation (timetable feasibility)  

For each train \(i\) and each consecutive pair of nodes \((n,n')\) that bound a traversed section \(s\):

\[
a_i(n') \ge d_i(n) + \tau_{i,s} - M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S,\; (n,n')\in s \tag{T1}
\]

Departure after minimum dwell:

\[
d_i(n) \ge a_i(n) + t^{\text{dwell}}_{i,n}^{\min}\,(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i\in T,\; n\in N \tag{T2}
\]

Upper bound by planning horizon:

\[
a_i(n)\le T^{\text{horizon}} \qquad\forall i\in T,\; n\in N \tag{T3}
\]

### 4.4 Delay definition  

Let \(n_i^{\text{dest}}\) be the destination node of train \(i\).

\[
D_i \ge a_i\bigl(n_i^{\text{dest}}\bigr) - t_i^{\text{orig}}\bigl(n_i^{\text{dest}}\bigr) - M\,c_i \qquad\forall i\in T \tag{D1}
\]

\(D_i\) is forced to zero if the train is cancelled (\(c_i=1\)).

### 4.5 Energy calculation  

\[
e_i = \sum_{s\in S} c^{\text{energy}}_{i,s}\,\tau_{i,s}\,z_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in T \tag{E1}
\]

### 4.6 Conflict‑avoidance on shared track (bidirectional)  

For every conflict pair \((i,j)\in\Omega\) and every section \(s\) that can be used by both directions:

\[
a_i^{\text{exit}}(s) \le a_j^{\text{enter}}(s) + M\,\delta_{i,j,s} \tag{C1}
\]
\[
a_j^{\text{exit}}(s) \le a_i^{\text{enter}}(s) + M\,(1-\delta_{i,j,s}) \tag{C2}
\]

where  

\[
a_i^{\text{enter}}(s)= d_i\bigl(\text{upstream node of }s\bigr) \\
a_i^{\text{exit}}(s)= a_i\bigl(\text{downstream node of }s\bigr)
\]

Only one of the two inequalities can be active, guaranteeing that the two trains are **separated in time** on the same physical track.

### 4.7 Blockage‑time feasibility  

If section \(s\in B\) is blocked on the *original* side during \([t^{\text{blk}}_{s},t^{\text{blk}}_{e}]\), any train using the opposite side must **avoid** that interval:

\[
a_i^{\text{enter}}(s) \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{e} \;\; \text{or}\;\; a_i^{\text{exit}}(s) \le t^{\text{blk}}_{s} \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in B \tag{BLK}
\]

A standard linearisation using a binary variable \(b_{i,s}\) (0 = before, 1 = after) can be applied:

\[
a_i^{\text{enter}}(s) \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{e} - M\,b_{i,s} \tag{BLK1}
\]
\[
a_i^{\text{exit}}(s) \le t^{\text{blk}}_{s} + M\,(1-b_{i,s}) \tag{BLK2}
\]

### 4.8 No‑overtaking on the same direction  

If two trains \(i\) and \(j\) travel **in the same direction** on the same section \(s\) (i.e. both belong to the same ordered set of sections), the following ordering must hold:

\[
a_i^{\text{enter}}(s) \le a_j^{\text{enter}}(s) \;\Rightarrow\; a_i^{\text{exit}}(s) \le a_j^{\text{exit}}(s) \qquad\forall (i,j,s)\in\Omega^{\text{same-dir}} \tag{OT}
\]

Linearised with big‑M:

\[
a_i^{\text{exit}}(s) \le a_j^{\text{exit}}(s) + M\,\gamma_{i,j,s} \tag{OT1}
\]
\[
a_j^{\text{enter}}(s) \le a_i^{\text{enter}}(s) + M\,(1-\gamma_{i,j,s}) \tag{OT2}
\]

where \(\gamma_{i,j,s}\) is a binary variable.

### 4.9 Cancellation logic  

If a train is cancelled, all its timing and route variables are forced to zero:

\[
a_i(n) \le M\,(1-c_i),\; d_i(n) \le M\,(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i\in T,\; n\in N \tag{CAN1}
\]
\[
z_{i,s} \le 1-c_i,\; x_{i,r} \le 1-c_i,\; y_{i,\phi} \le 1-c_i \qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S,\; r\in\Lambda_i,\; \phi\in\Phi_i \tag{CAN2}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP Formulation  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in T} D_i \;+\;(1-\alpha)\sum_{i\in T} e_i \;+\;\sum_{i\in T} p_i c_i \;+\;\beta\sum_{i\in T}\theta_i \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } & \text{(R1)}\!-\!\text{(R3)}\; \text{route constraints} \\
             & \text{(S1)}\!-\!\text{(S2)}\; \text{speed‑plan constraints} \\
             & \text{(T1)}\!-\!\text{(T3)}\; \text{timetable propagation} \\
             & \text{(D1)}\; \text{delay definition} \\
             & \text{(E1)}\; \text{energy calculation} \\
             & \text{(C1)}\!-\!\text{(C2)}\; \text{bidirectional conflict avoidance} \\
             & \text{(BLK1)}\!-\!\text{(BLK2)}\; \text{blocked‑section feasibility} \\
             & \text{(OT1)}\!-\!\text{(OT2)}\; \text{no‑overtaking constraints} \\
             & \text{(CAN1)}\!-\!\text{(CAN2)}\; \text{cancellation logic} \\
             & D_i,\;e_i,\;\tau_{i,s}\ge 0\quad\forall i,s \\
             & a_i(n),d_i(n)\ge 0\quad\forall i,n \\
             & x_{i,r},y_{i,\phi},z_{i,s},\delta_{i,j,s},b_{i,s},\gamma_{i,j,s},c_i,\theta_i\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall\text{indices}
\end{aligned}}
}
\]

---

## 6. Discussion of Model Features  

* **Integrated decision space** – The binary variables \(x_{i,r}\) and \(y_{i,\phi}\) couple the *routing* and *speed‑profile* decisions, guaranteeing that the selected travel times \(\tau_{i,s}\) are physically realizable.  
* **Conflict‑free guarantee** – Constraints (C1)–(C2), (OT1)–(OT2) and the blockage constraints (BLK1)–(BLK2) together enforce a **conflict‑free timetable** even when trains share a single track in opposite directions.  
* **Energy‑delay trade‑off** – The weighted objective allows the planner to emphasise punctuality (\(\alpha\) close to 1) or energy efficiency (\(\alpha\) close to 0).  
* **Robustness via cancellation** – Large penalty \(p_i\) makes cancellation a last resort, ensuring feasibility for heavily congested instances.  
* **Scalability** – The model is a classic MILP; in practice a decomposition (as described in the introductory text) can be applied: the master problem selects \((x_{i,r},y_{i,\phi})\) (an IP), while sub‑problems compute feasible \(\tau_{i,s}\) and verify conflict constraints.  

---

### End of formulation  

All variables, constraints and the objective are now fully specified. The model can be implemented in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) and solved directly for small‑medium instances, or used as the core of the decomposition‑based algorithm described in the accompanying research paper.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
*Goal: minimise the total secondary delay of all trains while respecting safety, capacity and operational rules. The model is split into three logical stages – **Rerouting**, **Reordering** and **Rescheduling** – but the formulation below can be used as a single‑shot MILP (all binary decisions are made simultaneously).*

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and basic assumptions  

| Symbol | Meaning | Remarks / Assumptions |
|--------|---------|------------------------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that have to be dispatched in the planning horizon. | All trains are already known (arrival‑time, type, length). |
| **N** = {1,…,|N|} | Set of nodes (stations, junctions, signal blocks) of the rail network. | Each node *n* has a capacity *Cⁿ* (max. number of trains that can occupy it simultaneously). |
| **A** ⊆ N × N | Set of directed arcs (track sections) connecting nodes. | Each arc *(i,j)∈A* has a deterministic travel time *τᵢⱼ* (in minutes) and a safety‑headway *hᵢⱼ* (minutes). |
| **Rᵗ** ⊆ **Pᵗ** | Feasible route set for train *t*.  *Pᵗ* is the set of all simple paths from the origin node *oᵗ* to the destination node *dᵗ*. | The route set is pre‑computed (e.g. by a routing‑graph or a‑priori pruning). |
| **πᵗ** = (π₁ᵗ,…,π_{|πᵗ|}ᵗ) | Ordered list of stations (or critical nodes) that train *t* must visit on any admissible route. | Used to define ordering variables. |
| **Δᵗ** | Planned (primary) departure time of train *t* from its origin node. | May be earlier or later than the scheduled time; primary delays are already accounted for. |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | Used to linearise logical conditions. |
| **ε** | Small positive number (e.g. 0.001) to break ties in the objective when needed. | Optional. |

**Assumptions (explicitly stated)**  

1. **Deterministic travel times** – No stochastic disturbances are considered; the model focuses on secondary delays caused by conflicts.  
2. **Single‑track sections** – Each arc can be occupied by at most one train at a time (capacity 1). If a line has multiple parallel tracks, each track is modelled as a separate arc.  
3. **Safety headway** – After a train leaves an arc, the next train may enter only after a fixed headway *hᵢⱼ*.  
4. **No overtaking** on the same arc – Trains keep their order on a given track section (handled by reordering variables).  
5. **Fixed train characteristics** – Length, acceleration, deceleration are embedded in the travel‑time *τᵢⱼ* and headway *hᵢⱼ*.  
6. **Secondary delay only** – Primary delays (Δᵗ) are parameters; the optimisation decides the *additional* (= secondary) delay *dᵗ*.  

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **xᵗʳ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r ∈ Rᵗ*, 0 otherwise. |
| **yᵗᵢⱼ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses arc *(i,j)∈A* (implied by the chosen route). |
| **sᵗᵢ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train *t* at node *i* (including primary delay Δᵗ). |
| **aᵗᵢ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Actual** arrival time of train *t* at node *i* after rescheduling. |
| **dᵗ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Total secondary delay of train *t* (objective variable). |
| **zᵗᵤᵥ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* is ordered **after** train *u* on the common arc (or node) *v* (re‑ordering variable). |
| **wᵗᵤᵥ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* must wait for train *u* at node *v* (waiting‑for variable, pair‑wise interpretation). |

*Auxiliary variables* (derived from the primary ones, used only in constraints):  

- **δᵗᵢⱼ** = aᵗⱼ – aᵗᵢ – τᵢⱼ – hᵢⱼ·zᵗᵤᵥ – M·(1‑yᵗᵢⱼ) ≥ 0 (see constraints).  

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} d^{t} \;+\; \varepsilon\!\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,j)\in A} a^{t}_{j}}
\]

*Explanation*  

- The primary term minimises the **total secondary delay** of all trains.  
- The second (optional) term with a tiny coefficient **ε** encourages earlier arrivals when several optimal delay solutions exist (helps the solver with tie‑breaking).  

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route selection  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in R^{t}} x^{t}_{r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Arc‑usage consistency** (link route and arc variables)  
   \[
   y^{t}_{i j}= \sum_{r\in R^{t}} \mathbf{1}_{(i,j)\in r}\; x^{t}_{r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in A
   \]
   where \(\mathbf{1}_{(i,j)\in r}=1\) if arc \((i,j)\) belongs to route *r*, 0 otherwise.

### 4.2 Timing (travel‑time and headway)  

3. **Travel time on each traversed arc**  
   \[
   a^{t}_{j} \ge a^{t}_{i}+ \tau_{i j}+h_{i j}\;z^{t u}_{i j} - M\,(1-y^{t}_{i j}) \qquad
   \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in A,\;\forall u\in T\setminus\{t\}
   \]
   *If train *t* uses arc (i,j) (yᵗᵢⱼ=1) and it is ordered **after** train *u* on that arc (zᵗᵤᵥ=1), the headway *hᵢⱼ* must be respected.*

4. **Reordering (no overtaking) on a common arc**  
   For any pair of distinct trains *(t,u)* that share an arc *(i,j)*:  

   \[
   z^{t u}_{i j}+z^{u t}_{i j}= y^{t}_{i j}+y^{u}_{i j}-1 \qquad
   \forall (i,j)\in A,\; \forall t<u
   \]

   *If both trains use the same arc, exactly one of the two ordering binaries must be 1 (i.e. one train follows the other). If only one train uses the arc, both ordering variables are forced to 0.*

5. **Waiting‑for relation at nodes (pair‑wise delay interpretation)**  
   \[
   w^{t u}_{i} \ge y^{t}_{i j} + y^{u}_{i k} -1 \qquad
   \forall i\in N,\; \forall (i,j),(i,k)\in A,\; \forall t\neq u
   \]
   *If train *t* arrives at node *i* on some outgoing arc and train *u* is still occupying node *i*, then *t* may have to wait for *u* (wᵗᵤᵢ =1).*

6. **Actual arrival time respects waiting‑for**  
   \[
   a^{t}_{i}\ge a^{u}_{i}+h_{i}\,w^{t u}_{i} -M\,(1-w^{t u}_{i}) \qquad
   \forall i\in N,\; \forall t\neq u
   \]
   where *hᵢ* is a node‑specific minimum clearance time (often the same as the headway of the outgoing arc).

### 4.3 Delay definition  

7. **Secondary delay of a train** – defined as the difference between its actual arrival at the **final destination** node *dᵗ* and the scheduled arrival (including primary delay).  
   Let *sᵗ_{dᵗ}=Δᵗ + \sum_{(i,j)\in\text{planned path}} τ_{i j}* (pre‑computed).  

   \[
   d^{t}= a^{t}_{d^{t}}- s^{t}_{d^{t}} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

   *Because *dᵗ* appears in the objective, the model will minimise it automatically.*

### 4.4 Capacity and safety constraints  

8. **Node capacity (e.g., platform or block occupancy)** – at any time *θ* only *Cⁿ* trains may be present. In a MILP we enforce this by a time‑indexed big‑M formulation (discretise the horizon into small intervals *θ∈Θ*).  

   \[
   \sum_{t\in T} \mathbf{1}\big\{ a^{t}_{i}\le \theta < a^{t}_{i}+h_{i}\big\}\;\le\; C^{i} \qquad
   \forall i\in N,\;\forall \theta\in\Theta
   \]

   *In practice, the discretisation step can be 1 min; the indicator is linearised with additional binaries (omitted here for brevity).*

9. **Arc capacity (single‑track)** – similar to node capacity, but usually *C^{i j}=1*.  

   \[
   \sum_{t\in T} y^{t}_{i j}\le 1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in A
   \]

### 4.5 Logical consistency  

10. **Big‑M linking of waiting‑for and actual times** (to avoid “inactive’’ w‑variables)  

    \[
    a^{t}_{i} \ge a^{u}_{i}+h_{i} - M(1-w^{t u}_{i}) \qquad
    \forall i\in N,\; \forall t\neq u
    \]

11. **Non‑negativity of delays**  

    \[
    d^{t}\ge 0 \qquad \forall t\in T
    \]

---

## 5. Model summary  

The MILP consists of:

* **Binary variables**:  
  *xᵗʳ* (route choice), *yᵗᵢⱼ* (arc usage), *zᵗᵤᵥ* (ordering on a shared resource), *wᵗᵤᵥ* (pair‑wise waiting).  

* **Continuous variables**:  
  *aᵗᵢ* (actual node arrival times), *dᵗ* (secondary delays).  

* **Objective**: minimise total secondary delay (plus an optional tie‑breaker).  

* **Constraints**: route selection, consistency between route and arc usage, travel‑time plus headway, re‑ordering (FIFO on each shared arc), pair‑wise waiting representation, definition of secondary delay, capacity/safety limits, and big‑M linearisations.

---

## 6. Remarks on computational tractability  

* The model is **NP‑hard** (rtRTMP is a known NP‑hard problem).  
* In practice, the following techniques are used to keep solution times within the required real‑time window (typically < 30 s):  

  1. **Pre‑selection of a small set of candidate routes** *Rᵗ* (e.g., 3‑5 per train) using a fast heuristic (A‑* or Dijkstra).  
  2. **Decomposition** – solve the **rerouting‑reordering** stage first (binary variables only) to obtain a reduced feasible set, then fix *xᵗʳ* and *zᵗᵤᵥ* while solving the **rescheduling** stage (continuous only).  
  3. **Cutting‑plane / symmetry breaking** – enforce FIFO order for trains with the same origin‑destination pair to reduce the number of *z* variables.  
  4. **Time‑window tightening** – compute earliest‑latest possible arrival times for each node (forward‑backward propagation) and use them to tighten the big‑M constants.  

---

## 7. Possible extensions (not included in the core model)  

| Extension | How to incorporate |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Energy consumption minimisation** | Add a linear term *αᵗᵢⱼ·yᵗᵢⱼ* (energy per km) to the objective, or a weighted multi‑objective (ε‑constraint). |
| **Passenger‑level delay weighting** | Replace the simple sum of *dᵗ* by a weighted sum ∑ wᵗ·dᵗ where *wᵗ* reflects train type (high‑speed, freight) or passenger load. |
| **Robustness to disturbances** | Introduce scenario indices *s∈S* with probability *pˢ* and duplicate the timing variables *aᵗᵢˢ*. Add chance‑constraints or a worst‑case bound on *dᵗ*. |
| **Safety‑relevant overlaps** | For each stop signal *σ*, add a binary “overlap‑clear’’ variable and enforce that the following train cannot enter the overlap until the preceding train has cleared the signal plus a safety margin. |
| **Crew‑or‑rolling‑stock constraints** | Add coupling constraints linking trains that share the same crew/vehicle set, forcing them to be scheduled consecutively. |

---

### End of MILP formulation  

The presented model captures the essential elements described in the introductory text: **rerouting**, **reordering**, **rescheduling**, **pair‑wise delay interpretation**, and **delay propagation**. All variables, constraints and the objective are expressed linearly (apart from the usual big‑M linearisation of logical conditions), making the formulation ready for direct implementation in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

**Variables**

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(x_{i,p}\) | Binary – 1 if train \(i\in\mathcal T\) selects speed‑plan \(p\in\mathcal P\). |
| \(y_{i,s}\) | Binary – 1 if train \(i\) uses segment \(s\in\mathcal S\) on the normal (non‑blocked) side. |
| \(u_{i,s}\) | Binary – 1 if train \(i\) uses segment \(s\) on the opposite side (detour). |
| \(z_{i,s}\) | Continuous – actual travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) (minutes). |
| \(d_i\) | Continuous – departure time of train \(i\) at its origin. |
| \(a_i\) | Continuous – arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination. |

**Parameters (assumed known)**  

* \(\mathcal T\) – set of trains, \(\mathcal S\) – set of bidirectional track segments, \(\mathcal P\) – set of admissible speed‑plans.  
* \(t_{i,s}\) – base travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) (minutes).  
* \(\text{cap}_s\) – capacity of segment \(s\) (max number of trains simultaneously on that side).  
* \([a_s,b_s]\) – disruption window on the normal side of segment \(s\) (empty if no blockage).  
* \(e_{i,p}\) – energy consumption of train \(i\) when using plan \(p\).  
* \(A_i^{\text{orig}}\) – originally scheduled arrival time of train \(i\).  
* \(r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) can still traverse segment \(s\) after rerouting (otherwise 0).  
* \(\lambda>0\) – weight for the energy term in the objective.  
* \(M\) – sufficiently large constant (big‑M).  

*Plan‑to‑segment mapping*  
\(\delta_{i,p,s}=1\) if plan \(p\) for train \(i\) includes traversal of segment \(s\); 0 otherwise. (Provided by the planner.)

**Objective function**

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\bigl(a_i-A_i^{\text{orig}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\lambda\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P} e_{i,p}\,x_{i,p}}_{\text{total energy}} .
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Plan selection** – each train chooses exactly one speed plan  
\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P} x_{i,p}=1\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T. \tag{1}
\]

2. **Link plan to segment usage** – a segment can be used only if the selected plan contains it  
\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\delta_{i,p,s}\,x_{i,p}\;\ge\; y_{i,s}+u_{i,s}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S. \tag{2}
\]

3. **Availability on sides** – a train may use a side only if it is feasible after rerouting  
\[
y_{i,s}+u_{i,s}\le r_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s. \tag{3}
\]

4. **Travel‑time definition (big‑M)**  
\[
z_{i,s}\ge t_{i,s}-M\bigl(1-y_{i,s}-u_{i,s}\bigr)\qquad\forall i,s, \tag{4}
\]
\[
z_{i,s}\le M\bigl(y_{i,s}+u_{i,s}\bigr)\qquad\forall i,s. \tag{5}
\]

5. **Timing consistency** – arrival equals departure plus summed travel times  
\[
a_i = d_i+\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T. \tag{6}
\]

6. **Segment capacity (static, non‑time‑indexed)**  
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T} y_{i,s}\le \text{cap}_s\qquad\forall s\in\mathcal S, \tag{7}
\]
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T} u_{i,s}\le \text{cap}_s\qquad\forall s\in\mathcal S. \tag{8}
\]

7. **Disruption blocking** – the normal side of a blocked segment cannot be used during its window (static formulation forbids it altogether)  
\[
y_{i,s}=0\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S \text{ with }[a_s,b_s]\neq\emptyset . \tag{9}
\]

8. **Opposite‑direction conflict** – at most one train may occupy the opposite side of a segment (static version)  
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T} u_{i,s}\le 1\qquad\forall s\in\mathcal S. \tag{10}
\]

9. **Non‑negativity / binary restrictions** – \(x_{i,p},y_{i,s},u_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\); \(z_{i,s},d_i,a_i\ge0\).

---

**Assumptions / remarks**

* The model uses a **static capacity** representation; a time‑indexed version would replace (7)–(8) by \(\sum_i y_{i,s,t}\le\text{cap}_s\) for each time interval \(t\).  
* Constraint (9) conservatively forbids any use of the normal side while the segment is blocked. If a train may cross after the blockage, a time‑indexed formulation is required.  
* The big‑M constant \(M\) must be larger than the maximal feasible travel time on any segment.  
* Energy \(e_{i,p}\) and delay are combined linearly; the weight \(\lambda\) allows the decision maker to trade off punctuality versus energy efficiency.  

The presented MILP fully describes the **integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial segment blockages, including plan selection, rerouting (opposite‑side use), capacity, disruption handling, and the joint minimisation of total delay and energy consumption.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  

The model below follows the description in the supplied text.  
It is divided into three sub‑problems that are solved sequentially (rerouting → re‑ordering → rescheduling) but the formulation is written as a single MILP so that the same set of decision variables can be used when the sub‑problems are combined.  
All symbols are defined in the *Sets* and *Parameters* sections; the *Variables* section distinguishes continuous (delay) and binary (routing / ordering) decisions.  
The model minimizes the total secondary delay of all trains while respecting railway safety (headway, overlap) and operational limits (track capacities, speed limits).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \mathcal{T} = \{1,\dots,T\} \) | Set of trains that have to be dispatched in the planning horizon. |
| \( \mathcal{N} = \{1,\dots,N\} \) | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, signal blocks). |
| \( \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{N} \) | Set of directed track‑segments (edges). |
| \( \mathcal{P}_i \) | Set of feasible **routes** (paths) for train \(i\). Each route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\) is a ordered list of edges \((e_1,\dots,e_{|p|})\). |
| \( \mathcal{S}_i \subseteq \mathcal{T}\setminus\{i\} \) | Set of trains that can potentially block train \(i\) (i.e. trains sharing at least one edge with any route of train \(i\)). |
| \( \mathcal{O}_i \subseteq \mathcal{S}_i \) | Subset of trains that are allowed to **precede** train \(i\) (ordering decisions). Typically \(\mathcal{O}_i=\mathcal{S}_i\). |

*Assumption 1*: The set of feasible routes \(\mathcal{P}_i\) is pre‑computed (e.g. by a routing‑selection stage or by a heuristic) and is small enough to keep the model tractable.  

*Assumption 2*: All trains travel at a constant **nominal speed** \(v_e\) on edge \(e\) (no acceleration/deceleration model). The nominal travel time on edge \(e\) is therefore \(\tau_e = \ell_e / v_e\) where \(\ell_e\) is the length of the edge.  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \( \tau_e \) | Nominal travel time on edge \(e\) (without any delay). | [h] |
| \( \overline{c}_e \) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy edge \(e\) simultaneously (usually 1 for single‑track, 2 for double‑track). | – |
| \( \Delta^{\max}_i \) | Upper bound on admissible secondary delay for train \(i\). | [h] |
| \( \beta_{ij} \) | Binary safety‑headway indicator: 1 if train \(j\) must finish edge \(e\) before train \(i\) can enter the same edge (depends on direction, signalling). | – |
| \( \gamma_{ij} \) | Overlap (clear‑behind) time that must be respected when train \(i\) stops before a signal that is held for train \(j\). | [h] |
| \( d^{\text{prim}}_i \) | Primary (exogenous) delay already suffered by train \(i\) before the optimisation starts. | [h] |
| \( w^{\text{max}} \) | Maximum allowed waiting (secondary) delay on any node (used to bound the model). | [h] |
| \( M \) | A large constant (big‑M) greater than the maximal possible time a train can be delayed on any edge (e.g. sum of all \(\tau_e\) + \(\Delta^{\max}_i\)). | [h] |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \( x_{i,p} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\); 0 otherwise. |
| \( y_{ij} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) **waits for** train \(j\) (i.e. \(j\) is the immediate predecessor of \(i\) on a shared edge); 0 otherwise. |
| \( s_{i,e} \) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Start time** of train \(i\) on edge \(e\). |
| \( f_{i,e} \) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Finish time** of train \(i\) on edge \(e\) ( \(f_{i,e}=s_{i,e}+\tau_e\) if the edge is traversed). |
| \( \delta_i \) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total **secondary delay** assigned to train \(i\) (the decision variable we minimise). |
| \( z_{i,e} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) actually traverses edge \(e\) (derived from route choice). |

*Assumption 3*: Each train traverses every edge of its selected route exactly once; therefore \(z_{i,e}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i:\,e\in p} x_{i,p}\).  

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_i}
\]

The objective is to minimise the sum of all secondary (controlled) delays, i.e. the total disruption caused by the rescheduling.

### 4.2 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i} x_{i,p}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\]

2. **Link route choice to edge‑usage**  

\[
z_{i,e}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i:\,e\in p} x_{i,p} \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T},\; e\in\mathcal{E}
\]

### 4.3 Timing constraints  

3. **Nominal travel on traversed edges**  

\[
f_{i,e}= s_{i,e}+ \tau_e \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T},\; e\in\mathcal{E}
\]

4. **Edge‑availability (capacity) – cumulative‑flow style**  

For each edge \(e\) the number of trains present at any time cannot exceed \(\overline{c}_e\). Using a classic time‑indexed big‑M formulation (continuous time, but linearised with binary ordering variables) we enforce pairwise ordering for every pair of trains that could be on the same edge:

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_{i,e} \; \ge \; f_{j,e} - M\,(1-y_{ij}) \\
s_{j,e} \; \ge \; f_{i,e} - M\,(y_{ij}) \\
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall i<j,\; e\in\mathcal{E}\; \text{with } z_{i,e}=z_{j,e}=1
\]

The binary variable \(y_{ij}=1\) means *train \(i\) goes after train \(j\)* on the shared edge.  

5. **Safety headway (FIFO, signalling)**  

If a signalling rule forces a minimum headway \(h_{ij}\) (often expressed as a binary parameter \(\beta_{ij}\)), we add:

\[
s_{i,e} \ge f_{j,e}+h_{ij} - M\,(1-\beta_{ij}) \qquad \forall i,j,e \text{ sharing }e
\]

When \(\beta_{ij}=0\) the constraint is relaxed.

6. **Overlap (clear‑behind) constraints**  

When train \(i\) must wait for an overlap after train \(j\) stops before a signal:

\[
s_{i,e} \ge f_{j,e}+ \gamma_{ij} - M\,(1-y_{ij}) \qquad \forall i,j,e
\]

### 4.4 Delay definition  

7. **Link secondary delay to start times**  

Assume that the **planned (ideal) departure time** of train \(i\) from its origin node is \(t^{\text{plan}}_i\). The secondary delay is the difference between the actual start time on the first traversed edge and the planned departure, after subtracting the primary delay already known:

\[
\delta_i = s_{i,e^{\text{first}}} - t^{\text{plan}}_i - d^{\text{prim}}_i \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\]

where \(e^{\text{first}}\) is the first edge of the selected route (identified through \(x_{i,p}\)).  

8. **Bounds on delay**  

\[
0 \le \delta_i \le \Delta^{\max}_i \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\]

### 4.5 Re‑ordering (pair‑wise waiting) constraints  

9. **Exactly one predecessor (or none) on each shared edge**  

For each train \(i\) and each edge it traverses, it either has no predecessor (it is the first on that edge) or it waits for exactly one other train that also uses the edge:

\[
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_i} y_{ij} \le 1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\]

If a FIFO rule is required for a particular node (e.g. station platform), we can enforce a total order by adding transitivity constraints:

\[
y_{ij}+y_{jk} \le 1 + y_{ik} \qquad \forall i,j,k\in\mathcal{T}
\]

(These constraints are optional and can be omitted for a pure pair‑wise model.)

### 4.6 Additional practical constraints  

10. **Maximum waiting at a node** (to avoid unrealistic holding times)

\[
s_{i,e_{\text{next}}} - f_{i,e_{\text{prev}}} \le w^{\text{max}} \qquad \forall i,\; e_{\text{prev}},e_{\text{next}} \text{ consecutive on the chosen route}
\]

11. **Logical linking of \(y_{ij}\) to actual edge sharing**  

If two trains never share an edge, they cannot wait for each other:

\[
y_{ij} \le \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}} z_{i,e}\,z_{j,e} \qquad \forall i\neq j
\]

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_i \\
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i} x_{i,p}=1 &&\forall i\\
&z_{i,e}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i:e\in p} x_{i,p} &&\forall i,e\\
&f_{i,e}= s_{i,e}+ \tau_e &&\forall i,e\\
&s_{i,e} \ge f_{j,e} - M(1-y_{ij}) &&\forall i<j,\; e\text{ with }z_{i,e}=z_{j,e}=1\\
&s_{j,e} \ge f_{i,e} - M(y_{ij}) &&\forall i<j,\; e\text{ with }z_{i,e}=z_{j,e}=1\\
&s_{i,e} \ge f_{j,e}+h_{ij} - M(1-\beta_{ij}) &&\forall i,j,e\\
&s_{i,e} \ge f_{j,e}+ \gamma_{ij} - M(1-y_{ij}) &&\forall i,j,e\\
&\delta_i = s_{i,e^{\text{first}}} - t^{\text{plan}}_i - d^{\text{prim}}_i &&\forall i\\
&0\le \delta_i \le \Delta^{\max}_i &&\forall i\\
&\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_i} y_{ij}\le 1 &&\forall i\\
&y_{ij}+y_{jk}\le 1 + y_{ik} &&\forall i,j,k\ (\text{optional FIFO})\\
&s_{i,e_{\text{next}}} - f_{i,e_{\text{prev}}}\le w^{\text{max}} &&\forall i,\; \text{consecutive edges}\\
&y_{ij}\le \sum_{e} z_{i,e}z_{j,e} &&\forall i\neq j\\
&x_{i,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,e}\in\{0,1\}\\
&s_{i,e},f_{i,e},\delta_i \ge 0 &&\forall i,e
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Remarks on the Model  

1. **Decomposition viewpoint** –  
   *Stage 1 (rerouting)* is captured by the binary variables \(x_{i,p}\) and constraints (1‑2).  
   *Stage 2 (re‑ordering)* is represented by the pair‑wise waiting binaries \(y_{ij}\) and constraints (9‑10).  
   *Stage 3 (rescheduling)* appears through the continuous timing variables \(s_{i,e},f_{i,e}\) and the delay definition (7).  

2. **Sub‑optimal version** –  
   If delay propagation is ignored, the model can be simplified by fixing \(s_{i,e}=t^{\text{plan}}_i+d^{\text{prim}}_i\) for the first edge and only using the binary ordering variables to compute \(\delta_i\) as a sum of pair‑wise waiting times. This yields the “pair‑wise interpretation” described in the paper.  

3. **Global‑optimal version** –  
   Keeping constraints (3‑8) ensures that the actual start/finish times respect the propagation of all previous waiting decisions, thus guaranteeing the optimal solution for the original rtRTMP.  

4. **Scalability** –  
   The number of binary variables grows with \(|\mathcal{T}|^2\) (pair‑wise waiting) and with \(\sum_i |\mathcal{P}_i|\) (route choice). In practice, a **pre‑selection** of a few promising routes per train (e.g. 2‑3) and a **conflict‑graph pruning** that removes pairs \((i,j)\) that never share an edge dramatically reduces the model size, as done in the cited literature.  

5. **Possible extensions** –  
   *Energy minimisation*: add a term \(\sum_i \alpha_i \, \delta_i\) where \(\alpha_i\) is the marginal energy cost of a unit delay.  
   *Passenger‑level objective*: incorporate weighted passenger‑kilometres to penalise delays of high‑load trains more heavily.  
   *Robustness*: introduce scenario‑based parameters for uncertain travel times and minimise the worst‑case total delay.  

---

### 7. Conclusion  

The MILP presented above captures the three‑stage decomposition (rerouting, re‑ordering, rescheduling) of the real‑time railway traffic management problem while remaining a **single linear model** that can be solved with any commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress). By fixing the route‑selection and ordering decisions obtained from the fast sub‑optimal stage, the second stage solves a reduced rescheduling problem that already respects delay propagation, delivering a globally optimal schedule for the original problem. The model can be readily adapted to include additional operational goals (energy, passenger satisfaction) or to be embedded in a rolling‑horizon decision support system for railway dispatchers.
