Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
The model below follows the description given in the text and adds the missing formal elements. All symbols are defined in the *Notation* section; any element that is not directly taken from the literature is marked as **(Assumption)**.

---

## 1.  Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains that have to be scheduled (|T| = *n*). |
| **\(N\)** | Set of nodes (stations, block‑sections, signal locations) of the rail network. |
| **\(A\subseteq N\times N\)** | Set of directed arcs (track sections) connecting nodes. |
| **\(R_t\)** | Set of admissible routes for train *t* (pre‑computed by a routing‑pre‑selection stage). |
| **\(r\in R_t\)** | One concrete route, i.e. an ordered list of arcs \((a_1,\dots ,a_{|r|})\). |
| **\(L_a\)** | Length (km) of arc *a* (Assumption: known). |
| **\(v^{\max}_a\)** | Maximum allowed speed on arc *a* (km h\(^{-1}\)). |
| **\(c_a\)** | Energy consumption coefficient of arc *a* (kWh per km) – used only if a secondary objective is added (Assumption). |
| **\(d^{\text{plan}}_{t,a}\)** | Planned (timetable) arrival time of train *t* at the **head** of arc *a* (minutes). |
| **\(M\)** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **\(S\subseteq T\times T\)** | Set of train pairs that may potentially conflict (i.e. share at least one arc). |
| **\(p_{t,a}\)** | Minimum dwell / safety time that train *t* must respect on arc *a* (minutes). |
| **\(\Delta^{\max}\)** | Maximum admissible secondary delay (Assumption). |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_{t,r}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* (∈ R_t), 0 otherwise. |
| **\(y_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from the **tail** of arc *a*. |
| **\(z_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at the **head** of arc *a*. |
| **\(w_{t,i}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Secondary (real‑time) delay of train *t* at event *i* (departure or arrival). |
| **\(o_{t,i}^{\text{ord}}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is ordered **before** another train on the same resource at event *i* (used for re‑ordering). |
| **\(b_{t_1,t_2,a}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t₁* must wait for train *t₂* on arc *a* (pair‑wise waiting indicator). |
| **\(s_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Slack (free time) left on arc *a* after the train has passed (used for overlap safety). |

---

## 2.  Model assumptions  

1. **Pre‑selected route set** – For each train a limited set *Rₜ* of feasible routes is given (generated by a routing‑pre‑selection heuristic).  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – Travel time on arc *a* for any train is \( \tau_a = \frac{L_a}{v^{\max}_a}\) (no stochasticity).  
3. **Single‑track sections** – When two trains share an arc they cannot occupy it simultaneously; a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) rule can be overridden by binary re‑ordering variables.  
4. **Safety headway** – After a train leaves an arc a safety margin *p* must be kept before the next train may enter (includes signal overlap).  
5. **Maximum secondary delay** – No train may be delayed more than \(\Delta^{\max}\).  
6. **Objective** – Primary objective is to minimise the sum of secondary delays (total passenger‑delay). A secondary energy‑minimisation term can be added if required.

---

## 3.  Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I_t} w_{t,i}}_{\text{Total secondary delay}}
\;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{a\in A} c_a \, L_a \, x_{t,r(a)}}_{\text{(optional) Energy consumption}}
}
\]

* \(I_t\) is the set of all events (departure/arrival) of train *t* (size = 2·|r|).  
* \(\lambda\) is a weighting factor (set to 0 if only delay is considered).  

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1 Route selection  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

\[
x_{t,r}=0 \quad \text{if arc } a\notin r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_{t,a}=z_{t,a}=0 \qquad \forall t,a,r \tag{R2}
\]

### 4.2 Time propagation along a chosen route  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of arcs \((a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}})\) on the selected route *r* :

\[
z_{t,a^{\text{out}}} + \tau_{a^{\text{out}}} \;+\; p_{t,a^{\text{out}}}
\; \le\; y_{t,a^{\text{in}}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,\; a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}} \in r \tag{T1}
\]

If the same arc is used again (loops) the constraint is applied for each occurrence.

### 4.3 Definition of secondary delay  

\[
w_{t,i} \;=\; y_{t,i} - d^{\text{plan}}_{t,i} \qquad \forall t,i \tag{D1}
\]

\[
0 \le w_{t,i} \le \Delta^{\max} \qquad \forall t,i \tag{D2}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict avoidance (pair‑wise waiting)  

For every pair \((t_1,t_2)\in S\) that share arc *a* :

\[
y_{t_1,a} \;\ge\; z_{t_2,a} + p_{t_2,a} - M\bigl(1-b_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{C1}
\]

\[
y_{t_2,a} \;\ge\; z_{t_1,a} + p_{t_1,a} - M\bigl(b_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{C2}
\]

\[
b_{t_1,t_2,a} \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in S,\; a\in A \tag{C3}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active, forcing one train to wait for the other.  

### 4.5 Re‑ordering (optional)  

If the dispatcher may change the FIFO order, binary ordering variables are introduced:

\[
o_{t_1,t_2,a} + o_{t_2,t_1,a}=1 \qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in S,\; a\in A \tag{O1}
\]

\[
y_{t_1,a} \ge z_{t_2,a}+p_{t_2,a} - M\bigl(1-o_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{O2}
\]

\[
y_{t_2,a} \ge z_{t_1,a}+p_{t_1,a} - M\bigl(1-o_{t_2,t_1,a}\bigr) \tag{O3}
\]

When re‑ordering is **forbidden** (e.g. FIFO policy), set \(o_{t_1,t_2,a}=0\) for all pairs.

### 4.6 Delay propagation (global‑optimal model)  

To capture the effect of a delay on downstream trains, we introduce cumulative delay variables \(\delta_{t,a}\) that are forced to propagate through the network:

\[
\delta_{t,a^{\text{in}}} \;\ge\; \delta_{t,a^{\text{out}}} + w_{t,a^{\text{out}}} \qquad \forall t,\; (a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}})\in r \tag{P1}
\]

\[
w_{t,a} = \delta_{t,a} \qquad \forall t,a \tag{P2}
\]

These constraints are activated only for the selected route (big‑M linearisation similar to (T1)).

### 4.7 Overlap / safety‑clearance (optional)  

\[
s_{t,a} \;\ge\; y_{t,a} - \bigl(z_{t,a}+p_{t,a}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl1}
\]

\[
s_{t,a} \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl2}
\]

A minimum required overlap \(\underline{s}_a\) can be imposed:

\[
s_{t,a} \ge \underline{s}_a \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl3}
\]

---

## 5.  Complete MILP formulation  

Putting together the objective and all constraints we obtain the following compact model:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I_t} w_{t,i}
\;+\;\lambda\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{a\in A} c_a L_a \Bigl(\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{t,r}\mathbf{1}_{\{a\in r\}}\Bigr) \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route selection} \\
&\text{(T1)} &&\text{time propagation on selected route} \\
&\text{(D1)–(D2)} &&\text{definition and bounds of secondary delay} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{pair‑wise conflict avoidance (waiting)}\\
&\text{(O1)–(O3)} &&\text{optional re‑ordering (if allowed)}\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{delay propagation (only in the optimal‑delay model)}\\
&\text{(Ovl1)–(Ovl3)} &&\text{overlap / safety clearance (optional)}\\
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; b_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\}\\
&y_{t,a},z_{t,a},w_{t,i},\delta_{t,a},s_{t,a}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,a,i .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on the two‑stage approach described in the paper  

1. **Stage 1 – Sub‑optimal model**  
   *Only constraints (R1)–(R2), (T1), (D1)–(D2) and the pair‑wise waiting variables **b** are kept.*  
   The model ignores (P1)–(P2) (delay propagation) and therefore yields a fast, but possibly sub‑optimal solution.

2. **Stage 2 – Full‑optimal model**  
   *All constraints above are activated, especially (P1)–(P2) that enforce delay propagation.*  
   The routes **x** are fixed to the solution of Stage 1 (or re‑optimised together), guaranteeing the global optimum for the original rtRTMP.

---

## 7.  Possible extensions  

| Extension | How to incorporate |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Energy minimisation** | Keep the term \(\lambda\sum c_a L_a x_{t,r}\) and possibly add a secondary objective using a weighted sum or a hierarchical (lexicographic) optimisation. |
| **Stochastic disturbances** | Replace deterministic travel times \(\tau_a\) by scenario‑dependent parameters \(\tau_{a}^{s}\) and add scenario‑indexed copies of the time‑propagation constraints; use a robust or chance‑constrained formulation. |
| **Multiple train classes (passenger / freight)** | Add class‑specific weighting in the objective (e.g. higher penalty for passenger‑train delays). |
| **Capacity of stations (platforms)** | Introduce additional binary variables for platform occupation and constraints that limit simultaneous occupancy. |

---

**The model above is a self‑contained MILP that captures the essential elements of the rtRTMP as described in the provided text, while filling the missing formal details with reasonable assumptions.**

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Blockage Scenario)**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) which route a train will take (including possible rerouting around a blocked segment), (ii) the speed level on every traversed segment (hence travel time and energy), and (iii) the exact arrival/departure times while guaranteeing conflict‑free use of the (now partially) shared track. All relationships are linear; binary variables are used only for routing, speed‑level choice and conflict ordering.

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Trains |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Directed track segments (arcs) |
| **R** ⊆ S×S | Feasible “continuation” pairs (i→j) – i.e. a train may go from segment *i* to segment *j* (including rerouting) |
| **V** = {1,…,|V|} | Discrete speed levels (e.g. low/medium/high) |
| **B** ⊆ S | Segments that are *partially blocked* during a known time window |
| **O** = { (t₁,t₂) | t₁<t₂, t₁,t₂∈T } | Ordered train pairs (used for bidirectional conflict) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| ℓ_s | Length of segment *s* (km) |
| b_s ∈ {0,1} | 1 if segment *s* is partially blocked, 0 otherwise |
| t⁽ᴮ⁾_s , t⁽ᴱ⁾_s | Beginning / end of the blockage window on *s* (minutes from horizon start) |
| v⁽ᵛ⁾_s | Nominal speed (km/min) achievable on *s* with speed level *v* |
| τ^{min}_s , τ^{max}_s | Minimum / maximum feasible travel time on *s* (min) |
| e⁽ᵛ⁾_s | Energy (MJ) needed to traverse *s* with speed level *v* |
| d^{orig}_t | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* from its origin (min) |
| a^{orig}_t | Planned (original) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (min) |
| p_t ≥ 0 | Weight for the delay of train *t* in the objective |
| q ≥ 0 | Global weight for total energy consumption |
| U | Big‑M constant (larger than the planning horizon, e.g. 1440 min) |
| c_{s,v} ∈ {0,1} | 1 if speed level *v* can safely pass the unblocked width of blocked segment *s*; 0 otherwise (assumed 1 for all non‑blocked segments) |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| x_{t,s} ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* |
| y_{t,(i,j)} ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* uses the continuation pair (i→j) (i.e. order of two consecutive segments) |
| z_{t,s,v} ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *v* |
| α_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the upstream end of segment *s* |
| β_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Departure time of train *t* from the downstream end of segment *s* |
| τ_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (β‑α) |
| ε_t ≥ 0 | Delay of train *t* (actual arrival – original arrival) |
| φ_t ≥ 0 | Energy consumed by train *t* |
| δ_{t₁,t₂,s} ∈ {0,1} | Ordering binary for bidirectional conflict on segment *s*: 1 if *t₁* passes before *t₂* |

---

### 4. MILP Formulation  

#### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \;\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} p_t\,\varepsilon_t}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\; \underbrace{q\;\sum_{t\in T}\phi_t}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

#### 4.2 Routing / Path construction  

1. **Exactly one incoming & one outgoing segment for each train** (origin & destination are fixed by data).  

\[
\sum_{s\in S:\,\text{up}(s)=\text{origin}_t} x_{t,s}=1,
\qquad
\sum_{s\in S:\,\text{down}(s)=\text{dest}_t} x_{t,s}=1
\quad\forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Flow balance for interior nodes**  

\[
\sum_{(i,s)\in R} y_{t,(i,s)} \;-\; \sum_{(s,j)\in R} y_{t,(s,j)} = 0,
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\notin\{\text{origin}_t,\text{dest}_t\}
\tag{R2}
\]

3. **Link arc‑selection to continuation variables**  

\[
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,i},\qquad
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,s},
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,s)\in R
\tag{R3}
\]

#### 4.3 Speed‑level selection  

\[
\sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,v}=x_{t,s},
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

#### 4.4 Travel‑time – speed coupling  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{t,s} &\ge \frac{\ell_s}{v^{v}_s} - U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v\\
\tau_{t,s} &\le \frac{\ell_s}{v^{v}_s} + U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v
\end{aligned}
\tag{S2}
\]

Together with (S1) this forces  

\[
\tau_{t,s}= \frac{\ell_s}{v^{v^\*}_s}\quad\text{where }v^\* \text{ is the selected speed level}.
\]

Physical feasibility:

\[
\tau^{min}_s\,x_{t,s}\le \tau_{t,s}\le \tau^{max}_s\,x_{t,s},
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{S3}
\]

#### 4.5 Timing (arrival / departure)  

\[
\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \tau_{t,s},
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{T1}
\]

Successive‑segment continuity (big‑M):

\[
\alpha_{t,j}\ge \beta_{t,i}-U\,(1-y_{t,(i,j)}),
\qquad\forall t,(i,j)\in R
\tag{T2}
\]

Origin / destination anchoring:

\[
\alpha_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}= d^{orig}_t,\qquad
\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}= a^{orig}_t+\varepsilon_t,
\qquad\forall t
\tag{T3}
\]

#### 4.6 Partial‑blockage handling  

*No occupation during the blockage window* (conservative version):

\[
\alpha_{t,s}\ge t^{E}_s - U\,(1-x_{t,s}),\qquad
\beta_{t,s}\le t^{B}_s + U\,(1-x_{t,s}),
\qquad\forall t,\; s\in B
\tag{B1}
\]

*If a speed level cannot fit through the remaining width*:

\[
z_{t,s,v}\le c_{s,v}+ (1-x_{t,s}),\qquad\forall t,\;s\in B,\;v\in V
\tag{B2}
\]

(When *c_{s,v}=0* the corresponding speed level is forbidden on that blocked segment.)

#### 4.7 Bidirectional conflict (track‑capacity)  

For every pair of distinct trains on the same physical segment *s*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{t_1,s} &\ge \beta_{t_2,s} - U\,\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\\
\alpha_{t_2,s} &\ge \beta_{t_1,s} - U\,(1-\delta_{t_1,t_2,s})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in O,\; s\in S
\tag{C1}
\]

Only one of the two inequalities is active; the binary \(\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\) decides the order.

A simpler (but stronger) capacity rule can be used when the planning horizon is coarse:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} x_{t,s}\le 1,\qquad\forall s\in S\text{ with }b_s=0
\tag{C2}
\]

Choose (C1) for exact bidirectional sequencing, (C2) for a quick upper bound.

#### 4.8 Energy accounting  

\[
\phi_t = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{v\in V} e^{v}_s \, z_{t,s,v},
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

#### 4.9 Delay definition  

\[
\varepsilon_t = \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - a^{orig}_t,
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

(If early arrival is allowed, replace by \(\varepsilon_t\ge \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}-a^{orig}_t,\; \varepsilon_t\ge0\).)

#### 4.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,s},\,y_{t,(i,j)},\,z_{t,s,v},\,\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&\alpha_{t,s},\,\beta_{t,s},\,\tau_{t,s},\,\varepsilon_t,\,\phi_t \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

### 5. How the model works  

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| **x, y** | Build a conflict‑free directed path for each train, allowing rerouting around the blocked segment. |
| **z** | Choose a discrete speed level on each traversed segment, fixing travel time and energy. |
| **α, β, τ** | Record the exact timetable (arrival, departure, travel time) consistent with the chosen speeds. |
| **δ** | Resolve bidirectional conflicts on shared track (only one train may occupy a segment at a time). |
| **B1‑B2** | Ensure that blocked segments are not used during their closure window, or only admissible speed levels are allowed. |
| **E1** | Accumulate energy consumption for the objective. |
| **OBJ** | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy, enabling a trade‑off between punctuality and sustainability. |

---

### 6. Complete Linear Model (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}p_t\varepsilon_t\;+\;q\sum_{t\in T}\phi_t\\[2pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{Routing: }(R1)-(R3)\\
&\text{Speed selection: }(S1)\\
&\text{Travel‑time – speed: }(S2),(S3)\\
&\text{Timing: }(T1)-(T3)\\
&\text{Blockage: }(B1),(B2)\\
&\text{Bidirectional conflict: }(C1)\;\text{or}\;(C2)\\
&\text{Energy: }(E1)\\
&\text{Delay: }(D1)\\
&\text{Domains: }(DOM)
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries \(x, y, z, \delta\). The model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). By adjusting the weights \(p_t\) and \(q\) the planner can explore different trade‑offs between service punctuality and energy efficiency while guaranteeing a feasible, conflict‑free timetable under partial‑segment blockages.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockages**  

All time is discretised into equal intervals of length Δt (e.g. 1 min).  
For each train we decide (i) which route (original or a rerouted alternative) it follows, (ii) the exact interval in which it arrives at every station on the chosen route, (iii) the interval in which it occupies each track segment, and (iv) whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode on that segment.  
The model minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while respecting timetable, blockages, capacity on bidirectional track pairs, and travel‑time limits.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **𝒯** | Set of trains *t*. |
| **𝒮** | Set of stations *s*. |
| **ℒ** | Set of directed track segments *l*. |
| **ℬ ⊂ ℒ×ℒ** | Set of **bidirectional pairs** \((l,l′)\) that share the same physical track (opposite directions). |
| **𝒫(t)** | Set of feasible routes for train *t* (original + possible rerouted alternatives). |
| **𝒦 = {1,…,K}** | Set of discrete time intervals in the planning horizon. |
| **Lₚ ⊆ ℒ** | Set of directed segments belonging to route *p*. |
| **𝒮ₚ ⊆ 𝒮** | Set of stations visited by route *p* (ordered). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| *aₜ,ₛ* | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *s* (continuous). | min |
| *dₜ,ₛ* | Scheduled departure time of train *t* from station *s*. | min |
| *dwellₜ,ₛ* | Minimum dwell time required at station *s* for train *t*. | min |
| *minRunₜ,ₗ*, *maxRunₜ,ₗ* | Minimum / maximum admissible travel time for train *t* on segment *l* (derived from speed limits). | min |
| *blockₗ,ₖ* | 1 if segment *l* is blocked during interval *k*, 0 otherwise. | – |
| *energyₜ,ₚ* | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per km) for train *t* on route *p*. | kWh |
| *eᵃᶜᶜₜ,ₗ* | Energy cost of using **accelerated** mode on segment *l* for train *t*. | kWh |
| *eᵈᵉᶜₜ,ₗ* | Energy cost of using **decelerated** mode on segment *l* for train *t*. | kWh |
| α, β | Weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| *M* | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| Δt | Duration of one time index (e.g. 1 min). | min |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| *xₜ,ₚ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *p*. |
| *yₜ,ₛ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **arrives** at station *s* in interval *k*. |
| *zₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **occupies** directed segment *l* during interval *k*. |
| *wₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *l* in interval *k* using **accelerated** mode. |
| *uₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *l* in interval *k* using **decelerated** mode. |
| *C* ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption (linked to *w* and *u*). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\!\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\!\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}\,y_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\!\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)}\! \text{energy}_{t,p}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

\((\cdot)^{+}=\max\{0,\cdot\}\).  
Because *y* is binary, the product equals the delay incurred if arrival is later than the scheduled time and zero otherwise. (A fully linear version can be obtained with auxiliary delay variables.)

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route selection  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad\forall\,t\in\mathcal T } \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Station‑visitation consistency  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} y_{t,s,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S } \tag{R2}
\]

#### 5.3 Segment‑occupation consistency  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} z_{t,l,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,l\in L_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; l\in\mathcal L } \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4 Arrival‑time and departure‑time variables (linearisation of *y*)  

\[
A_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s \tag{R4a}
\]
\[
D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+ \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}\qquad\forall t,s \tag{R4b}
\]

#### 5.5 Temporal ordering between successive stations  

For every ordered pair \((s,s')\) that are consecutive on route *p*,
let \(\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}\) be the set of directed segments between them.

\[
\boxed{
A_{t,s'}\;\ge\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}
- M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\;p\in\mathcal P(t),\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R5a}
\]

\[
\boxed{
A_{t,s'}\;\le\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}
+ M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\;p\in\mathcal P(t),\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R5b}
\]

The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when route *p* is not selected.

#### 5.6 Bidirectional‑track capacity (collision avoidance)  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l,k}+ \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l',k}\;\le\;1
\qquad\forall (l,l')\in\mathcal B,\; k\in\mathcal K } \tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7 Blockage avoidance  
\[
\boxed{ z_{t,l,k}\le 1-\text{block}_{l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R7}
\]

#### 5.8 Travel‑time bounds per segment  

Because each segment is traversed in exactly one interval (R3), the travel time on segment *l* equals one Δt.  
If a finer granularity is required, replace the left‑hand side by the sum of occupied intervals; the following linear bounds stay valid:

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\;x_{t,p}
\;\le\; 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;
\le\;
\frac{\text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\;x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R8}
\]

\(z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}\) is the binary variable indicating the interval when the train entered the segment (or left the previous segment); it can be introduced analogously to *y*.

#### 5.9 Dwell‑time enforcement (alternative linear form)  

For each consecutive station pair \((s,s')\) on the chosen route:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s',k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}
- M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,p,\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R9}
\]

#### 5.10 Linking speed‑mode to segment occupation  

\[
\boxed{ w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k}\;\le\; z_{t,l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R10}
\]

#### 5.11 Energy‑consumption definition  

\[
\boxed{ C = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{l\in\mathcal L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\,w_{t,l,k}+ e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\,u_{t,l,k}\bigr) } \tag{R11}
\]

If desired, the term \(C\) can be inserted directly into the objective instead of the separate energy term.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\!\sum_{t,s,k}\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}y_{t,s,k}
      \;+\;\beta\!\sum_{t,p}\text{energy}_{t,p}x_{t,p}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t.}&\;\text{Constraints (R1)–(R11)}\\
& x_{t,p},y_{t,s,k},z_{t,l,k},w_{t,l,k},u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\},\;
  C\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisations are used where a condition depends on a binary route‑selection variable). The model simultaneously decides **which route each train should take**, **when it arrives/departs each station**, **how it traverses each possibly‑blocked segment**, and **whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode**, while minimising a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7. Practical Remarks  

| Issue | Suggested handling |
|-------|--------------------|
| **Choice of M** | Set *M* larger than the maximum possible interval index (e.g., *K + 1*). |
| **Multiple‑interval travel on a long segment** | Replace (R3) by \(\sum_k z_{t,l,k}= \tau_{t,l}\) where \(\tau_{t,l}\) is the required number of intervals (derived from min/max run times). Adjust (R8) accordingly. |
| **Energy for cruise (no accel/decel)** | Add a constant term \(e^{\text{cruise}}_{t,l}\) multiplied by \(z_{t,l,k}\) in (R11). |
| **Robustness to data uncertainty** | Introduce slack variables for delay, heavily penalised in the objective. |
| **Solver** | The model is ready for CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.; typical size depends on |\𝒯|, |\𝒮|, |\ℒ|, |\𝒦|. |

The formulation above provides a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming model** for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem under partial segment blockages, matching the narrative’s key aspects (conflict‑free timetable, bidirectional track sharing, rerouting, and energy‑aware speed control).

Text:
**Variables**

* \(x_{t,s,h}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) during time‑interval \(h\)  
* \(y_{t,s,h}\in\{0,1\}\) – direction indicator on segment \(s\) (0 = forward, 1 = reverse)  
* \(p_{t,s,h}\ge 0\) – speed factor of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) during interval \(h\) (relative to the baseline speed)  
* \(\text{arr}_{t,n}\ge 0\) – arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(n\) (in interval units)  
* \(\text{dep}_{t,n}\ge 0\) – departure time of train \(t\) from station \(n\)  
* \(z_{t_1,t_2,s,h}\in\{0,1\}\) – ordering binary for two trains on the same segment in opposite directions (1 ⇒ \(t_1\) passes before \(t_2\))  
* \(r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\) is rerouted on segment \(s\) (uses the opposite track)  
* \(c_{t}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\) is cancelled  

---

**Parameters (illustrative, replace with data)**  

* \(a_{t,s}\) – original planned arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream station of segment \(s\)  
* \(d_{t,s}\) – original planned departure time of train \(t\) from the upstream station of segment \(s\)  
* \(\tau_{t,s}\) – baseline travel time on segment \(s\) for train \(t\) (in intervals)  
* \([u_s , v_s]\) – disruption window (interval indices) on segment \(s\) (if no disruption set \(u_s=v_s=-1\))  
* \(\text{cap}_s\) – capacity (max number of trains) per direction on segment \(s\)  
* \(e_{t,s}\) – energy cost coefficient of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (per unit speed factor)  
* \(p^{\min}_{t,s}, p^{\max}_{t,s}\) – admissible speed factor bounds  
* \(\Delta_h\) – length of one time interval (hours)  
* \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) – weighting coefficients in the objective  

---

### Objective function  

\[
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\!\!\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(\text{arr}_{t,N_{\text{last}}}-a_{t,S_{\text{last}}}\bigr)(1-c_t)
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\!\!\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{h\in H}
e_{t,s}\; p_{t,s,h}\;\Delta_h\;(1-c_t)
\]

The first term penalises total delay (difference between realised arrival at the final station and the original schedule). The second term accounts for total energy consumption, proportional to the speed factor.

---

### Constraints  

1. **Flow conservation (link segment occupation with arrivals/departures)**  

   For every train \(t\), segment \(s\) and interval \(h\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \text{arr}_{t,s} - M\bigl(1-x_{t,s,h}\bigr) &\le h,\\
   h+1 &\le \text{arr}_{t,s+1}+M\bigl(1-x_{t,s,h}\bigr),
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall t,s,h
   \]

   where \(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., \(|H|\)).  

2. **Travel‑time feasibility (speed‑dependent)**  

   Let \(\displaystyle \bar p_{t,s}= \frac{\sum_{h}p_{t,s,h}x_{t,s,h}}{\sum_{h}x_{t,s,h}}\) (average speed factor).  
   Using a big‑M linearisation:

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \text{arr}_{t,s+1}-\text{dep}_{t,s} &\ge \frac{\tau_{t,s}}{p^{\max}_{t,s}}-M\Bigl(1-\sum_{h}x_{t,s,h}\Bigr),\\
   \text{arr}_{t,s+1}-\text{dep}_{t,s} &\le \frac{\tau_{t,s}}{p^{\min}_{t,s}}+M\Bigl(1-\sum_{h}x_{t,s,h}\Bigr),
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall t,s
   \]

3. **Blockage (partial segment blockage)**  

   If interval \(h\) lies inside the disruption window \([u_s,v_s]\),

   \[
   x_{t,s,h}\le r_{t,s}, \qquad \forall t,s,\; u_s\le h\le v_s .
   \]

   Trains may occupy the blocked segment only when rerouting (\(r_{t,s}=1\)).  

4. **Capacity per direction**  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \sum_{t}x_{t,s,h}\bigl(1-y_{t,s,h}\bigr) &\le \text{cap}_s,\\
   \sum_{t}x_{t,s,h}\,y_{t,s,h} &\le \text{cap}_s,
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall s,h .
   \]

5. **Bidirectional conflict avoidance (ordering)**  

   For any two distinct trains \(t_1,t_2\) that could be on the same segment at the same interval:

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   x_{t_1,s,h}+x_{t_2,s,h}-1 &\le z_{t_1,t_2,s,h}+ (1-y_{t_1,s,h})+y_{t_2,s,h},\\
   x_{t_1,s,h}+x_{t_2,s,h}-1 &\le 1-z_{t_1,t_2,s,h}+ y_{t_1,s,h}+(1-y_{t_2,s,h}),\\
   \text{arr}_{t_1,s+1}+1 &\le \text{arr}_{t_2,s}+M\bigl(1-z_{t_1,t_2,s,h}\bigr),
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall s,h,\; t_1<t_2 .
   \]

   The first two constraints force exactly one ordering variable to be 1 when both trains occupy the segment in opposite directions; the third enforces a one‑interval separation in time.  

6. **Speed limits**  

   \[
   p^{\min}_{t,s}\;x_{t,s,h}\le p_{t,s,h}\le p^{\max}_{t,s}\;x_{t,s,h},
   \qquad\forall t,s,h .
   \]

7. **Dwell‑time at stations**  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \text{dep}_{t,n}-\text{arr}_{t,n} &\ge \text{dwell}^{\min} - M c_t,\\
   \text{dep}_{t,n}-\text{arr}_{t,n} &\le \text{dwell}^{\max} + M c_t,
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall t,n .
   \]

8. **Reroute–direction linking**  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   r_{t,s} &\le \sum_{h}y_{t,s,h},\\
   \sum_{h}y_{t,s,h} &\le M\, r_{t,s},
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall t,s .
   \]

   If a train uses the opposite direction on any interval, reroute must be activated, and conversely rerouting implies at least one opposite‑direction occupation.  

9. **Cancellation**  

   \[
   \sum_{s,h}x_{t,s,h}\le M(1-c_t),\qquad
   \text{arr}_{t,n},\text{dep}_{t,n}\le M(1-c_t),\qquad\forall t,n .
   \]

   When \(c_t=1\) the train does not occupy any segment and its times are dummy.  

10. **Logical consistency**  

    \[
    r_{t,s}\le 1-c_t,\qquad\forall t,s .
    \]

    A cancelled train cannot be rerouted.  

---

### Summary  

The MILP above simultaneously decides:

* **Rescheduling decisions** – new arrival/departure times, possible train cancellations, and reordering of conflicting trains.  
* **Rerouting decisions** – whether a train uses the opposite track on a blocked segment.  
* **Speed‑management decisions** – speed factor on each occupied interval, influencing travel times and energy consumption.  

The objective minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and energy use while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable, respecting segment capacities, blockage restrictions, speed limits, dwell‑time requirements, and the logical coupling between rescheduling and speed management.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRS‑MP)**  
The model simultaneously decides (i) a feasible, conflict‑free timetable (arrival / departure times, train order, route choice) for the set of high‑speed trains that are affected by a **partial‑segment blockage** and (ii) a set of admissible speed profiles for each train that realise the chosen timetable while minimising energy consumption.  

The formulation below follows the description in the introduction and completes the missing data with reasonable standard assumptions (all marked **[Assumption]**).  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains to be scheduled, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of stations (including the origin/depot and the terminal). Index \(s\). |
| \(L\) | Set of line‑segments (track sections) between consecutive stations, indexed by \(\ell\). Each \(\ell\) connects a pair \((s,s')\). |
| \(P\) | Set of **routes** (i.e. possible sequences of segments) that a train may use through the disruption area. Index \(p\). For every train \(t\) a subset \(P_{t}\subseteq P\) is feasible (e.g. original route, opposite‑track detour, etc.). |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of **speed‑profile intervals** (time‑distance discretisation) used to linearise the speed‑energy relationship, indexed by \(k\). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\) | Set of **bidirectional conflict zones** (segments that become single‑track because of the blockage), indexed by \(b\). |
| \(\mathcal{D}\) | Set of discrete **delay‑bins** used for the piece‑wise linear energy model, indexed by \(d\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / source |
|--------|---------|-----------------------|
| \(\underline{a}_{t}\) | Original (planned) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. | Schedule |
| \(\overline{a}_{t}\) | Latest admissible departure time (e.g. due to crew limits). | [Assumption]  \(\overline{a}_{t}= \underline{a}_{t}+30\) min |
| \(\underline{s}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(s\). | Regulation (e.g. 2 min) |
| \(\overline{s}_{t,s}\) | Maximum dwell time (e.g. due to platform capacity). | [Assumption] 10 min |
| \(\tau_{\ell}^{\min},\ \tau_{\ell}^{\max}\) | Minimum / maximum travel time on segment \(\ell\) (corresponds to max / min admissible speeds). | Derived from line speed limits and train dynamics |
| \(\beta_{b}\) | Capacity of conflict zone \(b\) (normally 1 train at a time). | 1 |
| \(\Delta_{b}^{\text{start}},\ \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}}\) | Start / end time of the blockage on conflict zone \(b\). | Disruption data |
| \(e_{k}^{\text{dist}}\) | Distance covered in speed‑interval \(k\) (km). | Discretisation of 0‑1 km |
| \(e_{k}^{\text{time}}\) | Time required to travel \(e_{k}^{\text{dist}}\) at the speed associated with interval \(k\). | \(e_{k}^{\text{time}} = e_{k}^{\text{dist}}/v_{k}\) |
| \(\gamma_{d}^{\text{energy}}\) | Energy consumption (kWh) associated with delay‑bin \(d\). | Obtained from a piece‑wise linear energy‑vs‑delay curve (Assumption) |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) used for conditional constraints. | 10⁵ |
| \(c^{\text{delay}}\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (penalty). | 1 |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}\) | Weight for total energy consumption. | 1 |
| \(c^{\text{cancellation}}\) | Penalty for cancelling a train (very large). | 10⁶ |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(a_{t}\) | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Continuous | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(u_{t,s}\) | Continuous | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from station \(s\) (after dwell). |
| \(x_{t,p}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route (detour) \(p\in P_{t}\). |
| \(y_{t,\ell}^{k}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(\ell\) using speed‑interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) **enters** conflict zone \(b\) (i.e. uses the opposite track). |
| \(z_{t,b}^{\text{exit}}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) **exits** conflict zone \(b\). |
| \(\delta_{t}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) is **cancelled** (i.e. not served). |
| \(\theta_{t,d}\) | Binary | 1 if the delay of train \(t\) (relative to original schedule) falls into delay‑bin \(d\). |
| \(\eta_{t,\ell}^{k}\) | Continuous | **Travel time** of train \(t\) on segment \(\ell\) when interval \(k\) is chosen (equals \(e_{k}^{\text{time}}\) if \(y_{t,\ell}^{k}=1\)). |

---

## 4. Linearisation of Speed‑Energy Relationship  

The energy consumption of a train is modelled as a piece‑wise linear function of its **total delay** (the extra time incurred compared with the original schedule). This avoids a non‑linear term while preserving the trade‑off between early/late arrival and energy use.

\[
\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}} \theta_{t,d}=1\qquad\forall t\in T\tag{4.1}
\]

Let the **actual delay** of train \(t\) be  

\[
\Delta t_{t}= a_{t}-\underline{a}_{t}+\sum_{s\in S}(u_{t,s}-d_{t,s})\; .
\]

(The first term is the departure shift, the second term is the sum of dwell‑time extensions.) We linearise the mapping into bins:

\[
\underline{\Delta}_{d}\,\theta_{t,d}\le \Delta t_{t}\le \overline{\Delta}_{d}\,\theta_{t,d} \qquad\forall t,d\tag{4.2}
\]

where \([\underline{\Delta}_{d},\overline{\Delta}_{d}]\) is the range of delays covered by bin \(d\).  

The **energy cost** contributed by train \(t\) is then  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}} \gamma_{d}^{\text{energy}}\;\theta_{t,d}\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{4.3}
\]

---

## 5. Objective Function  

A bi‑objective (weighted‑sum) is adopted: minimise total weighted delay, total energy, and train cancellations.

\[
\min\; 
c^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta t_{t}
\;+\;c^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}
\;+\;c^{\text{cancellation}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}\tag{5.1}
\]

All three terms are linear because \(\Delta t_{t}\) and \(E_{t}\) are linear expressions defined above.

---

## 6. Core Constraints  

### 6.1 Feasibility of Routing  

Each train chooses exactly one routing (original or detour) and the corresponding set of segments is activated.

\[
\sum_{p\in P_{t}} x_{t,p}= 1-\delta_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{6.1}
\]

For a given routing \(p\) we pre‑compute an incidence parameter  

\[
\rho_{p,\ell}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if route }p\text{ uses segment }\ell\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Then  

\[
y_{t,\ell}^{k}\le \sum_{p\in P_{t}} \rho_{p,\ell}\,x_{t,p}\qquad\forall t,\ell,k \tag{6.2}
\]

If a segment is not on the selected route, all \(y_{t,\ell}^{k}=0\).

### 6.2 Travel‑Time and Speed‑Interval Selection  

Exactly one speed‑interval must be selected for each traversed segment.

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,\ell}^{k}= \sum_{p\in P_{t}} \rho_{p,\ell}\,x_{t,p}\qquad\forall t,\ell \tag{6.3}
\]

The travel time contributed by the selected interval is fixed:

\[
\eta_{t,\ell}^{k}= e_{k}^{\text{time}} \, y_{t,\ell}^{k}\qquad\forall t,\ell,k \tag{6.4}
\]

The total travel time on segment \(\ell\) for train \(t\) is

\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \eta_{t,\ell}^{k}\qquad\forall t,\ell \tag{6.5}
\]

and must respect the admissible bounds:

\[
\tau_{\ell}^{\min}\!\!\sum_{p} \rho_{p,\ell}x_{t,p}\le \tau_{t,\ell}\le \tau_{\ell}^{\max}\!\!\sum_{p} \rho_{p,\ell}x_{t,p}\qquad\forall t,\ell \tag{6.6}
\]

### 6.3 Temporal Flow (time‑line)  

The classic train‑flow linking arrival, travel, and departure:

For every pair of consecutive stations \((s,s')\) connected by segment \(\ell\):

\[
d_{t,s'} = u_{t,s} + \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \ell=(s,s')\;\text{used by }t \tag{6.7}
\]

Dwell‑time limits at each station:

\[
\underline{s}_{t,s}\,(1-\delta_{t}) \le u_{t,s}-d_{t,s} \le \overline{s}_{t,s}\,(1-\delta_{t})\qquad\forall t,s \tag{6.8}
\]

Departure from origin (first station) respects the original schedule window:

\[
\underline{a}_{t}\,(1-\delta_{t}) \le a_{t} \le \overline{a}_{t}\,(1-\delta_{t})\qquad\forall t \tag{6.9}
\]

Link origin decision variable with the first station:

\[
a_{t}= d_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}\qquad\forall t \tag{6.10}
\]

### 6.4 Conflict‑Zone (Bidirectional) Capacity  

Only one train may occupy a conflict zone \(b\) at any instant. We use a time‑indexing trick by introducing **order variables** for any two trains that could conflict on the same zone:

For any pair \((t,i)\) (distinct trains) that share conflict zone \(b\) (i.e. both routes contain \(\ell\in b\)), introduce binary \(\omega_{t,i,b}\) = 1 if train \(t\) passes *before* train \(i\) on zone \(b\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Enter time of }t\text{ on }b: &&\;e_{t,b}= u_{t,s_{\text{enter}}^{b}}\\
&\text{Exit  time of }t\text{ on }b: &&\;f_{t,b}= d_{t,s_{\text{exit}}^{b}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Capacity constraints (big‑M formulation):

\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{t,b} + \beta_{b}\,M \, \omega_{t,i,b} \le f_{i,b} + M(1-\omega_{t,i,b}) \qquad\forall t\neq i,\, b\\
e_{i,b} + \beta_{b}\,M \, (1-\omega_{t,i,b}) \le f_{t,b} + M\;\omega_{t,i,b} \qquad\forall t\neq i,\, b
\end{aligned}\tag{6.11}
\]

The above enforces a strict ordering; because \(\beta_{b}=1\) the two inequalities together guarantee that the intervals \([e_{t,b},f_{t,b})\) and \([e_{i,b},f_{i,b})\) do not overlap.

**Blockage window** – a train may not occupy the zone during the blockage unless it uses the opposite‑track detour. If train \(t\) uses the opposite track, the binary \(z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}\) is forced to 1; otherwise the train must respect the unavailable window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& e_{t,b}\ge \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}}\quad\text{or}\quad f_{t,b}\le \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} \quad\text{if }z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}=0 \\
& e_{t,b}\ge \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} \;,\; f_{t,b}\le \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}}\quad\text{if }z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}=1
\end{aligned}\tag{6.12}
\]

These are linearised with big‑M, e.g.

\[
e_{t,b} \ge \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} - M (1- z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}) \qquad\forall t,b \tag{6.12a}
\]

\[
f_{t,b} \le \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} + M (1- z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}) \qquad\forall t,b \tag{6.12b}
\]

If a train chooses the opposite‑track detour, the corresponding routing variable enforces \(z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}=1\); otherwise it must stay outside the blockage window.

### 6.5 Coupling of Routing and Conflict‑Zone Decision  

If route \(p\) is a **detour** that uses the opposite track for conflict zone \(b\), we set  

\[
z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}} \ge x_{t,p}\qquad\forall t,b,p\in P_{t}^{\text{detour on }b}\tag{6.13}
\]

If the route is the original one, \(z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}=0\). This is ensured by the complementarity constraint:

\[
z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}} \le \sum_{p\in P_{t}^{\text{detour on }b}} x_{t,p}\qquad\forall t,b \tag{6.14}
\]

### 6.6 Train Cancellation  

If a train is cancelled (\(\delta_{t}=1\)), all its timing variables are forced to zero (or any dummy value) and all binary usage variables are forced to 0:

\[
a_{t}\le M\delta_{t},\qquad d_{t,s},u_{t,s}\le M\delta_{t}\quad\forall s \tag{6.15}
\]

\[
x_{t,p}\le 1-\delta_{t},\qquad y_{t,\ell}^{k}\le 1-\delta_{t},\qquad z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}}\le 1-\delta_{t}\quad\forall p,\ell,k,b \tag{6.16}
\]

---

## 7. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& c^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta t_{t}+c^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}+c^{\text{cancellation}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t} \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{(6.1)–(6.16)} \\
& \sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\theta_{t,d}=1,\;\; \underline{\Delta}_{d}\theta_{t,d}\le\Delta t_{t}\le\overline{\Delta}_{d}\theta_{t,d}\qquad\forall t,d \\
& \text{All variables respect their domains: } \\
&\quad a_{t},d_{t,s},u_{t,s},\Delta t_{t},E_{t}\ge 0; \\
&\quad x_{t,p},y_{t,\ell}^{k},z_{t,b}^{\text{enter}},z_{t,b}^{\text{exit}},\delta_{t},\theta_{t,d},\omega_{t,i,b}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Modeling Assumptions (explicit)

| # | Description |
|---|-------------|
| A1 | **Piece‑wise linear energy‑vs‑delay**: Energy is approximated by a set of linear bins (Eq. 4.2‑4.3). |
| A2 | **Detour routes are pre‑enumerated** (set \(P_{t}\)). Only one detour (opposite‑track) is considered per conflict zone. |
| A3 | **Speed discretisation**: The continuous speed‑profile is approximated by a small set \(\mathcal{K}\) of speed‑intervals (e.g. 0 km/h‑50 km/h, 50‑100 km/h, …). |
| A4 | **Single‑track capacity** in each conflict zone during the blockage (\(\beta_{b}=1\)). |
| A5 | **Big‑M value** \(M\) is sufficiently large to deactivate constraints when binaries are zero (e.g., 10⁵ s). |
| A6 | **Cancellation** is allowed but heavily penalised, ensuring it is used only if the disruption makes service impossible. |
| A7 | **Dwell‑time bounds** are identical for all trains (modifiable per train if required). |
| A8 | **No overtaking** on a segment – trains keep their order on each line‑segment, which is enforced implicitly by the conflict‑zone ordering constraints (6.11). |
| A9 | **Headway constraints** outside the disrupted zone are omitted for brevity (they can be added analogously to (6.11) on any segment). |
| A10 | **Train dynamics** (acceleration/deceleration limits) are embedded inside the admissible travel‑time bounds \([\tau_{\ell}^{\min},\tau_{\ell}^{\max}]\). |

---

## 9. Remarks on Solving the Model  

* The formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program** (MILP).  
* The number of binary variables grows with \(|T|\,|P|\) (routing choices), \(|T|\,|L|\,|\mathcal{K}|\) (speed‑interval selections) and \(|T|^{2}\,|B|\) (pairwise ordering).  
* In practice the model is tackled with the **decomposition strategy** described in the paper:  
  1. **Master IP** – decides the binary routing and ordering variables;  
  2. **Sub‑problems** – for each train, a pure linear program that selects the speed‑intervals (the “train plan”).  
* The master‑sub‑problem structure fits a **Benders‑type decomposition** or a **column‑generation** scheme where each column is a feasible train plan (IP‑equivalent to MILP when a fine enough set of speed‑intervals is used).  

---

### End of Model  

The above MILP captures, in a single linear optimisation framework, the intertwined decisions of **train rescheduling** (departure/arrival times, route selection, conflict‑zone ordering) and **speed management** (choice of admissible speed intervals that generate executable speed profiles) while simultaneously minimising **total delay**, **energy consumption**, and **train cancellations** under a partial‑segment blockage disruption.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

---

### 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t*. |
| **S = {L,R}** | Sides of a partially blocked segment (Left / Right). |
| **Seg** | Set of track segments, indexed by *g*. |
| **B ⊆ Seg** | Blocked segments (partial blockage). |
| **F = Seg \ B** | Free segments. |
| **Nₜ** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including origin & final). |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed profiles, indexed by *k* (k = 1 … K). |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment: *(i,j) ∈ P, i≠j*. |

Derived sets:  

* **Segₜ** – segments traversed by train *t*.  
* **Segᵢⱼ = Segᵢ ∩ Segⱼ** – common segments of trains *i* and *j*.  

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|--------|---------|------|
| **a⁰ₜₙ** | Planned arrival of train *t* at station *n*. | s |
| **hₜₙ** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n*. | s |
| **τ_{g,k}** | Travel time on segment *g* when speed profile *k* is used. | s |
| **e_k** | Energy consumption of speed profile *k* (per segment). | kWh |
| **L_g** | Length of segment *g*. | km |
| **T_start , T_end** | Start / end of the disruption window on blocked segments. | s |
| **Δ** | Minimum safety headway between two trains on the same side. | s |
| **M** | Big‑M constant (≥ maximal schedule horizon, e.g. 10 000 s). |
| **w₁ , w₂** | Positive weights (w₁ + w₂ = 1) for delay and energy. |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* of blocked segment *g* (g∈B∩Segₜ). |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on any common side. |
| **a_{t,n}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| **d_{t,n}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **τ_{t,g}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **v_{t,g,k}** | binary | 1 ⇔ speed profile *k* is chosen for train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **x_{t,g}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies any side of blocked segment *g*. (x_{t,g}=∑ₛ r_{t,g,s}) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}
}
\]

*First term*: total delay (difference between actual and planned final arrival).  
*Second term*: total energy consumption of the selected speed profiles.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side on each blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Speed‑profile selection – exactly one profile per segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}\tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.3 Travel time linked to speed choice  

\[
\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\,v_{t,g,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}\tag{S2}
\]

#### 5.4 Time propagation along a train’s path  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of stations *(n,n⁺)∈Nₜ* (where *g(t,n)* is the connecting segment):

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,n} &= a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t,\; \forall n\in N_{t}\tag{D1}\\
a_{t,n^{+}} &= d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,g(t,n)} &&\forall t,\; \forall n\neq\text{final}\tag{D2}
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 5.5 Ordering on a shared side of a blocked segment  

Let **enterₜ,g** be the departure time from the upstream station of segment *g* (i.e. the time the train enters the side).  
For any *(i,j)∈P* and any common blocked segment *g∈Segᵢⱼ∩B* and side *s∈S*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i,g}+ \tau_{i,g}+ \Delta &\le \text{enter}_{j,g}+ M\bigl(1-o_{i,j}\bigr) + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s}- r_{j,g,s}\bigr)\\
\text{enter}_{j,g}+ \tau_{j,g}+ \Delta &\le \text{enter}_{i,g}+ M\bigl(o_{i,j}\bigr)   + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s}- r_{j,g,s}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (i,j),g,s\tag{O1}
\]

If both trains use the **same** side (*r_{i,g,s}=r_{j,g,s}=1*), the big‑M term \(M(2‑r‑r)\) vanishes and the constraints enforce a classic “either‑or’’ ordering via binary *o_{i,j}*. If they use different sides the term deactivates the constraint, allowing simultaneous occupation.

#### 5.6 Transitivity of ordering (prevent cycles)  

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,k}-o_{i,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall i,j,k\in T,\; i\neq j\neq k\tag{O2}
\]

#### 5.7 Disruption‑window exclusion  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{t,g} &\ge T_{\text{end}} - M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr)\\
\text{enter}_{t,g} &\le T_{\text{start}} + M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\tag{W1}
\]

If a train uses the blocked segment (*x_{t,g}=1*), its entry time must lie **outside** the interval \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\).  

#### 5.8 Binary indicator definition  

\[
x_{t,g}= \sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\tag{X1}
\]

#### 5.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,g} &\ge 0 \\
r_{t,g,s},\; o_{i,j},\; v_{t,g,k},\; x_{t,g} &\in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\tag{B1}
\]

---

### 6. Full MILP (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
      + w_{2}\sum_{t}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s} r_{t,g,s}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t} \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{k} v_{t,g,k}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S1}\\
&\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k}\tau_{g,k}v_{t,g,k} &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S2}\\
&d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t,\; n\in N_{t} \tag{D1}\\
&a_{t,n^{+}}=d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,g(t,n)} &&\forall t,\; n\neq\text{final} \tag{D2}\\
&\text{Ordering (O1) for all }(i,j)\in P,\; g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; s\in S\\
&\text{Transitivity (O2) for all distinct }i,j,k\\
&\text{Disruption window (W1) for all }t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\\
&x_{t,g}= \sum_{s} r_{t,g,s} &&\forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\\
& a,d,\tau \ge 0,\; r,o,v,x\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linear products have been eliminated by the big‑M linearisation in (O1).  

---

### 7. How to use  

1. **Prepare data** (sets, parameters, original timetable).  
2. **Choose weights** *w₁, w₂* (e.g. w₁=0.7 for punctuality, w₂=0.3 for energy).  
3. **Set a big‑M** large enough (e.g. 10 000 s).  
4. **Load the formulation** into any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).  
5. **Solve** – the binary variables give the side choice, speed profile, and ordering; the continuous variables give the new timetable.  
6. **Interpret** – total delay, total energy, and the detailed schedule are directly read from the solution.

---

**The model above fully captures**  

* binary routing decisions on blocked segments,  
* binary ordering to avoid conflicts on a shared side,  
* discrete speed‑profile selection with associated travel‑time and energy,  
* propagation of arrival/departure times respecting dwell times,  
* exclusion of the disruption time window, and  
* a weighted delay‑plus‑energy objective.  

Thus it provides a complete, linear MILP representation of the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockages.

Text:
**Variables**

*Sets*  

\(T\) – set of trains, \(t\in T\)  
\(S\) – ordered set of stations, \(s\in S\) (first station \(s_{0}\), last station \(s_{L}\))  
\(L\) – set of line‑segments, \(l\in L\) (each segment connects two consecutive stations)  
\(K\) – set of discrete time‑intervals, \(k\in K\)  

*Decision variables*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{t,l} &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train }t\text{ traverses segment }l\text{ (any direction)}\\
c_{t}   &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train }t\text{ is cancelled}\\[2mm]
a_{t,s} &\ge 0      &&\text{arrival time of train }t\text{ at station }s\\
d_{t,s} &\ge 0      &&\text{departure time of train }t\text{ from station }s\\[2mm]
v_{t,l,k}&\ge 0      &&\text{speed of train }t\text{ on segment }l\text{ during interval }k\\
\tau_{t,l,k}&\ge 0   &&\text{travel time of train }t\text{ on segment }l\text{ during interval }k\\[2mm]
z_{t_{1},t_{2},l}&\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if }t_{1}\text{ precedes }t_{2}\text{ on shared segment }l\\
\text{opp}_{t,l}&\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train }t\text{ uses segment }l\text{ opposite to the normal direction}
\end{aligned}
\]

*Auxiliary piece‑wise variables* (for linearising the speed–energy relation)  

\[
\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}\ge 0,\qquad i=1,\dots ,I\;(I=5)
\]

with \(\sum_{i}\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}=y_{t,l}\).

---

**Parameters (assumed given)**  

\(\text{len}_{l}\) – length of segment \(l\) (km)  
\(v^{\min }_{l},\,v^{\max }_{l}\) – speed limits on segment \(l\) (km/h)  
\(e_{l}\) – energy coefficient on segment \(l\) (kWh per \((\text{km/h})^{2}\!\cdot\)h)  
\(\text{dwell}_{t,s}\) – minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (min)  
\(\text{sched}_{t}\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at the last station (min)  
\(B\) – big‑M (larger than any feasible horizon, e.g. 10 000)  
\(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}, w^{\text{opp}}\) – objective weights  

Disruption data (partial blockage):  

segment \(l^{\text{blk}}\) is blocked in its normal direction during \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\).  

---

**Objective function**

\[
\min\;
w^{\text{delay}}\!\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,s_{L}}-\text{sched}_{t}\bigr)(1-c_{t})
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\!\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{k\in K}
e_{l}\,v_{t,l,k}\,\tau_{t,l,k}
\;+\;
w^{\text{opp}}\!\sum_{t\in T}\text{opp}_{t,l^{\text{blk}}}
\]

(The term \(v_{t,l,k}\tau_{t,l,k}= \text{len}_{l}\) can be used to linearise the quadratic energy term; otherwise a piece‑wise linear approximation via \(\lambda\) is employed.)

---

**Constraints**

1. **Cancellation logic**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s} &\le B(1-c_{t}) &&\forall t,s\\
d_{t,s} &\le B(1-c_{t}) &&\forall t,s\\
v_{t,l,k}&\le B(1-c_{t}) &&\forall t,l,k\\
\tau_{t,l,k}&\le B(1-c_{t}) &&\forall t,l,k\\
y_{t,l}&\le 1-c_{t} &&\forall t,l
\end{aligned}
\]

2. **Maximum number of cancellations**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T}c_{t}\le \text{max\_cancellations}
\]

3. **Dwell‑time relationship**  

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+\text{dwell}_{t,s}\;(1-c_{t})\qquad\forall t,s
\]

4. **Speed limits**  

\[
v^{\min }_{l}\,y_{t,l}\le v_{t,l,k}\le v^{\max }_{l}\,y_{t,l}
\qquad\forall t,l,k
\]

5. **Travel‑time definition (piece‑wise linearisation)**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,l,k}&=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}\,p_{i}^{l} &&\forall t,l,k\\
\tau_{t,l,k}&=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}\,\frac{\text{len}_{l}}{p_{i}^{l}} &&\forall t,l,k\\
\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}&=y_{t,l} &&\forall t,l,k\\
\lambda_{t,l,k}^{i}&\ge 0 &&\forall t,l,k,i
\end{aligned}
\]

\(p_{i}^{l}\) are the speed break‑points (e.g., 5 equally spaced values between \(v^{\min }_{l}\) and \(v^{\max }_{l}\)).

6. **Time propagation along the line**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_{0}}&=0 &&\forall t\\
a_{t,s_{j+1}}&=d_{t,s_{j}}+\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{t,l_{j},k}
\qquad\forall t,\;j=0,\dots ,|S|-2
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(l_{j}\) is the segment connecting \(s_{j}\) and \(s_{j+1}\).

7. **Conflict avoidance on shared segments**  

For every pair \(t_{1}\neq t_{2}\) and segment \(l\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{t_{2},l}&\ge \text{exit}_{t_{1},l}-B\bigl(1-z_{t_{1},t_{2},l}\bigr)\\
\text{enter}_{t_{1},l}&\ge \text{exit}_{t_{2},l}-B\,z_{t_{1},t_{2},l}\\
z_{t_{1},t_{2},l}&\le y_{t_{1},l},\quad
z_{t_{1},t_{2},l}\le y_{t_{2},l}
\end{aligned}
\]

where  

\(\text{enter}_{t,l}=a_{t,s^{\text{start}}_{l}}\) and \(\text{exit}_{t,l}=d_{t,s^{\text{end}}_{l}}\).

8. **Disruption window – forbid normal direction**  

For the blocked segment \(l^{\text{blk}}\) and each interval \(k\) that overlaps \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\):

\[
v_{t,l^{\text{blk}},k}\le B\,\text{opp}_{t,l^{\text{blk}}}\qquad\forall t
\]

Outside the window the usual speed limits apply.  

Link opposite‑direction usage to routing:

\[
\text{opp}_{t,l^{\text{blk}}}\le y_{t,l^{\text{blk}}},\qquad
\text{opp}_{t,l^{\text{blk}}}\in\{0,1\}
\]

9. **Routing cardinality (each train follows its predefined path)**  

If train \(t\) must traverse a known set \(L_{t}\subseteq L\):

\[
\sum_{l\in L} y_{t,l}=|L_{t}|\qquad\forall t,\qquad
y_{t,l}=1\;\;\forall l\in L_{t}
\]

(If multiple feasible routes exist, the equality is replaced by a set‑covering formulation.)

---

**Assumptions (clearly stated)**  

* Time is discretised into equal intervals \(K\) (e.g., 5‑min slots).  
* Speed–energy relation is linearised by a 5‑point piece‑wise approximation; the exact quadratic term can be used if a quadratic solver is available.  
* The disruption blocks only one direction of a single segment; opposite‑direction travel is allowed but penalised.  
* All trains share the same ordered path (for simplicity); the model can be extended to multiple routes by adding binary routing variables per possible route.  
* Big‑M \(B\) is chosen larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min).  

The presented formulation constitutes a complete mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) that simultaneously decides train cancellations, routing (including possible opposite‑direction usage), arrival/departure times, and speed profiles while minimising a weighted sum of total delay, energy consumption, and disruption‑penalty, and guaranteeing conflict‑free operation under partial segment blockages.

Text:
**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑type formulation)**  

The model below follows the description in the prompt.  
It schedules a set of trains over a finite prediction horizon, decides **how many cars each train uses (flexible composition)**, **which stations each train stops at (stop‑skipping)** and **how rolling‑stock units are circulated** while respecting **time‑varying passenger demand** at every line section.  

All notation, variables, objective terms and constraints are listed explicitly.  
Where data are not given in the prompt, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption X)**.

---

## 1. Index Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains that may be operated in the horizon (indexed by \\(t\\)). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of stations on the line (indexed by \\(s\\)). |
| \\(L\\) | Set of line sections (ordered pairs of consecutive stations) \\(l=(s,s+1)\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible train‑composition types (different numbers of cars) (indexed by \\(k\\)). |
| \\(R\\) | Set of rolling‑stock units (individual train‑sets) (indexed by \\(r\\)). |
| \\(P\\) | Set of demand‑time‑intervals (piece‑wise constant approximation of passenger demand) (indexed by \\(p\\)). |
| \\(H\\) | Set of MPC horizons (normally one step, but we keep the notation for multi‑step). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \\(C_k\\) | Capacity (passenger seats) of composition type \\(k\\). | (Assumption 1): \\(C_k = k \times c_{\text{car}}\) with \\(c_{\text{car}} = 100\\) seats. |
| \\(c^{\text{run}}_{l}\\) | Minimum running time (seconds) to travel section \\(l\\) with a **full‑speed** train. | (Assumption 2): derived from line geometry. |
| \\(c^{\text{dwell}}_{s}\\) | Minimum dwell time (seconds) at station \\(s\\) for opening/closing doors. | (Assumption 3): e.g. 30 s. |
| \\(c^{\text{dwell}}_{s,\max}\\) | Maximum allowed dwell time (seconds) at station \\(s\\). | (Assumption 4): e.g. 120 s. |
| \\(d_{l,p}\\) | Expected passenger **arrival** demand (persons) on section \\(l\\) during interval \\(p\\). | Obtained from historic data, piece‑wise constant. |
| \\(h_{p}\\) | Length (seconds) of demand interval \\(p\\). | User‑defined (e.g. 15 min = 900 s). |
| \\(M\\) | Large constant for big‑M formulations (e.g. 10⁶). |
| \\(B\\) | Maximum number of trains that can be simultaneously on the line (capacity of signalling). | (Assumption 5). |
| \\(R^{\text{avail}}_r\\) | Availability binary of rolling‑stock unit \\(r\\) at the start of the horizon (1 if free). | From rolling‑stock management system. |
| \\(c^{\text{turn}}_r\\) | Minimum turn‑around time (seconds) required after a train finishes service before it can be reused. | (Assumption 6). |
| \\(c^{\text{op}}_k\\) | Operating cost per train of composition \\(k\\) (fuel/energy, crew, etc.). | (Assumption 7). |
| \\(c^{\text{wait}}\\) | Penalty cost per passenger‑minute of waiting. | (Assumption 8). |
| \\(c^{\text{trav}}\\) | Penalty cost per passenger‑minute of in‑train travel time (reflects passenger discomfort). | (Assumption 9). |
| \\(c^{\text{deviation}}\\) | Penalty cost per second of deviation from the nominal timetable (e.g. to keep service regular). | (Assumption 10). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{t,k}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses composition type \\(k\\). |
| \\(y_{t,r}\\) | Binary | 1 if rolling‑stock unit \\(r\\) is assigned to train \\(t\\). |
| \\(z_{t,s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) stops at station \\(s\\) (stop‑skipping). |
| \\(a_{t,s}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at station \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t,s}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from station \\(s\\). |
| \\(w_{l,p}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Passenger waiting time** accumulated on section \\(l\\) during interval \\(p\\). |
| \\(u_{l,p}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Passenger travel time** (in‑train) for passengers boarding on section \\(l\\) during interval \\(p\\). |
| \\(e_{t}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Operating cost** of train \\(t\\). |
| \\(v_{t}\\) | Continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Timetable deviation** of train \\(t\\) from its nominal schedule (absolute value). |

All binary variables enforce integer decisions (train composition, rolling‑stock assignment, stop‑skipping). The remaining variables are linear continuous.

---

## 4. Model Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Capacity linearity** – passenger capacity of a train equals the number of cars times a constant car capacity.  
2. **Running time** – the travel time on a section is the minimum running time plus a possible delay due to headway constraints (modelled later).  
3. **Dwell time limits** – each stop must respect a minimum and a maximum dwell time.  
4. **Demand approximation** – passenger arrival demand on each section is constant within each interval \\(p\\).  
5. **Signalling capacity** – at most \\(B\\) trains can occupy the line simultaneously (headway constraint).  
6. **Rolling‑stock turn‑around** – after a train finishes at the terminal, the same unit can be reused only after a minimum turn‑around time.  
7. **Cost linearity** – operating cost, waiting‑time cost, travel‑time cost and deviation cost are linear in the corresponding quantities.  
8. **No overtaking** – trains travel in the same direction on a single‑track line; ordering is preserved (implemented via head‑way constraints).  
9. **Zero‑initial‑stock** – at the beginning of the horizon each train may start from a depot (or a terminal) with a known time; this is encoded in parameters \\(a^{0}_{t}\\).  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{k\in K} c^{\text{op}}_{k}\,x_{t,k}}_{\text{Operating cost}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{p\in P} c^{\text{wait}}\; w_{l,p}}_{\text{Passenger waiting penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{p\in P} c^{\text{trav}}\; u_{l,p}}_{\text{Passenger travel‑time penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} c^{\text{deviation}}\; v_{t}}_{\text{Timetable regularity penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables (the waiting/travel times will be expressed linearly in Section 6).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Train‑composition selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T                                    \tag{C1}
\]

Each train uses exactly one composition type.

### 6.2. Rolling‑stock assignment  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} y_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T                                    \tag{C2}
\]

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,r}\le R^{\text{avail}}_r \qquad \forall r\in R                \tag{C3}
\]

A rolling‑stock unit can be assigned to at most one train during the horizon (if it is available).

### 6.3. Stop‑skipping (binary stop decision)  

If a train does **not** stop at a station, dwell time is zero:

\[
d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le M\,z_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S                \tag{C4}
\]

\[
d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\ge c^{\text{dwell}}_{s}\,z_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S   \tag{C5}
\]

\[
d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le c^{\text{dwell}}_{s,\max}\,z_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{C6}
\]

If \\(z_{t,s}=0\\) the inequality forces \\(d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}\\) (no dwell).

### 6.4. Travel‑time propagation  

For every consecutive pair of stations \\((s,s')\\) that belong to a line section \\(l\\):

\[
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s}+c^{\text{run}}_{l}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; l=(s,s')\in L \tag{C7}
\]

If the train skips station \\(s\\) (\\(z_{t,s}=0\\)), the departure time equals arrival time, therefore the above still holds.

### 6.5. Head‑way (signalling) constraints  

Let \\(h_{t,t'}\\) be the required minimum head‑way (seconds) between any two consecutive trains on the same line (assumed constant, e.g. 120 s). For any ordered pair \\((t,t')\\) with \\(t\\) scheduled **before** \\(t'\\) (ordering can be pre‑computed from nominal schedule):

\[
a_{t',s}\ge d_{t,s}+h_{t,t'}\qquad \forall s\in S,\; (t,t')\in \mathcal{O} \tag{C8}
\]

where \\(\mathcal{O}\\) is the set of ordered train pairs (derived from nominal timetable). This enforces the signalling capacity \\(B\\) indirectly; alternatively a cumulative‑train‑on‑track constraint can be added:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \mathbf{1}\bigl\{ a_{t,s}\le \tau \le d_{t,s}\bigr\}\le B \qquad \forall \tau\in[0,H_{\max}] \tag{C9}
\]

In a MILP this is approximated by discretising time; for brevity we keep the pairwise head‑way (C8).

### 6.6. Capacity – passenger boarding feasibility  

The number of passengers that can board a train on section \\(l\\) during interval \\(p\\) cannot exceed the train’s remaining seat capacity. Let \\(q_{t,l,p}\\) be the **boarded passengers** variable (continuous, ≥0).  

First, compute the **available seats** of train \\(t\\) (capacity of its composition):

\[
\sum_{k\in K} C_k\,x_{t,k}= \text{Cap}_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{C10}
\]

Then, for each train, the sum of boarded passengers over all sections it traverses in interval \\(p\\) must be ≤ capacity:

\[
\sum_{l\in L} q_{t,l,p}\le \text{Cap}_t \qquad \forall t\in T,\; p\in P \tag{C11}
\]

Boarding is only possible if the train actually stops at the upstream station of the section. Using binary stop variables we linearise:

\[
q_{t,l,p}\le d_{l,p}\; M\; z_{t,\,\text{up}(l)} \qquad \forall t,l,p \tag{C12}
\]

where \\(\text{up}(l)\\) denotes the upstream station of section \\(l\\) and \\(d_{l,p}\\) is the demand (passengers) on that section during interval \\(p\\).  

**Passenger waiting time** on section \\(l\\) during interval \\(p\\) is the demand that could not board any train:

\[
w_{l,p}= d_{l,p}-\sum_{t\in T} q_{t,l,p}\qquad \forall l,p \tag{C13}
\]

**Passenger travel time** is the sum of in‑train travel times for boarded passengers. The travel time for a passenger boarding on section \\(l\\) and alighting at the downstream terminal is approximated by the travel time of the train from the downstream station of \\(l\\) to the terminal. Let \\(\tau_{t,l}\\) be the travel time of train \\(t\\) from the downstream station of \\(l\\) to the terminal (computed from the arrival/departure variables). Then:

\[
u_{l,p}= \sum_{t\in T} q_{t,l,p}\; \tau_{t,l}\qquad \forall l,p \tag{C14}
\]

Because \\(\tau_{t,l}\\) is a linear expression of arrival/departure times (difference of two variables), (C14) stays linear.

### 6.7. Rolling‑stock turn‑around  

If a rolling‑stock unit finishes service at time \\(a_{t,\text{terminal}}\\), it cannot be reused before \\(a_{t,\text{terminal}}+c^{\text{turn}}_r\\). This is enforced by linking assignments of the same unit to different trains (big‑M):

\[
a_{t',\text{origin}} \ge a_{t,\text{terminal}}+c^{\text{turn}}_r - M\bigl(2-y_{t,r}-y_{t',r}\bigr) \qquad \forall r,\; t\neq t' \tag{C15}
\]

If both \\(y_{t,r}=y_{t',r}=1\\) the inequality is active; otherwise the big‑M deactivates it.

### 6.8. Timetable deviation  

Let \\(\hat a_{t,s}\\) and \\(\hat d_{t,s}\\) be the **nominal** arrival/departure times (e.g., from the schedule used at the beginning of the MPC step). Deviation variables are defined as absolute values:

\[
v_{t}\ge a_{t,s}-\hat a_{t,s}\qquad \forall t,s \tag{C16a}
\]
\[
v_{t}\ge \hat a_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\qquad \forall t,s \tag{C16b}
\]

(Only one station (e.g., the first) is needed, but we keep the generic form.)

### 6.9. Variable domains  

\[
x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\} \qquad \forall t,k,r,s
\]

\[
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},q_{t,l,p},w_{l,p},u_{l,p},v_{t}\ge 0 \qquad \forall \text{appropriate indices}
\]

---

## 7. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t,k} c^{\text{op}}_{k}x_{t,k}
        +\sum_{l,p} c^{\text{wait}}\, w_{l,p}
        +\sum_{l,p} c^{\text{trav}}\, u_{l,p}
        +\sum_{t} c^{\text{deviation}}\, v_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } & \text{(C1)–(C16)} \\
& x_{t,k},y_{t,r},z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
  a_{t,s},d_{t,s},q_{t,l,p},w_{l,p},u_{l,p},v_{t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on the MPC implementation  

* **Prediction horizon** – The MILP is solved at each MPC step for the next \\(H\\) seconds (e.g., 15 min). Only the first control action (the departure times and stop decisions for the first few minutes) is implemented; the horizon then slides forward.  
* **Presolve techniques** (as mentioned in the source text) can be applied before solving:  
  1. **Eliminate infeasible composition‑type‑train pairs** using capacity‑demand dominance.  
  2. **Fix stop‑skipping variables** for stations with negligible demand (set \\(z_{t,s}=0\\)).  
  3. **Aggregate low‑traffic sections** into a single “dummy” section to reduce \\(|L|\\).  
  4. **Pre‑assign rolling‑stock units** that are already at the depot, fixing \\(y_{t,r}=1\\) for those.  

These reductions lower the number of binary variables that a learning model (e.g., an LSTM) must predict.

* **Learning‑assisted integer fixing** – An LSTM trained on historic optimal solutions predicts a subset of the binary variables (e.g., \\(x_{t,k}\\) and \\(z_{t,s}\\)). Those predictions are then **fixed** in the MILP; the remaining continuous variables (arrival/departure times, passenger flows) are obtained by solving the reduced MILP, guaranteeing feasibility.

* **Scalability** – Because the objective and all constraints are linear, commercial MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) can exploit the structure, and the reduced binary space makes real‑time solution times (seconds) achievable for typical metro lines (≈10–20 trains, 15–30 stations).

---

### End of Model

The formulation above captures **time‑varying passenger demand**, **flexible train composition**, **stop‑skipping**, **rolling‑stock circulation**, and **MPC‑type receding‑horizon control**, exactly as described in the background text. All required components (variables, objective, constraints, and assumptions) are presented explicitly.

**Sets**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T & = \{i\}\; \text{set of trains} \\[2pt]
\mathcal S & = \{s\}\; \text{set of track segments (including possible detour segments)}\\[2pt]
\mathcal N & = \{n\}\; \text{set of stations ordered along the line}\\[2pt]
\mathcal P & = \{p\}\; \text{set of admissible speed‑plan profiles for each train}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Parameters**

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_i^{0}               &\; \text{original planned arrival time of train } i \text{ at the first station}\\
d_i^{0}               &\; \text{original planned departure time of train } i \text{ at the first station}\\[2pt]
t_{i s}^{0}           &\; \text{baseline travel time of train } i \text{ on segment } s\\[2pt]
u_s,\;v_s             &\; \text{start and end (in minutes) of the blockage on segment } s
                       \qquad (u_s=-1,\;v_s=-1 \text{ if segment } s \text{ is never blocked})\\[2pt]
e_{i p}               &\; \text{energy consumption (or cost) of using speed plan } p \text{ for train } i\\[2pt]
\tau_{i s p}          &\; \text{extra travel time (positive) or reduction (negative) on segment } s
                       \text{ when train } i \text{ follows plan } p\\[2pt]
c_{i j s}             &=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if trains } i \text{ and } j \text{ travel on segment } s\text{ in opposite directions}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}\\[2pt]
\text{bigM}           &\; \text{a sufficiently large constant for linearisation}\\[2pt]
\lambda_{\text{delay}},\;\lambda_{\text{energy}} &\; \text{weights in the objective (default = 1)}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Decision variables**

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{i p}               &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train } i \text{ uses speed plan } p\\[2pt]
A_{i n}               &\ge 0   &&\text{arrival time of train } i \text{ at station } n\\[2pt]
D_{i n}               &\ge 0   &&\text{departure time of train } i \text{ at station } n\\[2pt]
y_{i s}               &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train } i \text{ traverses segment } s\\[2pt]
r_{i s}               &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{1 if train } i \text{ reroutes around blocked segment } s\\[2pt]
z_{i j s}             &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{ordering variable: 1 if train } i \text{ passes segment } s
                       \text{ before train } j\\[2pt]
\end{aligned}
\]

The effective travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) is

\[
\widehat{t}_{i s}=t_{i s}^{0}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\tau_{i s p}\,x_{i p}.
\]

---

**Objective function**

\[
\min \;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\bigl(A_{i\,n_{1}}-a_i^{0}\bigr)
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P} e_{i p}\,x_{i p}
\]

where \(n_{1}\) denotes the first station (the delay is measured with respect
to the original arrival at that station).

---

**Constraints**

1. **Exactly one speed plan per train**

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P} x_{i p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T .
\]

2. **Segment‑usage vs. rerouting**

\[
y_{i s}+r_{i s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T,\;s\in\mathcal S .
\]

3. **Timing consistency along a segment**  
   Let \((u(s),v(s))\) be the upstream and downstream stations of segment \(s\).

\[
D_{i\,u(s)}+\widehat{t}_{i s}\le A_{i\,v(s)}+(1-y_{i s})\;\text{bigM}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T,\;s\in\mathcal S .
\]

4. **First‑station anchoring**

\[
A_{i\,n_{1}}=a_i^{0}, \qquad D_{i\,n_{1}}=d_i^{0}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T .
\]

5. **Minimum dwell time \(\delta\) (e.g. 2 min)**

\[
D_{i n}\ge A_{i n}+\delta \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T,\;n\in\mathcal N .
\]

6. **Blockage (partial segment blockage)**
   If segment \(s\) is blocked during \([u_s,v_s]\) the train may be on that
   segment only when it has rerouted:

\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{i\,u(s)} &\le u_s + \text{bigM}\, r_{i s} \qquad\forall i,s\text{ with }u_s\ge0,\\
D_{i\,u(s)} &\ge v_s - \text{bigM}\, r_{i s} \qquad\forall i,s\text{ with }v_s\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

7. **Conflict ordering for opposite‑direction trains**

   *a) Exactly one ordering direction*

\[
z_{i j s}+z_{j i s}=1 \qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S\text{ with }c_{i j s}=1 .
\]

   *b) Temporal precedence*

\[
D_{i\,u(s)}+\widehat{t}_{i s}\le A_{j\,u(s)}+\text{bigM}\,(1-z_{i j s})
\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;s\in\mathcal S\text{ with }c_{i j s}=1 .
\]

8. **Capacity of a segment (at most one train per direction)**

\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T} y_{i s}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in\mathcal S .
\]

9. **At most one reroute per train**

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i s}\le 1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal T .
\]

---

**Assumptions (clearly stated)**  

* The line is linear; each segment connects two consecutive stations.  
* All trains share the same set of speed plans; the parameters \(\tau_{i s p}\) capture
  the influence of a plan on the travel time of a particular train on a particular segment.  
* Blockage windows are known a‑priori and are deterministic.  
* Energy cost depends only on the chosen speed plan (no intra‑segment variation).  
* The big‑M constant is chosen large enough to deactivate constraints when the
  associated binary variable forces the condition to be irrelevant.  

The model above is a **complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation**
for the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial
segment blockages, incorporating bidirectional conflict resolution, rerouting
decisions, delay minimisation, and energy‑efficiency objectives.
