Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model)*  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Index sets and basic data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T**   | Set of trains  \(t\in T\) |
| **S**   | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD‑sections)  \(s\in S\) |
| **V**   | Set of stations (a subset of *S*)  \(v\in V\) |
| **N(s)**| Set of neighbour sections of *s* (up‑stream and down‑stream) |
| **\(\mathcal{P}_t\)**| Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (its route) – i.e. \(\mathcal{P}_t=(s_{t,1},s_{t,2},\dots ,s_{t,|P_t|})\) |
| **\(\mathcal{K}_t\)**| Set of admissible speed‑profile “modes’’ for train *t* (e.g. *cruise*, *slow‑down*, *stop*) |
| **\(\mathcal{B}\)**| Set of binary decision variables (see below) |

**Parameters (given by the timetable, infrastructure and train characteristics).**  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(L_s\) | Physical length of section *s* | [km] |
| \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\) | Maximum admissible speed of train *t* in section *s* (speed limit, rolling‑stock limit) | [km/h] |
| \(a^{\text{acc}}_{t}\) | Maximum acceleration of train *t* (positive) | [km/h²] |
| \(a^{\text{brk}}_{t}\) | Maximum service braking deceleration of train *t* (positive) | [km/h²] |
| \(d^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v)\) | Braking distance needed to stop from speed *v* (continuous function) – linearised later | [km] |
| \(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,v}\) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *v* | [s] |
| \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum headway (separation) required **at the entry of section *s*** when the preceding train is travelling at speed \(v\). For DTG this is the *speed‑dependent* braking distance plus a safety margin \(\Delta\).  | [s] |
| \(M\) | A big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time) | – |
| \(T^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\) | Original (possibly delayed) arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** boundary of section *s* (from the input timetable) | [s] |
| \(T^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}^{\text{dep}}\) | Original departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** boundary of section *s* (i.e. exit time) | [s] |
| \(\beta_{t,s}\) | Binary flag = 1 if section *s* is a **switch** (or a TTD‑section) for which a different safety rule applies; 0 otherwise. | – |

*Assumptions* (explicitly stated):  

1. The train route is fixed – only timing (retiming) and ordering (re‑sequencing) can be changed.  
2. Speed changes are represented by a **piece‑wise linear speed profile** per section; each profile is selected from a small set \(\mathcal{K}_t\).  
3. Braking distance is linearised: \(d^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v)\approx \alpha_{t} v + \gamma_{t}\) (parameters obtained from a linear regression on the true curve).  
4. Safety headway \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}\) is computed as \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}= \frac{d^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v_{t,s}^{\text{up}})}{v_{t,s}^{\text{up}}}+ \Delta\) where \(v_{t,s}^{\text{up}}\) is the speed of the **preceding** train when it reaches the upstream boundary of *s*.  
5. All times are measured from a common reference (e.g. midnight).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(A_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Actual arrival time** of train *t* at the upstream boundary of section *s* (after rescheduling). |
| \(D_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Actual departure time** (exit time) of train *t* from the downstream boundary of section *s*. |
| \(v_{t,s}^{k}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Speed of train *t* while traversing section *s* under speed‑profile mode \(k\in\mathcal{K}_t\). |
| \(x_{t,s}^{k}\) | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses speed‑profile mode \(k\) in section *s*, 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}\) | Binary | 1 if train *t₁* is scheduled **before** train *t₂* on (i.e. occupies) section *s*, 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{t_1,t_2,s}\) | Binary | 1 if a **re‑ordering** (swap) is performed between *t₁* and *t₂* on section *s* (i.e. the natural order given by the original timetable is reversed). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train *t* with respect to its original schedule (sum of all section‑wise delays). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Objective function  

The primary operational goal is to **minimise total accumulated delay** (or any weighted version).  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} \; w_t \; \Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}}
\]

- \(w_t\) is a priority weight (default = 1).  
- \(\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\) is defined later as the difference between the final (exit) time of the train and its original planned exit time at the last section of its route.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Core constraints  

#### 4.1  Route‑time propagation (travel time in a section)  

For each train *t* and each traversed section *s = s_{t,i}* :

\[
D_{t,s} = A_{t,s} + \frac{L_s}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_t} v_{t,s}^{k}\,x_{t,s}^{k}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t
\tag{1}
\]

The denominator is the selected speed (only one \(k\) can be active – see (4) below).

#### 4.2  Speed‑profile selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_t} x_{t,s}^{k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t
\tag{2}
\]

\[
v_{t,s}^{k}\le v^{\max}_{t,s}\,x_{t,s}^{k} \qquad \forall t,s,k
\tag{3}
\]

If a “stop’’ mode is present, its speed is forced to zero and the travel time becomes the dwell time (see §4.4).

#### 4.3  Speed‑dependent braking distance (linearised)  

For every train *t* and speed mode *k* that is **braking** (i.e. the train is preparing to stop at the downstream end of the section) we define a **brake‑indication point** \(B_{t,s}\) (time when the brake is applied). Using the linearised braking distance:

\[
B_{t,s}= D_{t,s} - \frac{ \alpha_{t}\,v_{t,s}^{k}+ \gamma_{t}}{v_{t,s}^{k}} \qquad \forall t,s,k\text{ with braking}
\tag{4}
\]

The term \(\frac{d^{\text{brk}}}{v}\) is the time needed to travel the braking distance at speed \(v\).  

#### 4.4  Minimum dwell time at stations  

If *s* is a station \(v\in V\) :

\[
D_{t,s} \ge A_{t,s} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,v} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s=v
\tag{5}
\]

If a “stop’’ mode is selected, the travel time (1) collapses to the dwell time only.

#### 4.5  **Speed‑dependent separation (headway) constraints** – the heart of DTG  

Consider two distinct trains \(t_1,t_2\) that share a common section *s* (i.e. \(s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2}\)). Exactly one of them must be scheduled first. The binary variable \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}\) encodes the order:

\[
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s}=1 \qquad \forall t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2}
\tag{6}
\]

If \(t_1\) precedes \(t_2\) on *s* we enforce that the **arrival** of \(t_2\) does not occur earlier than the **brake‑indication point** of \(t_1\) plus the required safety headway:

\[
A_{t_2,s} \;\ge\; B_{t_1,s} \;+\; \tau^{\text{head}}_{t_1,s}\;-\; M\,(1-y_{t_1,t_2,s}) \qquad \forall t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2}
\tag{7}
\]

Analogously, when \(t_2\) is first:

\[
A_{t_1,s} \;\ge\; B_{t_2,s} \;+\; \tau^{\text{head}}_{t_2,s}\;-\; M\,(1-y_{t_2,t_1,s})
\tag{8}
\]

The headway \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}\) is **speed‑dependent** and computed from the braking distance of the leading train (see Assumption 4). For a switch or TTD‑section (\(\beta_{t,s}=1\)) a possibly tighter headway \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}^{\text{switch}}\) can be used.

#### 4.6  Re‑ordering (swap) variables – optional but useful for real‑time traffic management  

If the dispatcher decides to **swap** the order of two trains on a given section, the binary \(z_{t_1,t_2,s}\) is set to 1 and the corresponding headway constraints are relaxed (the safety margin is increased to a pre‑defined “swap‑penalty’’ \(\psi\)):

\[
A_{t_2,s} \ge B_{t_1,s} + \psi - M(1-z_{t_1,t_2,s}) \qquad \forall t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2}
\tag{9}
\]

and

\[
z_{t_1,t_2,s} \le y_{t_1,t_2,s} \qquad
z_{t_1,t_2,s} \le y_{t_2,t_1,s}
\tag{10}
\]

Thus a swap can only be performed if the original order is overridden.

#### 4.7  Continuity of arrival/departure times along the route  

For each train *t* and every pair of consecutive sections \((s_{t,i},s_{t,i+1})\) in its route:

\[
A_{t,s_{t,i+1}} \ge D_{t,s_{t,i}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; i=1,\dots,|P_t|-1
\tag{11}
\]

Equality holds in an optimal solution (no unnecessary waiting) unless a deliberate hold is introduced (e.g. to create a larger headway).

#### 4.8  Definition of total delay  

Let \(s^{\text{last}}_t\) be the last section of train *t*’s route. The final exit time is \(D_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t}\). The original planned exit time is \(T^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t}^{\text{dep}}\). Then:

\[
\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}= D_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} - T^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t}^{\text{dep}} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{12}
\]

If a train finishes earlier than originally scheduled, \(\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\) is forced to be non‑negative (no “negative delay” reward) by the objective (or by adding \(\max\{0,\cdot\}\) using an auxiliary variable).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Additional practical constraints  

| Constraint | Reason |
|------------|--------|
| **Capacity of a section** – at most one train can occupy a section at any instant. Implemented by the ordering binaries \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}\) and (7)–(8). |
| **Maximum allowed delay** – for passenger‑service quality: \(\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\le \overline{\Delta}_t\). |
| **Priority handling** – for high‑priority trains (e.g. passenger vs. freight): set a large weight \(w_t\) or enforce \(\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}=0\) for the priority set. |
| **Switch‑specific safety** – if \(\beta_{t,s}=1\) (switch/TTD), replace \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}\) by a stricter value \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{t,s}^{\text{switch}}\) in (7)–(8). |
| **Speed‑limit adherence** – already covered by (3); optionally add a lower bound \(v_{t,s}^{k}\ge v^{\min}_{t,s}\) for cruising modes. |
| **Binary linearisation of product terms** – the term \(\frac{L_s}{\sum_k v_{t,s}^{k}x_{t,s}^{k}}\) is non‑linear. In practice it is linearised by pre‑computing travel‑time coefficients for each mode: \(\theta_{t,s}^{k}=L_s/v_{t,s}^{k}\) and then using \(\sum_k \theta_{t,s}^{k} x_{t,s}^{k}\) (since exactly one mode is active). This yields a linear travel‑time expression: \(\displaystyle D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_t}\theta_{t,s}^{k}x_{t,s}^{k}\). |
| **Big‑M selection** – \(M\) must be larger than the maximum possible schedule horizon (e.g. 24 h = 86 400 s). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Complete linearised formulation  

Using the travel‑time coefficients \(\theta_{t,s}^{k}=L_s/v_{t,s}^{k}\) (pre‑computed) and the linear braking‑time coefficient \(\beta_{t}^{k}= \frac{\alpha_{t} v_{t,s}^{k}+\gamma_{t}}{v_{t,s}^{k}}\) (also pre‑computed for each mode that represents braking), the model becomes fully linear:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{t\in T} w_t \Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}\quad 
& D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_t}\theta_{t,s}^{k}x_{t,s}^{k} &&\forall t,s\in\mathcal{P}_t \tag{1'}\\
& \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_t}x_{t,s}^{k}=1 &&\forall t,s\in\mathcal{P}_t \tag{2}\\
& A_{t,s_{i+1}}\ge D_{t,s_i} &&\forall t,\; i=1,\dots,|P_t|-1 \tag{11}\\
& A_{t_2,s}\ge A_{t_1,s}+ \beta_{t_1}^{k} + \tau^{\text{head}}_{t_1,s} - M(1-y_{t_1,t_2,s}) &&\forall t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2} \tag{7'}\\
& y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s}=1 &&\forall t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_{t_1}\cap\mathcal{P}_{t_2} \tag{6}\\
& D_{t,s}\ge A_{t,s}+ \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} &&\forall t,\; s\in V \tag{5}\\
& \Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}= D_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} - T^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t}^{\text{dep}} &&\forall t\in T \tag{12}\\
& \Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\le \overline{\Delta}_t &&\forall t\in T \\
& x_{t,s}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\},\; A_{t,s},D_{t,s},\Delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All remaining constraints (re‑ordering, switch‑specific headways, etc.) are added analogously using the binary variables \(z_{t_1,t_2,s}\) and the appropriate parameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Remarks on implementation  

* **Scalability** – The number of binary ordering variables grows quadratically with the number of trains that share a section. In practice one can restrict the set to *conflicting pairs* (identified by a preliminary conflict‑detection pass).  
* **Speed‑profile discretisation** – Typical choices for \(\mathcal{K}_t\) are:  
  * **Cruise** – \(v = v^{\max}_{t,s}\) (no braking inside the section).  
  * **Early‑brake** – a reduced speed that guarantees the brake point lies inside the section (used when the downstream block is occupied).  
  * **Stop** – \(v=0\) for stations.  
* **Linearisation of braking distance** – The linear approximation (Assumption 3) is sufficiently accurate for the optimisation stage; the resulting timetable can be validated with a high‑fidelity simulation afterwards.  
* **Objective extensions** – The model can be enriched with additional terms (e.g., number of re‑orderings, energy consumption, passenger‐carrying cost) by adding appropriate weighted variables.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Summary  

The formulation above captures the **core novelty of DTG signalling** – **speed‑dependent separation** – by linking the arrival of a following train to the **brake‑indication point** of the leading train and to a headway that depends on the leading train’s speed (through its braking distance).  

All other elements (route continuity, dwell times, capacity, re‑ordering) are inherited from the classic RECIFE‑MILP CDR model, while the **linearisation tricks** (pre‑computed travel‑time and braking‑time coefficients, big‑M) keep the problem within the MILP class, making it solvable with standard solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) for realistic railway instances.

Text:
**MILP model for Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed‑Management under Partial Segment Blockage (TRSMP)**  

The formulation simultaneously decides (i) which route a train uses when a segment is partially blocked, (ii) the arrival/departure times at every node, and (iii) the discrete speed level on each traversed segment.  
The objective minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable, respecting the blockage, and producing executable speed profiles.

---

### 1. Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of directed track segments, indexed by *s* |
| **Rₜ** ⊆ *S* | Set of admissible routes for train *t* (each route *r* is an ordered list of segments) |
| **K** | Set of discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* |
| **B** ⊆ *S* | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (only one direction usable) |
| *Dₛ* | Length of segment *s* (km) |
| *vₖ* | Speed (km/h) associated with speed level *k* |
| *eₖ* | Energy consumption (MJ) per kilometre at speed level *k* |
| *τₜ* | Planned departure time of train *t* from its origin (minutes from horizon start) |
| *Δₜ* | Desired arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (minutes) |
| *γ* | Minimum head‑way (minutes) between two trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment |
| *β* | Minimum separation (minutes) for opposite‑direction trains on a blocked segment |
| *θ* | Minimum dwell time at stations (minutes) |
| *w_d , w_e* | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |
| *M* | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶) |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| *xₜᵣ* | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* ∈ *Rₜ*; 0 otherwise |
| *aₜₛ* | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the upstream node of segment *s* |
| *dₜₛ* | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the downstream node of segment *s* |
| *yₜₛₖ* | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k*; 0 otherwise |
| *Eₜ* | continuous ≥0 | Total energy consumed by train *t* |
| *Δₜ^{delay}* | continuous ≥0 | Delay of train *t* (actual arrival – desired arrival) |

---

### 3. Objective  

\[
\min \; w_d\!\sum_{t\in T}\!\Delta_t^{delay}
\;+\; w_e\!\sum_{t\in T}\!E_t
\]

---

### 4. Constraints  

#### 4.1 Route selection  
\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

#### 4.2 Link speed choice to selected route  
\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t s k}\le \sum_{r\in R_t:\;s\in r} x_{t r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

#### 4.3 Travel‑time on a segment  
\[
d_{t s}\ge a_{t s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{60\,D_s}{v_k}\;y_{t s k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{T1}
\]

#### 4.4 Continuity between consecutive segments  
If segment *s′* follows *s* on the chosen route of *t* (denoted *nextₜ(s)=s′*), then  
\[
a_{t s'}\ge d_{t s}+ \theta - M\bigl(1- x_{t r}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; s,\; r\in R_t\text{ with }s\in r \tag{T2}
\]

First segment of a route:  
\[
a_{t,\,s_{t r 1}} = \tau_t \qquad\forall t,\; r\in R_t \tag{T3}
\]

Last segment of a route (delay definition):  
\[
\Delta_t^{delay}\ge d_{t,\,s_{t r |r|}}-\Delta_t - M\bigl(1- x_{t r}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; r\in R_t \tag{T4}
\]

#### 4.5 Blocked‑segment direction constraint  
For any two trains *t₁, t₂* that would use a blocked segment *s∈B* in opposite directions:  
\[
a_{t_1 s}\ge d_{t_2 s}+ \beta
 -M\bigl(1- y_{t_1 s k}\bigr)-M\bigl(1- y_{t_2 s k'}\bigr)
\qquad\forall s\in B,\; t_1\neq t_2,\; k,k'\in K \tag{B1}
\]

#### 4.6 Same‑direction head‑way  
For any two trains on the same segment (blocked or not):  
\[
a_{t_2 s}\ge d_{t_1 s}+ \gamma
 -M\bigl(1- y_{t_1 s k}\bigr)-M\bigl(1- y_{t_2 s k'}\bigr)
\qquad\forall s\in S,\; t_1\neq t_2,\; k,k'\in K \tag{H1}
\]

#### 4.7 Exactly one speed level per traversed segment  
\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t s k}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\;s\in r} x_{t r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{S1}
\]

#### 4.8 Energy calculation  
\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} e_k\,D_s\, y_{t s k}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1}
\]

#### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t r}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t,r\\
&y_{t s k}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t,s,k\\
&a_{t s},d_{t s},E_t,\Delta_t^{delay}\ge 0, &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5. Model summary  

* **Decision variables** – route choice (*x*), timing (*a*,*d*), speed level (*y*), delay and energy (*Δ^{delay}*,*E*).  
* **Objective** – minimise weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.  
* **Constraints** – enforce exactly‑one route, link speed to route, travel‑time consistency, continuity, blockage‑direction exclusivity, head‑way safety, unique speed per segment, and linear energy accounting.  

All constraints and the objective are linear; the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** and can be solved with any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (SCIP, HiGHS) MILP solver.  

The resulting solution provides a conflict‑free timetable, feasible speed profiles for each train, and the associated delay and energy figures, thereby addressing the integrated train rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockages.

**Variables**

* \(A_{t,s}\) – arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (continuous, \(\ge 0\)).  
* \(D_{t,s}\) – departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) (continuous, \(\ge 0\)).  
* \(y_{t,\ell}\) – travel time of train \(t\) on track segment \(\ell\) (continuous, \(\ge 0\)).  
* \(v_{t,\ell}\) – speed of train \(t\) on segment \(\ell\) (continuous, \(\ge 0\)).  
* \(z^{v}_{t,\ell,v}\) – binary variable, 1 if speed level \(v\) (from a discretised set \(\mathcal V\)) is chosen for train \(t\) on segment \(\ell\).  
* \(x_{t,\ell}\) – binary direction decision, 1 if train \(t\) uses its original direction on segment \(\ell\), 0 if it is rerouted to the opposite track.  
* \(o_{i,j,\ell}\) – binary ordering variable, 1 if train \(i\) passes segment \(\ell\) before train \(j\) (used for conflict avoidance).

**Parameters (assumed known)**  

* \(a^{0}_{t,s}\) – planned arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\).  
* \(d^{0}_{t,s}\) – planned departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\).  
* \(\text{dwell}_s\) – mandatory dwell time at station \(s\).  
* \(\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell},\;\tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\) – lower and upper bounds on feasible travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(\ell\).  
* \(e_t\) – energy cost coefficient of train \(t\) (energy per unit travel time).  
* \(\text{len}_{\ell}\) – length of segment \(\ell\).  
* \(\mathcal V\) – set of admissible speed levels (e.g., \(\{30,60,90,120\}\) km/h).  
* \(\ell^{\text{blk}}\) – segment that is partially blocked.  
* \(\text{side}^{\text{blk}}\in\{0,1\}\) – side of the blocked track (0 = original direction, 1 = opposite).  
* \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\) – disruption time window on the blocked side.  
* \(\text{origDir}_{t,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\)’s original direction on \(\ell\) coincides with the blocked side.  
* Mapping functions:
  * \(\text{seg}(t,s)\) – segment travelled after leaving station \(s\) by train \(t\).
  * \(\text{prevSt}(t,\ell),\;\text{nextSt}(t,\ell)\) – predecessor and successor stations of train \(t\) on segment \(\ell\).
  * \(\text{entrySt}(t,\ell),\;\text{exitSt}(t,\ell)\) – stations where train \(t\) enters and leaves segment \(\ell\).

**Objective function**

Minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption:

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\bigl(A_{t,s}-a^{0}_{t,s}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\alpha\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L} e_t\,y_{t,\ell}}_{\text{total energy cost}},
\]

where \(\alpha>0\) is a user‑defined weight.

**Constraints**

1. **Dwell time consistency**  
   \[
   D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+\text{dwell}_s\qquad\forall t,s.
   \]

2. **Link arrival‑departure across consecutive stations**  
   \[
   A_{t,s+1}=D_{t,s}+y_{t,\text{seg}(t,s)}\qquad\forall t,\; s\neq\max\mathcal S .
   \]

3. **Travel‑time bounds**  
   \[
   \tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}\le y_{t,\ell}\le \tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
   \]

4. **Speed‑time coupling (linearised by discretised speed levels)**  

   *Speed selection*  
   \[
   \sum_{v\in\mathcal V} z^{v}_{t,\ell,v}=1\qquad\forall t,\ell .
   \]

   *Speed value*  
   \[
   v_{t,\ell}= \sum_{v\in\mathcal V} v\;z^{v}_{t,\ell,v}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
   \]

   *Travel time definition* (linear because speed levels are fixed)  
   \[
   y_{t,\ell}= \sum_{v\in\mathcal V}\frac{\text{len}_{\ell}}{v}\;z^{v}_{t,\ell,v}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
   \]

5. **Direction decision for the blocked segment**  
   \[
   x_{t,\ell^{\text{blk}}}=1-\text{origDir}_{t,\ell^{\text{blk}}}\qquad\forall t .
   \]

6. **Disruption‑window feasibility on the blocked side**  
   For any train that would traverse the blocked side (\(x_{t,\ell^{\text{blk}}=1\)) the whole passage must lie outside the disruption window:

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   D_{t,\text{prevSt}(t,\ell^{\text{blk}})} &\ge T^{\text{start}} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{t,\ell^{\text{blk}}}),\\
   A_{t,\text{nextSt}(t,\ell^{\text{blk}})} &\le T^{\text{end}} \;+\; M\,(1-x_{t,\ell^{\text{blk}}}),
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   where \(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).

7. **Bidirectional conflict avoidance on a shared segment**  
   For any ordered pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) using the same direction on the same segment (\(x_{i,\ell}=x_{j,\ell}=1\)):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   A_{i,\text{exitSt}(i,\ell)} &\le A_{j,\text{entrySt}(j,\ell)} + M\bigl(1-o_{i,j,\ell}\bigr),\\
   A_{j,\text{exitSt}(j,\ell)} &\le A_{i,\text{entrySt}(i,\ell)} + M\,o_{i,j,\ell},
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall i<j,\;\forall \ell .
   \]

   The binary \(o_{i,j,\ell}\) selects which train passes first; the big‑M term deactivates the irrelevant inequality.

8. **Capacity on opposite direction (at most one train on the segment in the opposite direction at any time)**  

   \[
   \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\bigl(1-x_{t,\ell}\bigr)\le 1\qquad\forall \ell .
   \]

9. **Variable domains**  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &A_{t,s}, D_{t,s}, y_{t,\ell}, v_{t,\ell}\ge 0,\\
   &z^{v}_{t,\ell,v}\in\{0,1\},\; x_{t,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,\ell}\in\{0,1\}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]

**Assumptions (explicitly stated)**  

* Dwell times are known and identical for all trains at a given station.  
* Speed levels are discretised; the linearisation in (4) yields an exact representation of the piecewise‑constant speed‑time relationship.  
* The big‑M constant is chosen large enough not to restrict feasible solutions but not excessively large to avoid numerical difficulties.  
* All required mapping data (which segment follows each station, predecessor/successor stations for each train‑segment pair, etc.) are pre‑processed and provided as parameters.  

The model above constitutes a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the **integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP)** under a partial‑segment blockage, capturing delay minimisation, energy consumption, rerouting decisions, speed selection, and conflict‑free operation on a bidirectional high‑speed railway line.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP**  
*(partial‑segment blockage – each blocked segment can be travelled on two parallel “sides’’ – e.g. a detour track or the remaining free track)*  

Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming model** that simultaneously decides train‑order, side‑choice, speed‑profile and exact arrival/departure times while minimising a weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption.

---

### 1. Sets, parameters and data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \mathcal I \) | Set of trains, indexed by \(i\) |
| \( \mathcal K_i \) | Ordered set of stations visited by train \(i\) (including origin and destination). For a station \(k\in\mathcal K_i\) the next station is denoted \(k^{+}\). |
| \( \mathcal S=\{L,R\} \) | Set of “sides’’ of a blocked segment (left / right). |
| \( \mathcal B\subseteq \mathcal I\times\mathcal I \) | Set of unordered train pairs that share at least one blocked segment (potential conflict). |
| \( \mathcal G \) | Set of blocked segments (geographical sections). |
| \( \mathcal M \) | Set of admissible discrete speed profiles, indexed by \(m\). |
| \( L_{g} \) | Length of blocked segment \(g\) (km). |
| \( v_m \) | Nominal speed of profile \(m\) (km/h). |
| \( e_m \) | Energy consumption per kilometre when profile \(m\) is used (kWh/km). |
| \( \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k} \) | Minimum dwell time of train \(i\) at station \(k\) (minutes). |
| \( a_i^{\text{sched}} \) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (minutes from a common zero). |
| \( w^{\text{delay}}_i \) | Weight of delay for train \(i\) in the objective. |
| \( w^{\text{energy}} \) | Global weight of energy consumption in the objective. |
| \( M \) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| \( C_s \) | Maximum number of trains that may occupy side \(s\) simultaneously (capacity of the side). |
| \( \Delta^{\text{safety}} \) | Minimum safety headway between two successive trains on the same side (minutes). |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure geometry and the set of speed‑profile options.

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \( r_{i,g,s}\in\{0,1\} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) traverses blocked segment \(g\) on side \(s\). |
| \( o_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) **precedes** train \(j\) on side \(s\) (only defined for \((i,j)\in\mathcal B\)). |
| \( a_{i,k}\ge0 \) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(k\). |
| \( d_{i,k}\ge0 \) | continuous | Departure time of train \(i\) from station \(k\). |
| \( t_{i,g}\ge0 \) | continuous | Travel time of train \(i\) on blocked segment \(g\). |
| \( p_{i,g,m}\in\{0,1\} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses speed profile \(m\) on segment \(g\). |
| \( c_i\in\{0,1\} \) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) is cancelled (or completely delayed out of the horizon). |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\,
\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-a_i^{\text{sched}}\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\,
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\;\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\;\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}
e_m \; p_{i,g,m}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

*The first term penalises the deviation of the realised arrival at the final station from the original schedule; the second term adds the energy consumption of the chosen speed profiles.*

---

### 4. Constraints  

#### 4.1 Route‑choice on blocked segments  

1. **Exactly one side (or cancellation) is selected**  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,g,s} \;+\; c_i \;=\; 1 
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall g\in\mathcal G\text{ that train }i\text{ must cross}
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Side capacity (at most \(C_s\) trains may use side \(s\) on a segment)**  

\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} r_{i,g,s}\;\le\; C_s
\qquad\forall g\in\mathcal G,\;\forall s\in\mathcal S
\tag{R2}
\]

#### 4.2 Flow of a train through its stations  

3. **Minimum dwell time**  

\[
d_{i,k}\;\ge\;a_{i,k}+\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall k\in\mathcal K_i
\tag{F1}
\]

4. **Travel from a station to the next (including blocked segment)**  

Let \(g(i,k)\) be the (unique) blocked segment between station \(k\) and its successor \(k^{+}\) for train \(i\).  

\[
d_{i,k}+t_{i,g(i,k)} \;=\; a_{i,k^{+}}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall k\in\mathcal K_i\setminus\{\text{last}\}
\tag{F2}
\]

5. **Big‑M linking with cancellation**  

\[
a_{i,k}\le M(1-c_i),\quad d_{i,k}\le M(1-c_i),\quad t_{i,g}\le M(1-c_i)
\qquad\forall i,k,g
\tag{F3}
\]

#### 4.3 Speed‑profile selection and travel‑time link  

6. **Exactly one speed profile per traversed blocked segment**  

\[
\sum_{m\in\mathcal M} p_{i,g,m}\;=\;\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,g,s}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall g\in\mathcal G
\tag{S1}
\]

7. **Travel time equals length / speed of the chosen profile**  

\[
t_{i,g}\;=\;\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\frac{L_g}{v_m}\;p_{i,g,m}
\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall g\in\mathcal G
\tag{S2}
\]

#### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance on the same side  

For every unordered pair \((i,j)\in\mathcal B\) that share a blocked segment and for each side \(s\):

8. **Ordering definition (mutual exclusivity)**  

\[
o_{i,j,s}+o_{j,i,s}= r_{i,g,s}+r_{j,g,s}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal B,\;\forall s\in\mathcal S,\;\forall g\in\mathcal G
\tag{O1}
\]

9. **Safety headway when \(i\) precedes \(j\)**  

Define entry/exit times on segment \(g\):
\[
\text{entry}_{i,g}= d_{i,\text{up}(g)},\qquad
\text{exit}_{i,g}= d_{i,\text{up}(g)}+t_{i,g}
\]

Then  

\[
\text{entry}_{j,g}\;\ge\;\text{exit}_{i,g}+ \Delta^{\text{safety}}-M(1-o_{i,j,s})
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal B,\;\forall s\in\mathcal S,\;\forall g\in\mathcal G
\tag{O2}
\]

If \(o_{i,j,s}=1\) the headway constraint is enforced; otherwise it is relaxed by \(M\).

#### 4.5 Cancellation consistency  

\[
r_{i,g,s}\le 1-c_i,\qquad p_{i,g,m}\le 1-c_i
\qquad\forall i,g,s,m
\tag{C1}
\]

---

### 5. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i,g,s},\;o_{i,j,s},\;p_{i,g,m},\;c_i \in \{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},\;d_{i,k},\;t_{i,g}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-a_i^{\text{sched}}\bigr)
\;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\sum_{m\in\mathcal M} e_m\,p_{i,g,m}\\
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice and side capacity}\\
&\text{(F1)–(F3)} &&\text{time flow through stations, cancellation}\\
&\text{(S1)–(S2)} &&\text{speed‑profile selection and travel‑time link}\\
&\text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{conflict avoidance on the same side}\\
&\text{(C1)} &&\text{cancellation consistency}\\
&\text{variable domains.}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could arise (product of binary and continuous) have been eliminated by the big‑M technique.  

The model simultaneously decides:

* **Side choice** \(r_{i,g,s}\) for each blocked segment,  
* **Ordering** \(o_{i,j,s}\) of trains sharing a side,  
* **Speed profile** \(p_{i,g,m}\) (hence travel time \(t_{i,g}\)),  
* **Exact arrival/departure times** \(a_{i,k},d_{i,k}\),  
* **Whether a train is cancelled** \(c_i\).

The objective balances punctuality (delay) against operating cost (energy).  

---

### 7. How to use  

1. Populate the data (sets, lengths, speeds, energy values, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, safety headway, side capacities, big‑M).  
2. Load the formulation into a MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, etc.).  
3. Solve.  
4. Extract the solution:  
   * \(r_{i,g,s}=1\) → chosen side (detour).  
   * \(p_{i,g,m}=1\) → speed profile (hence speed).  
   * \(a_{i,k},d_{i,k}\) → rescheduled timetable.  
   * \(c_i=1\) → train to be cancelled/postponed.  

The same structure can be extended (e.g., crew/resource constraints, platform capacity, finer energy models) without breaking linearity – just add extra binary/continuous variables and linear linking constraints.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
The model is built in three logical stages – **Rerouting**, **Re‑ordering**, and **Rescheduling** – exactly as described in the paper summary.  
All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed below.  
Where the source text does not give a numeric value, a reasonable assumption is made and explicitly marked **(Assumption)**.

---

## 1. Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains that have to be dispatched in the planning horizon (indexed by \(i\)). |
| **\(N\)** | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, signal blocks) (indexed by \(n\)). |
| **\(E\subseteq N\times N\)** | Set of directed track segments (edges) \((n,m)\). |
| **\(R_i\)** | Set of admissible routes for train \(i\) (each route is a sequence of edges). |
| **\(P\)** | Set of precedence pairs \((i,j)\) that may conflict on a common resource (edge or station). |
| **\(c_{i,r}\)** | Estimated energy consumption of train \(i\) on route \(r\in R_i\) (kWh). |
| **\(t^{\text{plan}}_{i,n}\)** | Planned (timetable) arrival time of train \(i\) at node \(n\) (minutes from start of horizon). |
| **\(L_{i}\)** | Minimum travelling time of train \(i\) on any admissible route (minutes). |
| **\(M\)** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **\(\alpha,\beta\)** | Weight coefficients for the multi‑objective function (Assumption: \(\alpha=1,\;\beta=0.01\)). |
| **\(d^{\max}\)** | Upper bound on admissible secondary delay (Assumption: 120 min). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| \(x_{i,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) is assigned to route \(r\in R_i\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) is scheduled **after** train \(j\) on a shared resource (i.e. \(i\) waits for \(j\)); 0 otherwise. |
| \(s_{i,n}\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Start time** (actual departure) of train \(i\) from node \(n\). |
| \(a_{i,n}\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Arrival time** of train \(i\) at node \(n\). |
| \(\delta_i\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Secondary delay** of train \(i\) (difference between actual and planned arrival at its final destination). |
| \(p_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) **passes before** train \(j\) on a shared edge (used for the delay‑propagation model). |
| \(z_{i,j,n}\) | binary | 1 if trains \(i\) and \(j\) occupy edge \((n,m)\) at overlapping times (conflict indicator). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The primary goal is to **minimise total secondary delay**, while a secondary goal is to keep **energy consumption low**.  
Both are linear, so a weighted sum is used:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{i\in T}\delta_i}_{\text{Delay term}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{r\in R_i} c_{i,r}\,x_{i,r}}_{\text{Energy term}}
}
\]

*If only delay minimisation is required set \(\beta=0\).*

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link route choice to travel‑time on each edge** – for every edge \((n,m)\) that belongs to route \(r\) we define a parameter  
\( \tau_{i,nm}^{r}\) = travel time of train \(i\) on that edge when using route \(r\).  
If route \(r\) is not chosen, the corresponding travel time is forced to 0 by the big‑M:

\[
a_{i,m}\ge a_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} - M\,(1-x_{i,r}) \qquad \forall i\in T,\;(n,m)\in E
\tag{R2}
\]

(Only the chosen route contributes a non‑zero travel time.)

### 4.2 Timing (arrival / departure) constraints  

3. **Initial departure respects the planned time**  

\[
s_{i,\text{origin}(i)} \ge t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{origin}(i)} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{T1}
\]

4. **Propagation of times along the selected route**  

\[
a_{i,m}= s_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} \qquad \forall i\in T,\;(n,m)\in E \text{ that belong to the chosen route}
\tag{T2}
\]

5. **Departure from a node cannot be earlier than arrival**  

\[
s_{i,m}\ge a_{i,m} \qquad \forall i\in T,\; m\in N
\tag{T3}
\]

### 4.3 Delay definition  

6. **Secondary delay is the difference between actual arrival at the final destination and the planned arrival**  

\[
\delta_i \ge a_{i,\text{dest}(i)} - t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{dest}(i)} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

7. **Upper bound on secondary delay**  

\[
\delta_i \le d^{\max} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{D2}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance (re‑ordering) constraints  

For each pair of trains \((i,j)\in P\) that share at least one common edge or station, we enforce a **mutual‑exclusion** using the binary precedence variables \(y_{i,j}\) and \(y_{j,i}\).

8. **Exactly one precedence direction**  

\[
y_{i,j}+y_{j,i}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{C1}
\]

9. **If train \(i\) follows train \(j\), its entry time on the shared resource must be after the exit time of \(j\) plus a safety headway \(h\) (Assumption: \(h=2\) min).**  

Let \(\mathcal{S}_{ij}\subseteq E\) be the set of edges (or stations) that are common to both trains. For each such edge \((n,m)\):

\[
a_{i,m} \ge a_{j,n}+ \tau_{j,nm}^{r_j} + h - M\,(1-y_{i,j}) \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}
\tag{C2}
\]

(The big‑M de‑activates the inequality when \(y_{i,j}=0\).)

### 4.5 Delay‑propagation (optimal‑model extension)  

To capture the effect of a train waiting for another, we introduce the **pair‑wise waiting variables** \(p_{i,j}\) (1 if \(i\) waits for \(j\)). They are linked to the precedence variables:

\[
p_{i,j}\ge y_{i,j} \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{P1}
\]

The actual secondary delay of a train equals the **maximum** of all waiting times accumulated along its route. In a linear model we use an auxiliary variable \(\Delta_i\) that upper‑bounds the sum of all waiting contributions:

\[
\Delta_i \ge \sum_{j\in T\setminus\{i\}} \gamma_{i,j}\,p_{i,j} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{P2}
\]

where \(\gamma_{i,j}\) is the **minimum possible waiting time** on the first common resource (Assumption: equal to the headway \(h\)).  
Finally, the secondary delay variable is forced to be at least this propagated delay:

\[
\delta_i \ge \Delta_i \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{P3}
\]

### 4.6 Route‑selection consistency with re‑ordering  

10. **If two trains are ordered on a shared edge, they must be using routes that actually contain that edge.**  

\[
y_{i,j} \le \sum_{r\in R_i:\,(n,m)\in r} x_{i,r} \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}
\tag{RC1}
\]

(and analogously for \(y_{j,i}\)).

### 4.7 Optional safety‑overlap constraints (for the extended model)  

When a train stops at a signal, a **clear‑behind overlap** of length \(\ell^{\text{ov}}\) (Assumption: 300 m) must be kept free. Let \(\theta_{i,n}\) be the time needed to clear the overlap after departure from node \(n\). Then:

\[
s_{k,n} \ge a_{i,n} + \theta_{i,n} - M\,(1-z_{i,k,n}) \qquad \forall i,k\in T,\; n\in N
\tag{OV}
\]

where \(z_{i,k,n}=1\) indicates that train \(k\) would violate the overlap of train \(i\). The model forces \(z_{i,k,n}=0\) by minimising the objective, effectively preserving the overlap.

---

## 5. Full MILP Model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha \sum_{i\in T}\delta_i \;+\; \beta \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{r\in R_i} c_{i,r}\,x_{i,r} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1 && \forall i\in T \quad\text{(R1)}\\
& a_{i,m}\ge a_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} - M(1-x_{i,r}) && \forall i,(n,m)\in E \quad\text{(R2)}\\
& s_{i,\text{origin}(i)} \ge t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{origin}(i)} && \forall i\quad\text{(T1)}\\
& a_{i,m}= s_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} && \forall i,(n,m)\in\text{chosen route} \quad\text{(T2)}\\
& s_{i,m}\ge a_{i,m} && \forall i,m\quad\text{(T3)}\\
& \delta_i \ge a_{i,\text{dest}(i)}-t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{dest}(i)} && \forall i\quad\text{(D1)}\\
& \delta_i \le d^{\max} && \forall i\quad\text{(D2)}\\
& y_{i,j}+y_{j,i}=1 && \forall (i,j)\in P\quad\text{(C1)}\\
& a_{i,m} \ge a_{j,n}+ \tau_{j,nm}^{r_j}+h - M(1-y_{i,j}) && \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}\quad\text{(C2)}\\
& p_{i,j}\ge y_{i,j} && \forall (i,j)\in P\quad\text{(P1)}\\
& \Delta_i \ge \sum_{j\neq i}\gamma_{i,j}\,p_{i,j} && \forall i\quad\text{(P2)}\\
& \delta_i \ge \Delta_i && \forall i\quad\text{(P3)}\\
& y_{i,j} \le \sum_{r\in R_i:(n,m)\in r} x_{i,r} && \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}\quad\text{(RC1)}\\
& \text{(Optional) overlap constraints (OV)}\\
& x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; p_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,k,n}\in\{0,1\}\\
& s_{i,n},a_{i,n},\delta_i,\Delta_i\ge 0 \qquad && \forall i,n
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Remarks & Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Reason |
|---|------------|--------|
| 1 | \(\alpha=1,\;\beta=0.01\) | Gives a clear priority to delay minimisation while still penalising high‑energy routes. |
| 2 | Headway \(h=2\) min and safety‑overlap length \(\ell^{\text{ov}}=300\) m | Typical values used in European railway signalling. |
| 3 | Big‑M \(M=10\,000\) min | Guarantees de‑activation of conditional constraints. |
| 4 | Maximum secondary delay \(d^{\max}=120\) min | Reflects realistic operational limits for passenger services. |
| 5 | \(\gamma_{i,j}=h\) for all waiting pairs | Minimum waiting time equals the headway; any additional waiting will be captured by the cumulative \(\Delta_i\). |
| 6 | Energy consumption \(c_{i,r}\) is known a‑priori (e.g., from a power‑consumption model). | Required for the secondary objective term. |
| 7 | The set of admissible routes \(R_i\) is pre‑computed (e.g., by a routing heuristic). | Reduces the size of the MILP while preserving optimality for the chosen subset. |

---

### How the model works  

1. **Rerouting stage** – variables \(x_{i,r}\) choose a feasible path for each train.  
2. **Re‑ordering stage** – binary variables \(y_{i,j}\) decide which train yields to the other on each shared resource, guaranteeing conflict‑free schedules (FIFO, but the model can select any order).  
3. **Rescheduling stage** – continuous timing variables \(s_{i,n},a_{i,n}\) and delay variables \(\delta_i\) compute the actual timetable, while constraints (P1‑P3) propagate the waiting times caused by the chosen ordering.  

If the decision maker wishes to **ignore delay propagation** (sub‑optimal model), constraints (P1‑P3) can be omitted; the remaining MILP corresponds to the fast “rerouting + re‑ordering” stage described in the paper. Adding (P1‑P3) yields the **global‑optimal** formulation that accounts for secondary‑delay accumulation.

---

**End of MILP description**. The model is ready to be implemented in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) and to be solved within the short response times required by real‑time railway traffic management.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling‑and‑Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
*Partial‑segment‑blockage disruption, bidirectional single‑track sharing*  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains (both directions). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including fictitious origin 0 and destination |S|+1). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of track‑segments (directed arcs) that can be traversed. For a segment *e = (i,j)* the physical length is *ℓ_e* (km). |
| **B** ⊆ E | Sub‑set of segments that are *blocked* (partial blockage) during the disruption window \([τ^{start}, τ^{end}]\). |
| **D** = {1,…,|D|} | Set of *discrete speed‑profile plans* that can be assigned to a train on a given segment (see §2). |
| **K** = {1,…,|K|} | Set of *time‑intervals* used for the decomposition (e.g., 5‑min slots). |
| **dir(t)** ∈ {+1, –1} | Direction of train *t* ( +1  = “up‑track”, –1 = “down‑track”). |
| **Δt** | Length of a time‑interval (minutes). |

### Fixed parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(a^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum acceleration for train *t*. |
| \(d^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum deceleration (positive value) for train *t*. |
| \(v^{max}_t\) (m/s) | Maximum permissible speed for train *t*. |
| \(v^{min}_t\) (m/s) | Minimum operating speed (usually 0). |
| \(E^{run}_{t,e,d}\) (kWh) | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *e* when plan *d* is used (pre‑computed from physics). |
| \(T^{dwell}_{t,s}\) (min) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\) (min) | Minimum headway (separation) required between two trains *t* and *t'* on segment *e* (direction‑dependent). |
| \(τ^{start}, τ^{end}\) (min) | Beginning and end of the blockage window. |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant (large enough to deactivate constraints). |
| \(C^{delay}_t\) (\$ per minute) | Penalty cost for each minute of delay of train *t*. |
| \(C^{canc}_t\) (\$) | Penalty cost for canceling train *t*. |
| \(C^{energy}_d\) (\$/kWh) | Energy price used to convert energy consumption to cost (same for all trains). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s* (minutes from a reference zero). |
| \(y_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| \(z_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* (i.e. uses the “normal” direction), 0 otherwise (used for rerouting). |
| \(r_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses the **opposite** track on segment *e* (i.e. rerouted onto the blocked side). |
| \(p_{t,e,d}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if speed‑plan *d* is selected for train *t* on segment *e*. |
| \(c_t\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled**. |
| \(s_{t,k}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned to time‑interval *k* for the **headway‑checking** (used in the IP‑decomposition). |
| \(δ_{t,t',e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* precedes train *t'* on segment *e* (ordering variable). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum of operational cost, delay cost and energy cost** while heavily penalising cancellations.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;  & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{delay}_t \bigl( x_{t,|S|+1} - \hat{x}_{t,|S|+1} \bigr)}_{\text{Delay penalty}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{d\in D} C^{energy}_d \,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d}}_{\text{Energy cost}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{canc}_t \,c_t}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\hat{x}_{t,|S|+1}\) is the **original scheduled arrival time** at the final station (baseline).  
If a train is cancelled (\(c_t=1\)) all its timing variables are forced to zero (see constraints).

---

## 4. Core Constraints  

### 4.1 Feasibility of a train (cancellation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S\cup\{0,|S|+1\} \\
& y_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S .
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(c_t=1\) the train disappears from the schedule.

### 4.2 Logical link between arrival / departure

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,s} \ge x_{t,s} + T^{dwell}_{t,s} - M\,c_t &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.3 Travel time on a segment – coupling with speed plan  

For each traversed segment *e = (i,j)* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-z_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

- \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is the **deterministic travel time** (minutes) of plan *d* on segment *e* for train *t* (computed from acceleration/deceleration limits and speed‑limit \(v^{max}_t\)).  
- The big‑M term deactivates the constraint if the train does **not** use the segment in its normal direction.

If the train is rerouted onto the opposite track, the same constraint uses \(r_{t,e}\) instead of \(z_{t,e}\):

\[
x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) .
\]

### 4.4 Exactly one speed plan per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} p_{t,e,d}= z_{t,e}+r_{t,e} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If the segment is not used (\(z_{t,e}=r_{t,e}=0\)) all \(p_{t,e,d}=0\).

### 4.5 Rerouting feasibility (partial blockage)

A train may **only** use the opposite track on a blocked segment **during** the disruption window, and only if the segment is blocked for its original direction.

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,e} \le 1 &&\forall t, e\in B \\
& r_{t,e}=0 &&\forall t, e\notin B .
\end{aligned}
\]

Furthermore, the departure‑arrival times must respect the window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} \ge τ^{start} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B\\
& x_{t,j} \le τ^{end}+M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.6 Headway (conflict‑free) constraints – bidirectional sharing  

For any two distinct trains *t* and *t'* that occupy the **same physical track** (either both normal or one normal + one rerouted) on segment *e*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j)\\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

The binary ordering variable \(δ_{t,t',e}\) decides which train passes first.  
To guarantee a **minimum headway** \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} + T^{head}_{t,t',e} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) \\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} + T^{head}_{t',t,e} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a train is cancelled, the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0 (via big‑M).

### 4.7 Single‑track capacity (only one train at a time)

A compact alternative to the pairwise headway constraints uses the interval‑selection variables \(s_{t,k}\). For each time interval *k* and each physical segment *e*:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\bigr)\, s_{t,k} \le 1 \qquad \forall e\in E,\; k\in K .
\]

Linking \(s_{t,k}\) with actual timings:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,i} \le k\Delta t + M\,(1-s_{t,k}) \\
& y_{t,i} \ge (k-1)\Delta t - M\,(1-s_{t,k}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus a train occupies a segment only in the interval where its start‑time lies.

### 4.8 Physical speed‑profile consistency  

For each selected plan *d* on segment *e* the corresponding **average speed** must respect the train’s acceleration/deceleration limits. This is already embedded in the pre‑computed \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\); however, we enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \le v^{max}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 \\
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \ge v^{min}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is a constant for a given plan, these become simple bounds on the admissible plan set *D* (i.e., infeasible plans are removed a‑priori).

### 4.9 Route choice (normal vs opposite track)  

A train may travel on a segment either in its original direction or, if the segment is blocked, on the opposite track. The two binary variables must be **mutually exclusive**:

\[
z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If a segment is **not** blocked, the opposite‑track variable is forced to zero:

\[
r_{t,e}=0 \qquad \forall t,\; e\notin B .
\]

### 4.10 Continuity of route  

If a train uses the opposite track on a blocked segment, it must **switch back** to the normal track at the next station (no prolonged opposite‑track travel). This can be modelled by a simple “switch‑once” rule:

\[
\sum_{e\in B} r_{t,e} \le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

(If more complex multi‑segment rerouting is allowed, the constraint can be relaxed.)

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle \min\;  & \displaystyle
\sum_{t} C^{delay}_t\bigl(x_{t,|S|+1}-\hat{x}_{t,|S|+1}\bigr)
+ \sum_{t,e,d} C^{energy}_d\,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\,p_{t,e,d}
+ \sum_{t} C^{canc}_t\,c_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} & \text{(4.1)–(4.10) listed above} \\[2pt]
            & x_{t,s},y_{t,s}\ge 0,\; \forall t,s\\
            & z_{t,e},r_{t,e},p_{t,e,d},c_t,s_{t,k},δ_{t,t',e}\in\{0,1\},\;\forall\text{indices}.
\end{array}
}
\]

All constraints are *linear* because the travel‑time values \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and energy consumptions \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\) are pre‑computed constants for each admissible speed plan. The big‑M terms guarantee logical activation/deactivation.

---

## 6. Modeling Assumptions (explicitly stated)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | **Deterministic disruption window** \([τ^{start},τ^{end}]\) is known a‑priori and does not change during optimisation. |
| A2 | **Partial blockage** affects only one side of a double‑track segment; the opposite track is usable but only during the window. |
| A3 | **Rerouting** is limited to a single blocked segment per train (constraint 4.10). This keeps the model tractable; the formulation can be extended to multi‑segment rerouting by relaxing A3. |
| A4 | **Speed‑plan library** *D* is generated beforehand by solving the continuous speed‑profile sub‑problem for each train‑segment pair, respecting acceleration/deceleration limits and speed limits. The library is finite, making the problem MILP. |
| A5 | **Energy consumption** for each plan is pre‑computed (parameter \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\)). Energy price is assumed constant over the horizon. |
| A6 | **Headway times** \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\) are symmetric and cover safety, signalling and braking distance; they are taken as given data. |
| A7 | **Cancellation** is allowed for any train, but incurs a large penalty \(C^{canc}_t\) to discourage unnecessary cancellations. |
| A8 | **Time discretisation** for the IP‑decomposition uses intervals of equal length Δt (e.g., 5 min). The big‑M linking \(s_{t,k}\) to continuous times guarantees exact feasibility when Δt is sufficiently small. |
| A9 | **No overtaking** on a single‑track segment: ordering variable \(δ_{t,t',e}\) enforces a strict sequence. |
| A10| **Station dwell‑time minima** \(T^{dwell}_{t,s}\) are respected; additional dwell time may be introduced implicitly by the optimisation (through later departure). |

---

## 7. Remarks on Solving the Model  

* The MILP can be tackled directly with a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress).  
* For large networks, the **decomposition** described in the paper can be applied:  
  * **Step 1** – generate all feasible *train‑plans* \((z,r,p,δ)\) for each train (IP‑sub‑problem).  
  * **Step 2** – solve a master **integer‑program** that selects exactly one plan per train while respecting the capacity constraints \(\sum (z+r)s_{t,k}\le1\).  
* The **adaptive iterative refinement** starts with coarse Δt and a small plan set, then iteratively adds finer‑grained plans in the neighbourhood of the current solution.  
* The **local‑branching** technique can be used to explore the neighbourhood of a high‑quality incumbent, improving solution time.

---

**The formulation above provides a complete, linear (MILP) description of the *Train‑Rescheduling‑and‑Speed‑Management Problem* under a partial‑segment blockage, integrating timetable adjustments, rerouting decisions, speed‑profile selection and energy‑aware objectives while guaranteeing conflict‑free operation of bidirectional trains on a shared track.**

**Variables**

* \(x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\in I\) uses speed‑plan \(r\in R\), 0 otherwise.  
* \(y_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) precedes train \(j\) on shared segment \(s\in S\).  
* \(a_{i,n}\ge 0\) – arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(n\in N\).  
* \(d_{i,n}\ge 0\) – departure time of train \(i\) from station \(n\in N\).  
* \(t_{i,s}\ge 0\) – travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\in S\).  
* \(z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) is rerouted onto the opposite track on segment \(s\) during the disruption window.

**Parameters (assumed given)**  

* \(\hat a_{i}\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final station.  
* \(\text{dwell}_{i,n}\) – minimum dwell time of train \(i\) at station \(n\).  
* \(t^{\min}_{i,s,r},\; t^{\max}_{i,s,r}\) – minimum/maximum travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) under speed‑plan \(r\).  
* \(E_{i,r}\) – energy consumption of train \(i\) when using plan \(r\).  
* \(\text{safety}\) – safety head‑way time required between two trains on the same segment.  
* \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\) – disruption time window.  
* \(\text{blocked}_s\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if segment \(s\) is blocked during the disruption window.  
* \(\text{cap}^{\text{opp}}_s\) – capacity of the opposite track on segment \(s\).  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).  
* \(\text{seg\_start}_s,\text{seg\_end}_s\) – upstream/down‑stream stations of segment \(s\).  
* \(\text{SharedPairs}\subseteq I\times I\times S\) – unordered train pairs that share segment \(s\).  

**Objective (weighted sum of total delay and total energy)**  

\[
\min\; 
w^{\text{delay}}\!\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\!\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{r\in R} E_{i,r}\,x_{i,r}
\]

where \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train \(i\) at its final station.

**Constraints**

1. **Speed‑plan selection** (each train chooses exactly one plan)  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in R} x_{i,r}=1 \qquad \forall i\in I
   \]

2. **Dwell time consistency**  
   \[
   a_{i,n}+ \text{dwell}_{i,n}\le d_{i,n} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; n\in N
   \]

3. **Travel‑time definition** (segment \(s\) connects station \(\text{seg\_start}_s\) to \(\text{seg\_end}_s\))  
   \[
   t_{i,s}= d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}-a_{i,\text{seg\_end}_s}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

4. **Blockage handling – rerouting or avoidance**  
   For every blocked segment \(s\) (\(\text{blocked}_s=1\)):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\le T^{\text{end}} + M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \\
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\ge T^{\text{start}} - M\,(1-z_{i,s})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad \forall i\in I
   \]

5. **Opposite‑track capacity**  
   \[
   \sum_{i\in I} z_{i,s}\le \text{cap}^{\text{opp}}_s \qquad \forall s\in S
   \]

6. **Ordering on shared segments** (conflict‑free head‑way)  
   *Precedence sum*  
   \[
   y_{i,j,s}+y_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]
   *Safety head‑way*  
   \[
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}+ \text{safety}\le d_{j,\text{seg\_start}_s}+M\,(1-y_{i,j,s})
   \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]

7. **Speed‑plan feasibility for travel times** (big‑M linking)  
   \[
   t_{i,s}\ge \sum_{r\in R} t^{\min}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]
   \[
   t_{i,s}\le \sum_{r\in R} t^{\max}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

8. **Variable domains**  
   \[
   x_{i,r},\,y_{i,j,s},\,z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
   a_{i,n},\,d_{i,n},\,t_{i,s}\ge 0
   \]

**Assumptions (marked as such)**  

* The mapping of each segment to its upstream/down‑stream stations (\(\text{seg\_start}_s,\text{seg\_end}_s\)) is known.  
* Travel time on a segment is the difference between departure from the upstream station and arrival at the downstream station.  
* All trains share the same safety head‑way time.  
* The disruption affects only the specified blocked segments and the given time window.  
* Energy consumption depends only on the selected speed‑plan, not on the exact timing.  

The model above fully integrates train rescheduling (arrival/departure times, ordering, rerouting) with speed‑profile selection, ensuring a conflict‑free timetable that respects blockage constraints and minimizes a combination of passenger delay and energy use.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling + Speed‑Management MILP**  
(The model is written in a compact linear‑mixed‑integer form. All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed together with a short explanation of each element.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Sets and indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| **\(S\)** | Set of stations (including origins and terminals). |
| **\(E\)** | Set of directed track **segments**, indexed by \(e\). |
| **\(E^{\text{sh}}\subseteq E\)** | Sub‑set of **shared** segments that are blocked on one side. |
| **\(P_t\subseteq E\)** | Original (planned) route of train \(t\). |
| **\(Q_t\subseteq E\)** | Opposite‑track (detour) route of train \(t\) (used when the blockage forces a reroute). |
| **\(\mathcal C\)** | Set of conflict triples \((t,t',e)\) – two different trains that could occupy the same segment \(e\). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| \(L_e\) | Length of segment \(e\) | km |
| \(\underline v_e ,\overline v_e\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on \(e\) | km h\(^{-1}\) |
| \(\underline a ,\overline a\) | Minimum (braking) / maximum (acceleration) rate | km h\(^{-2}\) |
| \(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) | h |
| \(\hat a_{t,s}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) | h |
| \(\Delta^{\text{block}}=[\underline B,\overline B]\) | Time window in which the original track of a blocked segment is unavailable | h |
| \(\alpha,\beta>0\) | Weights of total delay and total energy in the objective | – |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_e\) | Linear coefficient converting average speed on segment \(e\) into energy consumption (kWh per km·km h\(^{-1}\)) | kWh·h km\(^{-1}\) |
| \(M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable equals 0 | h (or km) |
| \(\mathbf 1_{e\in P_t},\ \mathbf 1_{e\in Q_t}\) | Known 0/1 constants indicating whether segment \(e\) belongs to the original or detour route of train \(t\). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \(x_t\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Route‑choice: 0 → original route \(P_t\); 1 → opposite‑track route \(Q_t\). |
| \(\delta_{t,e}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Segment‑selection indicator (equals 1 iff train \(t\) traverses segment \(e\) on the chosen route). |
| \(y_{t,t',e}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Order on shared segment \(e\): 1 → train \(t\) passes **before** train \(t'\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) ( \(d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\) if the train stops). |
| \(v_{t,e}\ge0\) | continuous | Average speed of train \(t\) on segment \(e\). |
| \(\tau_{t,e}\ge0\) | continuous | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(e\). |
| \(\lambda^{k}_{t,e}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary (piece‑wise linear) | Break‑point selector for speed on segment \(e\) (see Section 4). |
| \(e_t\ge0\) | continuous | Total delay of train \(t\). |
| \(E_t\ge0\) | continuous | Energy consumption of train \(t\). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Linearisation of the speed–travel‑time relation  

The exact relation \(\tau_{t,e}=L_e/v_{t,e}\) is non‑linear.  
Choose a set of \(K\) speed break‑points \(\{v^{k}_e\}_{k=1}^{K}\) covering \([\underline v_e,\overline v_e]\).  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda^{k}_{t,e}= \delta_{t,e},\qquad 
v_{t,e}= \sum_{k=1}^{K} v^{k}_e\,\lambda^{k}_{t,e},\qquad 
\tau_{t,e}= \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{L_e}{v^{k}_e}\,\lambda^{k}_{t,e}.
\]

Because the break‑points lie inside the admissible speed interval, the speed bounds are automatically satisfied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min\; \alpha\sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T} E_t}
\]

The first term penalises total passenger delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Constraints  

#### 6.1   Route‑choice and segment selection  

\[
\delta_{t,e}= (1-x_t)\,\mathbf 1_{e\in P_t}+x_t\,\mathbf 1_{e\in Q_t}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;e\in E .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus a segment is active only on the selected route.

#### 6.2   Blockage‑window for opposite‑track usage  

If train \(t\) uses the opposite‑track detour \((x_t=1)\) and traverses a blocked segment \(e\in E^{\text{sh}}\) in the opposite direction, it must enter after the blockage starts and leave before it ends:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,\text{up}(e)} &\ge \underline B - M\,(1-x_t) &&\forall t,\;e\in E^{\text{sh}}\cap Q_t,\\
a_{t,\text{down}(e)} &\le \overline B + M\,(1-x_t) &&\forall t,\;e\in E^{\text{sh}}\cap Q_t .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

If \(x_t=0\) the constraints are relaxed by the big‑\(M\).

#### 6.3   Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments  

For every \((t,t',e)\in\mathcal C\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',\text{up}(e)} &\ge a_{t,\text{down}(e)} + M\,(1-y_{t,t',e}),\\
a_{t,\text{up}(e)}   &\ge a_{t',\text{down}(e)} + M\,y_{t,t',e},\\
y_{t,t',e}+y_{t',t,e}&=1,
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

and each inequality is multiplied by the corresponding \(\delta\)‑variables so that it is active only when both trains actually use segment \(e\).

#### 6.4   Speed limits  

\[
\underline v_e\,\delta_{t,e}\le v_{t,e}\le \overline v_e\,\delta_{t,e}
\qquad\forall t,e.
\tag{4}
\]

#### 6.5   Acceleration / deceleration limits  

For two consecutive segments \(e\rightarrow e'\) on the same train:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,e'}-v_{t,e} &\le \overline a\,\tau_{t,e}+M\bigl(2-\delta_{t,e}-\delta_{t,e'}\bigr),\\
v_{t,e}-v_{t,e'} &\le \underline a\,\tau_{t,e}+M\bigl(2-\delta_{t,e}-\delta_{t,e'}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

If either segment is not used the big‑\(M\) term deactivates the constraint.

#### 6.6   Time propagation (arrival–departure relationship)  

\[
a_{t,\text{down}(e)} \ge d_{t,\text{up}(e)} + \tau_{t,e} - M\,(1-\delta_{t,e})
\qquad\forall t,e.
\tag{6}
\]

If the train stops at a station \(s\) (\(\gamma_{t,s}=1\) known from the route data):

\[
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} - M\,(1-\gamma_{t,s})
\qquad\forall t,s.
\tag{7}
\]

#### 6.7   Delay definition  

\[
e_t \ge \sum_{s\in S}\bigl(a_{t,s}-\hat a_{t,s}\bigr)\,\gamma_{t,s},
\qquad e_t\ge0\qquad\forall t.
\tag{8}
\]

Only positive excess over the scheduled arrival is counted (early arrivals are ignored).

#### 6.8   Energy consumption (linearised)  

\[
E_t = \sum_{e\in E} c^{\text{energy}}_e\,v_{t,e}\,\delta_{t,e}
\qquad\forall t.
\tag{9}
\]

Because \(v_{t,e}\) is linear in the binary break‑point variables \(\lambda^{k}_{t,e}\), the expression is linear.

#### 6.9   Station capacity (pairwise ordering)  

Let \(C_s\) be the maximal number of trains that may dwell simultaneously at station \(s\).  
Introduce binary variables \(z_{t,t',s}\) for each unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t<t'\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge a_{t,s} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} - M\,(1-z_{t,t',s}),\\
a_{t,s}   &\ge a_{t',s} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t',s} - M\,z_{t,t',s},
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t<t',\;s\in S.
\tag{10}
\]

Summing the resulting order variables for a given station yields a bound that guarantees at most \(C_s\) overlapping dwell intervals. (For small‑scale tests the pairwise formulation suffices.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T} \sum_{e\in E} c^{\text{energy}}_e\,v_{t,e}\,\delta_{t,e}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(10) above,}\\
& x_t\in\{0,1\},\; \delta_{t,e},y_{t,t',e},z_{t,t',s},\lambda^{k}_{t,e}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},v_{t,e},\tau_{t,e},e_t,E_t\ge0\qquad\forall t,s,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (or linearised) and involve only continuous variables and binary decision variables; therefore the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8. Remarks on the model  

* **Route choice** – the binary \(x_t\) forces each train to follow either its original timetable (fast but possibly blocked) or the opposite‑track detour (slower but avoids the blockage).  
* **Blockage handling** – when the detour is taken the train must respect the time window \([\underline B,\overline B]\) of the blocked segment.  
* **Conflict avoidance** – binary order variables \(y_{t,t',e}\) guarantee a strict temporal ordering on every segment that could be occupied by more than one train, thus preventing collisions on the shared track.  
* **Speed–time coupling** – the piece‑wise linear speed representation together with the acceleration constraints lets the optimizer trade higher speed (lower delay) against higher energy consumption.  
* **Delay & energy** – the objective directly penalises the sum of train delays and the sum of energy consumptions, weighted by \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).  
* **Capacity** – simple pairwise ordering at stations limits the number of trains simultaneously dwelling, ensuring platform capacity is respected.  

The MILP can be solved with any commercial or open‑source solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, CBC, …). For large‑scale networks the model can be tightened with additional valid inequalities or decomposed (Benders, column generation), but the formulation above already captures the essential physics of **integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partial segment blockage**.
