Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a high‑speed railway experiences a *partial‑segment blockage* (one‑track operation) during a known disruption time window \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\).  

The formulation simultaneously decides  

1. **Timetable adjustments** – new arrival / departure times, possible train cancellations, and optional route changes (use of the opposite track).  
2. **Train‑order (re‑sequencing)** – binary precedence variables that avoid head‑way conflicts on the shared track.  
3. **Speed‑profile selection** – a set of pre‑computed feasible speed‑plans for each train‑run; the chosen plan determines the running time on every line segment and the associated energy consumption.  

All decisions are linearised, yielding a MILP that can be solved directly with a commercial solver or used as the master problem in the decomposition algorithm described in the paper.

---

## 1. Index Sets, Parameters and Assumptions  

| Symbol | Meaning | Remarks / Assumptions |
|--------|---------|------------------------|
| \(\mathcal{T}\) | Set of trains (indexed by \(i\)) | All trains that are scheduled to run during the planning horizon. |
| \(\mathcal{S}\) | Set of stations (indexed by \(s\)) | Includes the origin and destination of each train. |
| \(\mathcal{L}\) | Set of line‑segments (ordered pairs of consecutive stations \((s,s')\)) | Each segment is bi‑directional; during disruption only one direction may be usable. |
| \(\mathcal{P}_i\) | Set of feasible **speed‑plans** for train \(i\) on its original route | A speed‑plan \(p\) specifies a running time \(\tau^{p}_{i,\ell}\) and an energy consumption \(e^{p}_{i,\ell}\) for every segment \(\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i\). (Plans are generated offline by a detailed train‑dynamics model; linearisation is discussed later.) |
| \(\mathcal{K}_\ell\) | Set of *conflict‑pairs* on segment \(\ell\) | \((i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell\) if trains \(i\) and \(j\) ever use \(\ell\) (in either direction) in the original schedule. |
| \(\mathcal{B}\) | Set of *blocked* segments (subset of \(\mathcal{L}\)) | During \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\) only one track of the segment is available (i.e. bidirectional traffic must share the same physical line). |
| \(a^{\text{orig}}_{i,s}\) | Original scheduled **arrival** time of train \(i\) at station \(s\). | |
| \(d^{\text{orig}}_{i,s}\) | Original scheduled **departure** time of train \(i\) from station \(s\). | |
| \(\underline{t}^{\text{dwell}}_{i,s}\) | Minimum dwell time (boarding/alighting) required at station \(s\). | |
| \(\overline{t}^{\text{dwell}}_{i,s}\) | Maximum allowable dwell (e.g. due to platform capacity). | |
| \(\underline{t}^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}\) , \(\overline{t}^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible **running time** on segment \(\ell\) for train \(i\) (derived from physical limits). | |
| \(E^{\max}_i\) | Upper bound on total energy consumption for train \(i\). | Optional, to limit excessive acceleration. |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) used for linearising logical conditions. | Chosen larger than the planning horizon. |
| \(\Delta\) | Minimum head‑way (in minutes) required between two successive trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical line. | Typical safety margin (e.g. 3 min). |
| \(\Gamma\) | Minimum separation time between two opposite‑direction trains sharing a blocked segment (bidirectional conflict). | Usually larger than \(\Delta\) because of signalling constraints. |
| \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) | Weight of **energy** in the bi‑objective function (the remainder \(1-\alpha\) weights total delay). | Decision‑maker parameter. |

**Key modelling assumptions (explicitly stated):**

1. **Deterministic disruption** – the start/end times of the blockage are known a‑priori and do not change.  
2. **Pre‑computed speed‑plans** – for each train–segment pair a finite set of feasible speed‑profiles (running time / energy) is generated offline; the MILP only selects one plan.  
3. **Single‑track sharing** – on a blocked segment only one train can occupy the physical line at a time; head‑way constraints are enforced for both same‑direction and opposite‑direction pairs.  
4. **No crew‑change or rolling‑stock constraints** – the model focuses on train‑level decisions only.  
5. **Cancellation** – a train may be cancelled (binary variable) incurring a large penalty \(P^{\text{cancel}}_i\).  
6. **Rerouting** – a train can be forced to use the opposite track on a blocked segment (binary variable \(r_{i,\ell}\)); this does not change the physical distance, only the conflict‑type (same‑direction ↔ opposite‑direction).  

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(a_{i,s}\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | **New arrival time** of train \(i\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{i,s}\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | **New departure time** of train \(i\) from station \(s\). |
| \(x_{i,p}\) | Binary | **Speed‑plan selection** – 1 if plan \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\) is chosen for train \(i\). |
| \(c_i\) | Binary | **Cancellation flag** – 1 if train \(i\) is cancelled. |
| \(r_{i,\ell}\) | Binary | **Reroute flag** – 1 if train \(i\) uses the opposite track on blocked segment \(\ell\). |
| \(y_{i,j,\ell}\) | Binary | **Precedence** – 1 if train \(i\) passes *before* train \(j\) on segment \(\ell\) (same‑direction). |
| \(z_{i,j,\ell}\) | Binary | **Opposite‑direction precedence** – 1 if train \(i\) (direction \(+\)) passes before train \(j\) (direction \(-\)) on blocked segment \(\ell\). |
| \(\theta_i\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Total delay** of train \(i\) (difference between new and original arrival at its destination). |
| \(\varepsilon_i\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Total energy consumption** of train \(i\) (sum of selected plan energies). |

Auxiliary derived quantities (used in constraints, not independent variables):

- Running time on segment \(\ell\) for train \(i\):  
  \[
  t^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}\tau^{p}_{i,\ell}\,x_{i,p}\qquad\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i .
  \]
- Energy on segment \(\ell\) for train \(i\):  
  \[
  e_{i,\ell}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}e^{p}_{i,\ell}\,x_{i,p}\qquad\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i .
  \]

---

## 3. Objective Function  

A weighted sum of **total passenger delay** and **total energy consumption**, plus a large penalty for cancellations:

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \theta_i}_{\text{Delay}} \;+\;
(1-\alpha)\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \varepsilon_i}_{\text{Energy}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} P^{\text{cancel}}_i\,c_i}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}}
}
\]

where  

\[
\theta_i = \bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{dest}}} - a^{\text{orig}}_{i,s^{\text{dest}}}\bigr)\;(1-c_i)
\qquad\forall i,
\]
\[
\varepsilon_i = \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i} e_{i,\ell}\;(1-c_i).
\]

\(s^{\text{dest}}\) denotes the destination station of train \(i\).

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Feasibility of Speed‑Plan Choice  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i} x_{i,p}= 1-c_i \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{C1}
\]

If a train is cancelled (\(c_i=1\)) no plan is selected.

### 4.2 Time‑flow (timetable) constraints  

**Arrival–departure relationship at each station (including dwell):**

\[
d_{i,s} \;=\; a_{i,s} + \underline{t}^{\text{dwell}}_{i,s}\;(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{S}_i\setminus\{s^{\text{dest}}\}
\tag{C2}
\]

Optionally, a maximum dwell can be enforced:

\[
d_{i,s} \;\le\; a_{i,s} + \overline{t}^{\text{dwell}}_{i,s}\;(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{S}_i\setminus\{s^{\text{dest}}\}
\tag{C3}
\]

**Running‑time linking between consecutive stations:**  

Let \(\ell=(s,s')\) be the segment connecting station \(s\) to \(s'\) on train \(i\)’s route.  

\[
a_{i,s'} \;=\; d_{i,s} + t^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}\;(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i,\; \ell=(s,s')\in\mathcal{L}_i
\tag{C4}
\]

**Running‑time bounds (to keep the selected plan within physical limits):**  

\[
\underline{t}^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}\;(1-c_i) \;\le\; t^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell} \;\le\; \overline{t}^{\text{run}}_{i,\ell}\;(1-c_i)
\qquad\forall i,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i
\tag{C5}
\]

### 4.3 Disruption‑related feasibility  

**Blockage‑window occupancy:**  
If segment \(\ell\) is blocked (\(\ell\in\mathcal{B}\)) and train \(i\) traverses it, the entry time must be outside the blockage window *unless* the train uses the opposite track (i.e. is rerouted).  

Let the entry time on \(\ell\) be \(d_{i,s}\) (departure from the upstream station).  

\[
d_{i,s} \;\le\; T^{\text{start}} \;+\; M\bigl(r_{i,\ell}+c_i\bigr) \qquad\forall i,\;\ell=(s,s')\in\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{L}_i
\tag{C6a}
\]

\[
d_{i,s} \;\ge\; T^{\text{end}} \;-\; M\bigl(r_{i,\ell}+c_i\bigr) \qquad\forall i,\;\ell=(s,s')\in\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{L}_i
\tag{C6b}
\]

If \(r_{i,\ell}=0\) and \(c_i=0\), the two inequalities force the train to **avoid** the blockage window; otherwise the big‑M relaxes them.

**Reroute consistency:**  
A train can reroute on a blocked segment only once (binary decision per segment) and only if the segment is actually blocked:

\[
r_{i,\ell}\;\le\; \mathbf{1}_{\{\ell\in\mathcal{B}\}}\qquad\forall i,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i
\tag{C7}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance (head‑way) on shared physical line  

For every pair \((i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell\) that share segment \(\ell\) (same direction **or** opposite direction after rerouting) we enforce a *precedence* binary variable.

#### 4.4.1 Same‑direction precedence  

If both trains travel the **same direction** on \(\ell\) (i.e. either both use the original track or both have been rerouted to the same side), then

\[
d_{i,s} + \Delta \;\le\; a_{j,s'} + M\,(1-y_{i,j,\ell}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{C8a}
\]

\[
d_{j,s} + \Delta \;\le\; a_{i,s'} + M\,y_{i,j,\ell} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{C8b}
\]

where \(s\) is the upstream station of \(\ell\) for train \(i\) and \(s'\) the downstream station for train \(j\). The binary \(y_{i,j,\ell}\) decides which train goes first.

#### 4.4.2 Opposite‑direction precedence (blocked segment)  

When the segment is blocked (\(\ell\in\mathcal{B}\)) and the two trains travel in opposite directions (i.e. one of them may have been rerouted), a larger separation \(\Gamma\) is required:

\[
d_{i,s} + \Gamma \;\le\; a_{j,s'} + M\,(1-z_{i,j,\ell}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{C9a}
\]

\[
d_{j,s} + \Gamma \;\le\; a_{i,s'} + M\,z_{i,j,\ell} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{C9b}
\]

The binary \(z_{i,j,\ell}\) selects the crossing order.

#### 4.4.3 Linking precedence to reroute decisions  

The above constraints are only active when the two trains actually occupy the **same physical line**. This is modelled by the following logical activation:

\[
y_{i,j,\ell} \le 1 - r_{i,\ell} - r_{j,\ell} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\notin\mathcal{B}
\tag{C10a}
\]

\[
z_{i,j,\ell} \le r_{i,\ell} + r_{j,\ell} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{K}_\ell,\;\ell\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{C10b}
\]

Thus, if neither train reroutes on a blocked segment, they are treated as same‑direction (C8). If at least one reroutes, the opposite‑direction head‑way (C9) is enforced.

### 4.5 Energy and Energy‑limit  

Total energy for each train:

\[
\varepsilon_i = \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_i} e_{i,\ell}\;(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i
\tag{C11}
\]

Optional upper bound:

\[
\varepsilon_i \;\le\; E^{\max}_i \qquad\forall i
\tag{C12}
\]

### 4.6 Delay definition  

Destination station of train \(i\) is denoted \(s^{\text{dest}}_i\). Delay is measured only if the train is not cancelled:

\[
\theta_i = \bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{dest}}_i} - a^{\text{orig}}_{i,s^{\text{dest}}_i}\bigr)\;(1-c_i) \qquad\forall i
\tag{C13}
\]

If a train is cancelled, \(\theta_i=0\) (its penalty is captured by \(P^{\text{cancel}}_i\)).

### 4.7 Logical consistency  

- **Cancellation dominates all other decisions:**  

\[
a_{i,s} = a^{\text{orig}}_{i,s}\;,\; d_{i,s}=d^{\text{orig}}_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\;s\quad\text{if }c_i=1
\]

Implemented by big‑M relaxations or by fixing the variables through (C1)–(C13) which already set all other variables to zero when \(c_i=1\).

- **Exactly one speed‑plan per active train** (already enforced by C1).

- **Binary variables are 0/1** (standard integrality constraints).

---

## 5. Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{a,d,x,c,r,y,z,\theta,\varepsilon}\;&
\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\theta_i
+(1-\alpha)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\varepsilon_i
+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}P^{\text{cancel}}_i\,c_i \\
\text{s.t.}&\; \text{(C1)–(C13)} \\
&\; x_{i,p}\in\{0,1\},\; c_i\in\{0,1\},\; r_{i,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,j,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,j,\ell}\in\{0,1\} \\
&\; a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}, \theta_i, \varepsilon_i \ge 0 \quad \forall i,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Discussion of Linearisation  

1. **Speed‑plan linearisation** – The set \(\mathcal{P}_i\) is generated by solving the continuous train‑dynamics (acceleration, traction, braking) problem for each segment and discretising the feasible \((\text{running time},\text{energy})\) pairs. Because the selection is binary, the resulting relationship between running time and energy is linear (convex hull of the discrete points).  

2. **Big‑M values** –  
   * For head‑way constraints, \(M\) can be set to the planning horizon (e.g., 24 h) plus the maximum possible segment travel time.  
   * For blockage‑window constraints, \(M\) may be set to the horizon length as well.  

3. **Precedence activation** – The linking constraints (C10a,b) guarantee that only the appropriate set of head‑way constraints (C8 or C9) becomes binding, preserving linearity.  

4. **Cancellation handling** – By forcing all binary decisions to zero when \(c_i=1\) and fixing times to their original values through big‑M, the model remains linear.  

---

## 7. Possible Extensions (outside the core MILP)  

| Extension | How it would be added to the MILP |
|-----------|-----------------------------------|
| **Platform capacity limits** (max \(k\) trains at a station simultaneously) | Add binary occupation variables for each station‑time interval and a capacity constraint \(\sum_i \mathbf{1}_{[a_{i,s},d_{i,s})\cap\Delta t\neq\emptyset} \le k\). |
| **Crew‑working‑time constraints** | Introduce cumulative crew‑time variables and limit them per shift. |
| **Multiple disruption windows** | Duplicate the blockage‑window constraints for each interval, using separate binary flags \(r_{i,\ell}^{(q)}\). |
| **Stochastic disruption duration** | Replace deterministic \(T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}\) by scenario‑specific parameters and use a two‑stage stochastic MILP (first‑stage decisions \(x,c,r\), second‑stage recourse \(a,d\)). |

These extensions preserve the MILP structure but increase size; they can be handled by the same decomposition‑based algorithm described in the paper (master IP for binary decisions, sub‑problems for each train’s speed‑plan selection).  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above delivers a *complete* mixed‑integer linear model for the **Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial‑segment blockages. It integrates timetable adjustment, train‑order (conflict) resolution, rerouting decisions, and the selection of executable speed profiles, while jointly minimizing passenger delay, energy consumption, and cancellation penalties. The model is ready for implementation in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) and forms the mathematical core of the decomposition‑based solution framework proposed in the accompanying study.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP‑MILP)**  
*For a high‑speed railway line that suffers a partial‑segment blockage (one‑track closure) during a known disruption time window.*

---

## 1.  Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run on the line (including those that may be cancelled). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of the line). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of directed track segments (i,i′) that connect two consecutive stations. |
| **B** ⊆ E | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the physical track that is unavailable on one side during the disruption). |
| **K** = {1,…,K} | Set of *time‑intervals* used for linearisation of speed‑energy relations (e.g. 0–5 s, 5–10 s …). |
| **Δ** = {1,…,Δmax} | Set of *discretised speed‑levels* (Δ = 1 → minimum admissible speed, Δ = Δmax → maximum admissible speed). |
| **τᵣ** | Duration (in minutes) of the disruption time window (known a‑priori). |
| **tᵇᵤᵍ** | Beginning time of the disruption window (absolute clock time). |
| **M** | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) used in logical constraints. |
| **cᵗ** | Fixed penalty cost for cancelling train *t*. |
| **β⁺, β⁻** | Energy cost coefficients for acceleration (β⁺) and regenerative braking (β⁻). |
| **αᵗᵢᵢ′** | Minimum travelling time for train *t* on segment (i,i′) when travelling at the minimum admissible speed. |
| **γᵗᵢᵢ′** | Maximum travelling time for train *t* on segment (i,i′) when travelling at the maximum admissible speed. |
| **d⁽ᵗ⁾ᵢ** | Minimum dwell time required at station *i* for train *t* (including passenger boarding/alighting). |
| **Lᵗᵢᵢ′** | Length (km) of segment (i,i′) for train *t* (normally the same for all trains). |
| **a⁺, a⁻** | Maximum admissible acceleration / deceleration (km/min²). |
| **v⁽min⁾, v⁽max⁾** | Global minimum/maximum speed limits (km/min). |
| **Rᵗ** | Set of feasible *routing* alternatives for train *t* (normally two: original one‑track direction, or opposite‑track detour through the blocked segment). |
| **δᵗᵣ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* uses the *detour* (i.e. runs on the opposite track inside the blocked segment), 0 otherwise. |
| **πᵗᵢ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* occupies station *i* (i.e. arrives there), 0 otherwise. |
| **πᵗᵉ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* = (i,i′). |
| **τᵗᵢ** | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (continuous). |
| **σᵗᵢ** | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *i* (continuous). |
| **xᵗᵢᵢ′ᵏ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,i′) with speed‑level Δ = k (i.e. average speed that belongs to interval *k*). |
| **eᵗᵢᵢ′** ≥ 0 | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment (i,i′). |

**Assumptions (explicitly stated)**  

1. The line is *single‑track* in each direction; the disruption blocks **one** of the two parallel tracks for a known time window \([t^{b\_ug}, t^{b\_ug}+τ_r]\).  
2. All trains are high‑speed EMU sets with identical dynamical limits \((a^+,a^-,v^{min},v^{max})\).  
3. The timetable is discretised at the station level; only arrival and departure times are decision variables.  
4. Speed on each segment is approximated by a **piece‑wise constant** speed level \(k\); within a level the energy cost is linear (common linearisation of the non‑linear kinetic‑energy expression).  
5. Conflicts are prevented by **headway** constraints on any track segment: two trains cannot occupy the same segment at overlapping times.  
6. Trains may be **cancelled** (binary variable \(z_t\)). Cancellation removes all constraints concerning that train except a penalty in the objective.  
7. Rerouting (detour) is modelled by a binary variable \(\delta_{t}\) that switches the direction of the blocked segment for train *t* (i.e. uses the opposite track). When \(\delta_{t}=1\) the train traverses the segment in the opposite direction and must respect the opposite‑track capacity.  
8. Dwell times are enforced as *minimum*; longer dwell is allowed when required for conflict resolution.  
9. All parameters are known in advance (including disruption time window, segment lengths, minimum/maximum travelling times).  

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \(z_t\) | binary | 1 if train *t* is **cancelled**, 0 otherwise. |
| \(\delta_t\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the **detour** (opposite track) inside the blocked segment, 0 otherwise. |
| \(\pi_{t,i}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* arrives at station *i*, 0 otherwise (used to deactivate constraints for cancelled trains). |
| \(\pi_{t,(i,i')}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment \((i,i')\). |
| \(\tau_{t,i}\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *i*. |
| \(\sigma_{t,i}\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *i*. |
| \(x_{t,i,i',k}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment \((i,i')\) with speed‑level *k* (thus fixing travel time). |
| \(e_{t,i,i'}\) | continuous, ≥0 | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment \((i,i')\). |

---

## 3.  Linearised Travel‑Time – Speed‑Level Relation  

For each segment \((i,i')\) and speed level \(k\) we pre‑compute a **travel time** \( \theta_{i,i',k}\) (minutes) and an **energy coefficient** \(\eta_{i,i',k}\) (kWh) using the physical formulas

\[
\theta_{i,i',k}= \frac{L_{i,i'}}{v_k}, \qquad 
\eta_{i,i',k}= \beta^{+}\, v_k\, a^{+}\,L_{i,i'} - \beta^{-}\, v_k\, a^{-}\,L_{i,i'} ,
\]

where \(v_k\) is the representative speed of level *k* (the mid‑point of the interval).  
These values are *parameters* in the MILP.

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

The integrated model simultaneously **minimises total delay** (measured by deviation from the original scheduled times), **energy consumption**, and **cancellation penalties**.

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,
      \bigl(\tau_{t,i} - \tau^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr) }_{\text{Total delay cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,i')\in E} e_{t,i,i'}}_{\text{Energy cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} c_t\, z_t}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}}
}
\]

* \(w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\) – user‑defined weight (often 1) for delay at station *i* of train *t*.  
* \(\tau^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\) – originally planned arrival time (data).  

If a train is cancelled (\(z_t=1\)), the delay terms for that train are forced to zero by a big‑M linking \(z_t\) and \(\pi_{t,i}\) (see constraints).

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Cancellation and Activity  

\[
\pi_{t,i} \le 1- z_t \qquad \forall t\in T,\;i\in S \tag{C1}
\]

If train *t* is cancelled, it does not appear at any station.  

\[
\pi_{t,(i,i')} \le 1- z_t \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,i')\in E \tag{C2}
\]

### 5.2  Routing (detour) logic  

Only trains that truly need to pass the blocked segment may choose the opposite track:

\[
\pi_{t,(i,i')} = 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if segment }(i,i')\notin B,\\
\delta_t & \text{if }(i,i')\in B \text{ and original direction is blocked},\\
1-\delta_t & \text{if }(i,i')\in B \text{ and original direction is free}.
\end{cases}
\tag{R1}
\]

In MILP form we introduce a big‑M for each blocked segment \(b=(i,i')\):

\[
\pi_{t,b} \le 1- \delta_t + M(1-z_t) ,\qquad
\pi_{t,b} \ge \delta_t - M z_t .
\]

(Equivalent linear constraints guarantee \(\pi_{t,b}= \delta_t\) when the train is active.)

### 5.3  Speed‑level selection  

Each traversed segment is assigned **exactly one** speed level:

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K} x_{t,i,i',k} = \pi_{t,(i,i')} \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,i')\in E \tag{SL1}
\]

\[
x_{t,i,i',k} \in \{0,1\} .
\]

### 5.4  Travel‑time linking  

If a segment is travelled with speed level \(k\) the departure‑arrival relation must hold:

\[
\sigma_{t,i} + \theta_{i,i',k} \;-\; \tau_{t,i'} \le M\,(1- x_{t,i,i',k}) \qquad \forall t,i,i',k \tag{TT1}
\]

\[
\tau_{t,i'} + M\,(1- x_{t,i,i',k}) \le \sigma_{t,i} + \theta_{i,i',k} \qquad \forall t,i,i',k \tag{TT2}
\]

Thus, when \(x_{t,i,i',k}=1\) the equality \(\sigma_{t,i}+ \theta_{i,i',k}= \tau_{t,i'}\) is enforced.

### 5.5  Dwell‑time constraints  

\[
\sigma_{t,i} - \tau_{t,i} \ge d^{(t)}_i \;-\; M\,z_t \qquad \forall t,i \tag{DW1}
\]

Minimum dwell is waived for cancelled trains.

### 5.6  Head‑way (conflict‑avoidance) on **any** segment  

For any two *different* active trains \(t\neq t'\) that share a segment \((i,i')\) the order must be respected:

\[
\tau_{t',i'} \ge \sigma_{t,i} + \theta_{i,i',k}\;-\; M\bigl(2- x_{t,i,i',k} - x_{t',i,i',k'}\bigr)
\quad \text{or}
\]
\[
\tau_{t,i} \ge \sigma_{t',i'} + \theta_{i,i',k'}\;-\; M\bigl(2- x_{t,i,i',k} - x_{t',i,i',k'}\bigr),
\]

implemented with a binary ordering variable \(y_{t,t',i,i'}\in\{0,1\}\):

\[
\tau_{t',i'} \ge \sigma_{t,i} + \theta_{i,i',k} - M\,(1-y_{t,t',i,i'}) \tag{HW1}
\]
\[
\tau_{t,i} \ge \sigma_{t',i'} + \theta_{i,i',k'} - M\,y_{t,t',i,i'} \tag{HW2}
\]

Both constraints are enforced only if both trains traverse the segment:

\[
y_{t,t',i,i'} \le \pi_{t,(i,i')},\; y_{t,t',i,i'} \le \pi_{t',(i,i')}.
\]

### 5.7  Disruption‑time‑window feasibility  

If a train **uses** the blocked segment, it must **not** occupy it during the disruption window unless it takes the opposite track (detour).  

*Case 1 – original direction (blocked):*  

\[
\sigma_{t,i} + \theta_{i,i',k} \le t^{b\_ug} \;+\; M(1- \delta_t) \quad \text{or}\quad 
\tau_{t,i'} \ge t^{b\_ug}+ \tau_{r} \;+\; M(1- \delta_t) .
\]

*Case 2 – detour (opposite track, which is free):*  

No restriction; the train may pass anytime.

These logical constraints are linearised with binary variables and big‑M.

### 5.8  Energy accounting  

Energy on each segment is the sum of the level‑specific coefficients:

\[
e_{t,i,i'} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \eta_{i,i',k}\; x_{t,i,i',k} \qquad \forall t,i,i' \tag{EN1}
\]

Energy variables are non‑negative.

### 5.9  Variable domains  

\[
z_t,\; \delta_t,\; \pi_{t,i},\; \pi_{t,(i,i')},\; x_{t,i,i',k},\; y_{t,t',i,i'} \in \{0,1\}
\]

\[
\tau_{t,i},\; \sigma_{t,i},\; e_{t,i,i'} \ge 0
\]

---

## 6.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,
      \bigl(\tau_{t,i} - \tau^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr)
      + \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,i')\in E} e_{t,i,i'}
      + \sum_{t\in T} c_t\, z_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1) – (C2)    cancellation activity} \\
& \text{(R1) – routing / detour logic} \\
& \text{(SL1) – one speed level per traversed segment} \\
& \text{(TT1)–(TT2) – travel‑time linking} \\
& \text{(DW1) – minimum dwell time} \\
& \text{(HW1)–(HW2) – head‑way (conflict) constraints} \\
& \text{(Disruption window constraints) }\\
& \text{(EN1) – energy definition} \\
& \text{binary and non‑negativity domains.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7.  Remarks on Solving the MILP  

* **Decomposition** – As suggested in the article, the model can be decomposed into a *master* integer program that selects a feasible **train‑plan** (a combination of routing, speed‑level, and ordering decisions) for each train, and a set of *sub‑problems* (one per train) that compute the detailed arrival/departure times and energy given the chosen plan.  
* **Plan granularity** – The speed‑level set \(K\) determines the linearisation accuracy. A finer discretisation improves the representation of the true quadratic energy‑speed relation at the cost of larger model size.  
* **Adaptive refinement** – After solving a coarse‑grained model, the algorithm can introduce additional intermediate speed levels only for those trains whose schedules are near the disruption window, following the “local‑branching” idea.  
* **Scalability** – For a realistic high‑speed line (≈ 50 trains, 30 stations, 2‑3 speed levels), the MILP contains on the order of \( |T|\times|E|\times K \) binary variables (≈ a few thousand) and is tractable for modern MIP solvers when the above decomposition is used.  

---

**Thus, the formulation above constitutes a complete, linear (mixed‑integer) model that jointly optimises train rescheduling (arrival/departure times, routing, ordering) and speed‑profile selection, while explicitly handling bidirectional conflicts on a partially blocked segment and accounting for energy consumption.**

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model)*  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **N**   | Set of nodes (track points: block ends, switch‑points, station‑platform entry/exit, TTD‑section ends) |
| **A**   | Set of directed arcs (track segments)  \((i,j)\) with *i,j* ∈ N |
| **S**   | Set of speed‑profile options (e.g. *cruise*, *deceleration‑to‑stop*, *coasting*) |
| **K**   | Set of time‑discretisation points used for linearisation of continuous time (k = 0,…,K) |
| **B**   | Sub‑set of arcs that contain a switch (turnout) – “switch arcs” |
| **F**   | Sub‑set of arcs that are ordinary track (no switch) – “plain arcs” |
| **D**   | Set of DTG‑sections (TTD sections) – each section *d* is a contiguous set of arcs; the *end‑of‑authority* (EoA) of a train can only be placed at the downstream end of a section. |

*Assumption 1*: All physical blocks used in the timetable are aggregated into DTG‑sections *d* ∈ D.  
*Assumption 2*: The planning horizon is long enough to contain the latest possible arrival of any train after rescheduling.

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of arc \((i,j)\) | [km] |
| \(v^{\max}_t\) | Maximum permissible speed of train *t* (depends on train type) | [km/h] |
| \(a^{\text{acc}}_t\) | Maximum acceleration of train *t* | [km/h²] |
| \(a^{\text{brk}}_t\) | Maximum service braking deceleration of train *t* (positive value) | [km/h²] |
| \(B^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v)\) | Braking distance of train *t* when travelling at speed *v*: \(B^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v)=\frac{v^{2}}{2a^{\text{brk}}_t}\) (linearised, see §4) | [km] |
| \(s^{\text{dwell}}_{t,n}\) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station node *n* (0 if n not a station) | [s] |
| \(E^{\text{orig}}_{t,d}\) | Original (pre‑delay) planned entry time of train *t* into DTG‑section *d* | [s] |
| \(\Delta^{\text{init}}_t\) | Initial delay of train *t* at the beginning of the horizon (given) | [s] |
| \(M\) | Large positive constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | – |
| \(\epsilon\) | Small positive constant (e.g. 1 s) to enforce strict ordering | [s] |
| \(\alpha_{t,i}\) | Binary flag = 1 if train *t* is allowed to use node *i* (e.g. due to routing decisions) | – |
| \(\beta_{t,(i,j)}\) | Binary flag = 1 if train *t* traverses arc \((i,j)\) (routing decision) | – |
| \(\gamma_{t,d}\) | Binary flag = 1 if train *t*’s **end‑of‑authority** (EoA) is placed at the downstream end of DTG‑section *d* | – |

*Assumption 3*: All parameters are known a‑priori from the timetable, rolling‑stock data and signalling specifications.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,i} \) | Continuous ≥ 0 | **Arrival time** of train *t* at node *i* (seconds) |
| \(y_{t,i} \) | Continuous ≥ 0 | **Departure time** of train *t* from node *i* (seconds) |
| \(z_{t,d}\) | Continuous ≥ 0 | **EoA time** of train *t* at the downstream end of DTG‑section *d* (seconds) |
| \(v_{t,i}\) | Continuous ≥ 0 | Speed of train *t* when leaving node *i* (km/h) – used to compute braking distance |
| \(\beta_{t,(i,j)}\) | Binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* traverses arc \((i,j)\) |
| \(\gamma_{t,d}\) | Binary | 1 ⇔ train *t*’s EoA is placed at section *d* |
| \(\theta_{t,t',d}\) | Binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* is **ahead** of train *t'* on the same DTG‑section *d* (conflict‑ordering variable) |
| \(\delta_{t,t'}\) | Binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* is scheduled **after** train *t'* at a shared resource (node or switch) |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

Minimise the **total accumulated delay** of all trains at the end of their routes (or at a chosen reference node, e.g. last station).

\[
\min \; \sum_{t\in T}\bigl( x_{t,i^{\text{last}}} - E^{\text{orig}}_{t,i^{\text{last}}}\bigr)
\]

where \(i^{\text{last}}\) is the final node of train *t* (usually the last station).  
If a different performance measure is required (e.g., weighted delay, number of re‑routings), it can be added linearly.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Routing feasibility  

\[
\sum_{(i,j)\in A}\beta_{t,(i,j)} = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T   \tag{R1}
\]

Each train follows exactly one outgoing arc from a node (flow conservation) – expanded to a standard path‑flow model:

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}\beta_{t,(i,j)} - \sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}\beta_{t,(j,i)} = 
\begin{cases}
1 & i = o_t \\
-1 & i = d_t \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \qquad \forall t\in T,\, i\in N   \tag{R2}
\]

\(o_t\) and \(d_t\) are the origin and destination nodes of train *t*.

### 5.2. Time‑linking along traversed arcs  

If arc \((i,j)\) is used, departure from *i* plus travel time equals arrival at *j*:

\[
x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \frac{L_{ij}}{v_{t,i}} - M\bigl(1-\beta_{t,(i,j)}\bigr) \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in A   \tag{T1}
\]

\[
y_{t,i} \ge x_{t,i} + s^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i} - M\bigl(1-\alpha_{t,i}\bigr) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; i\in N   \tag{T2}
\]

The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when the arc is not selected.

### 5.3. Speed‑profile linearisation  

Train speed after leaving node *i* is limited by max speed and by acceleration from the previous node. A simple linear envelope (piecewise) can be introduced using the set *S*; for brevity we use a single bound:

\[
0 \le v_{t,i} \le v^{\max}_t \qquad \forall t,i   \tag{S1}
\]

If a more detailed profile is needed, binary variables selecting a speed‑profile *s* ∈ S can be added (omitted here for clarity).

### 5.4. End‑of‑Authority (EoA) placement  

The EoA of a train must be at the downstream end of exactly one DTG‑section that lies on its path:

\[
\sum_{d\in D}\gamma_{t,d} = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T   \tag{E1}
\]

If a train traverses arc \((i,j)\) that belongs to section *d*, then \(\gamma_{t,d}=1\) forces the EoA to be placed after the last arc of *d*:

\[
\sum_{(i,j)\in d}\beta_{t,(i,j)} \ge \gamma_{t,d} \qquad \forall t, d   \tag{E2}
\]

EoA time is linked to the departure from the last node of the section:

\[
z_{t,d} \ge y_{t,i^{\text{out}}(d)} - M\bigl(1-\gamma_{t,d}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,d   \tag{E3}
\]

where \(i^{\text{out}}(d)\) is the downstream node of section *d*.

### 5.5. Speed‑dependent separation (DTG‑specific)  

For any pair of trains \((t,t')\) that share the same DTG‑section *d* (i.e., both have \(\gamma_{t,d}=1\) and \(\gamma_{t',d}=1\)), the **brake‑indication point** of the following train must be at least the braking distance behind the front train’s EoA. Using the binary ordering variable \(\theta_{t,t',d}\) (1 if *t* is ahead of *t'*), we write:

\[
z_{t',d} \ge z_{t,d} + B^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v_{t,i^{\text{out}}(d)}) + \epsilon - M\bigl(1-\theta_{t,t',d}\bigr) \qquad \forall t\neq t', d   \tag{C1}
\]

\[
\theta_{t,t',d} + \theta_{t',t,d} = 1 \qquad \forall t\neq t', d \text{ with } \gamma_{t,d}=\gamma_{t',d}=1   \tag{C2}
\]

The braking distance term is linearised by piecewise approximation over a set of speed break‑points \(\{v^s\}_{s\in S}\). For each speed break‑point we introduce auxiliary continuous variables \(b_{t,d}^s\) and enforce:

\[
b_{t,d}^s \ge \frac{(v^s)^2}{2a^{\text{brk}}_t} - M\bigl(1-\lambda_{t,d}^s\bigr) \qquad \forall s
\]

\[
v_{t,i^{\text{out}}(d)} = \sum_{s}\lambda_{t,d}^s v^s ,\qquad 
\sum_{s}\lambda_{t,d}^s = 1 ,\qquad \lambda_{t,d}^s \in \{0,1\}
\]

Finally, the braking distance used in (C1) is \(B^{\text{brk}}_{t}(v_{t,i^{\text{out}}(d)}) = \sum_{s} b_{t,d}^s\).

### 5.6. Conflict resolution at switches and stations  

At a node that is a **resource** (station platform, switch, or TTD detector), at most one train may occupy it at a time. Using the ordering binary \(\delta_{t,t'}\) for any pair of trains that share node *i*:

\[
x_{t',i} \ge y_{t,i} + \epsilon - M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t'}\bigr) \qquad \forall i\in N_{\text{conflict}},\; t\neq t'   \tag{RSC1}
\]

\[
\delta_{t,t'} + \delta_{t',t} = 1 \qquad \forall i\in N_{\text{conflict}},\; t\neq t' \text{ with } \beta_{t,(i,\cdot)}=1,\beta_{t', (i,\cdot)}=1   \tag{RSC2}
\]

\(N_{\text{conflict}}\) includes all nodes where simultaneous occupation is forbidden (e.g., a switch point, a platform track, a TTD detector).

### 5.7. Initial delay incorporation  

The first arrival time of each train is forced to respect its known initial delay:

\[
x_{t,o_t} = E^{\text{orig}}_{t,o_t} + \Delta^{\text{init}}_t \qquad \forall t\in T   \tag{ID1}
\]

### 5.8. Non‑negativity and binary domains  

\[
x_{t,i},\, y_{t,i},\, z_{t,d},\, v_{t,i} \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,i,d
\]

\[
\beta_{t,(i,j)},\,\gamma_{t,d},\,\theta_{t,t',d},\,\delta_{t,t'} \in \{0,1\}
\]

---

## 6. Model Summary  

The MILP consists of:

* **Variables** – arrival/departure times, speeds, binary routing, EoA placement, and ordering variables.  
* **Objective** – minimise total train delay (linear).  
* **Constraints** – (i) routing feasibility, (ii) temporal consistency along selected arcs, (iii) speed limits, (iv) placement of the end‑of‑authority at DTG‑section boundaries, (v) **speed‑dependent separation** using braking‑distance based safety margins (the core DTG enhancement), (vi) mutual exclusion at switches/stations, (vii) incorporation of known initial delays.  

All constraints are linear (or linearised via standard piecewise‑linear approximations). The model therefore fits any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP).

---

## 7. Remarks & Possible Extensions  

1. **Piecewise‑linear braking distance** – the number of break‑points can be increased to improve fidelity without breaking linearity.  
2. **Multiple speed‑profile options** – introduce binary variables \(p_{t,s,i}\) to select a profile *s* on arc \((i,j)\); each profile has its own admissible speed and acceleration limits.  
3. **Weighted objective** – include penalties for re‑routing (switching arcs) or for exceeding a maximum allowable delay.  
4. **Moving‑block (virtual‑block) extension** – replace the DTG‑section set *D* by a set of dynamically generated virtual sections; the same constraints (E1–E3, C1) hold with the virtual boundaries.  
5. **Robustness** – add slack variables to allow limited violation of separation constraints at a high penalty, useful when the problem is infeasible due to extreme delays.  

---

**Thus, the presented MILP fully captures conflict detection and resolution for railway operations under distance‑to‑go signalling, accounting for train‑specific and speed‑dependent braking distances, while remaining a linear (mixed‑integer) optimisation problem suitable for real‑time decision support.**

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)  
Partial‑Segment‑Blockage Disruption Scenario**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) a **conflict‑free timetable** (arrival / departure times, train order and possible rerouting) and (ii) a **real‑time speed profile** for every train‑run segment so that the produced timetable can be executed by the train‑control system.  
All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  
Missing data are filled with *reasonable assumptions* that are clearly marked.

---

## 1.  Notation  

### 1.1   Sets  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(N\) | Set of stations (including origin and terminal), indexed by \(i\). |
| \(E\subseteq N\times N\) | Set of directed track sections (arcs) \((i,j)\) that a train can travel. |
| \(B\subseteq E\) | Subset of **blocked sections** (partial‑segment blockage). |
| \(\mathcal{D}\) | Set of discrete **time‑intervals** used for linearisation, indexed by \(d\).  Length of interval \(\Delta\) (e.g. 1 min). |
| \(K_{t}\) | Set of feasible **routing alternatives** for train \(t\) (original route + possible opposite‑track reroute through blocked area). |
| \(P_{t}^{k}\) | Set of **speed‑profile plans** for train \(t\) when using routing alternative \(k\). Each plan is a piece‑wise constant speed over the intervals in \(\mathcal{D}\) (see §2.3). |

### 1.2   Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / assumption |
|--------|---------|----------------------------|
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length (km) of section \((i,j)\). | – |
| \(v^{\max}_{ij}\) | Maximum admissible speed on \((i,j)\) (km/h). | 300 km/h for high‑speed line |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Maximum acceleration (km/h²). | 0.8 km/h² (≈0.22 m/s²) |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum deceleration (km/h², positive). | 0.9 km/h² |
| \(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i}\) | Minimum dwell time at station \(i\) (min). | 3 min |
| \(\tau^{\text{turn}}\_{t}\) | Minimum turnaround time for train‑type \(t\) after reaching terminal (min). | 10 min |
| \(C^{\text{energy}}_{t}\) | Energy cost coefficient (kWh per km·(speed/100)²) for train \(t\). | 0.12 kWh/km·(v/100)² |
| \(M\) | Large constant for “big‑M” linearisation (e.g. 10⁶). | – |
| \([s_{t}^{\text{orig}},e_{t}^{\text{orig}}]\) | Original scheduled **departure‑arrival window** for train \(t\) (min). | – |
| \(\Delta\) | Length of a time‑interval in \(\mathcal{D}\) (min). | 1 min |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight of total delay in objective (cost‑per‑min). | 1 \$/min |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of total energy consumption (cost‑per‑kWh). | 0.05 \$/kWh |
| \(\gamma\) | Weight of number of cancelled trains (penalty). | 10 000 \$/cancellation |
| \(b_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if section \((i,j)\) is **blocked** during the disruption window, 0 otherwise. (Only for \((i,j)\in B\)). | – |

> **Assumption A1** – The disruption window is known a‑priori (start \(t^{\text{disr}}_{s}\) – end \(t^{\text{disr}}_{e}\)). All blocked sections are unavailable for travel in the **original direction** during this interval; the opposite‑track can be used if a rerouting alternative is chosen.

### 1.3   Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t}^{k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses routing alternative \(k\in K_{t}\). |
| \(y_{t}^{p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if **speed‑plan** \(p\in P_{t}^{k}\) is selected (implicitly tied to the chosen route). |
| \(a_{ti}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Actual arrival time** of train \(t\) at station \(i\) (min from midnight). |
| \(d_{ti}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Actual departure time** of train \(t\) from station \(i\). |
| \(s_{tij}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies section \((i,j)\) during time‑interval \(d\). |
| \(z_{tij}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses section \((i,j)\) **in the opposite direction** during interval \(d\) (needed only for bidirectional conflict). |
| \(c_{t}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) is **cancelled**. |
| \(\delta_{ti}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Delay** of train \(t\) at station \(i\) w.r.t. original schedule: \(\delta_{ti}=a_{ti}-a_{ti}^{\text{orig}}\). |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train \(t\) (kWh). |

> **Assumption A2** – For each train‑route \(k\) we pre‑compute a *finite* set of feasible speed‑plans \(P_{t}^{k}\) (e.g. by discretising acceleration/deceleration decisions). Each plan provides the exact travel time on each traversed section and the associated energy use; the MILP only decides which plan to adopt.

---

## 2.  Model Overview  

The integrated MILP consists of three logical layers:

1. **Routing / cancellation layer** – choose a route (original or opposite‑track reroute) or cancel the train.  
2. **Timetabling layer** – enforce arrival/departure times, dwell times, turnaround, and **conflict‑free occupancy** of every track‑section for every time‑interval (including bidirectional conflicts).  
3. **Speed‑profile layer** – link the selected speed‑plan to the travel times on each traversed section; compute energy consumption.

All constraints are linear (or linearised with big‑M), making the model a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 3.  Objective Function  

A weighted sum of three practical goals:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in N}\delta_{ti}
\;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}
\;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t}
}
\]

* **Delay term** – penalises total passenger delay (minutes).  
* **Energy term** – penalises total electricity consumption (kWh).  
* **Cancellation term** – heavy penalty to avoid unnecessary cancellations.  

The weights \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are decision‑maker parameters.

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1   Routing / cancellation consistency  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{t}} x_{t}^{k} + c_{t} = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T                              \tag{1}
\]

Only one routing alternative (or cancellation) can be chosen.

If a train is cancelled, all timing variables are forced to a dummy value:

\[
a_{ti} \le M\,c_{t},\; d_{ti} \le M\,c_{t} \qquad \forall t,i                      \tag{2}
\]

### 4.2   Arrival / departure relationship  

\[
d_{ti} = a_{ti} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i}\;(1-c_{t}) \qquad \forall t,i          \tag{3}
\]

(If a train is cancelled, the constraint is relaxed by (2).)

### 4.3   Travel‑time coupling with speed plans  

For each train, the **total travel time** between successive stations must equal the travel time prescribed by the selected speed plan.

Let \(T_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\) be the travel time (in minutes) of plan \(p\) on section \((i,j)\) for route \(k\). This data are known a‑priori (pre‑computed).  

Define a binary indicator \(\chi_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)=1\) if plan \(p\) for route \(k\) traverses section \((i,j)\) (otherwise 0).  

Then for every consecutive station pair \((i,j)\) on train \(t\)’s *original* route:

\[
a_{t j} \ge d_{t i} + \sum_{k\in K_{t}}\sum_{p\in P_{t}^{k}} T_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\,\chi_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\, y_{t}^{p}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E_{t}^{\text{orig}}          \tag{4}
\]

where \(E_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) is the set of arcs that belong to the original route of train \(t\).  
If a reroute is selected, the corresponding arcs are alternatively defined in the data set for that route; the same constraint (4) is applied using the appropriate \(\chi\) and \(T\) values.

**Linking routing choice and speed‑plan selection**

\[
y_{t}^{p} \le x_{t}^{k}\qquad \forall t,\; p\in P_{t}^{k},\;k\in K_{t}           \tag{5}
\]

Only a plan belonging to the chosen routing alternative can be activated.

Exactly one plan must be chosen if the train is not cancelled:

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{t}}\;\sum_{p\in P_{t}^{k}} y_{t}^{p}= 1- c_{t}\qquad \forall t\in T   \tag{6}
\]

### 4.4   Section‑occupancy variables  

If train \(t\) traverses section \((i,j)\) using plan \(p\) that needs \(T_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\) minutes, we introduce the occupancy binary \(s_{tij}^{d}\) for each discrete interval \(d\).

We first compute the **starting interval** of the traversal:

\[
\theta_{tij} = \left\lfloor \frac{d_{ti}}{\Delta}\right\rfloor \quad\text{(continuous, relaxed by big‑M)}         \tag{7}
\]

To keep linearity we use a set of *pre‑defined* possible start‑times (e.g. every minute) and a big‑M linking:

\[
\theta_{tij} = \sum_{d\in \mathcal{D}} d\cdot s^{\ast}_{tij}{}^{d} \qquad
\sum_{d}s^{\ast}_{tij}{}^{d}=1 \qquad \forall t,(i,j)                 \tag{8}
\]

where \(s^{\ast}_{tij}{}^{d}\) is a binary indicating that the traversal of \((i,j)\) *starts* in interval \(d\).  

Now we enforce that the train occupies the section for the required number of intervals:

\[
s_{tij}^{d} \ge s^{\ast}_{tij}{}^{\ell} \qquad 
\forall t,(i,j),\; d\in\{\ell,\ell+1,\dots,\ell+\tau_{tij}^{k,p}-1\},\;
\forall \ell\in\mathcal{D}                                          \tag{9}
\]

where \(\tau_{tij}^{k,p}= \lceil T_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)/\Delta\rceil\) is the number of discrete intervals needed.  

If a train is cancelled, all its occupancy binaries are forced to 0:

\[
s_{tij}^{d}\le 1-c_{t}\qquad\forall t,i,j,d                                 \tag{10}
\]

### 4.5   Conflict‑free occupancy (unidirectional & bidirectional)  

#### 4.5.1   Single‑track capacity (one train at a time)

\[
\sum_{t\in T} s_{tij}^{d} \le 1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in E\setminus B,\; d\in\mathcal{D}   \tag{11}
\]

All **non‑blocked** sections can host at most one train in any direction.

#### 4.5.2   Blocked sections – opposite‑track usage  

For a blocked section \((i,j)\in B\) only **one direction** may be used at a time:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} s_{tij}^{d} \;+\; \sum_{t\in T} z_{tij}^{d} \;\le\; 1 
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in B,\; d\in\mathcal{D}                     \tag{12}
\]

where \(z_{tij}^{d}\) denotes occupancy of the *opposite* direction (i.e., train travelling from \(j\) to \(i\) on the opposite track).  

The opposite‑direction occupancy is linked to the same speed‑plan data (just reversed arcs) and obeys the same constraints (9)–(10) with indices swapped.

### 4.6   Delay definition  

\[
\delta_{ti}= a_{ti} - a_{ti}^{\text{orig}} \qquad \forall t,i           \tag{13}
\]

If the train is cancelled, \(\delta_{ti}=0\) automatically by (2).

### 4.7   Energy consumption  

Energy of a selected plan is directly taken from the pre‑computed data:

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{k\in K_{t}}\sum_{p\in P_{t}^{k}} 
      \Bigl( C^{\text{energy}}_{t}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in E} 
          \chi_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\,L_{ij}\,\bigl(\tfrac{v_{tij}^{k,p}}{100}\bigr)^{2}\Bigr)\; y_{t}^{p}
\qquad\forall t\in T                                            \tag{14}
\]

where \(v_{tij}^{k,p}\) is the **average speed** of plan \(p\) on section \((i,j)\) (derived from \(L_{ij}\) and \(T_{t}^{k,p}(i,j)\)).  
Because \(y_{t}^{p}\) is binary, (14) is linear.

### 4.8   Turn‑around and depot constraints (optional, for completeness)  

If a train returns to a depot after its final station \(i^{\text{last}}_{t}\):

\[
a_{t,\text{depot}} \ge d_{t,i^{\text{last}}_{t}} + \tau^{\text{turn}}_{t}\;(1-c_{t}) \tag{15}
\]

### 4.9   Logical linking of opposite‑track occupancy  

If a train uses a rerouting alternative that employs the opposite track for a blocked section \((i,j)\), we force the corresponding \(z\)-variables; otherwise they stay 0.

\[
z_{tij}^{d} \ge s^{\ast}_{tji}{}^{d}\;x_{t}^{k_{\text{opp}}} \qquad 
\forall t,(i,j)\in B,\; d\in\mathcal{D}                                   \tag{16}
\]

where \(k_{\text{opp}}\) denotes the routing alternative that traverses \((j,i)\) on the opposite track.

---

## 5.  Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t,i}\delta_{ti} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t}E_{t}\;+\;\gamma\sum_{t}c_{t}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(16)}\\
& x_{t}^{k},y_{t}^{p},s_{tij}^{d},z_{tij}^{d},c_{t},s^{\ast}_{tij}{}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{ti},d_{ti},\delta_{ti},E_{t}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.  

---

## 6.  Remarks & Modelling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Reasoning |
|---|------------|-----------|
| A1 | Disruption window and blocked sections are known a‑priori. | Enables the binary parameters \(b_{ij}\) and the definition of opposite‑track usage. |
| A2 | A **finite** set of pre‑computed feasible speed‑plans per routing alternative is available (generated by a lower‑level continuous optimisation or by enumerating admissible acceleration patterns). | Guarantees linearity; the plan data contains travel times, average speeds, and energy consumption. |
| A3 | Time is discretised into equal intervals \(\Delta\) (typically 1 min). | Allows binary occupancy variables \(s_{tij}^{d}\) and simplifies conflict constraints. |
| A4 | Maximum acceleration / deceleration are constant for all trains. | Simplifies the generation of the speed‑plan library; more detailed train‑specific dynamics could be added by expanding the plan set. |
| A5 | Energy consumption is approximated by a quadratic speed‑dependent term (common in high‑speed rail literature). | Keeps the energy term linear in the binary plan selection variables. |
| A6 | Dwell times are fixed (minimum dwell). Additional slack can be introduced by allowing \(d_{ti}\ge a_{ti}+ \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i}\) if desired. | Guarantees feasibility while keeping the model compact. |
| A7 | The “big‑M” constant is chosen sufficiently large (e.g., 10⁶) to relax constraints for cancelled trains. | Standard linearisation technique. |

---

## 7.  Possible Extensions  

* **Robustness** – introduce scenario‑based disruption start/end times and minimise worst‑case delay.  
* **Variable dwell time** – add a continuous slack variable \(w_{ti}\ge0\) to let trains wait longer if necessary, penalised in the objective.  
* **Crew/rolling‑stock constraints** – add coupling constraints linking trains sharing the same set of vehicles.  
* **Dynamic block‑duration** – allow binary variables that decide whether a blocked section is cleared earlier (investing resources).  

These extensions preserve the MILP structure but increase model size; they can be incorporated later once the basic TRSMP model is validated.

---

**The formulation above provides a complete, self‑contained MILP description of the **Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial‑segment blockage disruptions, ready to be implemented in any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).**

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model**  
*Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management under Partial Segment Blockage*

---  

### 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of stations, indexed by *s* |
| **L** | Set of track segments (between two successive stations), indexed by *ℓ* – each segment ℓ connects stations *(iℓ , jℓ)* |
| **H** | Set of discrete time‑steps in the planning horizon, indexed by *h* (Δh = length of a step) |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed levels, indexed by *k* (e.g. 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 km/h) |
| **R** | Set of admissible routes for a train; for train *t* the feasible subset is **Rᵗ** ⊆ **R** |
| **Rᵗℓ** | Subset of routes of train *t* that contain segment ℓ (used in linking constraints) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Δh | Length of a time step (h) |
| Lℓ | Length of segment ℓ (km) |
| v_k | Speed associated with level *k* (km/h) |
| e_k | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) at speed level *k* |
| cℓ | Capacity of segment ℓ (max. simultaneous trains) |
| Bℓ ⊆ H | Time‑steps during which segment ℓ is blocked |
| τ_t | Desired (original) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (h) |
| st₀t | Planned departure time of train *t* from its origin (h) |
| w_d , w_e | Weights for delay and energy in the objective |
| M | Large constant for big‑M linearisation (e.g. M = |H|·Δh) |
| δ_tr | 1 if route *r* is feasible for train *t*, 0 otherwise |
| p_trℓ | 1 if segment ℓ belongs to route *r* of train *t*, 0 otherwise |
| θ_kℓ = ⌈ Lℓ / (v_k·Δh) ⌉ | Number of time steps required to travel ℓ at speed level *k* (pre‑computed) |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| dep_th ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* departs its origin at time step *h* |
| arr_th ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* arrives at its final destination at time step *h* |
| y_tr ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* chooses route *r* |
| x_tℓkh ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* starts segment ℓ at speed level *k* at time step *h* |
| u_tℓh ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies segment ℓ during time step *h* |
| Δ_t ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *t* (h) |
| E_t ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption of train *t* (kWh) |

---

### 4. Derived Quantities  

Departure and arrival times (in hours):  

\[
t^{dep}_t = \sum_{h\in H} h\,\Delta h\; dep_{th},\qquad
t^{arr}_t = \sum_{h\in H} h\,\Delta h\; arr_{th}
\]

Delay definition (linear):  

\[
\Delta_t = t^{arr}_t - \tau_t \qquad (\Delta_t\ge 0)
\]

Energy consumption (linear):  

\[
E_t = \sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{h\in H} e_k\,L_\ell \; x_{t\ell k h}
\]

---

### 5. Objective  

\[
\min\;  w_d\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; w_e\sum_{t\in T}E_t
\]

Weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption.

---

### 6. Constraints  

#### 6.1 Route selection  
1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R^{t}} y_{tr}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Only feasible routes may be chosen**  

   \[
   y_{tr}\le \delta_{tr}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in R^{t}
   \]

#### 6.2 Departure / Arrival timing  
3. **Exactly one departure time**  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in H} dep_{th}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
   \]

4. **Exactly one arrival time**  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in H} arr_{th}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
   \]

5. **Departure cannot be earlier than the original plan** (optional)  

   \[
   t^{dep}_t\;\ge\; st_{0t}\qquad\forall t\in T
   \]

#### 6.3 Linking route, segment traversal and speed choice  
6. **If a route is chosen, the corresponding segments must be traversed**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{h\in H} x_{t\ell k h}= \sum_{r\in R^{t}} p_{tr\ell}\,y_{tr}
   \qquad\forall t\in T,\;\ell\in L
   \]

   (Left‑hand side = 1 iff segment ℓ is traversed, right‑hand side = 1 iff the selected route contains ℓ.)

7. **Only one speed level for a start of a segment**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} x_{t\ell k h}\le 1 \qquad\forall t,\ell,h
   \]

#### 6.4 Segment occupancy & capacity  
8. **Occupancy propagation** – a train that starts a segment at time *h* with speed *k* occupies the segment for the next `θ_kℓ` steps:  

   \[
   u_{t\ell (h+\sigma)} \;\ge\; x_{t\ell k h}
   \qquad\forall t,\ell,k,h,\;\sigma=0,\dots,\theta_{k\ell}-1
   \]

   (Indices that fall outside **H** are ignored.)

9. **Capacity limit**  

   \[
   \sum_{t\in T} u_{t\ell h}\le c_\ell \qquad\forall \ell\in L,\;h\in H
   \]

10. **Blockage constraint** – no occupancy during blocked steps  

    \[
    u_{t\ell h}=0 \qquad\forall t,\; \ell,\; h\in B_\ell
    \]

#### 6.5 Temporal precedence along a route  
11. **Flow conservation** – a train may start the successor segment only after it has finished the current one.  
    Let `succₜ(ℓ)` be the successor of ℓ on the selected route of train *t* (if any).  

    \[
    \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{h'\le h} x_{t\,succₜ(ℓ)\,k\,h'} \;\ge\; 
    \sum_{k\in K} x_{t\ell k h}
    \qquad\forall t,\;\ell \text{ with a successor},\;h\in H
    \]

12. **Final‑arrival linking** – the arrival binary must be set once the last segment of the selected route is finished.  
    If `ℓ_f(t)` is the last segment of the chosen route:  

    \[
    arr_{th}\;\ge\; \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\sigma=0}^{\theta_{k\ell_f(t)}-1}
    x_{t\ell_f(t)k\,(h-\sigma)}
    \qquad\forall t,\;h\in H
    \]

#### 6.6 Delay & energy definitions (linear)  
13. **Delay** (already expressed in Section 4, here written as a constraint)  

    \[
    \Delta_t = \sum_{h\in H} h\,\Delta h\; arr_{th} - \tau_t\qquad\forall t\in T
    \]

14. **Energy** (from Section 4)  

    \[
    E_t = \sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{h\in H} e_k\,L_\ell \; x_{t\ell k h}
    \qquad\forall t\in T
    \]

---

### 7. Model Summary  

| Component | Variable type | Linear? |
|-----------|---------------|---------|
| Route choice (`y`) | binary | yes |
| Departure / arrival (`dep`,`arr`) | binary | yes |
| Segment start with speed (`x`) | binary | yes |
| Segment occupancy (`u`) | binary | yes (derived from `x`) |
| Delay, energy (`Δ`,`E`) | continuous | yes |
| Objective | linear | – |
| All constraints | linear (or big‑M linear) | – |

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below is a *complete* mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem (TRSMP) described in the prompt.  
All symbols that appear in the objective or in the constraints are listed in the **parameter** and **variable** tables, after which the full mathematical program is given.  
The formulation is *linear* – every non‑linear term (product of a binary and a continuous variable, logical “or’’ statements, etc.) has been linearised by the usual big‑M or convex‑combination tricks, so the model can be handed directly to any commercial MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …).

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|--------|
| **\( \mathcal T =\{1,\dots ,T\}\)** | Set of trains (indexed by \(t\)). |
| **\( \mathcal S =\{1,\dots ,S\}\)** | Set of track segments (indexed by \(s\)). |
| **\( \mathcal D=\{+,-\}\)** | Set of travel directions ( +  = north‑bound, –  = south‑bound). |
| **\( \mathcal K=\{1,\dots ,K\}\)** | Set of admissible speed levels (ordered, e.g. 0 km/h, 150 km/h, 250 km/h, 300 km/h). |
| **\( \mathcal B\subseteq \mathcal S\times \mathcal D\)** | Set of *blocked* segment–direction pairs (partial blockage). |
| **\( \mathcal N_t =\{1,\dots ,N_t\}\)** | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) traverses in its (possibly rerouted) path. For each \(i\in\mathcal N_t\) we denote the concrete segment and direction by \((s_{t,i},d_{t,i})\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|--------|---------|-------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) | km |
| \(v^{\max}_k\) | Physical speed corresponding to level \(k\) | km/h |
| \(v^{\min}_{s,d}\) | Minimum admissible speed on blocked pair \((s,d)\) (often >0). | km/h |
| \(\alpha_{s,k}\) | Energy consumption (kWh) for traversing segment \(s\) at speed level \(k\) (linearised). | kWh |
| \(c^d_t\) | Penalty weight of one hour of delay for train \(t\). | $/h |
| \(w^e\) | Global weight for total energy in the objective. | $/kWh |
| \(w^d\) | Global weight for total delay in the objective (often =1). | – |
| \(M\) | Big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time, e.g. 10 000 min). | min |
| \(C_{s,d}\) | Track capacity (max. number of trains simultaneously on \((s,d)\)). | – |
| \(C^{\text{blk}}_{s,d}\) | Reduced capacity on a blocked pair \((s,d)\) (≤ \(C_{s,d}\)). | – |
| \(T^{\text{release}}_t\) | Earliest possible departure time of train \(t\) (planned). | min |
| \(T^{\text{due}}_t\) | Desired arrival time of train \(t\) at its final node (planned). | min |
| \(\tau^{\min}_{s,d}\) | Minimum dwell (stop) time required on segment \(s\) in direction \(d\) (e.g. station dwell). | min |
| \(\gamma_{s,d}\) | Minimum safe headway (time separation) for two trains travelling **in the same direction** on \((s,d)\). | min |
| \(\delta_{s}\) | Minimum safe separation for two trains travelling **in opposite directions** on a single‑track segment \(s\). | min |
| \(\widehat{t}_{t,i}^k = L_{s_{t,i}}/v^{\max}_k\) | Nominal travel time of train \(t\) on its i‑th segment when speed level \(k\) is used. | min |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,i,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses its i‑th segment with speed level \(k\). |
| \(y_{t,i}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) actually uses its i‑th segment (allows optional detours). |
| \(a_{t,i}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **up‑stream** node of its i‑th segment. |
| \(d_{t,i}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train \(t\) from the up‑stream node of its i‑th segment. |
| \(\Delta_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | Total (positive) delay of train \(t\) at its final node: \(\Delta_t = a_{t,N_t} - T^{\text{due}}_t\) (or 0 if early). |
| \(E\) | continuous ≥0 | Total energy consumption (kWh). |
| \(c_{t,t',i}^{\text{same}}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) passes **before** train \(t'\) on the same segment‑direction pair for the i‑th segment (same‑direction ordering). |
| \(c_{t,t',i}^{\text{opp}}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) passes **before** train \(t'\) on the same physical segment but opposite directions (opposite‑direction ordering). |

Auxiliary linear expressions (no additional variables)

* **Travel time on segment i of train t**:  
  \[
  p_{t,i}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\widehat{t}_{t,i}^k \, x_{t,i,k}.
  \tag{3.1}
  \]

* **Energy on segment i of train t**:  
  \[
  e_{t,i}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\alpha_{s_{t,i},k}\, x_{t,i,k}.
  \tag{3.2}
  \]

---

## 4. Objective Function  

Minimise a weighted sum of **total passenger delay** and **total energy consumption**:

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
w^{d}\,\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}c^{d}_{t}\,\Delta_{t}}_{\displaystyle \text{Delay cost}}
\;+\;
w^{e}\,\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_t} e_{t,i}}_{\displaystyle \text{Energy cost}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_{t}= \max\bigl\{0,\; a_{t,N_t}-T^{\text{due}}_t\bigr\}
\]

is linearised with a non‑negative slack variable \(\Delta_t\ge a_{t,N_t}-T^{\text{due}}_t\) and \(\Delta_t\ge0\).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing / speed‑selection  

1. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} x_{t,i,k}= y_{t,i}
   \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; i\in\mathcal N_t .
   \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Minimum speed on a blocked segment** (if \((s_{t,i},d_{t,i})\in\mathcal B\))  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal K:\; v^{\max}_k < v^{\min}_{s_{t,i},d_{t,i}}} x_{t,i,k}=0
   \qquad\forall t,i\;\text{with } (s_{t,i},d_{t,i})\in\mathcal B .
   \tag{R2}
   \]

### 5.2 Time‑flow (arrival / departure)  

3. **Release time at origin**  

   \[
   d_{t,1}\;\ge\;T^{\text{release}}_t \qquad\forall t .
   \tag{T1}
   \]

4. **Dwell / minimum stop time**  

   \[
   d_{t,i}\;\ge\; a_{t,i}+ \tau^{\min}_{s_{t,i},d_{t,i}}\, y_{t,i}
   \qquad\forall t,i .
   \tag{T2}
   \]

5. **Travel‑time definition (linearised)**  

   \[
   p_{t,i}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\widehat{t}_{t,i}^k\,x_{t,i,k}
   \qquad\forall t,i .
   \tag{T3}
   \]

6. **Propagation of timing**  

   \[
   a_{t,i+1}= d_{t,i}+p_{t,i}
   \qquad\forall t,\; i=1,\dots ,N_t-1 .
   \tag{T4}
   \]

7. **Delay definition**  

   \[
   \Delta_t \ge a_{t,N_t}-T^{\text{due}}_t ,\qquad 
   \Delta_t \ge 0
   \qquad\forall t .
   \tag{T5}
   \]

### 5.3 Track‑capacity and conflict avoidance  

Both same‑direction and opposite‑direction conflicts are modelled with binary ordering variables.

8. **Same‑direction headway** – for any unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) that occupy the **same** segment‑direction on the *i‑th* (or *j‑th*) position of their routes:

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   a_{t',j} &\ge d_{t,i}+ \gamma_{s_{t,i},d_{t,i}} - M\,c_{t,t',i}^{\text{same}},\\
   a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',j}+ \gamma_{s_{t,i},d_{t,i}} - M\,(1-c_{t,t',i}^{\text{same}}),
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{C1}
   \]

   for all \(t<t'\) and all \((i,j)\) such that \((s_{t,i},d_{t,i})=(s_{t',j},d_{t',j})\).

9. **Opposite‑direction exclusion on a single‑track segment** – if a segment \(s\) can be used by only one train at a time regardless of direction (typical for a blocked bidirectional line):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   a_{t',j} &\ge d_{t,i}+ \delta_{s_{t,i}} - M\,c_{t,t',i}^{\text{opp}},\\
   a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',j}+ \delta_{s_{t,i}} - M\,(1-c_{t,t',i}^{\text{opp}}),
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{C2}
   \]

   for all pairs \((t,t')\) with \((s_{t,i},d_{t,i})=(s_{t',j},-d_{t,i})\).

10. **Capacity on blocked segments** (if reduced capacity \(C^{\text{blk}}_{s,d}< C_{s,d}\))  

    \[
    \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_t}
        y_{t,i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{(s_{t,i},d_{t,i})=(s,d)\}}
    \;\le\; C^{\text{blk}}_{s,d}
    \qquad\forall (s,d)\in\mathcal B .
    \tag{C3}
    \]

    For unblocked segments the same expression is bounded by the nominal capacity \(C_{s,d}\).

### 5.4 Energy aggregation  

11. **Total energy**  

    \[
    E = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_t} e_{t,i}
      = \sum_{t}\sum_{i}\sum_{k}\alpha_{s_{t,i},k}\,x_{t,i,k}.
    \tag{E1}
    \]

### 5.5 Variable domains  

12. **Binary variables**  

    \[
    x_{t,i,k},\,y_{t,i},\,c_{t,t',i}^{\text{same}},\,c_{t,t',i}^{\text{opp}}\in\{0,1\}
    \qquad\forall\text{indices}.
    \tag{D1}
    \]

13. **Continuous variables**  

    \[
    a_{t,i},\,d_{t,i},\,p_{t,i},\,\Delta_t,\,E \ge 0
    \qquad\forall\text{indices}.
    \tag{D2}
    \]

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,a,d,\Delta,E,c}\;&
      w^{d}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} c^{d}_t\,\Delta_t
   \;+\;
      w^{e}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_t}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
          \alpha_{s_{t,i},k}\,x_{t,i,k}
\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{Routing / speed selection: } &&\eqref{R1},\eqref{R2}\\
&\text{Time flow: }               &&\eqref{T1}-\eqref{T5}\\
&\text{Capacity & conflict: }    &&\eqref{C1},\eqref{C2},\eqref{C3}\\
&\text{Energy aggregation: }     &&\eqref{E1}\\
&\text{Variable domains: }        &&\eqref{D1},\eqref{D2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only source of combinatorial difficulty is the binary variables, which makes the model a *Mixed‑Integer Linear Program*.

---

## 7. How the Model Works (Explanation)

| Component | Role in the model | Why it matters |
|-----------|------------------|----------------|
| **Binary speed variables \(x_{t,i,k}\)** | Choose the speed level for each train‑segment pair. | Different speeds generate different travel times (via \(p_{t,i}\)) and different energy consumptions (via \(\alpha_{s,k}\)). |
| **Arrival/Departure times \(a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\)** | Describe the timetable that results from the chosen speeds. | Needed to compute passenger delay and to enforce safe headways/conflicts. |
| **Dwell‑time constraints** | Force a minimum stop on stations or on blocked segments. | Guarantees realistic service times and respects operational rules such as minimum station dwell. |
| **Travel‑time linearisation (Eq 3.1)** | Translate a chosen speed level into a deterministic travel duration. | Keeps the model linear while linking speed decisions to timing. |
| **Blockage handling (R2, C3)** | Prevents the model from assigning a speed below the minimum allowed on a blocked segment and respects the reduced capacity caused by a partial blockage. | Ensures safety and feasibility under the disruption. |
| **Same‑direction headway (C1)** | Keeps a required time gap \(\gamma\) between two trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment. | Avoids collisions and respects signalling constraints. |
| **Opposite‑direction exclusion (C2)** | Guarantees that two trains travelling opposite ways on a single‑track segment are separated by \(\delta\). | Essential for bidirectional conflict resolution when a partial blockage forces the use of a single track. |
| **Objective (weighted sum)** | Minimises a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption. | Allows the planner to emphasise punctuality (\(w^d\)) or sustainability (\(w^e\)). |
| **Big‑M linearisation** | Turns logical “or’’ statements (who passes first) into linear constraints using ordering binaries. | Required to keep the whole formulation linear. |

---

## 8. Practical Remarks  

1. **Model size** – The pairwise conflict constraints (C1), (C2) grow quadratically with the number of trains sharing a segment. In practice generate them only for *potentially overlapping* trains (e.g., based on the original timetable).  
2. **Alternative routing** – If the network contains detours that bypass a blocked segment, enumerate the feasible routes for each train beforehand. The binary variable \(y_{t,i}\) then acts as a *route‑selection* indicator (the model above already supports optional skipping of a segment).  
3. **Energy refinement** – For a more accurate energy model (including acceleration/deceleration phases) introduce extra binary variables for acceleration phases and linearise the corresponding energy terms; the structure of the MILP stays unchanged.  
4. **Solver tips** – Provide the original timetable as a warm‑start, use strong branching on the ordering binaries \(c^{\text{same}},c^{\text{opp}}\), and apply a time limit or gap tolerance if the instance is very large.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential operational features of the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockages, while remaining a pure MILP that can be solved with any state‑of‑the‑art mixed‑integer optimizer.
