Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Full Linear Formulation**  

The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a partial‑segment blockage forces a high‑speed railway operator to (i) **retime** arrivals/departures, (ii) **reorder / reroute** trains that share the blocked track, and (iii) **choose feasible speed profiles** for every train‑run segment.  

All notation, sets, parameters and decision variables are defined first, followed by the objective function and the complete set of linear constraints. Where data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are explicitly stated (marked **Assumption**).

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning (Assumption) |
|--------|----------------------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run during the planning horizon (including those that may be cancelled). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) connecting two successive stations.  An edge *e = (i,j)* represents the line between station *i* and *j*. |
| **B ⊆ E** | Sub‑set of edges that are **blocked** (partial‑segment blockage). |
| **K** = {1,…,K} | Set of **speed‑profile types** that can be assigned to a train on a given edge (e.g., “fast”, “medium”, “slow”).  Each type k is characterised by a constant average speed *v_k* and a constant energy consumption rate *e_k* (Assumption). |
| **Δ** = {0,1,…,Δ_max} | Discrete time‑grid (in minutes) used to linearise continuous time.  All event times are forced to lie on this grid (Assumption). |
| **P** = {1,…,P} | Set of **pre‑computed feasible plans** for each train (see Section 4.2).  A plan *p* for train *t* specifies a complete sequence of (edge, speed‑type, departure‑time, arrival‑time) tuples that respects physical limits and the blockage window.  Plans are generated offline by a speed‑profile sub‑problem (Assumption). |

### Basic Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| *a_t* , *b_t* | Original (planned) **departure** and **arrival** times of train *t* at its origin and terminal (minutes from horizon start). |
| *τ_e* | Nominal travel time on edge *e* when travelling at the design speed *v_design* (minutes). |
| *L_e* | Length of edge *e* (km). |
| *v_k* | Average speed associated with speed‑type *k* (km/min). |
| *c_k* | Energy consumption per kilometre for speed‑type *k* (kWh/km). |
| *M* | A large constant (big‑M) used for logical constraints (e.g., 10⁶). |
| *T_start*, *T_end* | Beginning and end of the planning horizon (minutes). |
| *Δ_block_start*, *Δ_block_end* | Start and end of the blockage time window on every blocked edge *e∈B* (minutes). |
| *γ* | Weighting factor for the energy‑minimisation term (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1). |
| *β* | Penalty weight for train cancellation (high value to discourage cancellations). |
| *θ* | Maximum allowed dwell time at any station (minutes). |
| *ρ* | Minimum headway (time separation) required between two trains travelling in the **same direction** on the same edge (minutes). |
| *σ* | Minimum headway required between two trains travelling in **opposite directions** on a shared single‑track edge (minutes). |
| *π_t* | Priority level of train *t* (higher → more important, used in weighted tardiness). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| *x_{t,p}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if **plan p** is selected for train *t*, 0 otherwise. |
| *y_t* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* is **cancelled**, 0 otherwise. |
| *d_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *i* (if *i* is the origin of *t* or a intermediate stop). |
| *a_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *i*. |
| *z_{t,e,k}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses edge *e* with speed‑type *k* (implied by the selected plan). |
| *c_{t,e}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Entry time** of train *t* onto edge *e* (i.e., departure from upstream station). |
| *h_{t,e}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Exit time** of train *t* from edge *e* (i.e., arrival at downstream station). |
| *w_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Dwell time** of train *t* at station *i* (≥ 0). |
| *δ_{t,t',e}^{dir}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on edge *e* in the **same direction** (dir = “same”), 0 otherwise. |
| *δ_{t,t',e}^{opp}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on edge *e* in **opposite directions** (dir = “opp”), 0 otherwise. |

*Auxiliary variables* (used only in linearisation):  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|--------|
| *Δ_{t,t',e}* = *c_{t',e} – h_{t,e}* | Time gap between the entry of *t'* and exit of *t* on edge *e*. |
| *Δ'_{t,t',e}* = *c_{t,e} – h_{t',e}* | Symmetric gap. |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The planner seeks a **trade‑off between service quality (tardiness / cancellations) and energy consumption**. A weighted sum formulation is used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \underbrace{\gamma \; \sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{p\in P_t}\; \Bigl( \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in K} c_k \, L_e \, z_{t,e,k} \Bigr) \; x_{t,p}}_{\text{(1) Energy consumption}} \\
& \;+\; (1-\gamma)\; \Bigl[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( \pi_t \, \max\{0,\, a_{t,\text{dest}}-b_t\}\bigr)}_{\text{(2) Weighted tardiness}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} y_t}_{\text{(3) Cancellation penalty}} \Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

*Explanation*  

* (1) Energy: For each selected plan, the total energy equals the sum over all traversed edges of (energy‑rate × length). Because *z_{t,e,k}* is 1 only for the speed‑type used on edge *e*, the term is linear.  
* (2) Tardiness: Arrival at the destination station *dest(t)* is *a_{t,dest}*. The original scheduled arrival is *b_t*. Positive lateness is penalised proportionally to the train’s priority *π_t*. Early arrivals are not penalised (they can be absorbed by dwell time).  
* (3) Cancellation: A large penalty *β* discourages unnecessary cancellations but allows them when infeasibility would otherwise occur.

The weight *γ* (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1) lets the decision‑maker emphasise energy vs. service quality.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Plan‑selection consistency  

1. **Exactly one plan (or cancellation) per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P_t} x_{t,p} + y_t = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T. \tag{C1}
\]

2. **Link plan variables to edge‑speed variables**  

For each train *t* and each edge *e* that appears in plan *p* with speed‑type *k* (denoted by indicator *α_{t,p,e,k}* = 1 if plan *p* uses (e,k), 0 otherwise):

\[
z_{t,e,k} = \sum_{p\in P_t} \alpha_{t,p,e,k}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; k\in K. \tag{C2}
\]

3. **Derive entry/exit times from selected plan**  

If plan *p* specifies entry time *c_{t,p,e}* and exit time *h_{t,p,e}* on edge *e* (pre‑computed), then:

\[
c_{t,e} = \sum_{p\in P_t} c_{t,p,e}\; x_{t,p}, \qquad
h_{t,e} = \sum_{p\in P_t} h_{t,p,e}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t, e. \tag{C3}
\]

Similarly for station arrival/departure times:

\[
a_{t,i} = \sum_{p\in P_t} a_{t,p,i}\; x_{t,p}, \qquad
d_{t,i} = \sum_{p\in P_t} d_{t,p,i}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t, i\in S_t. \tag{C4}
\]

*(Here \(S_t\) denotes the ordered set of stations visited by train *t* in any feasible plan.)*  

If a train is cancelled (*y_t = 1*), all its timing variables are forced to a dummy value (e.g., 0) using big‑M constraints, which are omitted for brevity.

### 4.2 Physical feasibility of speed profiles  

4. **Travel‑time consistency on each edge**  

\[
h_{t,e} - c_{t,e} = \frac{L_e}{v_k} \; z_{t,e,k} \qquad \forall t, e, k\in K. \tag{C5}
\]

Because each edge is traversed with exactly one speed‑type (by (C2)), the RHS reduces to the appropriate travel time.

5. **Dwell‑time definition**  

For each intermediate station *i* (i.e., not origin or terminal of *t*):

\[
w_{t,i} = d_{t,i} - a_{t,i} \qquad \forall t, i\in S_t\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{dest}\}. \tag{C6}
\]

6. **Maximum dwell‑time bound**  

\[
0 \le w_{t,i} \le \theta \qquad \forall t,i\in S_t\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{dest}\}. \tag{C7}
\]

### 4.3 Blockage‑window feasibility  

For every blocked edge *e∈B* and every train that traverses it (i.e., *z_{t,e,k}=1*) the entry must lie **outside** the blockage interval:

\[
c_{t,e} \le \Delta_{\text{block\_start}} \;+\; M\,(1 - z_{t,e,k}) \quad \text{or} \quad
c_{t,e} \ge \Delta_{\text{block\_end}} \;-\; M\,(1 - z_{t,e,k}) \qquad \forall t, e\in B, k. \tag{C8}
\]

The logical “or” is linearised by introducing a binary *b_{t,e}* that selects which side of the window is used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{t,e} &\le \Delta_{\text{block\_start}} + M\,b_{t,e} ,\\
c_{t,e} &\ge \Delta_{\text{block\_end}} - M\,(1-b_{t,e}),\\
b_{t,e} &\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance on shared tracks  

The network contains **bidirectional single‑track sections** (edges where trains travelling in opposite directions must not occupy the track simultaneously). Two families of headway constraints are required.

#### 4.4.1 Same‑direction headway  

For any pair of distinct trains *t ≠ t'* that use the same edge *e* in the **same direction** (i.e., both travel from *i*→*j*), we enforce a minimum separation *ρ*:

\[
c_{t',e} \ge h_{t,e} + \rho \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}}\bigr) \qquad \forall t<t', e\in E. \tag{C9}
\]

The binary *δ_{t,t',e}^{same}* is forced to 1 when both trains actually occupy the edge:

\[
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \le \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k}, \qquad
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \le \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k}, \qquad
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \ge \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k} + \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k} -1. \tag{C10}
\]

If either train does not use the edge, *δ* becomes 0 and the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

#### 4.4.2 Opposite‑direction headway (single‑track)  

For edges that are **single‑track** (set *U ⊆ E*), we must guarantee that trains travelling in opposite directions do not overlap. Let *dir(t,e)* denote the direction of train *t* on edge *e* (0 = forward, 1 = reverse). For any pair *(t,t')* with opposite directions on *e∈U*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{t',e} &\ge h_{t,e} + \sigma \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}}\bigr),\\
c_{t,e} &\ge h_{t',e} + \sigma \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}}\bigr),\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\le \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k},\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\le \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k},\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\ge \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k} + \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k} -1.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t<t', e\in U. \tag{C11}
\]

The binary *δ^{opp}* becomes 1 only when both trains occupy the same single‑track edge, activating the mutual‑exclusion constraints.

### 4.5 Temporal bounds  

All event times must lie inside the planning horizon:

\[
T_{\text{start}} \le a_{t,i}, d_{t,i}, c_{t,e}, h_{t,e} \le T_{\text{end}} \qquad \forall t,i,e. \tag{C12}
\]

### 4.6 Logical linking of arrival / departure  

For each train *t* and each consecutive pair of stations *(i,j)* on its route:

\[
c_{t,(i,j)} = d_{t,i}, \qquad
a_{t,j} = h_{t,(i,j)}. \tag{C13}
\]

Thus the departure from the upstream station equals the entry onto the connecting edge, and the arrival at the downstream station equals the exit from that edge.

### 4.7 Cancellation handling (optional but useful)  

If a train is cancelled, all its timing variables are forced to a dummy value (e.g., *T_end+1*) and no conflicts are generated:

\[
c_{t,e} \ge T_{\text{end}}+1 - M y_t,\qquad
h_{t,e} \le T_{\text{end}} + M y_t,\qquad
\forall t,e. \tag{C14}
\]

Similarly for station times. This ensures that cancelled trains do not interfere with any headway constraints (the big‑M term deactivates them).

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

Putting everything together, the **TRSMP MILP** is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \text{(objective (1)–(3))} \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{Plan selection (C1)–(C4)}\\
& \text{Physical feasibility (C5)–(C7)}\\
& \text{Blockage avoidance (C8)}\\
& \text{Conflict‑avoidance (C9)–(C11)}\\
& \text{Temporal bounds (C12)–(C13)}\\
& \text{Cancellation logic (C14)}\\
& x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_t\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\},\; \delta^{\cdot}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,i},d_{t,i},c_{t,e},h_{t,e},w_{t,i}\in\Delta .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **purely linear**: all products involve a binary variable and a continuous (or integer) variable, which can be linearised with standard big‑M techniques.  

---

## 6. Remarks & Modeling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Rationale |
|---|------------|-----------|
| A1 | Time is discretised on a uniform minute grid Δ (Δ = {0,…,Δ_max}). | Guarantees integrality of all timing variables and enables linearisation of “max” tardiness. |
| A2 | A small finite set *K* of speed‑profile types (fast/medium/slow) is pre‑computed. | Real high‑speed trains can follow a limited number of admissible acceleration/deceleration patterns; each type is represented by a constant average speed *v_k* and energy rate *c_k*. |
| A3 | Feasible **train‑plans** *p∈P_t* are generated offline by solving a deterministic speed‑profile sub‑problem for each train under the blockage window. | This reduces the coupling between speed‑profile selection and timetable decisions to a binary plan‑selection problem, preserving linearity. |
| A4 | Energy consumption on an edge is approximated by *c_k·L_e* (average power × travel distance). | Detailed traction‑regeneration curves are non‑linear; the linear approximation is standard in high‑level railway optimisation. |
| A5 | Headway values ρ (same direction) and σ (opposite direction) are constant for all edges of the same type. | In practice, headways are dictated by signalling and safety standards and can be treated as uniform within a corridor. |
| A6 | Blockage affects the whole edge for the whole interval [Δ_block_start, Δ_block_end]; trains may either pass before the start or after the end (no partial occupancy). | Simplifies the logical “outside‑window” constraint while still representing the essential operational restriction. |
| A7 | Cancellation is allowed but heavily penalised (β large). | Provides a feasibility fallback when the disruption is too severe; the penalty ensures cancellations only occur when unavoidable. |
| A8 | All trains travel at a constant average speed on a chosen edge (no intra‑edge speed changes). | Guarantees linear travel‑time relation (C5). More detailed intra‑edge acceleration can be embedded by refining the set *K* or by splitting edges. |

---

## 7. Potential Extensions (outside the core MILP)  

* **Energy‑recovery**: introduce a negative coefficient for braking phases on descending gradients.  
* **Passenger‑level objective**: add a weighted sum of passenger‑minutes lost, using load factors per train.  
* **Robustness**: replace deterministic blockage times by intervals and enforce feasibility for all realizations (robust MILP).  
* **Dynamic re‑routing**: allow a train to switch from its nominal route to an alternative parallel line; this is modelled by adding extra edges and corresponding plan variables.  

---

**The formulation above constitutes a complete, linear, mixed‑integer model for the *Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)* under partial‑segment blockages, integrating timetable adjustments, bidirectional conflict resolution, and energy‑aware speed‑profile selection.**

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Blockage Scenario)**  

The model below captures the three decision layers described in the prompt:  

* **Route choice** – binary variables decide which admissible route a train will use (rerouting around a blocked segment).  
* **Timetable** – continuous variables give the exact arrival and departure times of every train on every segment that belongs to its chosen route.  
* **Speed profile** – a small discrete set of speed levels is selected for each traversed segment; the chosen speed determines travel time, energy consumption and feasibility with respect to the blockage window.  

The objective minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption, while guaranteeing conflict‑free operation on a single‑track line, respecting head‑way safety, and obeying the time windows of the partial blockages.

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments (blocks), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(R_t\) | Set of admissible routes for train \(t\). A route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of segments \(\text{seg}(r)=\{s_{r,1},\dots ,s_{r,|r|}\}\). |
| \(V\) | Set of admissible speed levels, indexed by \(v\) (e.g. low/medium/high). |
| \(D=\{+,-\}\) | Direction on a segment (forward / backward). |
| \(B\) | Set of partial‑blockage events. Each \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b^{\text{start}},b^{\text{end}},\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}})\) meaning that on segment \(s\) the sub‑interval \([b^{\text{start}},b^{\text{end}}]\) (metres from the segment start) is unavailable during the time window \([\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}}]\) (minutes). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(\underline v_s,\;\overline v_s\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(s\) (km h). |
| \(\tau^{\min}_t,\;\tau^{\max}_t\) | Earliest possible departure and latest allowed arrival for train \(t\) (minutes from a reference). |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight of total delay in the objective (e.g. € / min). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of total energy consumption (e.g. € / kWh). |
| \(c^{v}\) | Energy coefficient for speed level \(v\) (kWh / km). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{head}}\) | Minimum head‑way time between two trains travelling **in the same direction** on the same segment (minutes). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conf}}\) | Minimum separation time for two trains travelling **opposite directions** on a single‑track segment (minutes). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. \(M=10^5\)). |
| \(P_s\in\{0,1\}\) | Blockage indicator: 1 if segment \(s\) is partially blocked, 0 otherwise. |
| \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_s\) | Maximum extra travel time that may be incurred on a blocked segment \(s\) (minutes). |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in R_t\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(v\). |
| \(\delta_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Extra delay on segment \(s\) caused by a blockage. |
| \(E_t\ge0\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |
| \(D_t\ge0\) | continuous | Positive part of the final‑arrival delay of train \(t\). |
| \(z_{t,s}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) in direction \(d\) (used for bidirectional conflict). |
| \(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Ordering variable for two opposite‑direction trains on segment \(s\). |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T} E_t
}
\]

* \(D_t\) is the **positive** lateness of train \(t\) at its final destination (linearised, see constraint (9)).  
* \(E_t\) is the total energy used by train \(t\) (constraint (8)).

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑selection  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Activate time / speed variables only on the chosen route**  
   \[
   a_{t,s}\le M\!\sum_{r\in R_t:\,s\in\text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r},
   \qquad
   d_{t,s}\le M\!\sum_{r\in R_t:\,s\in\text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r},
   \qquad
   y_{t,s}^{v}\le\sum_{r\in R_t:\,s\in\text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}
   \quad\forall t,s,v. \tag{R2}
   \]

#### 5.2 Time feasibility along a chosen route  

3. **Travel time on a segment** (linearised with speed‑level binaries)  
   \[
   d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \underbrace{\frac{L_s}{v}}_{\displaystyle\theta_{s}^{v}}\;y_{t,s}^{v}
   \qquad\forall t,s,v. \tag{T1}
   \]

4. **Continuity between consecutive segments**  
   If \(s'\) follows \(s\) on the selected route of train \(t\):  
   \[
   a_{t,s'}\ge d_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route}. \tag{T2}
   \]

5. **Departure‑time window**  
   \[
   a_{t,s_0}\ge \tau^{\min}_t\qquad\forall t,
   \]
   where \(s_0\) is the first segment of the chosen route.

#### 5.3 Speed‑level selection  

6. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  
   \[
   \sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s}^{v}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\,s\in\text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}
   \qquad\forall t,s. \tag{S1}
   \]

7. **Speed bounds** (automatically satisfied because only one \(y\) can be 1)  
   \[
   \underline v_s\!\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\le\sum_{v} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\le\overline v_s\!\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}
   \qquad\forall t,s. \tag{S2}
   \]

#### 5.4 Energy calculation  

8. **Energy per train**  
   \[
   E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} c^{v}\,L_s\,y_{t,s}^{v}
   \qquad\forall t. \tag{E1}
   \]

#### 5.5 Blockage (partial‑segment) handling  

9. **Extra delay caused by a blocked segment**  
   \[
   \delta_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}-\sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v},
   \qquad
   0\le\delta_{t,s}\le \Delta^{\text{blk}}_s\,P_s
   \qquad\forall t,s. \tag{B1}
   \]

   The term \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_s\) limits the additional travel time that a blockage may force.

#### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict on a single‑track segment  

10. **Occupancy linking**  
    \[
    z_{t,s}^{d}\le\sum_{r\in R_t:\,\text{dir}(r,s)=d}x_{t,r}
    \qquad\forall t,s,d. \tag{C1}
    \]

11. **Ordering for opposite‑direction trains** (big‑M linearisation)  

    For every unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t\neq t'\), for every segment \(s\) and opposite directions \(d\) and \(-d\):

    \[
    \begin{aligned}
    a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\bigl(1-\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
    a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} - M\bigl(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
    \omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\le z_{t,s}^{d},\qquad
    \omega_{t,t',s}^{d} \le z_{t',s}^{-d},\\
    \omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\in\{0,1\}.
    \end{aligned}
    \qquad\forall t<t',s,d. \tag{C2}
    \]

    If both trains try to use the segment in opposite directions, \(\omega\) forces one of the two time‑ordering constraints to be active, guaranteeing a conflict‑free schedule.

#### 5.7 Delay definition (linearised positive part)  

12. **Positive lateness at final destination**  

    Let \(\text{last}(t)\) be the last segment of the route selected for train \(t\). Introduce an auxiliary variable \(D_t\) and impose  

    \[
    D_t \ge a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\max}_t,\qquad D_t\ge0
    \qquad\forall t. \tag{D1}
    \]

#### 5.8 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r},\;y_{t,s}^{v},\;z_{t,s}^{d},\;\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s},\;d_{t,s},\;\delta_{t,s},\;E_t,\;D_t\ge0
\qquad\forall t,s,v,d,t'<t.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Full compact MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t \tag{R1}\\

\]

All constraints are linear; the only products involve a binary variable and a constant, so the formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program** ready for any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 7. Interpretation of the model components  

| Component | Operational meaning |
|-----------|---------------------|
| **\(x_{t,r}\)** | Chooses a feasible route for each train, allowing rerouting around blocked segments. |
| **\(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\)** | Exact timetable – when a train enters and leaves each segment. |
| **\(y_{t,s}^{v}\)** | Determines the average speed on a segment; the speed fixes travel time (via \(\theta_{s}^{v}\)) and energy use (via \(c^{v}\)). |
| **\(z_{t,s}^{d}\) & \(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\)** | Enforce conflict‑free usage of a single‑track segment for opposite‑direction trains (head‑way for same direction, separation for opposite direction). |
| **\(\delta_{t,s}\)** | Captures extra travel time caused by a partial blockage; bounded by \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_s\). |
| **\(D_t\)** | Positive lateness of train \(t\) at its final destination – the part of the delay that the objective penalises. |
| **\(E_t\)** | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh), summed over all traversed segments and speed levels. |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of total delay (\(\alpha\)) and total energy (\(\beta\)), enabling the railway operator to explore the trade‑off between punctuality and energy efficiency. |

---

### 8. Remarks for practical use  

* **Big‑M selection** – choose \(M\) just larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min) to keep the formulation tight.  
* **Scalability** – the number of binary ordering variables \(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\) grows quadratically with the number of trains; in practice they are introduced only for train pairs that share a segment and have overlapping time windows.  
* **Speed‑level set** – a small discrete set (e.g., three levels) keeps the model size modest while still allowing a realistic trade‑off between travel time and energy.  
* **Extensions** – platform capacity, crew‑working‑time limits, or stochastic blockage durations can be added by extra binary variables and scenario‑based constraints without breaking linearity.

---

**Result** – The formulation above is a *complete, linear MILP* that simultaneously decides **where** each train should run, **when** it should be on every track block, and **how fast** it should travel, while minimising a combined delay‑energy objective and guaranteeing conflict‑free operation under partial‑segment blockages.

Text:
**Variables**

* \(x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\in T\) uses track segment \(s\in S\) (including the opposite‑track option for rerouting).  
* \(y_{t,\tau}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(t\) departs in discrete time period \(\tau\in\Tau\).  
* \(v_{t,s,\tau}\ge 0\) – speed of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) during period \(\tau\) (km h\(^{-1}\)).  
* \(a_{t,s,\tau}\ge 0\) – acceleration of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) during period \(\tau\) (km h\(^{-2}\)).  
* \(e_t\ge 0\) – total energy consumption of train \(t\).

**Parameters (assumed data)**  

* \(origDep_t\) – original departure period of train \(t\).  
* \(origArr_t\) – original arrival period of train \(t\).  
* \(\ell_s\) – length of segment \(s\) (km).  
* \(\underline{tt}_s,\overline{tt}_s\) – lower/upper bound on travel time on segment \(s\) (periods).  
* \(v^{\min},v^{\max}\) – global speed limits.  
* \(a^{\min},a^{\max}\) – global acceleration limits.  
* \(\alpha,\beta\) – energy‑cost coefficients (energy = \(\alpha v^2+\beta a^2\)).  
* \(\lambda\) – weight of the energy term in the objective.  
* \([b^{\text{start}}_s,b^{\text{end}}_s]\) – blockage time window for segment \(s\) (if no blockage set \(b^{\text{start}}_s>b^{\text{end}}_s\)).  

**Objective function**

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\tau\in\Tau} (\tau-origDep_t)\,y_{t,\tau}}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\lambda\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Departure‑time selection** – each train departs exactly once  

\[
\sum_{\tau\in\Tau} y_{t,\tau}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

2. **Segment usage** – a train can occupy a segment only after it has departed and before it has arrived  

\[
x_{t,s}\le \sum_{\tau\in\Tau} y_{t,\tau}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,
\]
\[
x_{t,s}\le 1-\sum_{\tau>origArr_t} y_{t,\tau}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S .
\]

3. **Time feasibility (arrival = departure + travel times)**  

\[
\sum_{\tau\in\Tau}\tau\,y_{t,\tau}=origDep_t+\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau\in\Tau}\tau\,x_{t,s}\,z_{t,s,\tau}\qquad\forall t\in T,
\]

where \(z_{t,s,\tau}\) is an auxiliary binary that equals 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) during period \(\tau\).  
(For a compact MILP we replace \(z_{t,s,\tau}=x_{t,s}\,y_{t,\tau}\) by linearization constraints.)

4. **Travel‑time definition (speed‑distance relation)**  

\[
\underline{tt}_s\,x_{t,s}\le \sum_{\tau\in\Tau} y_{t,\tau}\,(\tau-origDep_t)\le \overline{tt}_s\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,
\]

and linking speed to travel time  

\[
\frac{\ell_s}{v_{t,s,\tau}} \le \underline{tt}_s \;,\qquad
\frac{\ell_s}{v_{t,s,\tau}} \ge \overline{tt}_s
\qquad\forall t,s,\tau\text{ with }x_{t,s}=1 .
\]

(These are linearised by introducing a big‑M and the binary \(x_{t,s}\).)

5. **Speed limits**  

\[
v^{\min}\,x_{t,s}\le v_{t,s,\tau}\le v^{\max}\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t,s,\tau .
\]

6. **Acceleration limits**  

\[
a_{t,s,\tau}=v_{t,s,\tau}-v_{t,s,\tau-1}\qquad\forall t,s,\tau>1,
\]
\[
a^{\min}\,x_{t,s}\le a_{t,s,\tau}\le a^{\max}\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t,s,\tau .
\]

7. **Blockage constraint** – a blocked segment cannot be used during its blockage window  

\[
x_{t,s}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;\tau\in\Tau\text{ with }b^{\text{start}}_s\le\tau\le b^{\text{end}}_s .
\]

(If rerouting to the opposite track is allowed, introduce a second binary
\(x^{\text{opp}}_{t,s}\) and replace the above by \(x_{t,s}+x^{\text{opp}}_{t,s}=0\) during the window.)

8. **Bidirectional conflict avoidance** – at most one train may occupy a segment at a given period (including opposite directions)  

\[
\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(x_{t,s}+x^{\text{opp}}_{t,s}\bigr)\,y_{t,\tau}\le 1
\qquad\forall s\in S,\;\tau\in\Tau .
\]

9. **Energy consumption** (piece‑wise linearised)  

\[
e_t=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau\in\Tau}\bigl(\alpha\,v_{t,s,\tau}^2+\beta\,a_{t,s,\tau}^2\bigr)
\qquad\forall t\in T .
\]

(The quadratic terms are linearised by standard PWL or by introducing auxiliary variables and McCormick envelopes.)

---

**Assumptions made**

* Time is discretised into equal periods (e.g., minutes).  
* Each train traverses a segment in a single period; if a segment needs more than one period the model uses the lower/upper travel‑time bounds to aggregate several periods.  
* Speed–distance relation is linearised via big‑M; more accurate linearisation can be obtained with additional break‑points.  
* Rerouting is represented by a second binary variable for the opposite‑track usage; if no rerouting is allowed the opposite variable is omitted.  
* Energy is modelled as a weighted sum of squared speed and acceleration; the quadratic terms are linearised to keep the model MILP.  

The formulation above constitutes a complete mixed‑integer linear program that simultaneously decides train departure times, segment assignments (including possible rerouting), feasible speed/acceleration profiles, and minimizes a weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption while respecting blockage windows and bidirectional conflict constraints.

Text:
## Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)  
**Goal** – Minimise the total (i) passenger‑delay cost and (ii) energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable and feasible speed profiles for all trains after a partial‑segment blockage.  

The model is built on the following **sets**, **parameters**, **decision variables**, **objective function**, and **constraints**.  
All equations are linear (mixed‑integer) after suitable linearisation of the energy‑speed relationship (see Assumption A5).

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\( \mathcal{T}= \{1,\dots,T\}\\) | Set of trains that have to be operated (including those that may be cancelled). |
| \\( \mathcal{S}= \{1,\dots,S\}\\) | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of every train). |
| \\( \mathcal{L}= \{(i,j)\mid i,j\in\mathcal{S}, i<j\}\\) | Set of track **segments** between consecutive stations (ordered pair). |
| \\( \mathcal{B}\subseteq \mathcal{L}\\) | Set of **blocked segments** (the partial‑segment blockage). |
| \\( \mathcal{K}= \{1,\dots,K\}\\) | Set of **speed‑profile intervals** used to discretise a train’s run on a segment (see A4). |
| \\( \mathcal{D}\subseteq \mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}\\) | Set of ordered train‑pairs \((p,q)\) that travel in opposite directions on the same physical track (potential conflict pairs). |
| \\( \mathcal{P}_{t}\\) | Set of feasible **operation plans** for train \\(t\\) (see Section 4.1). Each plan combines a route (original or rerouted), a departure‑/arrival‑time pattern, and a speed‑profile choice for every travelled segment. |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| \\( \hat a_{ts}\\) | Planned (pre‑disruption) **arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at station \\(s\\). | s |
| \\( \hat d_{ts}\\) | Planned **departure time** of train \\(t\\) at station \\(s\\). | s |
| \\( \tau^{\min}_{ij}\\), \\( \tau^{\max}_{ij}\\) | Minimum/maximum feasible **travel time** on segment \\((i,j)\\) (derived from speed limits and safety headways). | s |
| \\( \eta^{k}_{ij}\\) | **Travel time** of a train on segment \\((i,j)\\) when using speed‑interval \\(k\\). (Linearised from the quadratic energy‑speed function). | s |
| \\( e^{k}_{ij}\\) | **Energy consumption** (kWh) incurred on segment \\((i,j)\\) when using speed‑interval \\(k\\). | kWh |
| \\( C^{\text{delay}}_{t}\\) | Unit penalty for **passenger delay** of train \\(t\\) (e.g. €/minute). | €/s |
| \\( C^{\text{energy}}\\) | Unit penalty for **energy consumption** (e.g. €/kWh). | €/kWh |
| \\( M\\) | Large constant for “big‑M’’ linearisation (greater than any feasible time). | s |
| \\( \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}\\) | Length of the **blocking time window** on segment \\((i,j)\\) (start‑time, end‑time). If \\((i,j)\\notin\mathcal{B}\\) then \\( \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}= [0,0]\\). |
| \\( \beta^{\text{reroute}}_{t}\\) | Fixed cost (or penalty) for **rerouting** train \\(t\\) (e.g. passenger inconvenience). | € |
| \\( \gamma^{\text{cancel}}_{t}\\) | Fixed cost for **cancelling** train \\(t\\) (large enough to avoid unnecessary cancellations). | € |
| \\( \alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\\) | Minimum **headway time** required between two trains travelling in opposite directions on the same physical track of segment \\((i,j)\\). | s |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

#### 3.1 Plan‑selection (binary)  

\[
x_{tp}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;p\in\mathcal{P}_{t}
\]

\(x_{tp}=1\) iff plan \(p\) is chosen for train \(t\).

#### 3.2 Time variables (derived from the selected plan)  

Because each plan already contains explicit times, we do not need separate continuous variables; however, for linear head‑way constraints we introduce:

\[
a_{ts}\ge 0,\;d_{ts}\ge 0\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S}
\]

represent the **actual** arrival / departure times. They are linked to the plan‑selection variables through assignment constraints (see Section 4.2).

#### 3.3 Speed‑interval activation (binary)  

\[
y^{k}_{tij}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{L},\;k\in\mathcal{K}
\]

\(y^{k}_{tij}=1\) iff train \(t\) traverses segment \((i,j)\) using speed interval \(k\).

#### 3.4 Auxiliary binary for conflict resolution  

\[
z_{pqij}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall (p,q)\in\mathcal{D},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}
\]

\(z_{pqij}=1\) iff train \(p\) passes segment \((i,j)\) **before** train \(q\) (in opposite directions).

#### 3.5 Cancellation indicator  

\[
c_{t}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\]

\(c_{t}=1\) iff train \(t\) is **cancelled** (all its plan‑variables forced to zero).

---

### 4. Model Formulation  

#### 4.1 Plan definition (pre‑processing)  

Each plan \(p\in\mathcal{P}_t\) is constructed *outside* the MILP and contains:

* a binary flag \(r_{tp}\) indicating whether the plan uses the **original route** (0) or the **rerouted (opposite‑track) route** (1);  
* a list of stations visited in order, hence the set of segments \(\mathcal{L}_{tp}\);  
* for every segment \((i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{tp}\) a feasible travel‑time value \(\tau^{p}_{tij}\) (chosen from the discretised set \(\{\eta^{k}_{ij}\}\)) and the corresponding energy \(e^{p}_{tij}\);  
* resulting arrival/departure times \(\{a^{p}_{ts}, d^{p}_{ts}\}\).

All \(\tau^{p}_{tij}\) respect the speed‑limit bounds \(\tau^{\min}_{ij}\le\tau^{p}_{tij}\le\tau^{\max}_{ij}\) and the blocking window:
\[
\bigl[a^{p}_{ti}, d^{p}_{tj}\bigr]\cap \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}= \emptyset\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{L}_{tp}.
\]

#### 4.2 Plan‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one plan (or cancellation) per train**

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{tp}+c_t = 1\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}.
\]

2. **Linking actual times to the chosen plan**  
For every train‑station pair that appears in at least one plan:

\[
a_{ts}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} a^{p}_{ts}\,x_{tp}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S},
\]
\[
d_{ts}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} d^{p}_{ts}\,x_{tp}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S}.
\]

If a station is **not visited** in a particular plan, its associated \(a^{p}_{ts},d^{p}_{ts}\) are set to 0; the big‑M technique guarantees the correct values when the plan is not selected.

3. **Speed‑interval activation from the chosen plan**  

For each segment \((i,j)\) that can be travelled by train \(t\):

\[
y^{k}_{tij}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t\;:\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{tp}\;\wedge\;\tau^{p}_{tij}= \eta^{k}_{ij}} x_{tp}\qquad\forall k\in\mathcal{K}.
\]

Hence exactly one speed‑interval is active for a traversed segment, and none if the segment is not used (the sum will be zero).

4. **Rerouting cost**  

Let \(r_{tp}\in\{0,1\}\) be a known attribute of plan \(p\) (1 if rerouted). Then the total rerouting penalty is

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}\beta^{\text{reroute}}_{t}\, r_{tp}\, x_{tp}
\]

which will appear in the objective.

5. **Cancellation cost**  

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \gamma^{\text{cancel}}_{t}\,c_{t}
\]

also part of the objective.

#### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance constraints (bidirectional headway)  

For every opposite‑direction pair \((p,q)\in\mathcal{D}\) and each physical segment \((i,j)\) they share (the same track, possibly after rerouting):

\[
a_{pj} - d_{qi} \ge \alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\,z_{pqij} - M\,(1-z_{pqij})\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{L},
\]

\[
a_{qi} - d_{pj} \ge \alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\,(1-z_{pqij}) - M\,z_{pqij}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{L}.
\]

If \(z_{pqij}=1\) the first inequality forces train \(p\) to finish the segment before train \(q\) enters it (plus required headway). The big‑M terms deactivate the opposite inequality.

Only pairs that actually **share** the segment in the selected plans need to be considered; this can be modelled by additional binary “share’’ variables or, more simply, by generating the constraints only for \((p,q)\)‑plan combinations where both trains use \((i,j)\). In the compact MILP we enforce it by coupling with plan‑selection:

\[
z_{pqij} \le \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_p}\!\!\!\!x_{p p}\; \mathbb{1}\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{pp}\},
\qquad
z_{pqij} \le \sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}_q}\!\!\!\!x_{q q}\; \mathbb{1}\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{qq}\},
\]

where \(\mathbb{1}\{\cdot\}\) is 1 if the statement holds, 0 otherwise.

#### 4.4 Blocking‑window feasibility  

For any train that uses a blocked segment \((i,j)\in\mathcal{B}\),

\[
a_{ti} \ge \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}^{\text{end}} \; \text{or}\; d_{tj} \le \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}^{\text{start}} .
\]

In the plan‑generation phase these constraints are already satisfied, so they do not need to be reproduced inside the MILP. Nevertheless, if we wish to keep them, we can write a linear big‑M formulation:

\[
a_{ti} \ge \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}^{\text{end}} - M\,u_{tij},
\]
\[
d_{tj} \le \Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}^{\text{start}} + M\,(1-u_{tij}),
\qquad u_{tij}\in\{0,1\}.
\]

At least one of the two inequalities must hold; the binary \(u_{tij}\) selects which side of the window the train passes.

#### 4.5 Energy‑consumption calculation  

\[
E = \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} e^{k}_{ij}\; y^{k}_{tij}.
\]

Because each traversed segment activates exactly one \(y^{k}_{tij}\), the expression yields the total energy of all selected plans.

#### 4.6 Delay‑cost calculation  

Passenger delay for train \(t\) is measured against the original schedule:

\[
\Delta_{t}= \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} \bigl( a_{ts} - \hat a_{ts} \bigr)^{+},
\]

where \((\cdot)^{+}\) denotes the positive part. This can be linearised with an auxiliary variable \(\delta_{ts}\ge0\):

\[
\delta_{ts} \ge a_{ts} - \hat a_{ts},\qquad
\delta_{ts}\ge 0,
\]
\[
\Delta_{t}= \sum_{s}\delta_{ts}.
\]

Total delay cost:

\[
\text{DelayCost}= \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} C^{\text{delay}}_{t}\, \Delta_{t}.
\]

#### 4.7 Objective function  

\[
\min\; 
\underbrace{\sum_{t} C^{\text{delay}}_{t}\, \Delta_{t}}_{\text{Passenger‑delay penalty}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{C^{\text{energy}}\;E}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t}\sum_{p} \beta^{\text{reroute}}_{t}\, r_{tp}\,x_{tp}}_{\text{Rerouting penalty}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t} \gamma^{\text{cancel}}_{t}\,c_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} .
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

### 5. Additional Linearisation Details (Assumptions)  

| # | Assumption | Description |
|---|------------|-------------|
| **A1** | **Finite plan set** – For each train, a *pre‑computed* set \(\mathcal{P}_{t}\) of feasible plans (original route, rerouted route, various speed‑interval choices) is enumerated before solving the MILP. The MILP only selects among them. |
| **A2** | **Discrete speed‑intervals** – The continuous speed range on each segment is discretised into a small number \(K\) of intervals (e.g., “slow”, “medium”, “fast”). Energy consumption is approximated linearly for each interval (see parameter \(e^{k}_{ij}\)). |
| **A3** | **Linear energy‑speed approximation** – The true \(E\!\propto\! v^{2}\) (or \(v^{3}\)) relationship is replaced by a piecewise‑linear function defined by the intervals; this guarantees linearity of the objective. |
| **A4** | **Big‑M values** – \(M\) is chosen larger than the longest feasible travel time on the network (e.g., 10 000 s) so that the associated constraints are activated only when needed. |
| **A5** | **Headway symmetry** – The minimum headway \(\alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\) is the same for both directions on a given physical track; this avoids asymmetric constraints. |
| **A6** | **Cancellation is allowed but heavily penalised** – \(\gamma^{\text{cancel}}_{t}\) is set high enough that cancellation occurs only when the disruption makes any feasible timetable impossible for that train. |
| **A7** | **No overtaking** – Within the same direction, trains keep their original order; thus no binary variables are needed for same‑direction conflicts. Only opposite‑direction conflicts are modelled. |
| **A8** | **Deterministic disruption window** – The start and end times of the blockage on each blocked segment are known a priori (no stochasticity). |

---

### 6. Summary of the MILP  

Putting everything together, the **complete linear mixed‑integer program** for the TRSMP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
\sum_{t} C^{\text{delay}}_{t}\,\Bigl(\sum_{s}\delta_{ts}\Bigr)
\;+\;
C^{\text{energy}}\!\!\sum_{t}\sum_{(i,j)}\sum_{k} e^{k}_{ij}\,y^{k}_{tij}
\;+\;
\sum_{t}\sum_{p}\beta^{\text{reroute}}_{t}\,r_{tp}\,x_{tp}
\;+\;
\sum_{t}\gamma^{\text{cancel}}_{t}\,c_{t} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{tp}+c_t = 1 &&\forall t \\
& a_{ts}= \sum_{p} a^{p}_{ts}\,x_{tp} &&\forall t,s \\
& d_{ts}= \sum_{p} d^{p}_{ts}\,x_{tp} &&\forall t,s \\
& y^{k}_{tij}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t:\tau^{p}_{tij}= \eta^{k}_{ij}} x_{tp} &&\forall t,i,j,k \\
& \delta_{ts}\ge a_{ts}-\hat a_{ts},\;\delta_{ts}\ge0 &&\forall t,s \\
& \sum_{k} y^{k}_{tij}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}\mathbb{1}\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{tp}\}\,x_{tp}
   &&\forall t,i,j\\
& a_{pj} - d_{qi} \ge \alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\,z_{pqij} - M\,(1-z_{pqij})
   &&\forall (p,q)\in\mathcal{D},\;(i,j)\\
& a_{qi} - d_{pj} \ge \alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\,(1-z_{pqij}) - M\,z_{pqij}
   &&\forall (p,q)\in\mathcal{D},\;(i,j)\\
& z_{pqij}\le \sum_{p}\mathbb{1}\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{pp}\}\,x_{pp},
   \quad
  z_{pqij}\le \sum_{q}\mathbb{1}\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{L}_{qq}\}\,x_{qq}
   &&\forall (p,q),\;(i,j)\\
& \text{(optional) blocking‑window big‑M constraints} &&\\
& x_{tp},\,y^{k}_{tij},\,z_{pqij},\,c_t \in\{0,1\},\;
  a_{ts},d_{ts},\delta_{ts}\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the model simultaneously chooses **(i)** whether a train is kept, rerouted, or cancelled, **(ii)** which pre‑computed speed‑profile (interval) to use on each traversed segment, and **(iii)** the relative order of opposite‑direction trains on shared tracks, thereby guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable that respects the blockage window and minimises the weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption.

---

### 7. How the Model is Used  

1. **Pre‑processing** – For every train \(t\) enumerate a modest set \(\mathcal{P}_t\) (typically < 20) that covers:  
   * original route with a few admissible speed‑interval combinations,  
   * rerouted route (using the opposite track) with analogous speed options,  
   * a “do‑nothing’’ cancellation plan.  

2. **Parameter estimation** – Compute \(\eta^{k}_{ij}\) and \(e^{k}_{ij}\) from the physics of high‑speed trains (e.g., using a piecewise‑linear approximation of \(P(v)=a_0 + a_1 v + a_2 v^2\)).  

3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress). The solution yields the selected plan for each train, the actual arrival/departure times, the head‑way ordering variables, and the associated energy and delay values.  

4. **Post‑processing** – Translate the chosen speed‑intervals back into continuous speed profiles (e.g., by applying a simple acceleration/deceleration ramp inside each interval) and dispatch the resulting timetable to the train‑control system.

---

### 8. Extensions (optional)

* **Stochastic blockage** – replace \(\Delta^{\text{block}}_{ij}\) by a scenario set with binary variables and a two‑stage robust formulation.  
* **Passenger‑share weighting** – let \(C^{\text{delay}}_{t}=w_t\cdot C^{\text{delay}}_{0}\) where \(w_t\) reflects the number of passengers on train \(t\).  
* **Dynamic headways** – make \(\alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}\) dependent on the chosen speed‑intervals (higher speed ⇒ larger safety distance). This remains linear by adding \(\alpha^{\text{headway}}_{ij}= \alpha_0 + \sum_k \alpha_k y^{k}_{tij}\).  

The presented MILP therefore constitutes a **complete, linear, integrated model** for the train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial‑segment blockages, ready for direct implementation and computational testing.

messages.content: You convert the text of an optimization model into a structured record. Report only what the text states as mathematics, that is, objective functions, equations and inequalities written with symbols. Do not complete, repair, improve or invent anything.

Read the text below and fill in the predefined form.

- ContainsFormulation: true only if the text writes out at least one objective function or constraint as a mathematical expression. False if the text only describes or outlines a model in words, discusses an approach, asks a question, or contains no model.
- variablesInModel: every decision variable that appears in the written expressions, numbered from 1. Parameters, sets and indices are not decision variables. An indexed family such as x_{ij} counts once. Domain: binary, integer or continuous as the text declares it, unknown if it does not say.
- objective_functions: every objective function written as an expression, numbered from 0, with the numbers of the decision variables it contains. Leave the list empty if no objective function is written out.
- constraints: every constraint written as an equation or inequality, numbered from 1, with the numbers of the decision variables it contains. Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear programme, the decision‑making required to (i) rebuild a conflict‑free timetable after a partial‑segment blockage, (ii) decide on possible rerouting of affected trains to the opposite track, (iii) choose a feasible speed profile for every train on every travelled segment, and (iv) minimise a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total electric energy consumption.  

All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  Where the source text does not provide numerical data, **reasonable assumptions** are made and marked as *Assumption X*.

---

## 1. Indices & Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\) |
| \(S\) | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train), indexed by \(s\) |
| \(E\) | Set of track‑segments (directed edges) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) |
| \(K\) | Set of *speed‑profile* classes (discrete speed‑levels) that can be assigned to a train on a segment, indexed by \(k\) |
| \(B\) | Set of *binary* conflict‑pair alternatives for two trains that could occupy the same track‑segment in opposite directions, indexed by \(b\) |
| \(W\) | Set of *disruption windows* (time intervals) during which a segment is blocked on one side, indexed by \(w\) |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / assumption |
|--------|---------|-----------------------------|
| \(L_e\) | Length of segment \(e\) (km) | given by infrastructure |
| \(v^{\max}_k\) | Nominal speed of profile class \(k\) (km/h) | Assumption 1: 8 discrete speeds 200, 260, … 400 km/h |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Maximum allowable acceleration (km/h²) | Assumption 2: 0.5 km/h² |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum allowable deceleration (km/h²) | Assumption 2: 0.6 km/h² |
| \(E^{\text{unit}}_{k}\) | Electrical energy consumption per km when using speed class \(k\) (kWh/km) | Assumption 3: monotone increasing with \(v^{\max}_k\) |
| \(\pi_t\) | Passenger‑carrying capacity of train \(t\) (persons) | given |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight of passenger‑delay in the objective (€/min per passenger) | Assumption 4: 0.10 €/min |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of energy consumption in the objective (€/kWh) | Assumption 4: 0.05 €/kWh |
| \(\tau^{\text{sched}}_{t,s}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (minutes from a common origin) | given |
| \(\Delta^{\text{min}}_{t}\) | Minimum dwell time required at any station (min) | Assumption 5: 2 min |
| \(\Delta^{\text{max}}_{t}\) | Maximum dwell time allowed (e.g. due to platform occupancy) (min) | Assumption 5: 10 min |
| \(M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant for linearisation | Set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min) |
| \([t^{\text{start}}_w,\,t^{\text{end}}_w]\) | Disruption time window for blockage \(w\) (minutes) | given – e.g. 120‑180 min |
| \(\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}}_w\subseteq E\) | Set of segments that are blocked (one‑track side) during window \(w\) | given |
| \(\rho_{t,e}\in\{0,1\}\) | Indicator whether train \(t\) *normally* traverses segment \(e\) (pre‑disruption) | derived from original timetable |
| \(\gamma_{t}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) is cancelled (i.e., removed from service) | Decision variable – see below |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous (min) | **Actual arrival time** of train \(t\) at station \(s\) |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous (min) | **Actual departure time** of train \(t\) from station \(s\) |
| \(x_{t,e,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(e\) using speed class \(k\) |
| \(z_{t,e}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(e\) at all (regardless of speed) |
| \(r_{t,e}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) *reroutes* on the opposite track for segment \(e\) (i.e., uses the blocked side) |
| \(p_{t,b}\) | binary | 1 if conflict‑pair alternative \(b\) (ordering of two opposite‑direction trains on a shared segment) is chosen |
| \(\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}}\) | continuous (min) | Positive lateness of train \(t\) at station \(s\) w.r.t. the original schedule |
| \(\eta_{t}\) | continuous (kWh) | **Total energy** consumed by train \(t\) on its realised route |
| \(\gamma_{t}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) is cancelled (no service) |

---

## 4. Model Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Discrete speed‑profile classes** are sufficient to approximate the optimal continuous speed profile; the travel time on a segment equals length divided by the selected speed class.  
2. **Acceleration / deceleration limits** are enforced by limiting speed jumps between consecutive segments (see Constraint (6)).  
3. **Energy** for a train on a segment is linear in length for a given speed class (no coasting, regenerative braking ignored).  
4. **Bidirectional conflict** on a segment blocked on one side is modelled by binary ordering variables \(p_{t,b}\). Only two trains can occupy the single usable track at the same time; the ordering is enforced by a pairwise disjunctive constraint.  
5. **Cancellation** is allowed – a cancelled train incurs a large penalty (implicitly via the objective if needed) but removes all constraints related to its movement.  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min \;\; 
\underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\pi_t \,\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}}}_{\text{Passenger‑delay cost}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}}_{\text{Energy cost}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{P^{\text{cancel}} \sum_{t\in T}\gamma_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty (optional)}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*The cancellation penalty \(P^{\text{cancel}}\) can be set high (e.g. 10 000 €) to discourage unnecessary cancellations.*

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1 Logical linking of travel decisions
\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,e,k}=z_{t,e} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;e\in E\tag{1}
\]

\[
z_{t,e}\le \rho_{t,e}+r_{t,e} \qquad\forall t,e\tag{6.1}
\]
*If the original route is blocked (\(\rho_{t,e}=0\)) the train may still traverse the segment only by rerouting (\(r_{t,e}=1\)).*

### 6.2 Speed‑profile selection
\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,e,k}=z_{t,e} \qquad\forall t,e\tag{2}
\]

### 6.3 Travel‑time on a segment
Let \( \tau^{\text{seg}}_{t,e}= \displaystyle\sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_e}{v^{\max}_k}\,x_{t,e,k}\).  
The departure‑arrival relationship over a segment connecting stations \(s_i\) and \(s_j\) is:

\[
a_{t,s_j}\;\ge\; d_{t,s_i}+ \tau^{\text{seg}}_{t,(s_i,s_j)} \;-\; M\gamma_{t}\qquad\forall t,\;(s_i,s_j)\in E\tag{3}
\]

The big‑\(M\) term de‑activates the constraint if the train is cancelled.

### 6.4 Dwell‑time limits
\[
\Delta^{\text{min}}_{t}\; \le\; d_{t,s}\!-\!a_{t,s}\; \le\; \Delta^{\text{max}}_{t} \qquad\forall t,\;s\in S\tag{4}
\]

### 6.5 Lateness definition
\[
\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}} \;\ge\; a_{t,s}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,s\tag{5}
\]
(and \(\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}}\ge0\) implicitly because it is a non‑negative continuous variable).

### 6.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (linearised)
For two consecutive segments \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) and \(e'=(s_j,s_k)\):
\[
\sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k \,x_{t,e,k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k \,x_{t,e',k}
\;\le\; a^{\max}\, \frac{L_e+L_{e'}}{2}+M\bigl(2-\!z_{t,e}-z_{t,e'}\bigr) \tag{6a}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k \,x_{t,e',k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k \,x_{t,e,k}
\;\le\; d^{\max}\, \frac{L_e+L_{e'}}{2}+M\bigl(2-\!z_{t,e}-z_{t,e'}\bigr) \tag{6b}
\]

If either segment is not traversed (\(z_{t,\cdot}=0\)), the constraint is relaxed.

### 6.7 Blockage‑time feasibility
A train using a blocked segment on the *unavailable* side must not occupy it during the disruption window:

\[
a_{t,s_j}\;\ge\; t^{\text{end}}_w \;-\;M\bigl(1-r_{t,e}\bigr) \quad\forall t,\;e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}}_w,\;w\in W \tag{7}
\]

If \(r_{t,e}=0\) (no rerouting) the constraint is vacuous.

### 6.8 Bidirectional conflict resolution on a single usable track  

For each segment \(e\) that is blocked on one side (so only one track is usable) and for every unordered pair of trains \((t,t')\) that would use the segment in opposite directions, introduce a binary ordering variable \(p_{t,t',e}\in\{0,1\}\) (this is a special case of \(p_{t,b}\)).  

Let  

\[
\underline{a}_{t,e}=a_{t,s_i},\qquad \overline{d}_{t,e}=d_{t,s_j}
\]

The disjunctive (big‑\(M\)) formulation is:

\[
\underline{a}_{t,e} \;\ge\; \overline{d}_{t',e} \;-\; M\, p_{t,t',e} \tag{8a}
\]
\[
\underline{a}_{t',e} \;\ge\; \overline{d}_{t,e} \;-\; M\,(1-p_{t,t',e}) \tag{8b}
\]

Both constraints are activated only if the two trains actually use the segment:

\[
p_{t,t',e}\le z_{t,e},\qquad p_{t,t',e}\le z_{t',e}\tag{8c}
\]

The ordering variable guarantees a conflict‑free passage of opposite‑direction trains on the single track that remains available during the disruption.

### 6.9 Energy accounting  
\[
\eta_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\;\sum_{k\in K} \Bigl(E^{\text{unit}}_{k}\,L_e\Bigr)\,x_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T\tag{9}
\]

### 6.10 Cancellation handling  

If a train is cancelled, all its timing variables are forced to a dummy value far outside the planning horizon:

\[
a_{t,s}=M\;\gamma_{t},\qquad d_{t,s}=M\;\gamma_{t}\qquad\forall t,s\tag{10}
\]

and all travel‑choice variables are forced to zero:

\[
z_{t,e}=0,\;x_{t,e,k}=0,\;r_{t,e}=0\qquad\forall t,e,k\tag{11}
\]

### 6.11 Domain restrictions  

\[
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}},\eta_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,s\tag{12}
\]

\[
x_{t,e,k},z_{t,e},r_{t,e},p_{t,b},\gamma_{t}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall t,e,k,b\tag{13}
\]

---

## 7. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\min\limits_{a,d,\delta,\eta,x,z,r,p,\gamma}\; & \displaystyle
\alpha \sum_{t}\sum_{s}\pi_t\delta_{t,s}^{\text{late}} \;+\;
\beta \sum_{t}\eta_{t}
\;+\; P^{\text{cancel}}\!\sum_{t}\gamma_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} & \text{(1)–(13) }\\
            & \text{All variables respect their domains.}
\end{array}}
\]

The formulation simultaneously:

* **Reschedules** arrival/departure times (\(a,d\)) while respecting dwell‑time windows, minimum/maximum journey times, and the disruption‑induced blockage constraints.  
* **Selects** whether a train uses the original track or the opposite‑track reroute (\(r_{t,e}\)).  
* **Chooses** a discrete speed class on every travelled segment (\(x_{t,e,k}\)), guaranteeing feasible acceleration/deceleration (Constraints 6a‑6b) and providing a linear estimate of energy consumption (Constraint 9).  
* **Enforces** conflict‑free usage of the single available track for each blocked segment by binary ordering variables (\(p_{t,b}\)).  
* **Optionally cancels** trains (\(\gamma_t\)) when recovery is impossible, at a high penalty.  

---

## 8. Remarks on Solving the Model  

* The model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**: the only nonlinearities stem from products of binary variables, which have been linearised by the standard big‑\(M\) technique.  
* **Scalability**: For realistic high‑speed networks the number of binary variables grows quickly (especially the pairwise conflict variables \(p\)). The decomposition strategy described in the source text (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems) can be applied directly: the master selects a feasible combination of binary decisions \((z,r,p,\gamma)\); for each train a sub‑problem fixes these binary choices and solves a linear programme to obtain optimal timings and speed‑profiles.  
* **Parameter calibration** (weights \(\alpha,\beta\), energy coefficients \(E^{\text{unit}}_k\), penalties) should be derived from the railway operator’s performance measures (e.g., passenger‑delay cost, electricity tariffs).  

The above MILP gives a **complete, linear, and implementable** representation of the **Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial‑segment blockage disruptions, fully aligned with the narrative and objectives of the provided introduction.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP**  
*(Partial segment blockage – one of the two parallel tracks of a segment is blocked for a known time window)*  

---

### 1. Sets and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* |
| **K(i)** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including origin and destination). Index *k* ∈ K(i). |
| **S = {L,R}** | Two parallel sides (Left / Right) of a segment that may be blocked. |
| **B ⊂ S** | Side that is *blocked* on the critical segment (e.g. **B = {L}**). |
| **SEG** | Set of track segments (including the blocked one). Index *seg*. |
| **len<sub>seg</sub>** | Physical length of segment *seg* (km). |
| **sched<sub>i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “on‑time’’ reference). |
| **dwell<sub>i,k</sub>** | Minimum dwell time required at station *k* for train *i* (minutes). |
| **v<sub>min</sub>, v<sub>max</sub>** | Global lower / upper speed limits (km /min). |
| **α, β** | Energy‑cost coefficients (α > 0, β ≥ 0). Energy on a segment is approximated by α v² + β v. |
| **T<sub>start</sub>, T<sub>end</sub>** | Start / end of the disruption window on the blocked side (minutes from the planning horizon origin). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **Δ<sub>safe</sub>** | Minimum safety headway between two consecutive trains on the same side of a segment (minutes). |
| **γ<sub>i</sub>** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (allows priority). |
| **w<sub>delay</sub>, w<sub>energy</sub>** | Global weights that balance the two parts of the objective. |
| **π<sub>seg</sub>** | Set of linearisation break‑points for speed (see § 4). |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r<sub>i,s</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* on the blocked segment (exactly one side must be chosen). |
| **o<sub>i,j,seg</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on the same side of segment *seg*. |
| **a<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k*. |
| **d<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **t<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **v<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **c<sub>i</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is cancelled (optional). |
| **e<sub>i,seg,p</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Portion of speed *v<sub>i,seg</sub>* allocated to linearisation piece *p* (see § 4). |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\min\;
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\;\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\;e_{i,seg,p}
\]

*First term*: weighted total delay (arrival at final station vs. scheduled).  
*Second term*: linearised energy consumption; \(\phi_{p}= \alpha p^{2}+ \beta p\) is the energy value at break‑point *p*.

---

### 4. Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

1. **Reconstruction of speed**  

\[
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p}\qquad\forall i,seg
\]

2. **Convex‑combination bounds**  

\[
0\le e_{i,seg,p}\le p_{\text{next}}-p_{\text{prev}}\qquad\forall i,seg,\;p\in\pi_{seg}
\]

(If the break‑points are dense the approximation is tight.)

3. **Linear energy expression**  

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}\;\approx\;\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\;e_{i,seg,p}
\]

All terms in the objective are now linear.

---

### 5. Model constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑choice on the blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

If side *s* is blocked permanently:  

\[
r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in B \tag{R2}
\]

(If the blockage is only temporary, use the time‑window constraints in § 5.6.)

#### 5.2 Flow conservation at stations  

\[
d_{i,k}= a_{i,k}+ \text{dwell}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{first}\} \tag{F1}
\]

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,\text{seg}(i,k)}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{last}\} \tag{F2}
\]

where **seg(i,k)** is the segment linking station *k* to *k+1* for train *i*.

#### 5.3 Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship (linearised)  

Introduce auxiliary variable \(u_{i,seg}=1/v_{i,seg}\).  

\[
t_{i,seg}= \text{len}_{seg}\; u_{i,seg}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T1}
\]

McCormick envelopes (valid because \(v_{min}\le v_{i,seg}\le v_{max}\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} \\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} \\
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}}-\frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}\bigl(v_{i,seg}-v_{\min}\bigr)\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}}-\frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}\bigl(v_{i,seg}-v_{\max}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T2}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\le v_{i,seg}\le v_{\max}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.5 Capacity / ordering on a shared side  

For any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that use the **same side** *s* of the **same segment** *seg* define:

\[
\text{enter}_{i,seg}= d_{i,\text{up}(seg)},\qquad
\text{exit}_{i,seg}= a_{i,\text{down}(seg)}
\]

Big‑M ordering constraints:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{exit}_{i,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{j,seg}+ M\,(1-o_{i,j,seg})\\
\text{exit}_{j,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{i,seg}+ M\,o_{i,j,seg}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C1}
\]

Mutual exclusivity:

\[
o_{i,j,seg}+o_{j,i,seg}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg \tag{C2}
\]

Linking to side‑choice:

\[
o_{i,j,seg}\le r_{i,s},\qquad o_{i,j,seg}\le r_{j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C3}
\]

If a train does not use side *s*, the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0.

#### 5.6 Disruption‑window (temporary blockage)  

If the blockage is only active during \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\) and a train *i* is assigned to the blocked side (*r<sub>i,B</sub>=1*), its passage must lie outside the window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i,blk} &\ge T_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-r_{i,B})\\
\text{exit}_{i,blk}  &\le T_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-r_{i,B})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in I \tag{D1}
\]

If the blockage is permanent, (R2) already forces \(r_{i,B}=0\).

#### 5.7 Optional cancellation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,k} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
d_{i,k} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
t_{i,seg} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg\\
v_{i,seg} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\tag{CAN}
\]

(If cancellations are to be penalised, add \(\sum_i \rho_i c_i\) to the objective.)

---

### 6. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\,e_{i,seg,p}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice on blocked segment}\\
&\text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{flow conservation at stations}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{travel‑time ↔ speed (linearised)}\\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{speed limits}\\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{capacity / ordering on shared side}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{no‑occupancy of blocked side during disruption window}\\
&\text{(CAN)} &&\text{optional cancellation}\\
&v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p} &&\forall i,seg\\
&0\le e_{i,seg,p}\le p_{\text{next}}-p_{\text{prev}} &&\forall i,seg,p\\
&r_{i,s},o_{i,j,seg},c_i\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,seg},v_{i,seg},e_{i,seg,p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy and division) have been replaced by standard MILP linearisation techniques (piecewise linear approximation and McCormick envelopes).  

---

### 7. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – fill the sets *I*, *SEG*, *K(i)*, the parameters (segment lengths, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, big‑M, safety headway).  
2. **Linearisation granularity** – choose a set of speed break‑points *π<sub>seg</sub>* (e.g., 0, v<sub>min</sub>, mid‑point, v<sub>max</sub>) to obtain the desired trade‑off between model size and energy‑approximation accuracy.  
3. **Solve** – feed the formulation to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, etc.).  
4. **Result interpretation** – the optimal solution provides for each train:  
   * which side of the blocked segment to use (`r_{i,s}`),  
   * exact arrival/departure times at every station (`a_{i,k}`, `d_{i,k}`),  
   * average speed on each segment (`v_{i,seg}`),  
   * ordering of trains on shared tracks (`o_{i,j,seg}`),  
   * and, if allowed, a cancellation decision (`c_i`).  

The solution simultaneously minimises total delay and energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable that respects the disruption, bidirectional track capacity, speed limits, and safety headways.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for rolling‑stock rescheduling with infrastructure‑availability constraints**  

The model combines two sub‑problems that appear in the paper:

* **Composition sub‑problem** – decides which rolling‑stock unit (RSU) will serve each passenger train trip and which shunting movements (SM) are required to realise the new circulation.  
* **Infrastructure sub‑problem** – checks whether the selected shunting movements can be performed on the available tracks of the stations (Utrecht C, Rotterdam C) while possibly allowing short delays of other (non‑shunting) trains.

The MILP below is written as a **single master problem** that can be solved directly (exact approach) or used inside a Benders/iterative scheme. All sets, parameters and variables are defined first, then the objective function, followed by the constraints. Wherever data are not supplied in the text, reasonable assumptions are explicitly marked.

---

## 1. Index sets and fundamental data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of passenger train trips that must be executed on the day (indexed by \\(t\\)). |
| \\(R\\) | Set of available rolling‑stock units (RSU) (indexed by \\(r\\)). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of stations where shunting may be performed (here \\(S=\{Utrecht, Rotterdam\}\\)). |
| \\(M\\) | Set of possible **shunting movements** (indexed by \\(m\\)). Each movement is a tuple \\((r, s, \tau^{\text{start}}_m, \tau^{\text{end}}_m)\\) meaning “RSU \\(r\\) is shunted at station \\(s\\) during the time window \\([\tau^{\text{start}}_m,\tau^{\text{end}}_m]\\)”. |
| \\(K\\) | Set of **ordinary (non‑shunting) train events** that occupy tracks (indexed by \\(k\\)). For each \\(k\\) we know the station \\(s(k)\\), the occupied time interval \\([\alpha_k,\beta_k]\\). |
| \\(P\\) | Set of **track‑slots** (track‑time resources) at each station (indexed by \\(p\\)). A slot is a pair \\((s, \ell)\\) where \\(\ell\\) is a physical track segment that can be used by at most one event at a time. |

*Assumption 1*: The timetable provides for each trip \\(t\\) a scheduled departure/arrival time \\(d_t, a_t\\) and a required capacity (number of seats).  

*Assumption 2*: Each RSU \\(r\\) has a fixed capacity \\(cap_r\\) (number of seats) and a known home depot location (used only for “night‑positioning” constraints, omitted here for brevity).  

*Assumption 3*: For each shunting movement \\(m\\) we know a **minimum duration** \\(len_m\\) (e.g. 5 min) and a **setup time** on the track (to be modelled as a resource consumption).  

*Assumption 4*: Short delays of ordinary trains are allowed up to a maximum \\(\Delta^{\max}\\) (e.g. 5 min).  

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{tr}\\) | binary | 1 if RSU \\(r\\) is assigned to trip \\(t\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{tm}\\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \\(m\\) is performed **after** trip \\(t\\) (i.e., RSU that served \\(t\\) must be moved by \\(m\\)). |
| \\(z_{km}\\) | binary | 1 if ordinary train event \\(k\\) is **delayed** to make room for shunting movement \\(m\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(d_k\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Additional delay (in minutes) applied to event \\(k\\). |
| \\(u_{mp}\\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \\(m\\) occupies track‑slot \\(p\\) (i.e. uses that physical track). |
| \\(v_{kp}\\) | binary | 1 if ordinary train event \\(k\\) (possibly delayed) occupies track‑slot \\(p\\). |
| \\(w_{r}\\) | binary | 1 if RSU \\(r\\) is **unused** (i.e. stays idle) – helps to minimise the number of extra RSUs that have to be kept as buffer stock. |

---

## 3. Objective function  

The model can balance several (often conflicting) goals. A **weighted linear combination** is used; the weights can be tuned by the decision maker.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & 
\underbrace{\alpha_1\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{r\in R} \bigl|cap_r - demand_t\bigr|\,x_{tr}}_{\text{(A) capacity‑matching penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\alpha_2\sum_{m\in M}\sum_{t\in T} y_{tm}}_{\text{(B) number of shunting movements (to keep it low)}}\\
&+ \underbrace{\alpha_3\sum_{k\in K} d_k}_{\text{(C) total extra delay introduced}}\\
&+ \underbrace{\alpha_4\sum_{r\in R} w_r}_{\text{(D) number of idle RSUs (buffer stock) to be minimised}}\\
&+ \underbrace{\alpha_5\sum_{m\in M}\sum_{p\in P} u_{mp}}_{\text{(E) track‑usage penalty (encourages using less congested tracks)}}\\
\end{aligned}
\]

Typical weight choices:  
* \\(\alpha_1\\) large (ensure passenger capacity).  
* \\(\alpha_2\\) medium (avoid unnecessary shunting).  
* \\(\alpha_3\\) small‑to‑medium (short delays are acceptable).  
* \\(\alpha_4\\) large (reduce capital stock).  
* \\(\alpha_5\\) small (helps the solver to spread movements over time).

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Assignment of rolling‑stock units  

1. **Each trip receives exactly one RSU**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{tr}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **An RSU can serve at most one trip at a time** (no overlap).  
   Let \\(O(t,t')\\) be a binary parameter =1 if the scheduled time windows of trips \\(t\\) and \\(t'\\) overlap (including a safety margin).  

\[
x_{tr}+x_{t'r}\le 1 \qquad \forall r\in R,\; \forall (t,t')\in T\times T \text{ with } O(t,t')=1
\]

3. **Capacity compatibility** (optional, can be relaxed with penalty A)  

\[
cap_r \, x_{tr} \ge demand_t \, x_{tr} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; r\in R
\]

### 4.2 Linking shunting movements to assignments  

A shunting movement \\(m=(r,s,\tau^{\text{start}}_m,\tau^{\text{end}}_m)\\) can only be used if the corresponding RSU actually serves a trip that finishes before the movement starts.

Define \\(F(t)\\) = scheduled finish time of trip \\(t\\).  

\[
y_{tm} \le x_{tr} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; m\in M \text{ with } r(m)=r
\]

\[
y_{tm}=0 \quad\text{if } F(t) > \tau^{\text{start}}_m \;\;(\text{pre‑computed infeasibility})
\]

### 4.3 Track‑resource capacity (infrastructure feasibility)  

For every track‑slot \\(p\\) and every point in time we must not exceed capacity 1. A classic way in MILP is to discretise the planning horizon into **time‑points** \\(q\in Q\\) (e.g., each minute). Let \\(B_{mpq}\\) = 1 if shunting movement \\(m\\) occupies slot \\(p\\) at time \\(q\\) (derived from its start/end times and the chosen slot). Similarly \\(B_{kpq}\\) for ordinary event \\(k\\) (including possible delay \\(d_k\\)).  

Then:

\[
\sum_{m\in M} u_{mp} B_{mpq} + \sum_{k\in K} v_{kp} B_{kpq} \le 1 \qquad \forall p\in P,\; q\in Q
\]

Because \\(u_{mp}\\) and \\(v_{kp}\\) are binary, the constraint guarantees that at most one movement uses a given track at a given minute.

### 4.4 Relation between shunting‑movement‑track choice and binary usage  

\[
u_{mp} \le \sum_{q\in Q} B_{mpq} \qquad \forall m\in M, p\in P
\]

If a movement never uses a slot, \\(u_{mp}=0\\).

### 4.5 Delaying ordinary trains to free a track  

If a shunting movement \\(m\\) would conflict with an ordinary event \\(k\\) on the same slot, we may delay \\(k\\) (by at most \\(\Delta^{\max}\\)).

1. **Conflict detection** (pre‑computed): let \\(C_{mk}=1\\) if movement \\(m\\) and event \\(k\\) overlap on the same station/track when \\(k\\) is on schedule.

2. **Delay activation**  

\[
z_{km} \ge y_{tm} \; C_{mk} \qquad \forall k\in K,\, m\in M,\, t\in T
\]

3. **Delay magnitude**  

\[
d_k \ge \bigl(\tau^{\text{start}}_m - \beta_k\bigr) \, z_{km} \qquad \forall k,m
\]

4. **Maximum allowed delay**  

\[
0 \le d_k \le \Delta^{\max} \qquad \forall k\in K
\]

If a movement cannot be rescued by a delay ≤ \\(\Delta^{\max}\\), the model will simply set \\(y_{tm}=0\\) (i.e., discard that movement).

### 4.6 Consistency of track‑occupation variables for ordinary events  

If event \\(k\\) is delayed, its occupied time interval shifts by \\(d_k\\). The binary variable \\(v_{kp}\\) must reflect the new slot usage:

\[
v_{kp} \ge \text{(event }k\text{ uses slot }p\text{ after shift)} \qquad \forall k,p
\]

In practice this is linearised by using the same discretisation as in (4.3) and adding:

\[
\sum_{p\in P} v_{kp}=1 \qquad \forall k\in K
\]

### 4.7 Idle‑RSU definition  

\[
w_r \ge 1 - \sum_{t\in T} x_{tr} \qquad \forall r\in R
\]

If an RSU is used for at least one trip, \\(w_r=0\\); otherwise \\(w_r=1\\).

### 4.8 Logical linking of shunting to the same RSU  

If a shunting movement is performed, the RSU that performed the preceding trip must be the same RSU that will be shunted:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{tm} = \sum_{t\in T} x_{t,r(m)} \qquad \forall m\in M
\]

(This ensures that each movement is attached to exactly one RSU.)

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \text{(weighted sum of objectives)}\\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4.1)–(4.8) } \\
& x_{tr}, y_{tm}, z_{km}, u_{mp}, v_{kp}, w_r \in \{0,1\}\\
& d_k \ge 0 \quad \forall k\in K .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; binary variables capture assignment, shunting‑selection, track‑usage and delay‑activation decisions. The model can be solved directly with a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) for small‑ to medium‑size instances (the paper reports instances with a few hundred trips and a few dozen shunting movements).  

For larger instances the **Combinatorial Benders** decomposition described in the paper can be applied:

* **Master problem** – the composition model (variables \\(x, y, w\\)) together with a Benders cut that forbids infeasible combinations of shunting movements.  
* **Sub‑problem** – the infrastructure model (variables \\(u, v, d, z\\)) that checks feasibility of the selected shunting set and returns a cut of the form  

\[
\sum_{m\in M'} y_{tm} \le |M'|-1 \qquad \forall \text{ infeasible set }M' .
\]

The iterative heuristic simply adds shunting movements one‑by‑one and resolves the sub‑problem each time.

---

### Remarks / Assumptions made  

1. **Time discretisation** (set \\(Q\\)) is assumed fine enough (e.g., 1 min) to capture all conflicts.  
2. **Track‑slot set** \\(P\\) is constructed from the real topology of Utrecht C and Rotterdam C; each slot can host at most one event per minute.  
3. **Maximum delay** \\(\Delta^{\max}\\) is a parameter (the paper mentions “a few minutes”).
