Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under a partial‑segment blockage**

---

### 1. Sets and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** = {L,R} | Two “sides’’ (Left, Right) of the blocked segment. |
| **B** ⊆ T | Trains that must cross the blocked segment ℓ\*. |
| **K** | Set of stations, indexed by *k*. |
| **L** | Set of free track segments (including the blocked one ℓ\*). |
| **ℓ\*** | The *blocked* segment (the only segment that can be travelled on either side). |
| **P(t,ℓ)** | 1 if train *t* traverses segment ℓ in its nominal route, 0 otherwise. |
| **Lℓ** | Length of segment ℓ (km). |
| **v̂₁,…,v̂_M** | Discrete admissible speed levels (km h⁻¹). |
| **αℓ** | Energy‑cost coefficient for segment ℓ (kWh·h·km⁻¹). |
| **Δt_k^{min}, Δt_k^{max}** | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station *k* (s). |
| **S_{i,j}** | Minimum safety headway between two successive trains on the same side (s). |
| **sched_a_{t,last}** | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (s). |
| **M_time** | Large constant > any feasible time difference (e.g. 10⁴ s). |
| **β₁, β₂** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective. |

*All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data and operational policies.*

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **r_{t,s}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* (s ∈ S) of the blocked segment. |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on a common side of a segment (i ≠ j). |
| **a_{t,k}**, **d_{t,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival / departure time of train *t* at station *k*. |
| **τ_{t,ℓ}** | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ. |
| **z_{t,ℓ,m}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* travels on ℓ with speed level *m*. |
| **w_{t,ℓ,m,m'}** | binary | Linearisation variable for the product of two speed‑level binaries (used for energy). |
| **delay_t** | continuous ≥0 | Total schedule deviation of train *t*. |
| **energy_t** | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption of train *t*. |

Auxiliary continuous variables:

* **v_{t,ℓ}** = Σₘ v̂ₘ z_{t,ℓ,m} (average speed on ℓ).  
* **e_{t,ℓ}** = Σₘ Σ_{m'} α_ℓ v̂ₘ² (L_ℓ / v̂_{m'}) w_{t,ℓ,m,m'} (energy on ℓ).

---

### 3. Linearised relations  

1. **Speed‑level selection**  

   \[
   v_{t,\ell}= \sum_{m=1}^{M}\hat v_{m}\,z_{t,\ell,m}\qquad\forall t,\ell
   \]
   \[
   \sum_{m=1}^{M}z_{t,\ell,m}=P(t,\ell)\qquad\forall t,\ell
   \]

2. **Travel‑time = length / speed (linearised)**  

   \[
   \tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{L_{\ell}}{\hat v_{m}}\,z_{t,\ell,m}\qquad\forall t,\ell
   \]

3. **Energy linearisation**  

   \[
   w_{t,\ell,m,m'}\le z_{t,\ell,m},\; w_{t,\ell,m,m'}\le z_{t,\ell,m'},\;
   w_{t,\ell,m,m'}\ge z_{t,\ell,m}+z_{t,\ell,m'}-1
   \]
   \[
   e_{t,\ell}= \sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{m'=1}^{M}
               \alpha_{\ell}\,\hat v_{m}^{2}\,\frac{L_{\ell}}{\hat v_{m'}}\,
               w_{t,\ell,m,m'}\qquad\forall t,\ell
   \]

4. **Delay definition**  

   \[
   delay_{t}= a_{t,\text{last}}-sched\_a_{t,\text{last}}\qquad\forall t
   \]

5. **Energy aggregation**  

   \[
   energy_{t}= \sum_{\ell\in L} e_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t
   \]

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
      \beta_{1}\sum_{t\in T}delay_{t}
      \;+\;
      \beta_{2}\sum_{t\in T}energy_{t}}
\]

The first term minimises total passenger delay, the second term minimises total energy consumption.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑choice for the blocked segment  
\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}= P(t,\ell^{*})\qquad\forall t\in B
\]

#### 5.2 Compatibility of ordering variables  
\[
c_{i,j}= \sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}\,r_{j,s}\qquad\forall i\neq j
\]
\[
o_{i,j}\le c_{i,j}\qquad\forall i\neq j
\]

#### 5.3 Disjunctive headway on any shared segment  
Let  

* \(enter_{t,\ell}= d_{t,\text{up}(\ell)}\) (departure from upstream station),  
* \(exit_{t,\ell}= a_{t,\text{down}(\ell)}= d_{t,\text{up}(\ell)}+\tau_{t,\ell}\).

For every pair of distinct trains *i*,*j* using segment ℓ **and** sharing a side:

\[
\begin{aligned}
exit_{i,\ell}+S_{i,j}&\le enter_{j,\ell}+M_{time}\,(1-o_{i,j})\\
exit_{j,\ell}+S_{i,j}&\le enter_{i,\ell}+M_{time}\,o_{i,j}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;\forall \ell\in L
\]

If the trains are on different sides, \(c_{i,j}=0\) forces \(o_{i,j}=0\) and the constraints are trivially satisfied.

#### 5.4 Dwell‑time limits at stations  
\[
\Delta t_{k}^{\min}\,P(t,k)\le d_{t,k}-a_{t,k}\le \Delta t_{k}^{\max}\,P(t,k)
\qquad\forall t,\;k\in K
\]

#### 5.5 Flow consistency (arrival–departure–travel)  

For each train *t* and each intermediate station *k* (except first/last):

\[
a_{t,k}= d_{t,\text{prev}(k)}+\tau_{t,\text{seg\_prev}(k)}
\]
\[
d_{t,k}= a_{t,k}+ (d_{t,k}-a_{t,k})\quad\text{(already bounded by (5.4))}
\]

The first station has a given scheduled departure, the last station supplies \(a_{t,\text{last}}\) used in the delay definition.

#### 5.6 Rerouting consistency (side propagation)  

If a train uses side *s* of the blocked segment, it must also use the corresponding side for all downstream segments that belong to the blocked‑area corridor.  
Let \(U_{\ell}^{s}=1\) if segment ℓ belongs to side *s* of the corridor, 0 otherwise.

\[
P(t,\ell)= r_{t,s}\,U_{\ell}^{s}\qquad\forall t\in B,\;\forall \ell\in\text{corridor},\; s\in S
\]

(Implementation: fix the binary routing variables of those downstream segments to the same side indicator.)

#### 5.7 Non‑negativity of delay and energy  

\[
delay_{t}\ge 0,\qquad energy_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t
\]

#### 5.8 Big‑M values (optional tightening)  

\[
M_{time}= \max_{t,\ell}\Big(\frac{L_{\ell}}{v_{\min}}+\max_{k}\Delta t_{k}^{\max}\Big)+\max_{i,j}S_{i,j}
\]

---

### 6. Summary  

* **Variables** – binary route choice \(r_{t,s}\), binary ordering \(o_{i,j}\), binary speed‑level selectors \(z_{t,\ell,m}\) (with auxiliary \(w\) for energy), continuous times \(a,d,\tau\), and auxiliary quantities \(delay_t, energy_t\).  
* **Objective** – minimise a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.  
* **Constraints** – enforce (i) exactly one side of the blocked segment per affected train, (ii) ordering only for trains sharing a side, (iii) headway (non‑overlap) on any shared segment, (iv) linearised travel‑time = length / chosen speed, (v) dwell‑time limits, (vi) flow consistency between stations and segments, (vii) side‑consistent rerouting, (viii) definitions of delay and energy, (ix) big‑M linking.

All relations are linear (or linearised with a small number of extra binaries), thus the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** ready for solution with any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

Now write the filled-in form for the text above as one JSON object, without code fences and without repeating the template.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial‑Segment‑Blockage Scenario**  

The model below is a *complete* mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that simultaneously decides  

* a conflict‑free timetable (arrival / departure times, train order and possible rerouting), and  
* a feasible speed‑profile for every train on every track segment (hence the travelled time on the segment).  

All symbols, sets and parameters are defined first, then the decision variables, the objective function and finally the linear constraints.  
Where the source text does not give a numeric value, a **reasonable assumption** is stated and highlighted in *italics*.

---

## 1.   Sets, Indices, and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning (assumption if not given) |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **T** = { t | t = 1,…,|T| } | Set of trains that have to be operated (including those that may be cancelled). |
| **S** = { s | s = 1,…,|S| } | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train). |
| **L** = { ℓ | ℓ = 1,…,|L| } | Set of *track‑segments* (directed links between two consecutive stations). |
| **B** ⊆ **L** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the disruption area). |
| **K** = { k | k = 1,…,|K| } | Set of *routing alternatives* for each train (k = 0 → original route, k = 1 → reroute to opposite track, …). |
| **I** = { i | i = 1,…,|I| } | Set of *time‑intervals* used to discretise the feasible travel‑time on a segment (see Section 3.2). |
| **Δt** | Length of a discretisation interval (e.g. 30 s). |
| **cᵗ** | Fixed cost of *cancelling* train *t* (large positive number to discourage cancellations). |
| **αℓ**, **βℓ** | Minimum and maximum admissible *travel time* on segment ℓ (derived from speed limits, acceleration/deceleration limits). *Assumption*: αℓ = 0.8·(nominal travel time), βℓ = 1.5·(nominal travel time). |
| **γℓ** | Energy consumption coefficient for travelling on ℓ (kWh per second of travel). *Assumption*: proportional to average speed on ℓ. |
| **τᵗˢ** | Minimum *dwell time* of train *t* at station *s* (e.g. 30 s). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶ s). |
| **[aᵢ, bᵢ]** | Time‑window of interval *i* (aᵢ = (i‑1)·Δt, bᵢ = i·Δt). |
| **Tᵗ₀ℓ** | Nominal (pre‑disruption) travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ. |
| **Rᵗ** ⊆ **K** | Feasible routing alternatives for train *t* (e.g. original route and a possible opposite‑track reroute). |
| **δℓ** | Binary indicator of whether segment ℓ is *single‑track* (δℓ = 1) or *double‑track* (δℓ = 0). In the disruption area the opposite track becomes single‑track, therefore δℓ = 1 for ℓ ∈ B after rerouting. |
| **Tᵈˢ**, **Tᵈᵉ** | Disruption start and end times (seconds from midnight). |
| **πᵗ** | Penalty weight for *delay* of train *t* (e.g. 1 €/s). |
| **πᵉ** | Penalty weight for *energy consumption* (e.g. 0.05 €/kWh). |
| **πᶜ** | Penalty weight for *cancellation* (e.g. 10 000 €). |

---

## 2.   Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **xᵗₖ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses routing alternative *k* (k ∈ Rᵗ). |
| **yᵗₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Actual *departure time* of train *t* from station *s* (seconds). |
| **aᵗₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Actual *arrival time* of train *t* at station *s*. |
| **zᵗℓi** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if the travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ falls into interval *i* (i.e., aᵗ_{s(ℓ)} + travel time = aᵗ_{s'(ℓ)}). |
| **cᵗ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* is *cancelled* (no service). |
| **dᵗ** ≥ 0 | continuous | *Delay* of train *t* relative to its original scheduled arrival at its final destination (dᵗ = aᵗ_{dest} – aᵗ₀_{dest}). |
| **eᵗ** ≥ 0 | continuous | *Energy consumption* of train *t* (kWh). |

*Auxiliary variables* (linearised products) are introduced where needed (e.g., xᵗₖ·zᵗℓi). They are handled by standard big‑M linearisation (see constraints (9)–(12)).

---

## 3.   Objective Function  

The planner wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total delay, total energy consumption and cancellation costs**:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\pi^{d}\,d^{t}}_{\text{Delay cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\pi^{e}\,e^{t}}_{\text{Energy cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\pi^{c}\,c^{t}}_{\text{Cancellation cost}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

All three components are linear because *dᵗ*, *eᵗ* and *cᵗ* are decision variables.

---

## 4.   Linear Constraints  

### 4.1  Routing‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one routing (or cancellation) per train**  

\[
\sum_{k\in R^{t}} x_{k}^{t} + c^{t}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{1}
\]

2. **If a train is cancelled, no timing variables are active** (big‑M)  

\[
y_{s}^{t}\le M\,(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{2}
\]

\[
a_{s}^{t}\le M\,(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{3}
\]

### 4.2  Timetable feasibility  

3. **Dwell‑time at each station**  

\[
y_{s}^{t} - a_{s}^{t} \ge \tau^{t}_{s}\;(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{4}
\]

4. **Travel‑time on each segment must lie in one admissible interval**  

\[
\sum_{i\in I} z^{t}_{\ell i}=1 - c^{t} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \ell\in L
\tag{5}
\]

5. **Link arrival / departure via selected interval**  

Let *s(ℓ)* be the upstream station of segment ℓ and *s'(ℓ)* the downstream station.  

\[
a^{t}_{s'(ℓ)} \;=\; y^{t}_{s(ℓ)} \;+\; \sum_{i\in I} \tilde{\theta}_{i}\,z^{t}_{\ell i} \;(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \ell\in L
\tag{6}
\]

where **\(\tilde{\theta}_{i}\)** is the *representative* travel time of interval *i* (e.g. the midpoint \((a_i+b_i)/2\)).  

6. **Travel‑time intervals respect speed limits**  

\[
\alpha_{\ell}\;(1-c^{t}) \le \sum_{i\in I}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\,z^{t}_{\ell i} \le \beta_{\ell}\;(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \ell\in L
\tag{7}
\]

### 4.3  Disruption‑time‑window constraints  

7. **Blocked segments cannot be used during the disruption window**  

If ℓ ∈ B and train *t* traverses ℓ during the blockage, the interval must be *outside* \([T^{d}_{s},T^{d}_{e}]\). This is enforced by forbidding intervals that overlap the window:

\[
z^{t}_{\ell i}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \ell\in B,\; i\in I\; \text{with}\;[a_i,b_i]\cap[T^{d}_{s},T^{d}_{e}]\neq\varnothing
\tag{8}
\]

(Implementation: pre‑process the set of admissible intervals for each blocked segment.)

### 4.4  Conflict‑avoidance on single‑track (including rerouted) segments  

8. **Head‑way (minimum separation) on a single‑track segment**  

Let **h** be the minimum safe head‑way (seconds, e.g. 120 s). For every pair of distinct trains \(t\neq t'\) that both use the *same* single‑track segment ℓ (i.e., δℓ = 1 and both have x‑variables that imply usage of ℓ), we impose a disjunctive ordering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a^{t}_{s'(ℓ)} &\le y^{t'}_{s(ℓ)} - h + M\,(1-\omega^{tt'}_{\ell}) \\
a^{t'}_{s'(ℓ)} &\le y^{t}_{s(ℓ)} - h + M\,\omega^{tt'}_{\ell} \\
\omega^{tt'}_{\ell} &\in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall \ell\in L,\; \delta_{\ell}=1,\; t<t'
\tag{9}
\]

The binary \(\omega^{tt'}_{\ell}\) decides which train passes first. The constraints are activated only if both trains actually occupy ℓ; this is enforced by big‑M terms using the routing‑selection variables:

\[
\omega^{tt'}_{\ell} \le x^{t}_{k(\ell)}\qquad
\omega^{tt'}_{\ell} \le x^{t'}_{k'(\ell)}\qquad
\text{(k(ℓ) is the routing alternative that includes ℓ)}
\tag{10}
\]

If either train does not use ℓ, the corresponding constraints become redundant.

### 4.5  Energy consumption calculation  

9. **Energy on a segment is proportional to travel time**  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_{\ell}\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}\,z^{t}_{\ell i}\;(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{11}
\]

(Linear because \(\gamma_{\ell}\) and \(\tilde{\theta}_{i}\) are data.)

### 4.6  Delay definition  

10. **Delay of each train relative to its original timetable**  

Let \(a^{t,0}_{\text{dest}}\) be the *original* scheduled arrival at the final destination (pre‑disruption). Then

\[
d^{t}= a^{t}_{\text{dest}} - a^{t,0}_{\text{dest}} \;(1-c^{t}) \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{12}
\]

If a train is cancelled, \(d^{t}=0\) (no penalty beyond the cancellation cost).

### 4.7  Logical linking of routing to segment usage  

11. **If a train chooses a routing that does not contain a segment, the corresponding interval variables must be zero**  

For each train *t*, segment ℓ and interval *i*:

\[
z^{t}_{\ell i} \le \sum_{k\in R^{t}:\,\ell\in L_{k}} x^{t}_{k} \qquad \forall t,\ell,i
\tag{13}
\]

where \(L_{k}\) is the set of segments belonging to routing alternative *k*.  

12. **If a train is cancelled, all segment‑usage variables are forced to zero** (already implied by (5)–(7) with the factor \(1-c^{t}\)).  

---

## 5.   Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\bigl(\pi^{d} d^{t} + \pi^{e} e^{t} + \pi^{c} c^{t}\bigr)\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(13)} \quad\text{(linear constraints listed above)}\\[1mm]
& x^{t}_{k}\in\{0,1\},\; z^{t}_{\ell i}\in\{0,1\},\; \omega^{tt'}_{\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; c^{t}\in\{0,1\}\\
& y^{t}_{s},a^{t}_{s},d^{t},e^{t}\ge 0 \qquad \forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries. The model therefore belongs to the class **MILP** and can be solved with any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, GLPK) MILP solver.

---

## 6.   Key Modeling Assumptions (explicitly stated)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | Travel‑time on a segment is approximated by a *piecewise‑constant* interval (Δt = 30 s is typical). This yields a linear representation of the speed profile while keeping the model tractable. |
| A2 | Energy consumption on a segment is assumed linear in travel time (γℓ coefficient). In practice γℓ can be calibrated from train‑specific power curves. |
| A3 | Minimum head‑way *h* on single‑track segments is constant for all trains (e.g., 120 s). This captures safety separation without modelling detailed signalling. |
| A4 | The disruption window \([T^{d}_{s},T^{d}_{e}]\) is known a‑priori and does not change during optimisation. |
| A5 | Cancelling a train is allowed but heavily penalised (πᶜ ≫ typical delay/energy costs). |
| A6 | Rerouting is limited to the *opposite* track of a blocked segment; no longer detours are considered. |
| A7 | All trains share the same maximum acceleration/deceleration limits, which are embedded in the interval bounds αℓ, βℓ. |
| A8 | The timetable is *conflict‑free* only on single‑track segments; on double‑track segments (δℓ = 0) trains may cross simultaneously without additional constraints. |
| A9 | Dwell‑time minima τᵗₛ are identical for all trains at a given station (e.g., 30 s). |

If a practitioner wishes to relax any of the above (e.g., variable head‑way, more detailed energy model, multi‑detour rerouting), the corresponding parameters and constraints can be replaced by the appropriate linear expressions without changing the overall structure of the MILP.

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets **T, S, L, B**, compute nominal travel times **Tᵗ₀ℓ**, the interval representatives **\(\tilde{\theta}_{i}\)**, and the energy coefficients **γℓ**.  
2. **Pre‑process** – For each blocked segment ℓ ∈ B, delete all intervals that intersect the disruption window (constraint (8)).  
3. **Model building** – Feed the MILP to a solver, optionally using the decomposition approach described in the accompanying paper (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems).  
4. **Post‑processing** – From the optimal **zᵗℓi** values retrieve the exact travel‑time on each segment, reconstruct the speed profile (piecewise‑constant speed = segment length / travel time), and compute the final timetable (**aᵗₛ**, **yᵗₛ**).  

The formulation guarantees that the produced timetable is **feasible** (no conflicts on single‑track sections, respects the blockage, respects dwell‑time and speed limits) and that the associated speed profiles are **executable**, while simultaneously **minimising delay, energy use and cancellations**.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP‑MILP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three tightly coupled decision layers that arise when a partial‑segment blockage disrupts a high‑speed railway line:

1. **Timetable decisions** – new arrival / departure times, possible re‑ordering of trains and binary routing (original track vs. opposite track).  
2. **Conflict‑avoidance decisions** – binary variables that guarantee that at any instant two trains never occupy the same track segment in opposite directions.  
3. **Speed‑profile decisions** – piece‑wise‑linear acceleration / cruising / coasting blocks that translate the timetable into feasible locomotive dynamics and that allow the energy consumption of each train to be evaluated.

The formulation is linear because all nonlinear train‑dynamics relations (e.g. kinetic energy, resistance) are linearised by a **time‑indexed piece‑wise‑linear speed envelope** (see Assumption A‑4).  

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Sets, parameters and indexing  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled (including those that may be cancelled). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of line segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations. |
| **D** ⊆ **S** | Sub‑set of *disrupted* segments (blocked on one side). |
| **K** = {1,…,|K|} | Set of **speed‑envelopes** (time‑indexed speed blocks) used to discretise a train’s speed profile on a segment. |
| **τ** = {0,Δ,…,H} | Discrete time horizon (Δ = time‑step, H = planning horizon). |
| **dir\_t** ∈ {+1,‑1} | Nominal travel direction of train *t* ( +1 = north‑bound, ‑1 = south‑bound). |
| **L\_s** | Length (km) of segment *s*. |
| **v\_max** | Maximum admissible speed (km h⁻¹) on any segment (assumed identical for all segments). |
| **a\_max**, **d\_max** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻²). |
| **E\_k** | Energy consumption (kWh) associated with speed‑envelope *k* (pre‑computed from a linearised power‑speed model). |
| **c\_t** | Fixed penalty (M $) for cancelling train *t*. |
| **M** | Large constant used in big‑M constraints (≥ maximal possible time value). |
| **β** ∈ (0,1] | Weight of the energy‑minimisation term (β = 1 → pure energy, β = 0 → pure delay). |
| **Δ\_t** | Original scheduled travel time of train *t* (baseline). |
| **t\_0\_t**, **t\_f\_t** | Original scheduled departure from first station and arrival at last station (baseline). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **a\_t** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* is **cancelled** (no service). |
| **r\_t ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* **uses the opposite (rerouted) track** on disrupted segments, 0 otherwise (uses its nominal track). |
| **π\_t** ∈ ℤ | integer | **Order index** of train *t* on its direction (used for conflict avoidance). |
| **arr\_{t,s}**, **dep\_{t,s}** ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Arrival** and **departure** times of train *t* at the *up‑stream* end of segment *s*. (If *s* is the first segment, arr\_{t,s}=departure from origin.) |
| **x\_{t,s,k}** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* **with speed‑envelope** *k* (i.e. the piece‑wise‑linear speed block *k* is selected). |
| **y\_{t,s}** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **occupies** segment *s* (any speed envelope). |
| **z\_{t,t',s}** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* **conflict** on segment *s* (i.e. occupy the same track at overlapping times). |
| **Δ\_{t}** ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Total delay** of train *t* (arrival at final destination minus original scheduled arrival). |
| **E\_t** ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of selected envelope energies). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Objective function  

The decision maker typically wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy**, while heavily penalising cancellations.

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} E_t}_{\text{energy term}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{(1-\beta)\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{delay term}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} c_t a_t}_{\text{cancellation penalty}}.
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*When β = 0 the model reduces to a pure delay‑recovery problem; when β = 1 it becomes a pure energy‑saving problem.*

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Model constraints  

### 4.1 Cancellation logic  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& a_t = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\;  \forall s\in S:\; y_{t,s}=0,\; x_{t,s,k}=0 \qquad &&\forall t\in T \tag{C1}\\
& a_t = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\;  \sum_{s\in S} y_{t,s} \ge 1 \qquad &&\forall t\in T \tag{C2}
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.2 Routing decision on disrupted segments  

If a segment *s* is disrupted (i.e. one side of the track is blocked), a train may either **wait** (stay on its original side) or **use the opposite track** (reroute). The model forces the same binary decision *r\_t* for **all** disrupted segments that train *t* traverses.

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_t = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{train } t \text{ may occupy } s \text{ only on its nominal side} &&\forall s\in D,\,t\in T \tag{R1}\\
& r_t = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{train } t \text{ occupies the opposite side on } s &&\forall s\in D,\,t\in T \tag{R2}
\end{aligned}
\]

In the linear model this is expressed by a **big‑M** coupling with the binary occupancy variable *y\_{t,s}* (see (C3) below).

### 4.3 Segment‑occupancy definition  

A train occupies a segment if **any** speed envelope is selected:

\[
\boxed{y_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t,s,k}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{C3}
\]

### 4.4 Speed‑envelope selection (piece‑wise‑linear speed profile)  

Only **one** envelope can be chosen for a given train‑segment pair:

\[
\boxed{\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{C4}
\]

Each envelope *k* is defined by a triple \((v_k,\,\tau_k^{\text{acc}},\,\tau_k^{\text{cruise}})\) pre‑computed such that the **time needed** to travel segment *s* when envelope *k* is used equals

\[
\theta_{k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k} + \tau_k^{\text{acc}} + \tau_k^{\text{cruise}} .
\]

(Assumption A‑4 guarantees linearity of this expression.)

### 4.5 Temporal consistency (travel time)  

For every non‑cancelled train the departure time from a segment equals the arrival time at the next segment plus the travel time induced by the selected envelope.

\[
\boxed{ dep_{t,s} + \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{k}\, x_{t,s,k}= arr_{t,s'} } 
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; s' = \text{successor}(s). \tag{C5}
\]

If a train is cancelled, all times are forced to zero by (C1).

### 4.6 Dwell‑time constraints at stations  

Let **St(s)** be the set of stations that bound segment *s*. For each station the **minimum dwell time** \(d^{\min}\) (minutes) must be respected:

\[
\boxed{ arr_{t,s} + d^{\min}\le dep_{t,s} } \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ that ends at a station}. \tag{C6}
\]

A **maximum dwell** \(d^{\max}\) can also be imposed if needed.

### 4.7 Conflict‑avoidance on shared tracks  

Two trains travelling in opposite directions may not occupy the **same physical track** at overlapping times. Let *dir\_t* be the nominal direction; the actual direction on a disrupted segment depends on *r\_t*:

\[
\text{effective\_dir}_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
\text{dir}_t & s\notin D,\\
\text{dir}_t \times (1-2 r_t) & s\in D .
\end{cases}
\]

A **conflict binary** \(z_{t,t',s}\) is activated if the two trains use the **same side** of the track on segment *s* **and** their time windows overlap. The linear big‑M formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& dep_{t,s} \le arr_{t',s} + M\, z_{t,t',s} &&\forall t<t',\, s\in S \\
& dep_{t',s} \le arr_{t,s} + M\,(1- z_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t<t',\, s\in S \\
& \text{if } \text{effective\_dir}_{t,s}= \text{effective\_dir}_{t',s}\;\Rightarrow\; z_{t,t',s}=0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C7}
\]

The last condition is linearised by adding a big‑M term that forces \(z_{t,t',s}=1\) (conflict) only when the two trains use the **same side**. Let  

\[
c_{t,s}= \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } s\notin D,\\
r_t & \text{if } s\in D .
\end{cases}
\]

Then the side used by train *t* on *s* is \(\text{side}_{t,s}= \frac{1+\text{dir}_t}{2}+c_{t,s}\) (0 = up‑track, 1 = down‑track). Equality of sides can be expressed with an auxiliary binary \(\sigma_{t,t',s}\) :

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \sigma_{t,t',s} \ge \text{side}_{t,s} - \text{side}_{t',s} \\
& \sigma_{t,t',s} \ge \text{side}_{t',s} - \text{side}_{t,s} \\
& \sigma_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{C7a}
\]

Finally, enforce  

\[
z_{t,t',s} \ge 1-\sigma_{t,t',s}\qquad\forall t<t',\,s\in S . \tag{C7b}
\]

Thus, if the sides differ (\(\sigma=1\)) the conflict binary may be 0; if the sides coincide (\(\sigma=0\)) the model forces a non‑overlap via the time‑ordering constraints in (C7).

### 4.8 Train‑order (sequencing) on the same direction  

For trains travelling **in the same direction** on the same side, a **precedence index** \(\pi_t\) ensures a consistent order (helps the solver to break symmetry).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \pi_t \neq \pi_{t'} \qquad &&\forall t\neq t',\; \text{if } \text{effective\_dir}_{t,s}= \text{effective\_dir}_{t',s} \text{ and } y_{t,s}=y_{t',s}=1\\
& dep_{t,s} \le arr_{t',s} + M\bigl(1- \mathbf{1}_{\pi_t<\pi_{t'}}\bigr) &&\forall t,t',s .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C8}
\]

(Only a subset of the constraints is needed; the model can also drop \(\pi\) variables and rely solely on the big‑M time‑ordering constraints.)

### 4.9 Delay definition  

The **total delay** of train *t* equals the difference between its final arrival (last segment) and the original scheduled arrival:

\[
\Delta_t = arr_{t,s^{\text{last}}} - t_f^{\text{orig}} + M a_t \qquad \forall t\in T . \tag{C9}
\]

The big‑M term forces \(\Delta_t\) to a large value when the train is cancelled (so the penalty *c\_t* dominates).

### 4.10 Energy accounting  

Energy is the sum of the envelope energies selected for every traversed segment:

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K} E_k \, x_{t,s,k}\qquad \forall t\in T . \tag{C10}
\]

### 4.11 Feasibility of acceleration / deceleration limits  

Because each envelope *k* has been constructed to respect the acceleration/deceleration caps (Assumption A‑4), the selection constraint (C4) already guarantees feasibility. If a finer model is required, the following linear constraints can be added:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& v_{k}^{\text{start}} + a_{\max}\,\tau_k^{\text{acc}} \ge v_{k}^{\text{cruise}} &&\forall k\in K \\
& v_{k}^{\text{cruise}} - d_{\max}\,\tau_k^{\text{dec}} \ge v_{k}^{\text{end}} &&\forall k\in K .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C11}
\]

These are *pre‑processing* constraints used to generate the admissible envelope set *K*.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Summary of assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Explanation |
|---|------------|--------------|
| **A‑1** | **Deterministic disruption window** – The start and end times of the partial blockage are known a‑priori and are incorporated in the big‑M constraints (the segment is unavailable for the blocked side for the whole horizon). |
| **A‑2** | **Single‑track per direction** – Each physical track can be used by at most one train at a time; the opposite side of a double‑track line is treated as a separate resource that can be accessed only via the binary rerouting variable *r\_t*. |
| **A‑3** | **Fixed train set** – No new trains are inserted during the recovery; only existing scheduled services may be delayed, rerouted or cancelled. |
| **A‑4** | **Piece‑wise‑linear speed envelope** – The continuous speed‑time relationship of a high‑speed train is approximated by a finite set *K* of linear blocks; each block respects the physical limits *v\_max*, *a\_max*, *d\_max*. This yields a linear travel‑time expression \(\theta_k\). |
| **A‑5** | **Energy linearisation** – Energy consumption of each block is pre‑computed (e.g., by integrating the power‑speed curve) and treated as a constant *E\_k*. The total energy is therefore a linear function of the binary envelope variables. |
| **A‑6** | **No overtaking on the same side** – Trains travelling in the same direction on the same track cannot overtake; this is enforced by the ordering variables \(\pi_t\) (or equivalently by the time‑ordering big‑M constraints). |
| **A‑7** | **Sufficiently large M** – The constant *M* is chosen larger than the planning horizon *H* plus the longest possible travel time, guaranteeing that the big‑M constraints are never active when they should be relaxed. |
| **A‑8** | **Station dwell times are deterministic** – Minimum (and optionally maximum) dwell times are known and identical for all trains; they are enforced by (C6). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\beta\sum_{t\in T} \underbrace{\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}E_k x_{t,s,k}}_{E_t}
      +(1-\beta)\sum_{t\in T}\underbrace{\bigl(arr_{t,s^{\text{last}}}-t_f^{\text{orig}}+M a_t\bigr)}_{\Delta_t}
      +\sum_{t\in T}c_t a_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C11) as listed above} \\[2pt]
& a_t\in\{0,1\},\; r_t\in\{0,1\},\; \pi_t\in\mathbb Z,\;
x_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s},z_{t,t',s},\sigma_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& arr_{t,s},dep_{t,s},\Delta_t,E_t\ge 0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K.
\end{aligned}
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### How the model works  

* **Cancellation** – If \(a_t=1\) all occupancy and timing variables are forced to zero; the large penalty \(c_t\) makes cancellation a last‑resort decision.  
* **Rerouting** – The binary \(r_t\) switches the side used on every disrupted segment. The side‑equality binaries \(\sigma_{t,t',s}\) together with the conflict binaries \(z_{t,t',s}\) guarantee that two trains never occupy the same physical track at overlapping times.  
* **Speed‑profile selection** – For each traversed segment the model chooses exactly one envelope \(k\). Because each envelope encodes a feasible acceleration / deceleration pattern, the resulting timetable is **automatically feasible at the control level**.  
* **Energy–delay trade‑off** – The weighted objective lets the planner decide how much extra delay is acceptable in exchange for reduced energy consumption (e.g., by favouring coasting envelopes).  
* **Conflict‑free schedule** – The combination of (C7)–(C8) ensures that the final timetable respects both **bidirectional conflicts on the shared track** and **same‑direction sequencing**.  

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### Remarks for implementation  

* The size of the envelope set *K* is the main driver of model size. In practice a **small catalogue** (e.g. 3–5 envelopes per segment: “accelerate‑cruise”, “cruise‑coast”, “full‑stop”) is sufficient to capture the main energy‑delay trade‑off while keeping the MILP tractable.  
* The decomposition approach described in the introductory text (IP for interactions + train‑plan generation) can be built on top of this formulation by **pre‑computing** for each train a set of feasible *train‑plans* (a vector of \((x_{t,s,k})\) together with the induced travel times) and then using the IP to select one plan per train while respecting the conflict constraints.  
* Commercial solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) handle the binary‑continuous structure efficiently; the big‑M values should be tightened using the known horizon *H* (e.g., \(M = H + \max_{s,k}\theta_k\)).  

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**The model above constitutes a complete, linear (MILP) representation of the integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) for high‑speed railways under partial‑segment blockages, including bidirectional conflict handling, rerouting decisions, and an explicit energy‑delay trade‑off.**

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Blockage Case)**  

---

### 1. Sets & indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `N`    | Set of network nodes (stations, block‑entry/exit points). |
| `A`    | Set of directed arcs (track segments) ` (i,j) `. |
| `B⊂A`  | Subset of arcs that are **partially blocked** (only one track usable). |
| `K`    | Set of discrete speed levels (e.g., `k=1,…,K`). |
| `S_i`  | Successors of node `i` (`{j|(i,j)∈A}`); `P_i` predecessors. |
| `β_{ij}`| =1 if arc `(i,j)` is bidirectional (i.e. also `(j,i)∈A`), 0 otherwise. |

All arcs are directed to model opposite‑direction conflicts.

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `t_i^{sched}` | Scheduled arrival time at node `i`. |
| `Δ_i^{max}`   | Maximum admissible delay at node `i`. |
| `L_{ij}`      | Length of arc `(i,j)` (km). |
| `v_k`         | Speed associated with level `k` (km/h). |
| `c_k`         | Energy consumption rate at speed `v_k` (kWh/km). |
| `τ_{ij}`      | Minimum travel time on a **free** arc `(i,j)` (`L_{ij}/v_max`). |
| `τ_{ij}^k`    | Travel time on a **blocked** arc `(i,j)∈B` at speed `v_k` (`L_{ij}/v_k`). |
| `δ_i`         | Minimum dwell time at station `i` (minutes, 0 if not a station). |
| `M`           | Large constant for big‑M linearisation. |
| `w_d , w_e`   | Positive weights for total delay and total energy. |
| `γ_{ij}`      | Minimum safety headway (minutes) for opposite‑direction use of the same physical segment (used only for bidirectional conflict). |

All data are assumed known a‑priori.

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| `x_{ij}` | binary | `1` if the train traverses arc `(i,j)`, `0` otherwise. |
| `a_i`    | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time at node `i`. |
| `d_i`    | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time from node `i`. |
| `y_{ij}^k`| binary | `1` if on a blocked arc `(i,j)∈B` the train uses speed level `k`. (If `(i,j)∉B` the variable is not defined.) |
| `e_i`    | continuous, ≥0 | Cumulative energy spent up to node `i` (optional, only for reporting). |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\; 
w_d\sum_{i\in N}\bigl(a_i-t_i^{sched}\bigr) \;+\;
w_e\sum_{(i,j)\in B}\sum_{k\in K} c_k\,L_{ij}\,y_{ij}^k }
\]

*First term = total delay; second term = total energy on blocked arcs (energy on free arcs is constant and can be omitted).*

---

### 5. Core constraints  

#### 5.1. Flow conservation (single‑path routing)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\in S_s} x_{sj} &= 1 &&\text{(leave origin exactly once)}\\
\sum_{i\in P_t} x_{it} &= 1 &&\text{(enter destination exactly once)}\\
\sum_{j\in S_i} x_{ij} - \sum_{j\in P_i} x_{ji} &= 0 &&\forall i\in N\setminus\{s,t\}
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 5.2. Timing on free arcs  

\[
a_j \;\ge\; d_i + \tau_{ij} - M\,(1-x_{ij}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in A\setminus B
\]

#### 5.3. Speed‑choice on blocked arcs  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{ij}^k = x_{ij} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B
\]

\[
a_j \;\ge\; d_i + \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{ij}^k\,y_{ij}^k - M\,(1-x_{ij}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B
\]

#### 5.4. Dwell time at stations  

\[
d_i \;\ge\; a_i + \delta_i \qquad\forall i\in N_{\text{station}}
\]

#### 5.5. Delay bounds  

\[
0 \;\le\; a_i - t_i^{sched} \;\le\; \Delta_i^{max} \qquad\forall i\in N
\]

#### 5.6. Bidirectional conflict on a partially blocked segment  

\[
x_{ij}+x_{ji} \le 1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B \text{ with } \beta_{ij}=1
\]

(If the model were extended to several trains, a time‑indexed version of this constraint would be needed; with a single train the binary sum already prevents a “turn‑back”.)

#### 5.7. Energy accumulation (optional, for reporting)  

\[
e_j = e_i + \sum_{k\in K} c_k\,L_{ij}\,y_{ij}^k \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B
\]

For free arcs a constant term can be added or the equation omitted.

---

### 6. Model summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_d\sum_{i}(a_i-t_i^{sched}) + w_e\sum_{(i,j)\in B}\sum_{k} c_k L_{ij} y_{ij}^k\\[2pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{Flow conservation } (5.1)\\
& a_j \ge d_i + \tau_{ij} - M(1-x_{ij}) &&\forall (i,j)\in A\setminus B\\
& \sum_{k} y_{ij}^k = x_{ij} &&\forall (i,j)\in B\\
& a_j \ge d_i + \sum_{k}\tau_{ij}^k y_{ij}^k - M(1-x_{ij}) &&\forall (i,j)\in B\\
& d_i \ge a_i + \delta_i &&\forall i\in N_{\text{station}}\\
& 0\le a_i - t_i^{sched}\le \Delta_i^{max} &&\forall i\in N\\
& x_{ij}+x_{ji}\le 1 &&\forall (i,j)\in B,\; \beta_{ij}=1\\
& x_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{ij}^k\in\{0,1\},\; a_i,d_i\ge0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries `x_{ij}` and `y_{ij}^k`. The model can be solved directly with any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 7. How the model works  

| Element | Role |
|--------|------|
| `x_{ij}` | Chooses a feasible route that avoids or uses blocked segments. |
| `a_i , d_i` | Capture the (possibly delayed) timetable; they link directly to the objective (delay). |

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
The formulation below is a complete, linear model that can be used directly in a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  It is built by extending the classic RECIFE‑MILP CDR model (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with the DTG‑specific elements described in the paper excerpt.  

All symbols are defined in the *Sets* and *Parameters* sections; any symbol marked with “*Assumption*” is introduced because the source text does not provide a numeric value or a precise definition.  The model is **deterministic** (the timetable and the set of delayed events are known at the time of optimisation) and **static** (the planning horizon is a single day/shift).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD sections), indexed by *s*. |
| **P** | Set of stations, a subset of *S*. |
| **N(t)** | Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (its route). |
| **E** | Set of events (arrival/departure at a section), indexed by *(t,s)* with *s*∈N(t). |
| **K** | Set of feasible speed‑profile options (e.g. “full‑speed”, “reduced‑speed”). |
| **B** | Set of binary decision variables for ordering conflicts (defined later). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| **L_s** | Length of section *s* (km). | Network data |
| **v_k** | Constant cruising speed associated with speed‑profile *k* (km/h). | Assumption – e.g. 200 km/h, 160 km/h, 120 km/h |
| **a_brk** | Uniform service‑braking deceleration (km/h²). | Assumption – e.g. 1.0 km/h² (≈ 0.28 m/s²) |
| **τ_dwell** | Minimum dwell time at stations (minutes). | Timetable data |
| **τ_buf** | Safety buffer (minutes) added to all separation constraints to guarantee robustness. | Assumption – e.g. 0.5 min |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}** | Planned (reference) arrival time of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}^{dep}** | Planned departure time of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **δ_{t,s}** | Exogenous delay (minutes) already observed for train *t* at the entry of *s* (≥0). | Real‑time input |
| **M** | Large constant (“big‑M”) for linearising logical constraints. | Set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary indicator = 1 if train *t* uses speed‑profile *k* on section *s*, 0 otherwise. | Decision variable (see below). |
| **b_{s}** | Binary flag = 1 if section *s* is a **switch** (or a TTD section with special rules), 0 otherwise. | Network data |
| **γ** | Factor converting kilometres to minutes at speed *v_k*: γ_{k}=60 / v_k (min/km). | Derived from v_k |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **a_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted arrival time** of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s* (minutes from horizon start). |
| **d_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted departure time** of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary | Speed‑profile selection: 1 if train *t* travels on section *s* with profile *k*. |
| **y_{t,s}** | Binary | 1 if train *t* **stops** (dwells) at station *s* ∈ P, 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{(t1,t2),s}** | Binary, (t1,t2)∈C_s | **Ordering variable** for a pair of conflicting trains on the same section *s*: 1 if *t1* passes before *t2*, 0 otherwise. |
| **z_t** | Continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between adjusted arrival at its last section and the planned arrival). |
| **w_{t}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Penalty** for applying a speed‑profile slower than the fastest one (used to discourage unnecessary speed reductions). |

*Note:* The set **C_s** contains all unordered pairs of trains whose routes intersect section *s*:  

\[
C_s = \{(t_1,t_2)\mid t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in N(t_1)\cap N(t_2)\}.
\]

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The primary operational goal is to **minimise total passenger/traffic delay** while penalising unnecessary speed reductions (to keep the solution realistic).  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_t}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in N(t)}\sum_{k\in K} w_{t}\, \beta_{t,s,k}}_{\text{speed‑reduction penalty}}
}
\]

* **λ** is a weighting factor (e.g. λ = 0.1 min) that trades off delay versus speed‑profile changes.  

The total delay of a train is defined later (constraint (9)).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Speed‑profile selection  

Each train must choose **exactly one** speed‑profile on every traversed section.

\[
\sum_{k\in K} \beta_{t,s,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{1}
\]

### 5.2. Travel time on a section (DTG‑specific)  

The **minimum travel time** on section *s* for train *t* using profile *k* is the sum of:

* **running time** = length / speed,
* **braking time** needed to stop at the *end of authority* (EoA).  
  Under DTG, the brake‑indication point (IP) is placed at the *braking distance* from the EoA, which depends on the current speed. The braking distance (in km) for speed *v_k* with deceleration *a_brk* is  

\[
\text{brkDist}_{k}= \frac{v_k^{2}}{2\,a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(km)} .
\]

The corresponding **braking time** (minutes) is  

\[
\text{brkTime}_{k}= \frac{v_k}{a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(min)} .
\]

Because the EoA is always at the **end of the section**, the train must start braking **brkDistₖ** before the end. If the section is longer than the braking distance, the train can cruise at *vₖ* for the remaining part; otherwise the whole section is covered by the braking curve (the model automatically handles this via a big‑M linearisation – see (5)–(6)).  

For linearity we pre‑compute the **minimum feasible travel time** on section *s* for profile *k*:

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \underbrace{\frac{L_s-\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_k}\,60}_{\text{cruise time (min)}} \;+\; \text{brkTime}_{k} \quad\text{if }L_s>\text{brkDist}_{k},
\]

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\,60 \quad\text{if }L_s\le \text{brkDist}_{k}\; (\text{pure braking}).
\]

*Assumption:* The same braking curve is used for all trains (homogeneous rolling stock).  

The **adjusted departure time** must respect the minimum travel time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{s,k}\,\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{2}
\]

### 5.3. Dwell time at stations  

If a train stops at a station (*y_{t,s}=1*), it must stay at least **τ_dwell** minutes; otherwise it may pass through (zero dwell).

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \tau_{dwell}\,y_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P\cap N(t) \tag{3}
\]

### 5.4. Propagation of times along the route  

The departure from section *s* becomes the arrival at the next section *s′* (the exit of *s* is the entry of *s′*).  

\[
a_{t,s'} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive in }N(t) \tag{4}
\]

### 5.5. Conflict‑avoidance (DTG separation)  

Two trains *t₁* and *t₂* that occupy the same section *s* must respect a **speed‑dependent separation distance**. Under DTG the separation is expressed as a **minimum time gap** between the *brake‑indication points* of the two trains. The brake‑indication point of a train on section *s* occurs **brkDistₖ** before the end of the section; therefore the **earliest safe entry** of the following train is:

\[
\text{SafeEntry}_{t_1,s}= a_{t_1,s} + \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\text{time from entry to IP}} .
\]

Because the model already enforces the minimum travel time (2), we can impose the separation directly on the **arrival times**:

\[
a_{t_2,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_1,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_1,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{(t_1,t_2),s}) \tag{5a}
\]

\[
a_{t_1,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_2,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_2,s}}}{v_{k_{t_2,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_2,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,x_{(t_1,t_2),s} \tag{5b}
\]

where **x_{(t₁,t₂),s}** decides the ordering (0 → *t₁* before *t₂*, 1 → *t₂* before *t₁*).  

The **Δ‑terms** are linearised by introducing auxiliary continuous variables:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_{k}}\,60\;\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{5c}
\]

Constraint (5a)–(5b) together with (5c) guarantee that **exactly one ordering** is selected:

\[
x_{(t_1,t_2),s}+x_{(t_2,t_1),s}=1 \qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s \tag{5d}
\]

*Special handling for switches / TTD sections* (b_s = 1): the separation distance can be reduced by a factor **ρ < 1** (e.g., 0.8) because the detection is more accurate. This is modelled by scaling the Δ‑term:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}^{\text{eff}} = \Delta_{t,s}\; \bigl(1-\rho\,b_s\bigr) \tag{5e}
\]

and using **Δ_{t,s}^{eff}** in (5a)–(5b).

### 5.6. Initial conditions (exogenous delays)  

The adjusted arrival must be at least the original planned arrival plus any observed delay:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s} \;+\; \delta_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{6}
\]

### 5.7. Definition of total train delay  

The **total delay** of train *t* is measured at its **last section** (the final destination). Let *s^{\text{last}}_t* be the last element of N(t).  

\[
z_t \;=\; a_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \;-\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{7}
\]

(If a train is scheduled to arrive earlier than the horizon start, the RHS can be negative; the model will simply not select that solution.)

### 5.8. Speed‑reduction penalty (optional)  

If a train uses a slower profile than the fastest one (*k\* = arg max vₖ*), we charge a small penalty:

\[
w_t \;\ge\; \bigl(1-\beta_{t,s,k^{\*}}\bigr) \quad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{8}
\]

This forces **w_t = 1** if any section uses a slower speed; otherwise **w_t = 0**. The term appears in the objective with weight λ.

### 5.9. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s},\, d_{t,s},\, \Delta_{t,s},\, z_t &\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
\beta_{t,s,k} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
y_{t,s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s\in P\\
x_{(t_1,t_2),s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s,\, s\in S\\
w_t &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the Model  

* **Decision variables** – adjusted arrival/departure times, speed‑profile choices, dwell‑stop decisions, conflict‑ordering binaries, and a total‑delay variable.  
* **Objective** – minimise the sum of all train delays while discouraging unnecessary speed reductions.  
* **Constraints** – (1) enforce a single speed profile per section, (2) enforce DTG‑based minimum travel times, (3) enforce mandatory dwell times, (4) propagate times along each train’s route, (5) enforce speed‑dependent separation (the core DTG enhancement), (6) respect observed exogenous delays, (7) compute total delay, (8) optional penalty for slower profiles, (9) variable domains.  

The model is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable times a constant) and therefore solvable to optimality with any MILP solver.  By adjusting the data (section lengths, speed‑profile set, braking deceleration, switch‑factor ρ, safety buffer τ_buf) the same formulation can be applied to any railway network equipped with ETCS L2 (or similar DTG) signalling.  

--- 

**How to use the model in practice**

1. **Data preparation** – extract the network topology (sections, switches), the timetable (Δt⁰), current delays (δ), and define the speed‑profile catalogue (K).  
2. **Parameter computation** – compute braking distances/braking times for each profile, the minimum travel times θ_{s,k}, and the Δ‑terms.  
3. **Model building** – feed the sets, parameters, and the above MILP formulation to a solver.  
4. **Solution interpretation** – the optimal *a_{t,s}* give the new schedule; *β_{t,s,k}=1* tells which speed profile each train should adopt; *x_{(t1,t2),s}* indicates the resolved ordering on every conflicted section.  

With this complete MILP formulation you can now evaluate, for a given set of disruptions, how much total delay can be avoided by exploiting the **speed‑dependent separation** that DTG signalling makes possible, exactly as described in the paper’s contribution.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a partial‑segment blockage forces a high‑speed railway operator to (i) **retime** trains, (ii) **reorder / reroute** them on the opposite track, and (iii) **choose feasible speed profiles** for every train‑run segment.  

All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  Where data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption X)**.

---

## 1.  Index Sets and Basic Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run during the planning horizon. |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train). |
| **L** = {1,…,|L|} | Set of line‑segments (track sections) connecting two consecutive stations. Each segment ℓ ∈ L has a *direction* d(ℓ) ∈ {+ , – } (forward / backward). |
| **B** ⊆ L | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the disruption area). |
| **K** = {1,…,Kmax} | Set of *speed‑profile* alternatives (discrete speed‑time plans) that can be assigned to a train on a given segment. |
| **P** = {1,…,Pmax} | Set of *order‑position* indices used for train‑reordering on a shared segment (see constraint (13)). |
| **Δ** = {0,1,…,Δmax} | Set of discrete time‑interval indices used for linearising quadratic speed‑energy relations (Assumption 4). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Value / Source |
|--------|--------------|------------------------|
| **τ₀ₜₛ** | Planned (pre‑disruption) arrival time of train *t* at station *s*. | timetable data |
| **δₜₛ** | Minimum dwell time required at station *s* for train *t* (including passenger exchange). | Assumption 1: 2–5 min |
| **Lℓ** | Physical length of segment ℓ (km). | infrastructure data |
| **vᵐₖ** | Maximum admissible speed for profile *k* (km/h). | Assumption 2: 200–350 km/h |
| **aᵐₖ**, **bᵐₖ** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration for profile *k* (km/h²). | Assumption 2 |
| **eₖ** | Energy consumption (kWh) associated with completing a segment with profile *k* (averaged over the segment). | derived from train‑performance curves |
| **M** | Large constant for “big‑M” linearisation (≥ planning horizon, e.g. 10⁶ s). | Assumption 3 |
| **Tmax** | Upper bound on the planning horizon (seconds). | e.g. 24 h |
| **Δt** | Length of a discretisation interval for the piece‑wise linear speed‑energy relation (seconds). | Assumption 4: 10 s |
| **c₁**, **c₂** | Weight coefficients for the two competing objectives (delay minimisation, energy consumption). | c₁ = 1, c₂ = 0.01 (typical) |
| **βℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Indicator: 1 if segment ℓ is *bidirectional* (i.e. both directions share the same physical track). | Assumption 5 |
| **γℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Indicator: 1 if segment ℓ belongs to the blocked set **B**. | problem data |
| **Δ₍ℓ₎** = [tᵇ₍ℓ₎ , tᵉ₍ℓ₎] | Disruption time window on blocked segment ℓ (seconds). | given by incident report |
| **Rₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Feasibility indicator: 1 if train *t* is allowed to use segment ℓ (i.e. the train’s original route contains ℓ). | derived from original timetable |
| **Uₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Feasibility indicator for *rerouting*: 1 if train *t* may use the opposite‑track version of ℓ (only when βℓ = 1). | Assumption 6 |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **aₜₛ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Actual *arrival* time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| **dₜₛ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Actual *departure* time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **xₜℓk** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment ℓ using speed‑profile *k*. |
| **yₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses segment ℓ (either original direction or rerouted). |
| **zₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses the *opposite* direction of a bidirectional segment ℓ (i.e. rerouting). |
| **pₜℓp** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | Position of train *t* on segment ℓ in the ordered sequence *p* (used for conflict‑avoidance on shared track). |
| **wₜℓδ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ (seconds). |
| **uₜℓδ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment ℓ (kWh). |
| **θₜℓδ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | Indicator that the travel time of train *t* on ℓ falls into discretisation interval δ (used for piece‑wise linear energy‑time relation). |

---

## 4.  Model Assumptions (explicitly stated)

1. **Assumption 1 – Minimum dwell time** – Each train must stay at a station for at least δₜₛ minutes; additional dwell may be imposed by conflict resolution.  
2. **Assumption 2 – Discrete speed profiles** – The continuous speed‑time space is approximated by a finite set **K** of admissible profiles, each characterised by a constant cruising speed, acceleration and deceleration limits.  
3. **Assumption 3 – Big‑M value** – M is chosen larger than any feasible arrival/departure time (e.g. M = 10⁶ s).  
4. **Assumption 4 – Piece‑wise linear energy‑time relation** – Energy consumption on a segment is approximated by a set of linear segments indexed by δ ∈ Δ.  
5. **Assumption 5 – Bidirectional sharing** – Only segments with βℓ = 1 are physically shared by opposite‑direction trains; all others are dedicated tracks.  
6. **Assumption 6 – Rerouting feasibility** – A train may be rerouted onto the opposite track of a bidirectional segment only if Uₜℓ = 1 (e.g. signalling permits it).  

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

The planner wishes to **(i)** minimise total passenger delay (difference between actual and planned arrival times) and **(ii)** minimise total energy consumption of all trains. A weighted sum is used:

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  c_{1}\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\bigl(a_{t s}-\tau^{0}_{t s}\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}} 
\;+\; c_{2}\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} u_{t\ell}\,}_{\text{Total energy}}
}
\tag{1}
\]

where  

\[
u_{t\ell}= \sum_{\delta\in\Delta}\theta_{t\ell\delta}\,e_{\delta} \qquad\text{(see constraints (23)–(26))}
\]

---

## 6.  Core Constraints  

### 6.1 Temporal consistency at stations  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& d_{t s} \;\ge\; a_{t s} + \delta_{t s} \qquad &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{2}\\
& a_{t s'} \;\ge\; d_{t s} + w_{t\ell} \qquad &&\forall t\in T,\; (\ell = (s,s'))\in L \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

### 6.2 Segment‑travel‑time definition  

\[
w_{t\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t\ell k}\; \underbrace{\frac{L_{\ell}}{v^{m}_{k}}}_{\text{cruising time}} \qquad \forall t,\ell \tag{4}
\]

(If acceleration/deceleration phases are modelled, the term can be refined; the linearisation above follows Assumption 2.)

### 6.3 Segment usage linking  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t\ell k} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{5}\\
& y_{t\ell}\le R_{t\ell}+U_{t\ell}\,z_{t\ell} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{6}\\
& z_{t\ell}\le \beta_{\ell}\,U_{t\ell} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]

Constraint (6) forces a train to use a segment either in its original direction (Rₜℓ = 1) or, if allowed, on the opposite track (zₜℓ = 1).  

### 6.4 Blockage‑time window (partial blockage)  

A train may occupy a blocked segment only **outside** the disruption window, unless it is rerouted onto the opposite track:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& a_{t s} + w_{t\ell} \;\le\; t^{b}_{\ell} \;+\; M\,(1-\gamma_{\ell}) \quad &&\forall t,\ell\in B,\; \text{if } z_{t\ell}=0 \tag{8}\\
& a_{t s} \;\ge\; t^{e}_{\ell} \;-\; M\,(1-\gamma_{\ell}) \quad &&\forall t,\ell\in B,\; \text{if } z_{t\ell}=0 \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]

If the train is rerouted (zₜℓ = 1) the constraints are relaxed (big‑M term).

### 6.5 Conflict‑avoidance on shared bidirectional segments  

For every bidirectional segment ℓ (βℓ = 1) we order the trains that occupy it (including those using the opposite direction). Let **P** be a sufficiently large set of positions (|P| ≥ number of trains that may use ℓ).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{p\in P} p_{t\ell p}= y_{t\ell} &&\forall t,\ell \tag{10}\\
& \sum_{t\in T} p_{t\ell p}= 1 \quad\text{or}\;0 &&\forall \ell,\;p\in P \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]

The ordering variables enforce a *first‑come‑first‑served* sequence. To guarantee temporal separation we use a big‑M disjunctive constraint:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& a_{t' s'} \;\ge\; d_{t s} + \varepsilon \;-\; M\bigl(1- \underbrace{(p_{t\ell p} \;+\; p_{t'\ell p+1})}_{\text{t precedes t′}}\bigr) \\
&\qquad\qquad\forall \ell\in L,\; \forall (t,t')\in T^{2},\; \forall p\in P\setminus\{ |P|\} \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]

where **ε** is a safety margin (e.g., 30 s). Constraint (12) states that if train *t* is placed immediately before train *t′* on segment ℓ, then *t′* may not enter ℓ before *t* has cleared it.

### 6.6 Energy‑time linearisation (piece‑wise)  

For each segment ℓ and train *t* we introduce binary variables θₜℓδ that select the interval δ in which the travel time wₜℓ lies:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& w_{t\ell}= \sum_{\delta\in\Delta} \bigl( \underline{w}_{\delta} + \overline{w}_{\delta}\bigl) \theta_{t\ell\delta} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{13}\\
& \sum_{\delta\in\Delta} \theta_{t\ell\delta}= y_{t\ell} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{14}\\
& u_{t\ell}= \sum_{\delta\in\Delta} e_{\delta}\,\theta_{t\ell\delta} \qquad &&\forall t,\ell \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]

The parameters \(\underline{w}_{\delta},\overline{w}_{\delta}\) are the lower/upper bounds of travel time for interval δ (e.g., 30–40 s, 40–50 s, …). The energy coefficient \(e_{\delta}\) is the average energy consumption for that interval (derived from the train’s power‑speed curve).  

### 6.7 Logical linking of speed‑profile selection and travel time  

Because each speed profile *k* implies a deterministic travel time, we enforce:

\[
w_{t\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{k\ell}\,x_{t\ell k} \qquad \forall t,\ell \tag{16}
\]

where \(\tau_{k\ell}=L_{\ell}/v^{c}_{k}+ \text{acc/dec phases}\) (pre‑computed).  

### 6.8 Rerouting feasibility and capacity  

If a train is rerouted onto the opposite track, the opposite direction must be *free* during the same time interval. This is already covered by the ordering constraints (12) because the opposite‑track trains share the same set of ordering variables **pₜℓp** (βℓ = 1).  

### 6.9 Binary‑variable consistency  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t\ell k} \le y_{t\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,k \tag{17}\\
& \sum_{k\in K} x_{t\ell k}= y_{t\ell} &&\forall t,\ell \tag{18}\\
& z_{t\ell} \le y_{t\ell} &&\forall t,\ell \tag{19}
\end{aligned}
\]

### 6.10 Upper bound on total makespan (optional)  

\[
a_{t s}\le \text{Tmax} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{20}
\]

---

## 7.  Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& c_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\bigl(a_{t s}-\tau^{0}_{t s}\bigr) \;+\; c_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} u_{t\ell} \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{(2)–(20)} \\
& a_{t s}, d_{t s}, w_{t\ell}, u_{t\ell}\ge 0 \\
& x_{t\ell k}, y_{t\ell}, z_{t\ell}, p_{t\ell p}, \theta_{t\ell\delta}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (e.g., product of binary variables in (12)) are handled by standard big‑M linearisation, preserving the MILP structure.

---

## 8.  Remarks on Model Use  

1. **Scalability** – The number of ordering variables **pₜℓp** grows with the number of trains that may share a bidirectional segment. In practice, a *conflict‑graph* can be built to restrict ordering only to pairs of trains whose time windows overlap, dramatically reducing the size.  
2. **Decomposition** – Following the paper’s suggestion, the model can be decomposed into (i) an *integer‑program* that decides the binary variables \((y,z,x,p,\theta)\) (i.e., the *train‑plan selection*), and (ii) a set of *continuous sub‑problems* that compute the exact arrival/departure times and energy values for each selected plan. The decomposition is exact because the continuous sub‑problems are linear and have a unique optimal solution given the binary decisions.  
3. **Iterative refinement** – If the initial discretisation of speed profiles **K** or the piece‑wise energy intervals **Δ** is too coarse, the solution can be refined iteratively by adding intermediate profiles or splitting Δ‑intervals around the current travel times (local branching).  

---

### End of Formulation  

The MILP above provides a **complete, linear** representation of the **Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial‑segment blockages, explicitly handling (i) retiming, (ii) rerouting on opposite tracks, (iii) bidirectional conflict resolution, and (iv) energy‑aware speed‑profile selection. All assumptions required to close the model are clearly identified.

Text:
**Variables**

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(D_i\) | continuous | actual departure time of train \(i\) |
| \(A_i\) | continuous | actual arrival time of train \(i\) |
| \(u_{i,s}\) | continuous | start time of the traversal of segment \(s\) by train \(i\) |
| \(v_{i,s}\) | continuous | duration of the traversal of segment \(s\) by train \(i\) |
| \(x_{i,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses segment \(s\) in its original direction, 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{i,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses the opposite track on segment \(s\) (only allowed for the blocked segment \(s^{*}\)), 0 otherwise |
| \(z_{i,k,s}\) | binary | ordering variable for two trains \(i,k\) that share the **same** direction on segment \(s\) ( \(z_{i,k,s}=1\) ⇒ train \(i\) precedes train \(k\) ) |
| \(z^{\text{op}}_{i,k}\) | binary | ordering variable for a train using the original direction and a train using the opposite track on the blocked segment \(s^{*}\) |
| \(w_i\) | binary | side‑choice of the disruption window for train \(i\) on the blocked segment ( \(w_i=0\) ⇒ traversal before the window, \(w_i=1\) ⇒ after) |

**Parameters (assumed / given)**  

* \(I\) – set of trains, indexed by \(i\).  
* \(S\) – set of track segments, indexed by \(s\).  
* \(s^{*}\in S\) – the segment that is partially blocked.  
* \(a_i^{0}\) – planned (original) arrival time of train \(i\).  
* \(d_i^{0}\) – planned (original) departure time of train \(i\).  
* \(\tau^{\min }_{i,s},\;\tau^{\max }_{i,s}\) – lower and upper bounds on the travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\).  
* \(e_s\) – energy cost per unit of traversal time on segment \(s\).  
* \([t_{\text{start}},t_{\text{end}}]\) – disruption time window on segment \(s^{*}\).  
* \(\lambda\) – weight of the energy term in the objective.  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).  

**Assumptions**  

1. Single‑track per direction; the opposite track of the blocked segment can be used only by rerouted trains.  
2. Energy consumption is linear in traversal time.  
3. All trains must be scheduled (no cancellations).  
4. Dwell times at stations are bounded by \(\underline{d}\) and \(\overline{d}\) (optional).  

**Objective function**

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(A_i-a_i^{0}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S} e_s \, v_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy consumption}} .
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Departure–arrival consistency** (total travel time equals sum of segment durations)  

\[
D_i + \sum_{s\in S} v_{i,s}= A_i \qquad \forall i\in I .
\]

2. **Travel‑time bounds**  

\[
\tau^{\min }_{i,s}\,x_{i,s}\;\le\; v_{i,s}\;\le\;\tau^{\max }_{i,s}\,x_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;s\in S .
\]

If \(x_{i,s}=0\) then \(v_{i,s}=0\) (enforced by the above bounds).

3. **Rerouting relationship on the blocked segment**  

\[
y_{i,s^{*}} = 1 - x_{i,s^{*}}\qquad\forall i\in I,
\]
\[
y_{i,s}=0\qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\neq s^{*}.
\]

4. **Sequencing on each segment for trains using the same direction**  

For every pair \(i,k\in I,\; i<k\) and every segment \(s\in S\):

\[
u_{i,s}+v_{i,s}\;\le\; u_{k,s}+M\bigl(1-z_{i,k,s}\bigr)+M\bigl(2-x_{i,s}-x_{k,s}\bigr),
\]
\[
u_{k,s}+v_{k,s}\;\le\; u_{i,s}+M z_{i,k,s}+M\bigl(2-x_{i,s}-x_{k,s}\bigr).
\]

If at least one of the trains does not use segment \(s\) (\(x_{i,s}=0\) or \(x_{k,s}=0\)), the big‑M terms deactivate the constraints.

5. **Bidirectional conflict on the blocked segment**  

For every pair \(i,k\in I,\; i<k\):

\[
u_{i,s^{*}}+v_{i,s^{*}}\;\le\; u_{k,s^{*}}+M\bigl(1-z^{\text{op}}_{i,k}\bigr)+M\bigl(2-x_{i,s^{*}}-y_{k,s^{*}}\bigr),
\]
\[
u_{k,s^{*}}+v_{k,s^{*}}\;\le\; u_{i,s^{*}}+M z^{\text{op}}_{i,k}+M\bigl(2-x_{k,s^{*}}-y_{i,s^{*}}\bigr).
\]

These constraints order a train that stays on the original track with a train that uses the opposite track on the same physical resource.

6. **Disruption‑window avoidance for trains staying on the original track**  

For each train \(i\):

\[
u_{i,s^{*}} \;\ge\; t_{\text{end}}\, w_i - M\bigl(1-x_{i,s^{*}}\bigr),
\]
\[
u_{i,s^{*}}+v_{i,s^{*}} \;\le\; t_{\text{start}} + M w_i + M\bigl(1-x_{i,s^{*}}\bigr).
\]

If \(x_{i,s^{*}}=0\) the constraints are inactive; otherwise \(w_i=0\) forces the traversal completely before the window, \(w_i=1\) forces it completely after.

7. **Dwell‑time bounds at stations (optional)**  

Assuming a fixed order of segments \(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(|S|)\) (e.g., \(s_1\rightarrow s_2\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow s^{*}\)):

\[
\underline{d}\;-\;M\bigl(2-x_{i,\sigma(p)}-x_{i,\sigma(p+1)}\bigr)
\;\le\;
u_{i,\sigma(p+1)}-\bigl(u_{i,\sigma(p)}+v_{i,\sigma(p)}\bigr)
\;\le\;
\overline{d}+M\bigl(2-x_{i,\sigma(p)}-x_{i,\sigma(p+1)}\bigr)
\]
for all \(i\in I\) and \(p=1,\dots,|S|-1\).

8. **Linking departure/arrival to first/last segment (optional)**  

\[
D_i = u_{i,\sigma(1)},\qquad
A_i = u_{i,\sigma(|S|)}+v_{i,\sigma(|S|)}\qquad\forall i\in I .
\]

9. **Variable domains**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& D_i, A_i, u_{i,s}, v_{i,s} \ge 0 &&\forall i,s,\\
& x_{i,s}, y_{i,s}, z_{i,k,s}, z^{\text{op}}_{i,k}, w_i \in \{0,1\} &&\forall i,k,s.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

The model above fully captures the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under a partial‑segment blockage: it decides departure/arrival times, segment traversal durations (i.e., speed profiles), whether a train is rerouted onto the opposite track, and the ordering of trains on shared resources, while minimizing a weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption.

Text:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockage**

---

### 1. Sets & indices
| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Trains to be scheduled (including the disrupted one). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Track segments (between two consecutive nodes). |
| **V** = {1,…,|V|} | admissible speed‑profile types (e.g. slow, normal, fast). |
| **R** = {1,…,|R|} | feasible routes for a train (detour routes around the blocked part). |
| **P** ⊆ S | Segments that are *partially blocked* (disruption zone). |
| **B** ⊆ S | Segments that are *fully closed* (no train may use them). |
| **A** ⊆ S | Bidirectional (single‑track) segments – opposite directions share the same physical line. |

For a train *t* and a route *r* let  

\[
\text{seg}(t,r)=\bigl(s^ {t,r}_1,s^ {t,r}_2,\dots ,s^ {t,r}_{|seg(t,r)|}\bigr)
\]

be the ordered list of segments that constitute the route.

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(L_s\) | length of segment *s* | km |
| \(v_p\) | average speed of profile *p* | km · min⁻¹ |
| \(e_p\) | energy consumption rate of profile *p* | kWh · km⁻¹ |
| \(\tau^{\min}_s\) | minimum traversal time of *s* (fastest admissible speed) | min |
| \(\tau^{\max}_s\) | maximum permissible traversal time of *s* | min |
| \(D^{\text{orig}}_t\) | scheduled departure of train *t* (pre‑disruption) | min |
| \(A^{\text{orig}}_t\) | scheduled arrival of train *t* (pre‑disruption) | min |
| \(\underline{t}_s ,\overline{t}_s\) | start / end of the disruption window on segment *s∈P* | min |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}\) | weight (cost) per minute of passenger delay | $ · min⁻¹ |
| \(w^{\text{energy}}\) | weight (cost) per kWh of energy used | $ · kWh⁻¹ |
| \(M\) | a large constant (big‑M) | – |
| \(\overline{C}_s\) | capacity of segment *s* (normally 1 for single‑track) | – |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r*. |
| \(z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if segment *s* belongs to the chosen route of *t*. |
| \(y_{t,p,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed profile *p*. |
| \(d_t\ge0\) | continuous | actual departure time of train *t*. |
| \(a_t\ge0\) | continuous | actual arrival time of train *t*. |
| \(u_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | entry time of train *t* into segment *s*. |
| \(v_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | exit time of train *t* from segment *s*. |
| \(\beta_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | logical selector for the “or’’ in the blockage avoidance (see §5.5). |
| \(\gamma_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | ordering selector for two trains on a bidirectional segment *s*. |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_t\ge0\) | continuous | total energy used by train *t*. |
| \(c^{\text{delay}}_t\ge0\) | continuous | delay of train *t* (actual – scheduled arrival). |

---

### 4. Model  

#### 4.1 Objective – weighted sum of delay and energy  

\[
\min\;\; w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}c^{\text{delay}}_{t}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}c^{\text{energy}}_{t}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

---

#### 4.2 Route selection  

\[
\sum_{r\in R}x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

\[
z_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R:\;s\in\text{seg}(t,r)} x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

Thus exactly one route per train, and \(z_{t,s}=1\) iff *s* belongs to that route.

---

#### 4.3 Speed‑profile assignment  

\[
\sum_{p\in V} y_{t,p,s}=z_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{SP1}
\]

Exactly one speed profile on every used segment.

---

#### 4.4 Traversal‑time linking (linear)  

\[
v_{t,s}-u_{t,s}= \sum_{p\in V}\frac{L_s}{v_p}\,y_{t,p,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{TT1}
\]

\[
\tau^{\min}_s\,z_{t,s}\le v_{t,s}-u_{t,s}\le
\tau^{\max}_s\,z_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t,s \tag{TT2}
\]

When a segment is not used (\(z_{t,s}=0\)) the rhs collapses to 0.

---

#### 4.5 Temporal continuity along the chosen route  

Let the ordered list of segments on the selected route of train *t* be   
\(s^{t}_1,s^{t}_2,\dots ,s^{t}_{K_t}\).

\[
u_{t,s^{t}_1}=d_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{TC1}
\]

\[
v_{t,s^{t}_{K_t}}=a_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{TC2}
\]

\[
u_{t,s^{t}_{k+1}}\;\ge\;v_{t,s^{t}_{k}}
\qquad\forall t,\;k=1,\dots ,K_t-1 \tag{TC3}
\]

The inequality permits waiting (dwell) at intermediate stations.

---

#### 4.6 Partial‑blockage avoidance (or‑condition linearised)  

For every partially blocked segment \(s\in P\) and every train that uses it:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{t,s}&\ge \overline{t}_s - M\beta_{t,s}\\
v_{t,s}&\le \underline{t}_s + M(1-\beta_{t,s})\\
\beta_{t,s}&\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P \tag{BLK}
\]

If \(\beta_{t,s}=0\) the train must finish before the disruption starts;  
if \(\beta_{t,s}=1\) it must start after the disruption ends.

Closed segments are simply forbidden:

\[
z_{t,s}=0 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B \tag{CLS}
\]

---

#### 4.7 Bidirectional (single‑track) conflict – ordering  

For every bidirectional segment \(s\in A\) and every unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) that both use it (\(z_{t,s}=z_{t',s}=1\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{t',s}&\ge v_{t,s} - M\gamma_{t,t',s}\\
u_{t,s }&\ge v_{t',s} - M(1-\gamma_{t,t',s})\\
\gamma_{t,t',s}&\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall s\in A,\; t<t',\; z_{t,s}=z_{t',s}=1 \tag{BI}
\]

Exactly one of the two ordering inequalities is enforced, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the segment simultaneously.

(If a segment admits capacity \(\overline{C}_s>1\), the pairwise ordering can be replaced by a cumulative‑capacity formulation.)

---

#### 4.8 Energy consumption  

\[
c^{\text{energy}}_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{p\in V} L_s\,e_p\,y_{t,p,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{EN}
\]

---

#### 4.9 Delay calculation  

\[
c^{\text{delay}}_{t}= a_t - A^{\text{orig}}_{t}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{DL}
\]

(If early arrivals are to be ignored, replace by   
\(c^{\text{delay}}_{t}= \max\{0, a_t-A^{\text{orig}}_{t}\}\)  – linearised with an auxiliary variable.)

---

#### 4.10 Domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{t,r},\,z_{t,s},\,y_{t,p,s},\,\beta_{t,s},\,\gamma_{t,t',s}&\in\{0,1\}\\
d_t, a_t, u_{t,s}, v_{t,s}, c^{\text{energy}}_t, c^{\text{delay}}_t &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5. Remarks & modelling choices  

| Feature | MILP element |
|---------|--------------|
| **Reroute decision** | binary \(x_{t,r}\) (R1‑R2). |
| **Departure / arrival times** | continuous \(d_t, a_t\) (TC1‑TC2, DL). |
| **Speed‑profile selection** | binaries \(y_{t,p,s}\) (SP1, TT1). |
| **Weighted objective** | (OBJ) – linear combination of total delay and total energy. |
| **Time feasibility** | (TT1‑TT2) links segment travel time to speed; (TC3) ensures continuity. |
| **Partial blockage** | (BLK) – linearised “or’’ using \(\beta_{t,s}\). |
| **Closed segment** | (CLS). |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | (BI) – pairwise ordering on single‑track segments. |
| **Energy consumption** | (EN) – linear sum of length × energy‑rate. |
| **Delay** | (DL). |
| **Capacity >1** | can be added with a time‑slice cumulative constraint (not shown). |

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries listed above. The formulation can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). Additional practical aspects (minimum dwell times, rolling‑stock circulation, crew‑working limits, etc.) can be introduced as extra linear constraints without changing the overall structure.
